Metal detecting sits in a contested space: in some countries, notably through voluntary recording schemes, it is integrated into knowledge production, while in others unlicensed detecting is a serious offense, and the debate over its benefits and harms remains genuinely unresolved. Relationships with living communities and descendant peoples are central to modern ethics. Landscapes surveyed by archaeologists are often the homelands, sacred grounds, and cultural property of Indigenous and local communities, whose knowledge, interests, and rights must inform the work. Ethical survey involves consultation and, increasingly, collaboration, respecting that some places and knowledge are not to be publicized or intruded upon, and recognizing community authority over heritage. Curation and preservation form a further duty. Because survey generates records, samples, and sometimes collected artifacts, these must be conserved and made accessible for the long term, held in trust rather than treated as private data, so that the knowledge outlives the project. The guiding principle across these obligations is stewardship: archaeologists hold a fragile, finite, and non-renewable record on behalf of the public and of future generations, and survey, as the least destructive way to learn from that record, carries a corresponding responsibility to gather knowledge without diminishing the heritage it studies, to report honestly, and to share the results in ways that respect both the evidence and the people connected to it.

sections.heading: Limitations, Misconceptions, and Onward Connections
sections.body: For all its power, survey has firm limits that must be understood to use it well and to avoid common misreadings. The most important misconception is that survey provides a straightforward, ground-truthed map of past settlement. It does not; it provides a map of what surviving traces could be detected under the conditions and by the methods used, a signal heavily filtered by preservation, visibility, and technique, as earlier sections stressed. A related error is to treat blank areas on a survey map as genuinely empty in the past, when they may be areas no method could see into, whether under alluvium, forest, water, or modern building. A third misconception is that remote sensing and geophysics identify what features are: they do not date anything, and they reveal form and physical contrast, not function or period, so a rectilinear enclosure detected by magnetometry could be prehistoric, Roman, or modern, and only comparison with excavated parallels, or targeted excavation itself, can resolve it. Survey and excavation are therefore complementary rather than rivals. Survey excels at breadth, distribution, and the non-destructive detection of pattern across landscapes; excavation excels at depth, chronology, stratigraphy, and the recovery of the fragile organic, environmental, and dating evidence that survey cannot reach. A mature project uses survey to decide where and whether to excavate, and uses the few excavated points to calibrate and interpret the broad survey picture, each method answering the questions the other cannot. Practical limitations recur across techniques. Almost every method depends on ground conditions, so the same site may be visible one season and invisible the next, and different geologies favor different instruments, meaning no single method works everywhere. Costs and skills vary widely, from the near-free labor of fieldwalking to the specialist equipment and processing of lidar and multi-method geophysics. Data volumes from modern remote sensing are enormous and demand curation, and poorly processed data can invent or erase features. The discipline continues to evolve. Advances in sensor technology are making airborne and vehicle-mounted geophysics faster and finer; machine learning is being applied, with appropriate caution, to detect features automatically in imagery and geophysical data, though such tools inherit and can amplify the training biases discussed earlier. Integration deepens as more data layers, including three-dimensional and time-series records, are combined in geographic information systems. Survey connects onward to nearly every part of archaeology and beyond: to landscape and environmental archaeology, which reconstruct the settings survey maps; to settlement and social archaeology, which read distribution patterns for evidence of hierarchy, exchange, and land use; to heritage management and public policy; and to geography, geology, and remote-sensing science, whose methods it borrows and adapts. Understood honestly, as a distinct and non-destructive mode of inquiry with characteristic strengths and blind spots, survey is the discipline's principal way of asking not what happened at one place, but how people organized the whole world they inhabited.

guides.title: Stratigraphy and the Harris Matrix
guides.summary: How archaeologists establish the order in which things happened, from the geological laws of superposition through the context-based recording system to the Harris matrix itself. It covers building and checking a matrix, phasing, attaching dates through terminus post quem reasoning, Bayesian modelling, and the method's genuine limits.

sections.heading: Why Sequence Is the Foundation of Archaeology
sections.body:
Excavation destroys the thing it studies. A trench can be dug only once, and once a layer of soil has
been removed it can never be put back and re-examined in place. Everything an archaeological site can
ever tell the world about the order in which events happened must therefore be observed, understood
and written down at the moment of digging, by the person holding the trowel. This is the harsh fact
that makes stratigraphy, the study of layers and their relationships, the central discipline of field
archaeology rather than one specialism among many.

What stratigraphy delivers is sequence: a demonstration that this floor was laid before that wall was
built, that the wall stood before the pit was dug through it, and that the pit had already filled up
before the whole area was buried under a demolition spread. None of those statements depends on
knowing a single date. They are relative statements, and they are far more robust than absolute ones,
because they rest on physical relationships visible in the ground rather than on interpretation of
artefacts or on laboratory measurements with their own error ranges. A radiocarbon determination has
a standard error of decades; a stratigraphic relationship, correctly observed, is simply true.

That robustness carries the whole discipline. Dating evidence, whether coins, pottery, radiocarbon or
dendrochronology, is attached to sequence rather than the other way round. A coin does not date the
layer it sits in by itself, because a coin can circulate for a century before being lost and can be
dug up and redeposited long afterwards. What a coin does is set a limit: the layer containing it
cannot have been formed before the coin was struck. It is the stratigraphic sequence that converts
scattered limits like that into a chronology, by insisting that dates assigned to a series of layers
must run in the order the layers demonstrably formed. Without sequence there is a bag of objects and
some guesses. With it there is history.

The stakes are practical as well as intellectual. Most excavation now takes place ahead of
construction, under time and cost pressure, on sites that will be destroyed by foundations within
months. The record produced is the only surviving version of the site, and it will be consulted by
researchers decades later who never saw the ground. If the sequence in that record is wrong or
ambiguous, every later conclusion built on it inherits the error, and there is no way to check.

This is why the field developed a formal, almost mathematical apparatus for recording sequence. The
Harris matrix, devised in 1973, is the best known expression of it: a diagram which strips a site down
to nothing but its units of stratification and the order in which they came into being. It looks
austere, even bureaucratic, but it exists to answer the question every excavation must answer and
cannot afford to get wrong.

sections.heading: The Geological Inheritance
sections.body:
Archaeological stratigraphy is a borrowed science, adapted from geology across roughly two centuries,
and its foundational principles were formulated long before anyone applied them to human remains.
Understanding the geological originals explains both the strength of the archaeological versions and
the precise points where they had to be modified.

The starting point is the work of Nicolas Steno, the Danish anatomist also known as Niels Stensen,
whose 1669 treatise usually cited by its short Latin title as De solido intra solidum set out the
principles still taught today. His law of superposition states that in an undisturbed sequence of
layers, each layer is younger than the one beneath it and older than the one above. The reasoning is
simply that a layer must have something to rest on, so the surface it lies upon must already have
existed. His principle of original horizontality holds that sediments are deposited in approximately
horizontal sheets under gravity, so strongly tilted strata have been disturbed since deposition. His
principle of lateral continuity holds that a layer originally extended sideways until it thinned out
or met a barrier, so a layer appearing on both sides of a valley was once continuous across it.

A fourth principle, cross-cutting relationships, developed later through the work of James Hutton in
the late eighteenth century and Charles Lyell in the nineteenth: any feature that cuts across a body
of rock must be younger than the rock it cuts. A fault is younger than the strata it displaces; an
intrusion is younger than the rock it invades. This becomes indispensable in archaeology, where human
activity consists very largely of cutting into things.

William Smith added the other half of the toolkit. Working as a canal surveyor in England around
1800, he observed that particular assemblages of fossils appeared in a consistent order wherever the
strata were exposed, and that this order could be used to correlate rocks between distant places.
His geological map of England and Wales, published in 1815, was the first demonstration that
sequence could be extended across a landscape. The archaeological equivalent, using pottery types
and other artefacts to correlate deposits between sites, follows exactly the same logic and inherits
exactly the same weaknesses.

Underpinning all of it is uniformitarianism, the principle set out at length in Lyell's Principles of
Geology between 1830 and 1833: the processes observable today are the processes that formed the
record of the past. Where the geologist watches a river deposit silt to understand ancient
sediments, the archaeologist watches a modern building collapse, a ditch silt up, or a floor accumulate
trampled dirt, and uses those observations to interpret the same phenomena centuries old. The
discipline that studies these formation processes systematically is now called archaeological site
formation theory, and it is the direct descendant of Lyell's insight.

sections.heading: How Archaeological Layers Differ from Geological Ones
sections.body:
Borrowing geology's principles wholesale would produce serious errors, because the deposits an
archaeologist digs through are made by people and behave quite differently from those made by rivers
and oceans. Four differences matter enough to change the method.

The first is speed and scale. A geological stratum may represent tens of thousands of years and
extend for hundreds of kilometres. An archaeological layer may represent a single afternoon, a
building's demolition, one flood, or one dumped barrowload of rubbish, and may be two metres across
and three centimetres thick. Time in an archaeological sequence is wildly unevenly distributed: a
thick homogeneous layer may represent a century of gradual accumulation while the thin dark line
above it represents a fire that lasted one night. Thickness is not a measure of duration, and
assuming it is has produced many badly wrong site narratives.

The second is that people dig. Human beings cut pits, graves, ditches, post-holes, wells, cellars,
robber trenches and foundation trenches, and each of those destroys part of the sequence already
present and inserts something younger into the middle of something older. A pit dug in the twelfth
century through Roman layers puts twelfth-century material physically below Roman material at the
edges. Superposition still applies, but only to the relationship between the pit's fills and the
layers the pit cuts through, not to a naive reading of what is higher and lower on the section face.
This is the single commonest source of error made by inexperienced excavators.

The third is horizontality. Geological original horizontality is a reasonable default. Archaeological
deposits are frequently anything but horizontal at the moment of formation: a rampart is built as a
sloping bank, a rubbish tip accumulates on an incline, a road has a deliberate camber, a ditch fills
with material sliding in from the sides. Harris reformulated the principle accordingly, holding that
archaeological strata deposited against a face or an obstruction will have an original slope, and
that a horizontal surface should be read as the deliberate work of levelling rather than as the
natural default.

The fourth difference is lateral continuity. A geological bed can be assumed to have continued until
it thinned or met a basin edge. An archaeological layer very often had a real, deliberate edge from
the start: a floor stopped at a wall, a yard surface at a fence, a midden at the limit of where
people threw things. Harris's restatement is that the original extent of a deposit will either thin
to a feather edge, be bounded by the limit of the basin of deposition, or be truncated by later
removal, and that any abrupt vertical edge must be explained rather than assumed to be original. This
matters enormously, because a truncated edge is itself evidence of a later event that must be placed
in the sequence.

sections.heading: From Antiquarianism to Method: A Short History
sections.body:
The idea that the ground records time in layers took a long while to become excavation practice, and
the history explains why several competing techniques still coexist.

The earliest systematic use of sequence in archaeology was typological rather than stratigraphic.
Christian Jürgensen Thomsen, curator at the Danish National Museum, organised its collections in the
1810s and 1820s into stone, bronze and iron, publishing the scheme in 1836. It was a hypothesis about
order with no excavated proof. The proof came from his younger colleague Jens Jacob Worsaae, who from
1843 onward dug Danish peat bogs and burial mounds specifically to test whether the three ages
appeared in the predicted stratigraphic order. They did. That combination, a typological hypothesis
verified by excavated superposition, is arguably the founding move of scientific archaeology.

Excavation technique improved unevenly. Giuseppe Fiorelli, appointed to direct the excavations at
Pompeii in 1860, insisted on clearing buildings downward from the top rather than tunnelling in
laterally for objects, and on recording what was found in place. In Britain, Augustus Henry Lane Fox
Pitt Rivers, excavating on Cranborne Chase in the 1880s and 1890s, established that everything found
must be recorded, including the ordinary and the broken, and published his sites in exhaustive detail
at his own expense. His often-quoted principle was that excavation is destruction, and that the
excavator's obligation is to record what is destroyed.

The twentieth century's dominant technique came from Mortimer Wheeler, who set it out in Archaeology
from the Earth in 1954. Wheeler dug in a grid of square boxes separated by standing baulks of unexcavated
earth, usually about a metre wide. The vertical faces of those baulks gave permanent, drawable
sections through the deposits, and the section drawing became the primary record of sequence.
Kathleen Kenyon applied the method with great rigour at Jericho from 1952, and the approach became
known as the Wheeler-Kenyon method. It taught a generation to read layers properly.

Its weakness was that the baulks concealed exactly the horizontal relationships that reveal what a
site was: a building's plan, a yard's extent, the shape of an occupation surface. Philip Barker's
Techniques of Archaeological Excavation, published in 1977 and drawing on his work at Wroxeter, argued
forcefully for open-area excavation, in which large areas are stripped one stratigraphic unit at a
time with no permanent baulks. This exposes whole surfaces and reveals faint features that a grid
would slice into meaninglessness. But it removes the section drawing as the main record of sequence,
because there is no permanent standing face to draw.

That created a genuine problem. Open-area excavation gives a far better picture of what a site looked
like at each moment and a far worse mechanism for demonstrating the order of moments. Something was
needed that could record sequence independently of any section face. That gap is precisely what the
Harris matrix was invented to fill.

sections.heading: The Context: The Basic Unit of Excavation
sections.body:
Modern excavation is organised around a single conceptual unit, called a context in British practice
and variously a locus, a stratigraphic unit or a feature elsewhere. A context is the smallest
recognisable event in the formation of the site: one deposition, one cut, one construction. Every
context receives a unique number, and that number is the permanent identifier tying together the
written record, the drawings, the photographs, the finds and the samples from that event.

Contexts come in a small number of kinds and distinguishing them is the first skill an excavator
learns. A deposit is material that accumulated or was placed: a dump of rubbish, a layer of trampled
occupation dirt, the silt in the bottom of a ditch, a spread of demolition rubble, the fill of a
grave. A cut is not material at all but a void, the negative shape produced when someone removed
earth: the sides and base of a pit, a post-hole, a foundation trench, a ditch. A masonry or structural
context is a built thing, a wall, a floor surface, a hearth, treated as one unit if it was made in one
operation. A skeleton in a grave is normally recorded as its own context.

The cut is the conceptually hard one, because it is defined by absence. When a pit is excavated the
archaeologist removes the fills, which are contexts in their own right, and is then looking at the
surfaces of the cut, which is a separate, earlier context: the pit was dug before it was filled. The
cut and its fills therefore always occupy different positions in the sequence, and confusing a pit
with its fill is one of the classic errors. The rule is that the act of digging and the act of filling
are different events and get different numbers.

Deciding where one context ends and another begins is a judgement, made in the field, on the basis of
colour, texture, compaction, inclusions and boundary sharpness. Two dumps of similar clay tipped an
hour apart may be genuinely indistinguishable and will be recorded as one context, in which case the
record under-reports events. Conversely a single deposit that dried unevenly may look like two. There
is no way to eliminate this judgement, and it is why context definition is treated as an
interpretative act rather than a neutral observation. Good practice is to record the reasoning, so a
later reader can see why the excavator drew the line where they did.

Each context is written up on a pro forma record sheet, standardised so that nothing is forgotten
under pressure. It carries the number, a physical description, the excavator's interpretation, a
plan, a list of finds and samples, and, critically, a stratigraphic relationships box in which the
excavator records which contexts this one lies above, which it lies below, and which it may equate
to. Those boxes are the raw material of the matrix.

sections.heading: Deposits and Interfaces
sections.body:
One of the genuine conceptual advances of the 1970s was the insistence that surfaces are units of
stratification in their own right, equal in status to the material deposits, and must be numbered,
recorded and placed in the sequence like anything else. Edward Harris made this argument central to
his system, and it is the point most often skipped by those learning it.

The reasoning is that a great deal of what happened on a site left no material behind at all, only a
surface. When people dig a pit, the event of digging produces no deposit; it produces a hole. When a
building is levelled and the ground scraped flat, the scraping produces a surface that destroyed
whatever was above it. When a river erodes across an abandoned settlement, or a Victorian cellar is
cut through Roman levels, the event is recorded only as a boundary. If only material deposits were
numbered, these events, some of the most important on any site, would be invisible in the record, and
the sequence would appear to jump inexplicably from early to late.

Harris distinguished several kinds of interface. A feature interface is the surface produced by
removing earlier material, and it divides naturally into vertical feature interfaces, meaning the
sides and base of a cut such as a pit, post-hole or ditch, and horizontal feature interfaces, meaning
broad truncation surfaces produced by levelling, erosion or ploughing. A layer interface is the upper
surface of a deposit, the surface that was exposed and walked on before the next deposit covered it.
A period interface is a surface that can be shown to have been exposed across the whole site at one
time, marking a genuine horizon in the site's history.

In routine British recording practice, a compromise has settled. Cuts are always numbered as
independent contexts, because their relationships genuinely differ from their fills, and this is
non-negotiable. The upper surfaces of ordinary deposits, by contrast, are usually not given separate
numbers, because doing so roughly doubles the size of the record for little analytical gain; the
deposit's own number is treated as standing for both the material and its surface. Harris argued
against that simplification and there is a reasonable case that something is lost, particularly where
a surface was exposed for a long time and accumulated wear, but the practical convention has largely
won.

Where the distinction bites hardest is in truncation. A layer that has been cut away has lost part of
its own history, and any dating evidence in the missing part is gone forever. Recognising a
truncation surface, drawing it, numbering it and placing it in the sequence is what converts an
apparent absence of evidence into positive evidence of a destructive event. Sites where a whole
century seems to be missing usually turn out, on careful reading, to have a truncation surface that
was recorded as nothing at all.

sections.heading: The Four Laws of Archaeological Stratigraphy
sections.body:
Edward Harris set out four laws specific to archaeological deposits, adapting three from geology and
adding one that has no geological equivalent. They are short, and everything else in the method
follows from them.

The law of superposition states that in a series of layers and interfacial features, as originally
created, the upper units are younger and the lower are older, because each must have been supported
by something already in existence. The wording matters: the qualification "as originally created" is
what excludes situations where later disturbance has inverted things. Upcast from a ditch thrown onto
a bank places older material above younger; a wall that has fallen over lies with its original top
furthest from its base. Superposition applies to the order of the events, not naively to present
vertical position.

The law of original horizontality holds that any archaeological layer deposited in an unconsolidated
form will tend toward a horizontal position, because strata resting against a sloping face will
either slump to the horizontal or reflect the contours of the basin they lie in. Its practical
consequence is diagnostic: strongly tilted deposits indicate either that they were deposited against
something now removed, or that they have subsided, slumped or been dumped from a fixed point. Each of
those is an event that the sequence must accommodate.

The law of original continuity holds that any deposit or interfacial feature will be bounded by the
edge of its basin of deposition, or will thin to a feather edge. Therefore, if any edge is exposed
in a vertical plane, a part of its original extent must have been removed by later excavation or
erosion. This turns a blunt vertical edge from a puzzle into a positive statement: something later
cut it, and that something is a context to be found and numbered.

The fourth, the law of stratigraphic succession, is Harris's own and is the one that makes the matrix
possible. It states that a unit of archaeological stratification takes its place in the stratigraphic
sequence of a site from its position between the undermost of the units that lie above it and the
uppermost of all the units that lie below it, and with which it has a physical contact. All other
relationships are redundant. This is a startling claim on first reading. It says that most of the
relationships one could write down are not information at all, and that the true sequence is defined
only by immediate contacts.

The consequence is enormous in practice. On a site with a thousand contexts there are, in principle,
nearly half a million possible pairwise relationships. The law says the great majority are logically
implied by others and should be deleted, leaving a few thousand genuine, immediate, physically
observed contacts. Without that pruning rule the diagram would be an unreadable thicket. With it, the
sequence becomes a compact structure that a human being can actually read, check and argue with.

sections.heading: Edward Harris and the Invention of the Matrix
sections.body:
The matrix has a precise origin. In 1973 Edward Cecil Harris, a Bermudian archaeologist then in his
twenties, was working on the Lower Brook Street excavations in Winchester, England, under the
direction of Martin Biddle. Winchester was among the first genuinely large open-area urban
excavations, and it had run headlong into the problem the technique creates. The site had a very deep
and complex sequence, thousands of stratigraphic units, and, because it was dug in open area without
permanent baulks, no single section face on which the whole sequence could be read.

The existing tools were inadequate in a specific way. A section drawing shows the layers that happen
to intersect one arbitrary vertical plane, which on a complex urban site is a small and unrepresentative
sample. It also mixes two quite different kinds of information: the shape and thickness of deposits,
which is descriptive, and their order of formation, which is chronological. Harris's insight was to
separate those completely. Shape belongs on plans and sections. Order belongs on a diagram that
records nothing except which unit came before which, with no scale, no thickness, no shape and no
spatial position at all.

The result is a diagram of boxes and lines. Each unit of stratification is a box containing its
number. A vertical line from one box down to another means the upper unit is directly above, and
therefore later than, the lower. Units with no relationship to each other sit side by side with no
connecting line, which is itself a meaningful statement: their relative order is genuinely unknown
from stratigraphy alone. Time runs from bottom to top, oldest at the base. The diagram is nothing
more than that, and its power comes from what it excludes.

Harris first published the method in 1975, in a paper titled "The stratigraphic sequence: a question
of time" in the journal World Archaeology, and set it out fully in his book Principles of
Archaeological Stratigraphy in 1979, with a substantially revised second edition in 1989 that
remains the standard reference and has been translated into many languages and made freely available.

Adoption was rapid in Britain and Ireland, particularly through urban units such as the Department of
Urban Archaeology in London, whose site manual made single-context recording with a matrix the
standard method. It spread widely across northern Europe. In North America and parts of the
Mediterranean world, uptake has been more partial, with many projects retaining locus-based or
level-based systems and treating the matrix as an optional analytical tool rather than a recording
requirement. The result is that a reader consulting excavation reports from different traditions will
find genuinely different assumptions about what constitutes a record of sequence, which is worth
knowing before comparing them.

sections.heading: The Three Possible Relationships
sections.body:
The entire method rests on a claim of exhaustive simplicity: between any two units of stratification
on a site there are exactly three possible relationships, and no others. Every observation made in
the field must be forced into one of them, and the discipline of doing so is what makes the resulting
diagram checkable.

The first relationship is no direct relationship. Two contexts on opposite sides of the site that
never touch and are not linked by any chain of contacts have no stratigraphic relationship at all.
This is not a failure of observation. It is a positive finding: stratigraphy alone cannot tell which
of them is earlier, and any claim about their relative order must come from elsewhere, from dating
evidence, from spatial logic, or from correlation. On the diagram they appear side by side, unlinked.
Beginners very often invent a relationship here because the two contexts appear at similar depth, and
similar depth means nothing whatsoever.

The second is superposition, meaning one context is directly above or below the other and physically
in contact. This is the workhorse relationship and produces almost all the lines on a matrix. The
phrasing conventionally used on record sheets is that context 105 is "above" or "later than" context
112, and correspondingly 112 is "below" or "earlier than" 105. A cut is always earlier than its own
fills and later than everything it cuts through, which is the relationship that trips people most
often. Only immediate, physical contacts should be recorded; a context four layers down is later
handled by the chain, not by a direct line.

The third is correlation, the assertion that two separately numbered contexts are in fact parts of
one original unit, now divided. A floor cut through by a later pit survives as two patches with
different numbers; a bank sectioned in two trenches produces two records of one bank. Where the
excavator is confident they are the same event, the contexts are correlated, drawn on the matrix as
two boxes joined by a horizontal line with a distinctive connector, or merged into a single box.

Correlation is by far the most dangerous of the three, because unlike the other two it is an
interpretation rather than an observation. Nobody saw the two patches connect; someone inferred it
from similarity of colour, texture and level. If the inference is wrong, the two halves of the
sequence are welded together incorrectly and every relationship downstream of the join is corrupted.
Worse, correlations are the usual cause of the one thing a matrix must never contain, a loop, in
which following the relationships upward eventually leads back to where you started. Because such a
loop asserts that a context is both earlier and later than itself, it is a logical impossibility and
a signal that at least one recorded relationship, very often a correlation, is wrong.

sections.heading: Constructing a Matrix Step by Step
sections.body:
Building a matrix is mechanical once the relationships are recorded honestly, and that is the point:
the diagram can be checked by someone who never saw the site, and errors surface as logical
contradictions rather than matters of opinion.

The work is done in two passes. During excavation each context sheet's relationships box is filled in
immediately, while the physical contacts are still visible, and a running matrix is drawn on a
whiteboard in the site hut and updated daily. That running version is a working tool: it exposes
contradictions while the ground is still open and can still be re-examined, which is the only moment
at which a problem can genuinely be resolved. The second pass happens in post-excavation analysis,
when relationships are entered into software, the diagram is generated formally, and it is checked
for loops and redundancy.

The governing discipline is recording only direct physical contacts. If context 40 lies on 41 and 41
lies on 42, then 40 is later than 42, but that must not be written down. It is implied by the chain,
and recording it explicitly creates a redundant line that may survive as a false direct relationship
if 41 is later reinterpreted.
steps: Assign every unit of stratification a unique number as it is identified: every deposit, cut, wall, floor and skeleton. Never reuse a number, even for one later found to be an error; retire it with a note instead.

Before removing each context, examine its boundaries and record what it physically touches. Ask three questions: what does this lie directly on, what lies directly on it, and what does it cut or get cut by?
Write those into the relationships box as 'earlier than' and 'later than' lists. Record only immediate contacts, never inferred ones, and never a relationship deduced by following a chain.
For a cut and its fills, record the cut as earlier than all its fills and later than every context it passes through. Record the fills in their own order of deposition, lowest first.
Note suspected correlations separately as 'same as', with a written justification, and keep them flagged as provisional rather than merging the numbers.
Draw each context as a box on a large surface, placing later contexts higher up the sheet. Leave generous space, because sequences reorganise repeatedly as digging proceeds.
Join each pair with a single vertical line, later above earlier. Draw no line between contexts with no observed relationship, and resist tidying the diagram by inventing one.

Check continuously for loops by tracing any path upward and confirming it never returns to its starting box. A loop means at least one recorded relationship is wrong; re-examine the ground before it is destroyed.
Remove redundant lines: if a line from A to C exists alongside a path A to B to C, delete the direct A to C line, which carries no new information.

After excavation, enter all relationships into stratigraphic software, regenerate the diagram, and reconcile every discrepancy with the hand-drawn site version, treating each as a question about the site rather than a clerical slip.

sections.heading: The Mathematics Underneath: Graphs, Loops and Reduction
sections.body:
Although Harris devised the matrix as a practical field tool and described it in plain language, it
turns out to be an exact instance of a well-studied mathematical object, and recognising that has
made it possible to check and manipulate sequences by computer with complete rigour.

Formally, a Harris matrix is a directed acyclic graph, usually abbreviated DAG. The contexts are the
vertices, or nodes. Each relationship of superposition is a directed edge running from the later
context to the earlier one. Directed means the relationship has an orientation and is not symmetric:
if A is later than B, then B cannot be later than A. Acyclic means the graph contains no closed loop,
which in this application encodes the physical impossibility of a context being both earlier and later
than itself. When stratigraphic software reports a cycle error it is applying exactly this test, and
the finding is not a matter of interpretation. Something recorded is definitely wrong.

The law of stratigraphic succession corresponds to an operation known in graph theory as transitive
reduction. Given a graph, the transitive reduction is the unique smallest graph that preserves
exactly the same reachability relations: any node reachable from another in the original is still
reachable in the reduced version, and no additional connections are implied. For a directed acyclic
graph the transitive reduction is unique and can be computed efficiently, which is why software can
take a raw list of hundreds of thousands of recorded relationships and return a clean diagram with
the redundant ones stripped out. Harris arrived at the correct operation by reasoning about
stratigraphy years before it was widely described in these terms.

The reciprocal operation, transitive closure, adds every relationship implied by any chain. It is
occasionally useful for querying, for instance to ask whether context 812 is earlier than context 44
by any route at all, but it must never be used as a record, because it obliterates the distinction
between what was observed and what was deduced.

Turning the sequence into a list, oldest to youngest, corresponds to topological sorting. A crucial
property is that for any interesting archaeological site there are very many valid topological
orderings, not one, because contexts on opposite sides of a site have no relationship and can be
ordered either way. This is not a defect of the method; it is an accurate statement about what the
evidence supports. A published sequence presented as a single definite ordering of every context is
almost certainly asserting more than the stratigraphy can bear.

One further consequence deserves emphasis. Because the graph records only relative order, it contains
no metric information whatsoever. The vertical distance between boxes on the page means nothing. Two
contexts drawn one above the other may be separated by an hour or by four centuries, and nothing in
the diagram distinguishes those cases. Time enters only when dating evidence is attached, which is a
separate operation entirely.

sections.heading: Single-Context Recording in Practice
sections.body:
The recording system that grew up around the matrix, generally called single-context recording,
reorganises the whole practice of excavation around the unit rather than around the trench. It is
demanding, and understanding what it costs as well as what it delivers is necessary to using it
sensibly.

The governing rule is that contexts are removed strictly in reverse order of deposition: the latest
surviving context anywhere in the area is excavated first, then the next latest, and so on downward.
This is harder than it sounds, because the latest context is often a small patch in one corner while
a large early deposit occupies most of the area, so the surface being worked is rarely flat and
progress looks chaotic to an untrained eye. Digging in arbitrary horizontal spits, by contrast, is
easy and produces an unusable record, because a spit slices through several unrelated contexts at once
and mixes their finds irretrievably.

Each context is planned individually, at a standard scale, most commonly 1:20, showing its full
extent in plan. In the classic system every plan is drawn on a separate sheet of translucent film, so
that overlaying successive sheets on a light table reconstructs the site in three dimensions and any
subset can be combined to show a single phase. Levels are taken across each context relative to a
site datum tied to the national height network. Photographs are taken with a scale and north arrow.
Finds are bagged by context, never by area or spit. Environmental samples, typically 10 to 40 litres
of soil for flotation, are taken by context with the context number written on the bag before it
leaves the ground.

The benefits are real and cumulative. The record is modular, so a specialist studying pottery decades
later can ask precisely which contexts a sherd group came from and where those contexts sit in the
sequence. Reinterpretation is possible without re-excavation, because the primary units and their
relationships are preserved independently of the excavator's narrative. Different excavators working
in different corners produce records that combine without translation.

The costs are equally real. It is slow, typically slower per cubic metre than any alternative, and on
commercial projects with fixed budgets that pressure is constant. It generates a very large archive:
a substantial urban excavation may produce five to fifteen thousand context records, several thousand
plans, and a matrix that when plotted runs to many metres of paper. It demands a high and consistent
standard from every excavator, since one person's careless relationships box corrupts the whole
sequence. And it front-loads a great deal of description while deferring interpretation, which some
practitioners regard as an intellectual weakness rather than a virtue.

sections.heading: Phasing, Grouping and the Site Narrative
sections.body:
A matrix with four thousand boxes is a complete statement of sequence and an almost unreadable account
of a site. Turning it into history requires aggregating contexts into progressively larger
interpretative units, and this is where excavation stops being observation and becomes argument.

The usual hierarchy runs in three or four levels. Individual contexts are combined into groups, also
called sub-groups, which represent a single recognisable action or entity: a pit and all its fills; a
wall, its foundation trench and the backfill of that trench; a hearth and its rake-out. Groups are
combined into larger land-use units or blocks representing a coherent activity in one place, such as
a building with its floors and walls, or a yard with its surfaces and drains. Those are assigned to
phases, meaning periods of activity across the whole excavated area that can be argued to be broadly
contemporary. Phases may then be gathered into periods spanning centuries.

The critical logical point is that each level of aggregation adds interpretation and subtracts
certainty. Contexts and their relationships are, as far as anything in archaeology can be, observed
fact. Groups are usually secure, since a pit and its fills obviously belong together. Phasing is
frankly an argument, because it asserts that things in different parts of the site, often with no
stratigraphic relationship whatsoever, were in use at the same time. That assertion rests on dating
evidence, on shared alignments, on the logic of access and circulation, and on the excavator's
judgement. Good reports keep the levels visibly separate, so a later reader can accept the contexts
while rejecting the phasing. Reports that present phases as though they were observations make their
own reasoning unfalsifiable.

Phase boundaries are best anchored on genuine site-wide horizons: a destruction layer, a comprehensive
levelling, a fire, a flood deposit, or a major replanning that cuts across the whole area. Where no
such horizon exists, phase boundaries are conveniences and should be labelled as such. Many sites
simply do not have clean phases, because one building was rebuilt while its neighbour stood
untouched, and forcing a tidy scheme onto continuous, overlapping change misrepresents how places
actually change.

A useful discipline is to produce a reduced matrix at group and phase level alongside the full one.
The full context matrix is the primary record and belongs in the archive; the reduced version is what
appears in the published report and what most readers will ever see. Both should be available, and
the relationship between them should be documented, because the reduction embodies exactly the
interpretative decisions that a future researcher may want to challenge. The commonest failing in
published reports is that only the reduced diagram survives, leaving a reader who doubts the phasing
with no way to reconstruct the evidence it was built from, and therefore no way to propose an
alternative without returning to an unpublished archive that may be difficult to access or, in some
older cases, no longer exists at all.

sections.heading: Attaching Dates to a Sequence
sections.body:
Stratigraphy establishes order. Chronology requires attaching dates to that order, and the logic of
doing so correctly is precise and frequently mishandled.

The two governing concepts are Latin phrases in universal use. A terminus post quem, commonly
abbreviated TPQ, is a limit after which: the date after which a context must have formed. A coin
struck in 1247 found in a pit fill gives that fill a TPQ of 1247, because the fill cannot have been
deposited before the coin existed. A terminus ante quem, or TAQ, is a limit before which: the date
before which a context must have formed. If a sealed layer is covered by a floor independently dated
to 1310, the layer has a TAQ of 1310. A context bracketed by both is dated to a range, and the whole
craft of site chronology consists of assembling enough brackets to constrain the sequence.

The datable material in a context gives a TPQ, never a TAQ, and this asymmetry is the source of most
errors. The latest datable object in a deposit dates the deposit's formation, because a single
intrusive late sherd proves the whole deposit is at least that late, whereas any number of early
objects proves nothing beyond their own manufacture. This is why excavators speak of a context being
dated by its latest material, a rule that feels counterintuitive but follows directly from the logic.

Two contaminating processes must be understood. Residuality is the presence of genuinely old material
in a later deposit, and it is extremely common, because digging a pit through earlier levels throws
earlier artefacts into the pit's fill. A twelfth-century pit cut through a Roman street will contain
abundant Roman pottery. Intrusion is the opposite, later material working down into an earlier
deposit through worm action, root channels, animal burrows, or unnoticed small cuts, and it is far
more dangerous, because a single intrusive object can shift a context's apparent date by centuries.
The defence against both is the sequence itself: dates assigned to contexts must run consistently with
the stratigraphic order, and a context whose apparent date contradicts its stratigraphic position is
signalling contamination, not revising the sequence.

Radiocarbon requires particular care about what is being dated. The measurement dates the death of
the organism, not the deposition of the deposit. Charcoal from the heartwood of an oak felled at 300
years old carries an inbuilt age offset of up to three centuries, the so-called old wood problem. The
preferred samples are short-lived single entities, cereal grains, twigs, nutshells or articulated
bone, from securely sealed contexts. Where a sample's stratigraphic position is uncertain, the
determination is close to worthless regardless of laboratory precision, which is a point worth
repeating whenever budget pressure suggests dating whatever is convenient.

sections.heading: Extensions, Software and Bayesian Chronology
sections.body:
The matrix was designed for buried deposits on open-area urban excavations, and much of its
subsequent development consists of stretching it to other kinds of evidence and connecting it to
statistical methods that did not exist when it was devised.

Standing buildings were the first extension. A wall is a stratified object: its footings precede its
superstructure, a blocked doorway postdates the opening it blocks, a re-pointing episode postdates
the masonry it covers, and a raised roofline postdates the wall it sits on. Buildings archaeology
records these as contexts and constructs matrices for elevations exactly as for excavated deposits.
The complications are that relationships are often lateral rather than superimposed, and that
buildings are repaired repeatedly in ways that leave subtle traces, so the resulting matrices tend to
be wide and shallow where excavation matrices are narrow and deep. The method transfers, but the
diagrams look quite different.

The same logic has been applied to landscapes, where field boundaries, trackways, ridge and furrow
and enclosures cut and respect one another in readable ways, and to individual complex artefacts and
to rock art panels, where superimposed motifs can be sequenced by which overlies which. In each case
the requirement is the same: identifiable units and observable direct contacts.

Software has become standard. Purpose-built programs including Stratify, ArchEd and the Harris Matrix
Composer take a list of relationships, perform the transitive reduction, detect cycles, handle
correlations and lay out a readable diagram automatically, a task that by hand on a large site
consumes weeks. Most integrate with the site database so that context records, finds and matrix are a
single system, and with geographic information systems so that each context's plan is linked to its
node.

The most consequential development is the marriage of stratigraphy with Bayesian statistics.
Radiocarbon determinations calibrate to probability distributions rather than points, often spanning
150 to 300 years, and calibration curve wiggles can produce frustrating multi-peaked results. Bayesian
chronological modelling, implemented in widely used programs such as OxCal, developed by Christopher
Bronk Ramsey at Oxford, treats the stratigraphic sequence as prior information: if context 50 is
demonstrably earlier than context 48, then whatever the raw calibrations suggest, the true dates must
respect that order. Imposing the order dramatically narrows the resulting posterior distributions,
frequently reducing uncertainty from centuries to a few decades, occasionally to within a generation.

This has made the matrix considerably more valuable than it was, because a rigorously recorded
sequence now converts directly into chronological precision. It also raises the stakes: an incorrect
stratigraphic relationship fed into a Bayesian model does not merely go unnoticed, it actively forces
the dates into a wrong arrangement and returns a confident, precise, false answer.

sections.heading: Criticisms, Failure Modes and Limits
sections.body:
The matrix is a powerful instrument with well-understood weaknesses, and practitioners argue about it
seriously. Knowing where it fails is part of using it competently.

Its most fundamental limitation is that it records order and nothing else. It carries no information
about duration, and two boxes adjacent on the diagram may be separated by minutes or by five hundred
years. It carries no information about importance: a scrape of mortar and a cathedral foundation are
identical boxes. It carries no spatial information, so a matrix alone cannot tell you where anything
was. These are deliberate exclusions rather than oversights, but readers unfamiliar with the
convention persistently over-read the diagrams, treating vertical spacing as elapsed time.

Contemporaneity is handled poorly, and this is a genuine structural weakness rather than a matter of
taste. The diagram can say that A is later than B, or that their relationship is unknown, but it has
no clean way to assert that A and B were in use simultaneously, which is exactly what a site
narrative most needs. Two floors in adjacent rooms of one building were certainly contemporary, yet
if no context touches both they appear on the matrix as unrelated. Practitioners bridge this with
grouping and phasing, but those are interpretative layers bolted on rather than something the formal
system supports.

A more searching criticism, developed by writers including Gavin Lucas and Adrian Chadwick, targets
single-context recording rather than the matrix itself. The argument is that atomising a site into
thousands of separately recorded units, filled in on standardised forms, encourages excavators to
believe they are producing neutral observations, when context definition is unavoidably
interpretative. It also separates the person who understood the deposit in the ground from the person
who later writes the narrative, potentially losing knowledge that was never written down because the
form had no box for it. The proposed remedies, reflexive recording with narrative diaries and
interpretation at the trowel's edge, associated particularly with the long-running project at
Çatalhöyük in Turkey, aim to supplement the pro forma rather than replace it.

The practical failure modes are more mundane and more common. Loops in the diagram are the classic
symptom and almost always trace back to a wrong correlation or a cut misidentified as its own fill.
Contexts recorded with no relationships at all become orphan nodes floating unattached, usually
because a busy excavator left the relationships box blank; these are unrecoverable once the ground is
gone. Redundant relationships recorded as direct contacts survive the reduction and misrepresent the
sequence. Unrecognised truncation makes a century vanish. Numbers reused for two different contexts
corrupt everything associated with them.

Nearly all of these are detectable while the site is still open and nearly all are irrecoverable
afterwards. That asymmetry is the whole argument for maintaining the matrix daily during excavation
rather than assembling it afterwards from the paperwork. The diagram's real function is not to be a
tidy appendix in a report. It is a live error-detection device that works only while there is still
ground left to look at.

guides.title: Radiocarbon Dating
guides.summary: How radiocarbon dating works, from the cosmic-ray production of carbon-14 to the laboratory measurement and calendar calibration of a date. Covers the chemistry, the instruments, sample selection, reservoir effects, and how to read a published date critically.

sections.heading: A Clock Buried in Every Living Thing
sections.body:
Before 1949, an archaeologist who dug up a hearth, a wooden post, or a bundle of grass sandals had no direct way to say how old it was. Ages came from stratigraphy, from stylistic comparison of pottery and stone tools, and from occasional links to written histories. Those methods can order events reliably enough, but they float free of the calendar: a sequence of five occupation layers might span two centuries or two thousand years, and two sites on different continents could not be tied together at all. Radiocarbon dating changed that. It supplies an absolute age, in years, from a fragment of anything that was once alive, using a physical process that runs at the same rate everywhere in the universe and cannot be sped up or slowed down by heat, pressure, or chemistry.

The idea rests on a striking coincidence. Cosmic rays striking the upper atmosphere continually manufacture a radioactive isotope of carbon, carbon-14, which mixes into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide. Plants take that carbon dioxide up in photosynthesis; animals eat plants or eat animals that ate plants. So every living organism carries carbon whose radioactive fraction matches, to a good approximation, the fraction in the air around it. At death the exchange stops. No new carbon-14 comes in, and the carbon-14 already present decays away at a fixed rate, halving roughly every 5,730 years. Measure how much is left, compare it with how much a living thing would have, and the arithmetic gives you the time since death.

The practical reach of the method is about ten half-lives. After roughly 50,000 years so little carbon-14 survives that the signal drowns in laboratory background, and even the most careful modern work struggles past about 55,000 years. At the young end, the method is precise to a few decades for most of the Holocene, and for the last seventy years an entirely different trick, using the fallout from atmospheric nuclear testing, can pin a date to within a year or two. Between those limits lies the whole span of the human story that matters most to archaeology: the peopling of Australia and the Americas, the end of the Ice Age, the invention of agriculture, the rise of cities, and the collapse of empires. Almost every date you have ever read for a prehistoric event traces back, directly or through a chain of cross-checks, to a radiocarbon measurement.

It is worth being precise about what is actually being dated, because this is the source of more bad archaeology than any laboratory error. The method dates the death of the organism whose carbon you are measuring, and nothing else. A charcoal fragment from a hearth dates the year the tree stopped growing, which may be centuries before someone burned it, and the interior rings of a long-lived oak can be four hundred years older than the outer bark. A date on a seed found in a pit dates the seed; whether the seed belongs to the pit is an archaeological judgement, not a physical measurement. Understanding how these measurements are made, and where they go wrong, is therefore not a technical footnote but the foundation of how we know when anything happened before writing.

sections.heading: Cosmic Rays and the Manufacture of Carbon-14
sections.body:
Carbon-14 is not left over from the formation of the Earth. Its half-life is far too short for that; any primordial supply would have vanished a hundred thousand times over. It is manufactured fresh, continuously, in the upper atmosphere, and understanding that factory explains both why the method works and why it needs correcting.

The raw material is galactic cosmic radiation: mostly bare protons, accelerated to enormous energies by supernova shock fronts elsewhere in the Milky Way, arriving at the top of the atmosphere at a rate of a few particles per square centimetre per second. When one of these primary protons collides with a nucleus of nitrogen or oxygen some 15 to 20 kilometres up, it shatters it and produces a shower of secondary particles, among them free neutrons. Those neutrons slow down through repeated collisions until they are moving at roughly thermal speeds, and a slow neutron striking a nitrogen-14 nucleus undergoes a particularly efficient reaction: the neutron is absorbed and a proton is ejected. In nuclear shorthand this is written n + 14N gives 14C + p. Nitrogen-14 makes up about 78 percent of the atmosphere by volume, so there is no shortage of targets, and this single reaction accounts for the overwhelming majority of natural carbon-14 production.

The newly minted carbon-14 atom is chemically reactive and within hours to weeks oxidises, first to carbon monoxide and then to carbon dioxide. As carbon dioxide it becomes ordinary atmospheric gas, indistinguishable in behaviour from the far more abundant carbon-12 and carbon-13, and it mixes through the whole atmosphere on a timescale of one to two years. Global production runs at something like two atoms per square centimetre of the Earth's surface per second, which sounds like nothing and amounts to perhaps seven or eight kilograms of new carbon-14 worldwide each year. Balanced against decay, this maintains a steady-state atmospheric inventory in which about one carbon atom in a trillion is carbon-14. Written as a ratio, roughly 1.2 times ten to the minus twelve.

Two things modulate that production rate, and both matter enormously in practice. The first is the Earth's magnetic field, which deflects incoming charged cosmic rays; when the field is strong, fewer cosmic rays penetrate and less carbon-14 is made, and the geomagnetic dipole has varied by a factor of roughly two over the last fifty thousand years. The second is the Sun. Solar wind and the heliospheric magnetic field also shield the inner solar system, so during periods of high solar activity production falls, and during quiet spells such as the Maunder Minimum of the late seventeenth century it rises. The consequence is unavoidable and central to everything that follows: the atmospheric carbon-14 concentration has never been truly constant, and a raw radiocarbon measurement therefore does not give a calendar age directly.

sections.heading: The Carbon Reservoirs and How Living Things Take Carbon Up
sections.body:
Carbon-14 made in the stratosphere does not stay there. It joins the global carbon cycle, and where it goes, how fast, and how thoroughly it mixes determines whether a given material is datable and whether its date needs correction. Thinking in terms of reservoirs makes the whole subject tractable.

The atmosphere is a small, fast, well-stirred reservoir holding on the order of 800 gigatonnes of carbon. It exchanges with the terrestrial biosphere, roughly 550 gigatonnes in living plants plus perhaps 1,500 gigatonnes in soils, on timescales of a growing season to centuries. It exchanges with the surface ocean, about 900 gigatonnes, within a few years. And the surface ocean exchanges with the vast deep ocean, some 37,000 gigatonnes, only sluggishly, on a global overturning timescale of roughly a thousand years. The deep ocean is the crucial complication. Water sinking in the North Atlantic or around Antarctica carries its carbon-14 out of contact with the atmosphere and does not return for centuries, during which decay proceeds unreplenished. Deep water is therefore radiocarbon-depleted, and where it upwells it makes the local surface water look artificially old.

For a land plant the situation is beautifully simple. A leaf fixes carbon dioxide drawn straight from the air it is standing in, so its carbon-14 ratio tracks the contemporary atmosphere with a lag of weeks. A tree ring formed in a particular summer locks in that summer's atmospheric signal and never exchanges it again, which is exactly why tree rings became the backbone of calibration. A herbivore eating that plant inherits the same signal within the turnover time of its tissues, which varies from days for liver protein to years for bone collagen and effectively never for tooth enamel laid down in childhood. This tissue-turnover difference is why a bone and a tooth from the same individual can, legitimately, give slightly different answers, and why forensic scientists deliberately sample enamel when they want a birth year and collagen when they want a death year.

Aquatic organisms are a different matter. A fish, a shellfish, or a person who eats a great deal of either draws carbon from water that may carry an old, depleted signal. A plant growing in a hard-water lake fed by springs running through limestone takes up dissolved carbonate that is millions of years old and radiocarbon-dead. In both cases the organism is born looking old, and the measured age must be corrected or the sample avoided. The single most common blunder in the whole field is dating a material whose carbon did not come from the open atmosphere and forgetting to say so. Establishing the carbon pathway into a sample, before any laboratory work begins, is not a formality; it decides whether the resulting number means anything at all.

sections.heading: Radioactive Decay, Half-Life, and the Age Equation
sections.body:
Carbon-14 decays by beta-minus emission. Inside the nucleus a neutron converts to a proton, ejecting an electron and an antineutrino, and the atom becomes stable nitrogen-14 again, closing the loop with the atmospheric reaction that made it. The emitted electron carries at most 156 kiloelectronvolts, a low energy by nuclear standards, and this softness matters practically: the beta particles are stopped by a few tens of centimetres of air or a sheet of paper, which makes carbon-14 harmless to handle but hard to detect efficiently.

Radioactive decay is a memoryless process. Any given carbon-14 nucleus has a fixed probability of decaying in the next second, independent of how long it has already existed, of temperature, of pressure, and of the chemical compound it sits in. This gives the exponential law N of t equals N-zero times e to the power minus lambda t, where lambda is the decay constant. Half-life and decay constant are linked by lambda equals the natural logarithm of 2 divided by the half-life, about 0.693 divided by the half-life. Rearranging for time gives the fundamental age equation: t equals the mean lifetime, which is 1 over lambda, multiplied by the natural logarithm of N-zero over N. Practitioners usually write it as t equals 8033 times ln of the ratio of modern to sample activity, in radiocarbon years.

That constant 8033 conceals a historical wrinkle worth knowing, because it confuses almost every newcomer. Willard Libby's team originally measured the half-life as 5,568 years, plus or minus 30. Later and better measurements put the true value at 5,730 years, plus or minus 40. By international agreement the discipline nevertheless continues to compute and publish raw ages using the old Libby half-life of 5,568 years, whose corresponding mean life is 8,033 years. This is not an error left uncorrected out of inertia. Because raw ages are always converted to calendar dates through a calibration curve that was itself built using the same convention, the two half-life choices cancel exactly, and freezing the convention keeps the entire historical literature mutually comparable. If you recompute a published age with the true half-life and then calibrate, you will get a wrong answer.

A worked example fixes the ideas. Suppose a charcoal sample yields 25 percent of the modern carbon-14 activity. Then t equals 8033 times ln of 4, and ln of 4 is 1.386, giving about 11,130 radiocarbon years before present. Note that the ratio, not the absolute amount, sets the age, so sample size affects only precision and not accuracy. Note also the brutal consequence of exponential decay at the old end: after 50,000 years only about 0.2 percent of the original carbon-14 remains, so a contamination of one percent modern carbon would make a genuinely 50,000-year-old sample appear to be about 37,000 years old. Old samples are exquisitely vulnerable to young contamination, and this asymmetry drives almost all laboratory practice.

sections.heading: Libby, the First Measurements, and the Birth of the Method
sections.body:
The method was conceived and demonstrated by Willard Frank Libby and his group at the University of Chicago in the years immediately after the Second World War, and the reasoning that led there is instructive because it shows how many separate facts had to be in place at once.

Libby had worked during the war on isotope separation for the Manhattan Project and knew the behaviour of light isotopes intimately. The key precursor was the 1939 discovery by Serge Korff, flying detectors on balloons, that cosmic rays produce a shower of neutrons in the upper atmosphere. Libby reasoned that those neutrons must be absorbed almost entirely by atmospheric nitrogen, that the resulting carbon-14 must be oxidised and mixed globally, and that it must therefore be present in all living matter at a low but measurable and roughly constant concentration. He estimated the equilibrium abundance before anyone had measured it, arriving at a figure close to the true one part in a trillion.

Proving it required detecting a handful of beta decays against an overwhelming background of cosmic rays and ambient radioactivity, a formidable problem in the 1940s. Libby's group first confirmed the existence of natural carbon-14 by concentrating it from methane produced by Baltimore sewage, a genuinely biological carbon source, and showing that petroleum-derived methane, being millions of years old, contained none. That contrast between living and fossil carbon was the proof of principle. They then built a counter using carbon black smeared inside a screen-wall Geiger tube and surrounded it with a thick iron shield and a ring of anticoincidence counters that vetoed any pulse coincident with a passing cosmic-ray muon.

The decisive test came in 1949, when Libby and James Arnold published dates for samples of known age, the so-called curve of knowns. Wood from the funerary boat of the Egyptian pharaoh Sesostris III, acacia from the tomb of Djoser at Saqqara, and a piece of a Ptolemaic coffin all returned ages agreeing with Egyptological dates within the stated uncertainties. Redwood and fir samples cross-checked against tree-ring counts likewise agreed. The 1949 paper in Science is one of the great demonstrations in twentieth-century science: an entirely new physical technique validated against an entirely independent body of historical knowledge. Libby received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1960.

His original assumptions were not all correct. He assumed atmospheric carbon-14 had been constant, which it has not, and he used a half-life now known to be about three percent too short. Yet the structure of his argument was sound, and the discrepancies his method eventually revealed, when radiocarbon dates for European megaliths came out older than the Egyptian monuments they were supposed to derive from, forced a wholesale rewriting of European prehistory. A technique good enough to overturn the framework that validated it is a technique that has genuinely learned something new.

sections.heading: Decay Counting: Gas Proportional and Liquid Scintillation
sections.body:
For the first three decades, radiocarbon dating meant sitting and waiting for atoms to decay. The arithmetic of that is sobering. One gram of modern carbon contains about 6 times ten to the twenty-two carbon atoms, of which roughly 6 times ten to the ten are carbon-14. With a mean life of 8,267 years in seconds, that gram produces about 13.6 decays per minute. A five-thousand-year-old sample gives about seven. A forty-thousand-year-old sample gives about a tenth of a decay per minute, so counting a statistically useful number of events takes days or weeks of continuous measurement in a heavily shielded room.

Two detector designs dominated. In gas proportional counting the sample is chemically converted to a pure counting gas, usually carbon dioxide but sometimes methane or acetylene, and that gas becomes the fill of the detector itself, so every decay happens inside the sensitive volume and essentially none is lost to absorption. The tube runs at a few thousand volts; each beta particle ionises the gas, the electrons avalanche toward a central wire, and the resulting pulse is amplified and counted. In liquid scintillation counting the sample carbon is converted to benzene, a synthesis that packs six carbon atoms into every molecule and yields an excellent solvent, and a scintillator such as PPO is dissolved in it. A beta particle excites the benzene, the energy is transferred to the scintillator, which emits a brief flash of ultraviolet-blue light, and two photomultiplier tubes in coincidence register the flash while rejecting their own random noise.

Both approaches live or die by background suppression. A typical installation sits in a basement under several metres of concrete, inside a lead or iron castle twenty centimetres thick, with the shielding iron often salvaged from pre-1945 ships or sunken vessels because steel smelted after the atmospheric nuclear tests carries traces of cobalt-60 and other activation products. Around the counter sits a ring or blanket of anticoincidence detectors: if the guard fires at the same instant as the sample counter, the event was a cosmic-ray muon punching through, and the pulse is vetoed. Even so, background may be a few counts per minute, comparable to the signal from an old sample, so blanks made from geologically ancient carbon such as anthracite or marble are counted alongside every batch and subtracted.

The defining limitation of decay counting is sample size. A conventional gas or liquid measurement needs on the order of one to ten grams of pure carbon, which means perhaps five to twenty grams of charcoal, fifty to a hundred grams of wood, or several hundred grams of bone. That is a fist-sized lump of an artefact, destroyed. You cannot date a single seed, a thread from a textile, a fleck of pigment, or a milligram of collagen from a precious hominin fossil. Decay counting still has a niche, because for large, clean, young samples it can achieve superb precision cheaply, but the transformation of archaeology came when it became possible to count the atoms themselves rather than waiting for them to fall apart.

sections.heading: Accelerator Mass Spectrometry: Counting Atoms Instead of Decays
sections.body:
Accelerator mass spectrometry, universally abbreviated AMS, was demonstrated for radiocarbon in 1977 and now performs the overwhelming majority of measurements. Its logic is simple and its engineering is not: rather than waiting the eight thousand years it takes an average carbon-14 atom to decay, ionise the sample, separate the isotopes by mass, and count the carbon-14 atoms one at a time as they arrive at a detector. Because you detect essentially every atom you inject rather than the tiny fraction that happens to decay during your measurement, sensitivity improves by something like six orders of magnitude. Sample requirements fall from grams to around one milligram of carbon, and often to a hundred micrograms or less, and measurement time falls from weeks to under an hour.

The obstacle is that a conventional mass spectrometer cannot do this, because carbon-14 is swamped by two interferences of almost identical mass. Nitrogen-14 is an isobar, an atom of the same mass number, and it is astronomically more abundant. Molecular fragments such as carbon-13 with a hydrogen atom, or carbon-12 with two hydrogens, also weigh about fourteen atomic mass units and are present at levels that would utterly bury the real signal. AMS defeats both with a specific and rather elegant sequence of tricks.

The sample is first reduced to graphite, pressed into a small target, and bombarded with caesium ions in a sputter source, which knocks off negative ions. This first step alone eliminates nitrogen, because the nitrogen negative ion is unstable and simply does not survive; the interference that no ordinary spectrometer can remove is removed by chemistry. The negative carbon ions are accelerated toward the positive high-voltage terminal of a tandem accelerator, typically at 0.5 to 5 million volts, though modern compact instruments manage at 200 kilovolts. At the terminal the ions pass through a thin foil or a stripper canal of argon gas, which strips several electrons away, converting each ion to a positive charge state of 1 plus, 3 plus, or higher. Any molecule reaching that point is violently broken apart by the sudden loss of its bonding electrons, so molecular interferences are destroyed outright. The now-positive ions are repelled from the same terminal, gaining energy a second time, and are then sorted by a sequence of magnetic and electrostatic analysers before landing in a gas ionisation detector that identifies each particle individually by its energy loss.

Meanwhile the abundant carbon-12 and carbon-13 beams are measured as electric currents in Faraday cups, since counting them individually would be hopeless. The instrument therefore reports isotope ratios directly. Standards of known activity, usually oxalic acid supplied by the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology, and blanks of radiocarbon-dead carbon are run in the same wheel as the unknowns to normalise the result and quantify the background.

sections.heading: Isotopic Fractionation and the Delta-13C Correction
sections.body:
Nature does not treat the three carbon isotopes identically. Carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 have masses in the ratio 12 to 13 to 14, and that difference, small as it is, changes how fast molecules diffuse, how tightly bonds vibrate, and how readily enzymes act. Lighter isotopes generally move and react slightly faster. The result is that a plant does not have quite the same isotopic composition as the air it grew in, and unless this is corrected it introduces an error of many centuries.

The magnitude is quantified as delta-13C, the per-mille deviation of the sample's carbon-13 to carbon-12 ratio from an agreed standard, originally a belemnite fossil from the Pee Dee formation in South Carolina and now the equivalent Vienna PDB scale. Atmospheric carbon dioxide sits near minus 8 per mille in the pre-industrial era. Plants using the common C3 photosynthetic pathway, which includes trees, wheat, rice and most temperate vegetation, discriminate strongly against the heavy isotope and land around minus 25 per mille. C4 plants such as maize, millet, sorghum and tropical grasses discriminate far less and cluster near minus 12. Marine carbonates such as shell sit close to zero. Bone collagen from a terrestrial herbivore falls near minus 21, reflecting a further enrichment of about five per mille at each trophic step.

The physics that saves the situation is that fractionation scales almost exactly with mass difference. The mass difference between carbon-14 and carbon-12 is twice that between carbon-13 and carbon-12, so whatever depletion a process produces in carbon-13 it produces very nearly twice as much in carbon-14. This means a single measurement of delta-13C, which is easy and can be made on the same AMS run, lets you correct the carbon-14 result exactly. By convention every reported age is normalised to a delta-13C of minus 25 per mille, the typical value for wood, so that all materials are placed on a common footing. The correction is not trivial in size: the difference between a marine shell at zero and the minus 25 reference corresponds to about 400 radiocarbon years.

There is a bonus. Because delta-13C is diagnostic of diet, the number measured for correction is also palaeodietary evidence in its own right. A human skeleton with collagen at minus 12 ate a great deal of maize or another C4 crop; one at minus 20 ate C3 plants and the animals that grazed them; values between minus 15 and minus 12 combined with elevated nitrogen-15 point to substantial marine protein. Some of the most important findings about the spread of maize agriculture through the Americas, and about the abrupt Neolithic shift away from seafood in coastal Britain, came from delta-13C values measured only because the radiocarbon laboratory needed them for a correction.

sections.heading: Radiocarbon Years Are Not Calendar Years
sections.body:
The single most misunderstood fact about the method is that the number a laboratory measures is not a calendar date. It is a conventional radiocarbon age, expressed in radiocarbon years before present, where present is fixed by international convention at 1950, the year before atmospheric bomb testing began to distort the atmosphere. A result reported as 3200 plus or minus 30 BP does not mean the object is from 1250 BC. It means the object contains as much carbon-14 as a sample would if the atmosphere had always held exactly the 1950 concentration and the Libby half-life were correct. Neither assumption is true, and converting from one to the other is called calibration.

The need for calibration became undeniable in the 1960s, when Hans Suess and others compared radiocarbon measurements on wood whose exact calendar age was known from tree-ring counting. The two scales did not match. They wandered apart by up to eight hundred years in the earlier Holocene, and the discrepancy did not vary smoothly; it wiggled, sometimes reversing direction over a few decades.
