These deviations, still called Suess wiggles, are the direct fingerprint of the varying production rate driven by solar activity and the geomagnetic field, superimposed on longer-term changes in ocean circulation that alter how quickly carbon-14 is diluted into the deep sea.

The consequence is that a raw radiocarbon age must be run backwards through a curve of measured radiocarbon age against true calendar age, and the shape of that curve determines how precise the answer can be. Where the curve is steep, a narrow band of radiocarbon ages maps onto a narrow band of calendar years and the date is sharp. Where the curve is flat, an entire span of calendar centuries produced almost identical radiocarbon ages, and any measurement falling on that plateau is hopelessly vague no matter how precisely it was measured. The most notorious example is the Hallstatt plateau between roughly 800 and 400 BC, where samples from four hundred years of European Iron Age all return about 2450 BP. There is a comparable flat stretch around 1450 to 1650 AD that frustrates historical archaeology, and another in the early Neolithic. Where the curve reverses, a single measurement can yield two or three separate possible calendar intervals with gaps between them, which is why calibrated results are often reported as multiple ranges.

Calibrated results are written with the qualifier cal, as in 1490 to 1310 cal BC, and always with a stated confidence, conventionally 68.3 percent for one sigma and 95.4 percent for two sigma. The probability distribution that comes out of calibration is usually lumpy and asymmetric rather than a neat bell curve, so quoting a single central date with a plus-or-minus is misleading and increasingly discouraged. A responsible publication gives the uncalibrated measurement with its laboratory code, the calibration curve used, the software, and the 95.4 percent ranges, so that a reader in twenty years can recalibrate the original number against an improved curve.

sections.heading: Building the Calibration Curve: Rings, Corals, Varves and Speleothems
sections.body:
A calibration curve is an empirical object. Someone had to find material whose calendar age is known independently and exactly, measure its radiocarbon content, and plot one against the other. The internationally agreed curves, published by the IntCal working group, are revised roughly every seven years as new data accumulate; the current generation comprises IntCal20 for the Northern Hemisphere terrestrial record, SHCal20 for the Southern Hemisphere, and Marine20 for oceanic samples.

The gold standard is dendrochronology. Trees in seasonal climates add one growth ring per year, and by matching the distinctive pattern of wide and narrow rings between overlapping timbers, from living trees back through historic buildings, archaeological posts and subfossil trunks buried in river gravels and bogs, dendrochronologists have assembled continuous ring-by-ring chronologies. The German oak and pine sequence and the Irish bog oak sequence together reach beyond 12,000 years without a gap. Each ring can be dissected out and dated individually, giving a calibration point of absolute calendar accuracy. Because the ring counting is independent of any physical model, this part of the curve is as close to ground truth as the field possesses, and it now anchors the record to roughly 14,000 years ago.

Beyond the tree rings, calibration relies on materials that can be dated by a second radiometric clock. Corals are ideal: they grow annual bands, live in the surface ocean, and incorporate uranium, which decays to thorium-230 on a completely independent schedule. Measuring both uranium-thorium and radiocarbon on the same coral band gives a paired point, and floating coral records now extend the curve to about 50,000 years. Speleothems, the layered calcite of stalagmites, work the same way and have contributed heavily to the oldest part of IntCal20, particularly the Hulu Cave record from China, whose annual layers and precise uranium-series dates cover the last 54,000 years. Annually laminated lake sediments, called varves, provide a further check; the sediment of Lake Suigetsu in Japan preserves a countable layer for every year across more than 50,000 years and contains terrestrial leaf fragments that can be radiocarbon dated directly, which makes it uniquely valuable because it avoids the marine reservoir problem entirely. Foraminifera in ocean cores tied to ice-core chronologies fill remaining gaps.

Two properties of the resulting curve deserve emphasis. First, it is hemispherically asymmetric. The Southern Hemisphere has proportionally more ocean surface, so its atmosphere is slightly diluted with old upwelled carbon, and southern samples appear about 30 to 80 radiocarbon years older than contemporaneous northern ones. Using the wrong hemispheric curve is a real and avoidable error. Second, the curve is not a line but a band with its own uncertainty, and modern calibration software propagates that uncertainty into the final answer rather than pretending the curve is exact.

sections.heading: Choosing and Collecting a Sample in the Field
sections.body:
Most bad radiocarbon dates are created in the field, not in the laboratory, and no amount of instrumental precision can rescue a sample that was the wrong thing, in the wrong place, handled badly. The two questions that must be answered before anything is bagged are what event the carbon actually records, and whether that event is genuinely the one you want to date.

The concept that governs the first question is the old-wood problem. Wood and charcoal date the year a tree ring formed, not the year the wood was used. A structural beam of oak may have been cut from a three-hundred-year-old trunk, seasoned for a decade, used for a generation, salvaged, and reused, so the innermost sampled ring may predate the archaeological event by four centuries. Driftwood, common on Arctic sites, may have floated for decades before anyone burned it. Peat and dung fuel carry their own inbuilt age. The remedy is to prefer short-lived material whose life span is close to the event: a cereal grain, a nutshell, a twig, a leaf, a fruit stone, a single-year plant stem, an insect remain, or, if wood must be used, the outermost rings including bark. A single carbonised barley grain from a storage pit is worth more than a kilogram of ambiguous charcoal.

The second question is one of association, and it is archaeological rather than chemical. A datable object in a pit dates the pit only if it entered the pit while the pit was in use. Burrowing, tree throw, ploughing and worm action move small objects vertically through a deposit, and a modern weed seed can travel down a root channel into a Neolithic layer. Where a date must carry weight, take several samples from one context and expect agreement; irreconcilable scatter is itself the finding.
steps: Decide the target event first, then work backwards to the material that dates it. Write down explicitly what a date on this sample will and will not prove.

Prefer short-lived, single-entity samples: one seed, one nutshell, one twig, one bone, one thread. Avoid bulking many fragments together, which averages several unrelated deaths into a meaningless composite date.
Record the exact three-dimensional position, context number, and stratigraphic relationships before lifting anything. A date without secure provenance is uninterpretable.
Handle with clean tools. Use a trowel or tweezers cleaned between samples, and avoid touching the sample with bare skin, which transfers modern carbon in the form of oils and amino acids.
Never use consolidants, glues, varnishes or paraffin wax near the sample. Conservation resins are petroleum-derived and radiocarbon-dead; they make a sample look older and resist removal.
Package in inert material: aluminium foil, or a clean glass vial, or a new polythene bag if the sample is dry. Do not use paper, cotton wool, or labelled bags where the ink can transfer.
If the sample is wet, keep it cool and get it to the laboratory quickly, or air-dry it below about 40 degrees Celsius. Mould growth introduces new carbon; heating above that risks altering collagen.
Collect a background sample of the surrounding sediment where contamination is plausible, and submit replicates from the same context so that internal consistency can be checked.

sections.heading: Laboratory Pretreatment: Getting Rid of the Wrong Carbon
sections.body:
Everything that reaches a radiocarbon laboratory is contaminated. Groundwater deposits carbonate; plant roots grow through and leave rootlets; humic and fulvic acids from decaying vegetation percolate through soil and adsorb onto porous material; conservation resins, fingerprints and packaging leave organic residues. Pretreatment is the chemistry that strips all of this away and leaves only carbon that was part of the original organism, and it is where most of a laboratory's skill lives.

The workhorse for plant material is the acid-base-acid sequence, universally abbreviated ABA. The sample is first examined under a microscope and any visible rootlets and soil are picked out with tweezers. It is then treated with hot dilute hydrochloric acid, typically one molar at around 80 degrees Celsius, which dissolves carbonates from groundwater and shell fragments. Next comes dilute sodium hydroxide, again around one molar, which dissolves humic acids; the solution turns brown, and the wash is repeated until it runs clear. Because the alkali step leaves the sample able to absorb carbon dioxide from the air, a second acid wash follows to reprotonate it and drive off any absorbed modern carbon dioxide. The sample is then rinsed to neutrality and dried. Each step costs material, and a fragile sample can be entirely consumed, so laboratories weigh the aggressiveness of the treatment against how much carbon they must have left at the end.

Bone requires a different approach because the mineral fraction, hydroxyapatite, readily exchanges carbonate with groundwater and is generally untrustworthy. What is dated is the protein, collagen. The bone is demineralised in cold dilute acid, the residue is gelatinised in slightly acidic water at around 58 degrees Celsius, filtered to remove particulates, and then ultrafiltered through a membrane that retains molecules above about 30 kilodaltons. That last step, introduced widely in the 2000s, discards short degraded peptides and small contaminant molecules and retains only large intact collagen chains. It transformed Palaeolithic archaeology: many early modern human and Neanderthal dates obtained before ultrafiltration proved to be thousands of years too young, and the redating of key European sites substantially compressed the apparent period of Neanderthal and modern human overlap. Quality is judged by collagen yield, ideally above one percent of bone weight, by carbon-to-nitrogen atomic ratio, which should sit between 2.9 and 3.6, and by amino acid composition.

Specialised protocols exist for other materials. Textiles and paper get solvent extraction to remove waxes and sizing. Iron artefacts can be dated through the charcoal carbon absorbed during smelting. Lime mortar can be dated through the carbon dioxide it absorbed from air while setting, though incompletely burned limestone aggregate makes this notoriously difficult. Whatever the material, the purified carbon is finally combusted to carbon dioxide with copper oxide in a sealed quartz tube, and for AMS that gas is reduced to graphite over an iron or cobalt catalyst with hydrogen at about 550 degrees Celsius.

sections.heading: Reservoir Effects: Marine, Freshwater and Volcanic Carbon
sections.body:
A reservoir effect occurs when an organism's carbon did not come from the open atmosphere, so it was already deficient in carbon-14 at the moment of death and appears older than it is. These offsets are large, systematic, and responsible for a great many published errors, some of which took decades to unpick.

The marine reservoir effect is the best characterised. The surface ocean mixes with deep water that has been isolated from the atmosphere for centuries, so surface seawater carries a carbon-14 deficit corresponding globally to about 400 radiocarbon years. Marine samples are therefore calibrated against a dedicated curve, Marine20, which already builds in that global average. On top of it sits a local correction called delta-R, which accounts for regional departures from the global mean. Where cold, old, deep water upwells, delta-R is strongly positive: several hundred years off Peru, off Namibia, in parts of the Southern Ocean, and in Arctic waters. In enclosed warm seas it may be near zero or slightly negative. Values of delta-R are determined empirically from shells collected live before 1950 whose collection year is documented, or from paired marine and terrestrial samples from the same archaeological context, and are compiled in an online database. Choosing an appropriate delta-R, with its own uncertainty, is a required step and not an optional refinement.

Human remains complicate this further, because a person eating both land and sea food carries a mixture of both carbon sources. The correction depends on the proportion of marine protein in the diet, which is estimated from stable isotopes, principally delta-13C and delta-15N. This is not a minor adjustment: a coastal individual with a heavily marine diet can appear four centuries too old. The Mesolithic and Neolithic burials of Scandinavia and Scotland required systematic redating once this was properly handled.

Freshwater systems produce an analogous but far less predictable hardwater effect. Rivers and lakes draining limestone or chalk carry dissolved bicarbonate derived from rock that is geologically ancient and contains no carbon-14 at all. Aquatic plants using that bicarbonate, and the fish and molluscs that eat them, can be apparently thousands of years old while still alive, and offsets vary from negligible to more than two thousand years within a single catchment and even between seasons. There is no global correction curve; each water body must be characterised on its own, ideally by dating modern specimens. Volcanic regions produce a similar effect where magmatic carbon dioxide, radiocarbon-dead, vents into the air and is taken up by plants growing nearby, an effect measurable around fumaroles in Italy, Iceland and Yellowstone. The general rule is simple: if the carbon might not have come from open air, assume there is an offset and prove otherwise.

sections.heading: The Bomb Spike and the Dating of the Very Recent Past
sections.body:
Between 1955 and 1963 the atmospheric testing of thermonuclear weapons released an enormous pulse of neutrons into the atmosphere, and those neutrons did to atmospheric nitrogen exactly what cosmic-ray neutrons do: they made carbon-14. Atmospheric levels nearly doubled, peaking in 1963 at about 100 percent above the pre-war baseline in the Northern Hemisphere and somewhat later and lower in the Southern. The Partial Test Ban Treaty of 1963 ended atmospheric testing, and since then the excess has been drawn down as the pulse mixes into the ocean and the biosphere, falling with an effective half-life of about eleven years, quite unrelated to the radioactive half-life. By the early 2020s atmospheric levels had fallen back through the pre-bomb value and, because fossil fuel burning adds radiocarbon-dead carbon dioxide, are now dropping below it.

For archaeology this was an irritation, which is why the convention fixes present at 1950 and why laboratories jealously guard pre-bomb standards. For everything else it is a gift. The rise and fall traces a steep, well-mapped, almost monotonic curve over the last seventy years, so measuring the carbon-14 content of any material formed in that window pins its year of formation to within one to three years. This is a precision that no other dating method approaches for the recent past.

The forensic applications are the best known. Because tooth enamel is laid down in childhood at known ages and never remodelled afterwards, the bomb-curve value in a molar gives an unidentified person's year of birth to within about one and a half years. Tissues with faster turnover, such as hair, nails, blood lipids and soft tissue, record the last months or years of life and can indicate year of death. Combining the two brackets a life. The same logic dates ivory: enforcement of the ban on elephant ivory depends on distinguishing pre-ban from post-ban material, and bomb-curve dating shows whether a tusk came from an animal that died before or after the CITES cutoff, evidence that has been used in prosecutions. It has been applied to fake wine, where the vintage claimed on a bottle can be tested against the carbon-14 in the alcohol, and to art forgery, where a canvas or a pigment binder made after 1955 exposes a supposed old master instantly.

Biomedical research exploited the same signal to settle a question that had resisted every other approach. By measuring the bomb-derived carbon-14 in the DNA of cells sorted from human tissue, researchers dated when those cells were born. The results showed that heart muscle cells do renew, though slowly, at under one percent per year in adulthood, and that some neurons in the hippocampus are generated throughout life while cortical neurons are essentially as old as the person.

sections.heading: Bayesian Chronological Modelling and Wiggle-Matching
sections.body:
A single calibrated date is often disappointingly vague, especially where the calibration curve is flat. The most important methodological advance of the last thirty years has been the realisation that dates should not be interpreted one at a time. Archaeologists usually know things about a site independently of the radiocarbon measurements, and that prior knowledge can be combined with the measurements formally, using Bayes's theorem, to produce far sharper results than any date could give alone.

The prior information is usually stratigraphic. If layer three sits beneath layer two, which sits beneath layer one, then whatever their individual dates suggest, the true sequence must run oldest at the bottom. A Bayesian model takes the probability distribution from each calibrated date, imposes the ordering constraint, and computes a revised posterior distribution for every date simultaneously. Any part of a date's probability that would violate the known order is suppressed, and uncertainty collapses dramatically. Ranges that were two centuries wide routinely tighten to two or three decades. The technique also estimates quantities that were never measured at all, such as the probable start date, end date, and total duration of a phase, complete with credible intervals, from a set of dates that individually fall within it.

The standard software is OxCal, written by Christopher Bronk Ramsey at Oxford, with BCal and Chronomodel as alternatives. Models are specified in a small language of nested phases, sequences, boundaries and gaps. Crucially, the software reports an agreement index for each date and for the model as a whole; a date whose individual index falls below about 60 percent is fighting the constraints, which usually means it is an outlier or that the assumed stratigraphy is wrong. The model is thus falsifiable rather than merely persuasive, and outlier models exist that downweight suspect measurements automatically instead of the analyst deleting them by hand.

The results have been transformative. Alasdair Whittle and colleagues applied this approach to early Neolithic enclosures in southern Britain and produced a chronology at generational resolution, showing that causewayed enclosures appeared over roughly a century rather than the vague half-millennium previously assumed, and that individual monuments were used for a few decades, within a single human lifetime. That is a qualitatively different kind of history.

A related technique, wiggle-matching, applies where a sample carries its own internal ordering. Take a timber with fifty preserved rings but no matching dendrochronological master curve. Date rings 1, 11, 21, 31 and 41 separately. The five results must lie exactly ten radiocarbon-relevant years apart in true calendar time, so the whole block can be slid along the calibration curve until the pattern of wiggles matches. Because the curve's fine structure is distinctive, the fit is usually unique, and the final precision can reach plus or minus ten years or better, even in a period where a single date would be useless. Wiggle-matching has resolved bitter disputes, most famously over the date of the Minoan eruption of Thera. It should be said that a Bayesian model is only as good as its priors: a wrong stratigraphic assumption produces a confident and precisely wrong answer.

sections.heading: Limits, Failure Modes, and How to Read a Date Critically
sections.body:
Every method has an envelope outside which it fails, and the honest use of radiocarbon depends on knowing where the edges are. Several distinct failure modes account for nearly all bad dates in the published literature.

The first is the hard age limit. Beyond about 50,000 years, less than 0.2 percent of the original carbon-14 remains, and the measurement becomes a contest between a vanishing signal and laboratory background. Results in that range should be treated as minimum ages unless the laboratory has demonstrated its blanks are exceptional. The asymmetry of contamination is brutal here: adding one percent of modern carbon to a truly infinite-age sample yields an apparent age of about 37,000 years, which is why a great many purportedly Palaeolithic dates from older literature are simply the contamination background of the equipment that produced them. Conversely, adding one percent of dead carbon to a 5,000-year-old sample shifts it by only about eighty years. Old samples are ruined by young contamination; young samples are barely affected by old.

The second is dating the wrong event. Inbuilt age in long-lived wood, redeposited charcoal, reused timber and residual material in a later deposit all date something real but not what the excavator wanted. There is no chemical test for this; it is defeated only by choosing short-lived samples and thinking hard about association.

The third is an uncorrected reservoir offset, which silently adds centuries to anything that ate fish, drank hardwater, grew beside a volcanic vent, or lived in the sea. The fourth is calibration-curve structure, where a plateau produces an irreducibly wide answer no matter how good the measurement, and an inversion produces multiple disjoint intervals that must both be reported. The fifth is misinterpreting the statistics: a two-sigma range excludes the truth one time in twenty, so with twenty dates in a study, one being wrong is the expectation and not a scandal.

When a date looks wrong, work through the possibilities in order rather than dismissing it. Check the material and what it dates. Check whether the context could contain intrusive or residual material. Check whether the carbon source was atmospheric. Check that the correct hemispheric or marine curve and an appropriate delta-R were used. Check the collagen quality indicators if it is a bone. Then, if the date still resists, submit replicates, ideally to a second laboratory, since inter-laboratory comparison exercises consistently find small systematic offsets between facilities. Radiocarbon dating is not fallible in mysterious ways; it fails for a short and well-understood list of reasons, nearly all of them decided before the sample ever reached an instrument, and a reader who knows that list can assess a published date almost as well as the person who commissioned it.

guides.title: Dendrochronology (Tree-Ring Dating)
guides.summary: How annual tree rings are formed, crossdated and assembled into chronologies that date timber to an exact calendar year, and how the method is used in archaeology, climate reconstruction and radiocarbon calibration.

sections.heading: What Dendrochronology Is and Why It Matters
sections.body:
Dendrochronology is the science of dating events by the annual growth rings of trees, and it occupies a peculiar and privileged position among all methods of reconstructing the past: alone among the major dating techniques, it can assign a piece of wood to a single named calendar year, and in favourable cases to a season within that year. Radiocarbon dating returns a probability distribution spanning decades or centuries. Thermoluminescence, potassium-argon and uranium series methods carry errors measured in percentages. A well-crossdated tree ring carries no statistical error at all in the ordinary sense: the ring either matches the reference chronology at a unique position or it does not, and when it does, the date is exact. This is why dendrochronology is described as an absolute rather than a relative or an estimated method, and why archaeologists prize it so highly where wood survives.

The reach of the technique is broad. Its core archaeological application is dating structures: the roof timbers of a cathedral, the piles of a lake village, the planking of a shipwreck, the panel on which a Renaissance painting was made, the belly of a violin. Beyond archaeology, tree rings furnish annually resolved records of temperature, rainfall, river flow, volcanic eruptions, forest fires, insect outbreaks, landslides, glacier advances and solar activity, extending in the best cases back more than twelve thousand years. And the technique underpins the accuracy of radiocarbon dating itself, because the calibration curves that convert a radiocarbon measurement into a calendar date are built from radiocarbon measurements on tree rings of known year.

The whole edifice rests on a simple biological fact and a simple statistical one. The biological fact is that trees growing in temperate and other seasonal climates lay down one distinguishable layer of wood per year, so that counting layers counts years. The statistical fact is that in a climate-limited stand, the year-to-year variation in ring width is driven largely by weather common to the whole region, so that trees kilometres or even hundreds of kilometres apart record recognisably the same sequence of wide and narrow years. That shared pattern acts as a barcode. Match the barcode from an undated timber against a dated reference sequence and the timber acquires the reference's calendar years.

The limits are equally simple to state. The method works only where trees produce clear annual rings, which excludes most of the wet tropics; only where the wood survives, which is a matter of waterlogging, aridity, charring or continuous shelter; only where enough rings are present to give a statistically unique pattern, conventionally at least fifty and preferably a hundred; and only where a reference chronology already exists for that species and region. Where those conditions hold, however, the results are of a precision no other archaeological method approaches.

sections.heading: How a Tree Ring Forms
sections.body:
The ring is a product of a thin sleeve of dividing cells called the vascular cambium, which lies just beneath the bark and wraps the entire living trunk, branches and roots. The cambium divides outward to produce phloem, the tissue that carries sugars down from the leaves, and inward to produce xylem, the water-conducting tissue that becomes wood. Only the inward production accumulates, which is why a trunk thickens and why the record is read from the inside out: the innermost ring at the pith is the oldest, the outermost beneath the bark the youngest.

Seasonality creates the visible boundary. In spring, when water is abundant and the tree is flushing new leaves, the cambium produces cells that are large in diameter with thin walls, optimised for conducting water. This tissue is called earlywood or springwood and appears pale. As the season advances and water becomes limiting, the cells produced become progressively smaller and thicker-walled, prioritising mechanical strength over conduction, forming latewood or summerwood, which appears dark and dense. Growth then ceases entirely for the dormant season. When growth resumes the following spring, large thin-walled cells abut the previous year's dense latewood, producing the sharp boundary the eye reads as a ring line. The ring is therefore not a line but a whole year's block of wood bounded by that abrupt transition.

Species differ in how they organise this. Conifers such as pine, spruce, larch and fir have a simple xylem of tracheids and show the earlywood to latewood gradient very clearly, which is why they are the classic dendrochronological material. Among broadleaves, the ring-porous species, notably oak, ash, elm and chestnut, produce a distinct band of very large vessels at the start of each season, giving an unmistakable ring boundary and making oak the backbone of European archaeological dating. Diffuse-porous species such as beech, birch, maple and lime scatter their vessels evenly through the ring and are much harder, sometimes impossible, to read.

Two further structures matter for archaeology. Heartwood is the older, inner wood in which the conducting cells have died and become blocked with resins, tannins and other extractives, often darkening in colour; sapwood is the outer living zone still conducting water. The sapwood band is what makes precise felling dates possible, because its outermost ring is the last one the tree grew. Finally, the bark itself: if a fragment of bark or the boundary immediately beneath it, called the waney edge, survives on an archaeological timber, the felling year can be fixed exactly, and often the felling season too, since a complete latewood band means winter felling while a partial earlywood band means the tree came down in spring or early summer.

sections.heading: The Governing Principles of the Discipline
sections.body:
Dendrochronology is unusual among archaeological sciences in having an explicit, teachable set of principles, formalised largely by Harold Fritts in the 1970s and still taught in the same form. The first is uniformitarianism, borrowed from geology: the physical and biological processes that link climate to tree growth today operated in the same way in the past, so a modern calibration of growth against weather can be projected backwards. This is an assumption, and a defensible one, but it is not a certainty, and the possibility that the relationship has changed over time is a live research question rather than a settled matter.

The second is the principle of limiting factors, drawn from Liebig's law of the minimum: the rate of a biological process is constrained by whichever necessary resource is scarcest. A tree growing at the arid lower treeline is limited by moisture, so its rings record rainfall. A tree at the cold upper or northern treeline is limited by summer warmth, so its rings record temperature. A tree growing in the middle of its comfortable range is limited by nothing in particular, grows steadily, and produces what dendrochronologists call a complacent series, uniform rings that carry almost no dateable signal. Site selection is therefore not an incidental practicality but a principle in its own right: samples are deliberately sought from stressed, marginal sites where the climate signal is strong.

The third and most important is crossdating, the recognition that trees in a region share a common growth pattern and that this pattern can be used to assign exact years. Simple ring counting is not dendrochronology and is not reliable, because it is defeated by missing rings, in which a severely stressed tree fails to produce a ring at all around part or all of its circumference, and by false or double rings, in which a mid-season drought produces a latewood-like band that mimics a boundary. Crossdating catches both, since a missing or spurious ring throws the pattern out of alignment against the reference and the error announces itself.

The fourth is replication: no date rests on one sample. The convention is to take at least two cores from each tree and to sample many trees, so that individual quirks average out and the shared signal emerges. The fifth is aggregate tree growth, the recognition that a measured ring width is the sum of several superimposed influences, an age-related growth trend, the climate signal, disturbance events, endogenous factors and unexplained noise, and that extracting any one of them means removing the others. The sixth is ecological amplitude, the recognition that each species has a limited range within which it is useful, so material must be matched to a reference of the same or a closely comparable species.

sections.heading: A. E. Douglass and the Origins of the Method
sections.body:
The idea that tree rings record years is very old. Leonardo da Vinci noted around 1500 that rings reveal a tree's age and that their thickness reflects wet and dry years. Carl Linnaeus, Alexander von Humboldt, Charles Babbage and the Swedish naturalist Bartholin all made similar observations. What none of them did was work out how to use the pattern rather than the count, and it was an astronomer, not a botanist, who took that step.

Andrew Ellicott Douglass arrived in Arizona in 1894 to help site the Lowell Observatory and became interested in whether the roughly eleven-year sunspot cycle left a trace in terrestrial climate. Lacking long weather records, he turned to ponderosa pines around Flagstaff as a proxy, and by 1904 he had grasped that the sequence of wide and narrow rings was consistent from tree to tree across the region. That insight, crossdating, is the foundation of the whole discipline, and Douglass spent the following decades extending it. He founded the Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research at the University of Arizona in 1937, an institution that remains the field's centre of gravity, and he coined the term dendrochronology from the Greek for tree, time and study.

The archaeological breakthrough came from a practical problem. Douglass could build a long chronology backwards from living trees, and a separate floating chronology from beams in Ancestral Puebloan ruins, but the two would not join; a gap of unknown length lay between them. Working with archaeologists on a National Geographic Society project, he searched for a timber old enough to bridge it. On 22 June 1929, at the Whipple Ruin at Show Low, Arizona, a charred beam catalogued as HH-39 was recovered whose rings overlapped both sequences. The bridge closed, and in a single stroke hundreds of southwestern ruins that had been placed only in a relative sequence acquired exact calendar dates. Sites such as Mesa Verde, Chaco Canyon and Betatakin could now be discussed in terms of specific construction years, and the great thirteenth-century Puebloan depopulation could be set against a reconstructed drought running from 1276 to 1299.

The method spread outward from there. Bruno Huber built the first German oak work from the 1940s; Ernst Hollstein and Bernd Becker extended the central European oak chronologies through the second half of the twentieth century; Michael Baillie and Jon Pilcher constructed the Irish oak sequence at Queen's University Belfast, publishing a chronology reaching back to 5289 BC by 1984. Edmund Schulman's work on bristlecone pines in the 1950s established that the oldest trees grow in the harshest places, a finding that made the very long American chronologies possible. Douglass's original motive, incidentally, was never fulfilled: the sunspot signal he set out to find in tree rings proved far weaker and less consistent than he hoped, and the search for it is a minor footnote beside the dating method that emerged as a by-product.

sections.heading: Building a Chronology from Living Trees Backwards
sections.body:
A chronology is a dated reference sequence of ring widths for a species and region, and it is built by a process of successive overlap called bridging. The starting point must be a sample of known date, which in practice means living trees: a core taken from a living tree in, say, 2020 has its outermost complete ring in 2019, and every ring inward can be counted and confirmed against its neighbours. Cores from many living trees of the same species and area are crossdated against one another and averaged to produce a master chronology covering the lifespan of the oldest, perhaps two to four hundred years for most temperate species.

The chronology is then pushed backwards using dead wood. Standing dead trees, fallen logs, driftwood, timbers from old houses, barns, bridges and churches, mine props, ship planks and archaeological finds all provide sequences that end before the present. Each such sequence, undated in isolation, is compared against the master. If its later portion matches the master's earlier portion at a statistically convincing position, the sequence is dated and its earlier portion extends the master further back. Repeat this hundreds of times with progressively older material and the chronology grows. In the German oak sequence the process ran through medieval buildings, then Roman waterlogged timbers, then Neolithic lake-village piles, then subfossil oaks recovered from river gravels in the Main, Danube and Rhine valleys, ultimately reaching beyond 10,000 years before the present.

Sequences that cannot yet be tied to the master are called floating chronologies. A floating chronology is internally consistent, so it gives exact relative years within itself, but its absolute position is unknown. Many important archaeological sequences existed for years in this state, and they are anchored either when a bridging sample is found or, increasingly, by radiocarbon wiggle-matching, which fixes the float against the calibration curve with an uncertainty of a decade or two rather than the centuries an isolated radiocarbon date would give.

Two quality measures govern how far a chronology can be trusted at its extremes. Sample depth is simply the number of individual series contributing to each year; a chronology's oldest decades may rest on two or three samples and are correspondingly fragile. The expressed population signal, EPS, developed by Wigley, Briffa and Jones in 1984, estimates how well the available sample represents the theoretical infinite population, and a value of 0.85 is the conventional threshold for a reliable chronology. Published chronologies plot both against year, and a careful user checks them before relying on a date near the ends.

Chronologies are also regional rather than universal, and this is not a defect but a consequence of the climate signal being regional. A southern German oak chronology will date a Bavarian roof beam confidently and an Irish one poorly, so national and regional networks are maintained separately and an unknown sample is routinely tested against dozens of them. The pattern of which chronologies it matches, and how strongly, is itself informative, and it is the raw material of provenance work as well as of dating.

sections.heading: Crossdating and the Statistics of a Match
sections.body:
Crossdating begins as a visual craft and ends as a statistical test, and competent practitioners insist on both. The classic visual technique is the skeleton plot, taught by Douglass and still used. The analyst works along the sample under a microscope and, on a strip of graph paper with one column per ring, draws a vertical line whose length represents how narrow a ring is relative to its immediate neighbours; wide rings are left blank and exceptionally wide ones marked with a B. Absolute width is deliberately discarded, since it varies with tree age and site, and only the relative pattern of pointer years, the conspicuously narrow or wide years that most trees in a region share, is retained. Two skeleton plots slid along one another until the marks align give the offset, and hence the date.

The quantitative approach measures each ring to 0.01 or 0.001 millimetres and compares series numerically at every possible offset. Three statistics dominate the literature. The Student's t-value derived from the correlation between the two series, usually after the Baillie-Pilcher transformation which high-pass filters the data against a five-year running mean, is the most commonly quoted; values above 3.5 are considered a possible match, above 4.0 to 5.0 a good one, and above 6.0 to 8.0 essentially decisive when supported by other evidence. Gleichläufigkeit, sometimes anglicised as percentage of parallel variation or the coefficient of agreement, counts the proportion of year-to-year intervals in which the two series move in the same direction; values above about 65 percent are meaningful, above 70 percent good. The COFECHA program, written by Richard Holmes in 1983 and still the standard quality-control tool, segments each series into overlapping fifty-year windows and flags any segment whose correlation with the master falls below a threshold, which is how dating errors are hunted down.

A responsible date requires convergence. A single high t-value at one position, with nothing else supporting it, is not sufficient, because with a short series and many possible offsets a spurious high value will occur by chance. What is wanted is a high statistic at one position and nothing comparable elsewhere, agreement between the visual pattern and the numbers, agreement across several independent samples from the same structure, agreement against more than one reference chronology, and a date that is not absurd in its archaeological context. Where those conditions are met the result is genuinely secure; where a report offers one t-value of 3.6 and no replication, it should be read as a suggestion rather than a date.

It is worth being explicit about what the statistics do and do not prove. A t-value is not a probability that the date is correct; it summarises how unusual the correlation is under an assumption of independence that ring series notoriously violate, because consecutive ring widths are autocorrelated. This is precisely why the Baillie-Pilcher filtering step exists and why practitioners quote thresholds derived from experience with real material rather than from theory. Judgement, not a number, closes the case.

sections.heading: Sampling Wood in the Field
sections.body:
Getting the sample is where most avoidable errors are introduced, and the fundamental tension is between obtaining the fullest ring sequence and doing the least damage to a living tree or a historic structure. The instrument that resolves it for living trees is the increment borer, a hollow tempered-steel auger invented in Sweden in the late nineteenth century, threaded at the tip so that it screws into the wood and extracts a pencil-thin core, typically 4.3 or 5.15 millimetres in diameter, without felling anything. The wound it leaves is small and normally compartmentalised by the tree within a season.

For archaeological and historic timbers, coring is often preferred because it is minimally destructive, but the ring-porous structure of oak and the frequent presence of nails, rot or dense heartwood make a thin transverse slice cut with a fine saw the better option where the timber is already broken or an offcut is available. Charcoal cannot be cored at all: it is handled as fragments, consolidated if necessary, and given a polished transverse face. Waterlogged wood must never be allowed to dry unsupported, since it will shrink and collapse catastrophically; it is kept wet and either measured wet or conserved with polyethylene glycol before analysis.

The single most valuable feature to preserve is the outermost surface. A timber retaining bark or the waney edge gives a felling year to the season; a timber whose sapwood has been trimmed away in shaping gives only a terminus post quem, an earliest possible date, with an estimated allowance for the missing rings. When sampling a building, prefer timbers where bark or the rounded outer surface survives.
steps: Record the context first: sketch or photograph the timber in place, number it, note its structural role, orientation and any evidence of reuse such as redundant joints or nail holes.
Choose a sampling point at or just above the widest part of the trunk cross-section, avoiding knots, reaction wood, wounds and any point where the ring sequence is visibly disturbed.
For a living tree, assemble the borer, brace it against the trunk at chest height, aim precisely at the pith, and start it with firm pressure until the threads bite.
Turn the borer steadily clockwise with both hands, keeping the axis perpendicular to the trunk, until the depth marks show you have passed the centre.
Insert the extractor spoon fully, reverse the borer half a turn to break the core free, and withdraw the spoon slowly so the core does not snap.
Transfer the core immediately into a labelled paper straw or slotted wooden mount, marking which end was the bark end, since a reversed core is worse than no core.
Withdraw the borer, clean and oil it, and leave the wound open, since sealants impede natural compartmentalisation.
For a dead timber, cut a full transverse slice with a fine-toothed saw where the section is already broken, taking at least 50 millimetres of thickness and keeping bark and outer surface intact.
Bag waterlogged samples wet and cool; never allow archaeological wood to air-dry before it is measured or conserved.

sections.heading: Preparation, Measurement and Standardisation
sections.body:
A core straight from the borer shows almost nothing. It must be dried slowly, glued into a grooved wooden mount with the tracheids or vessels oriented vertically so the transverse face is presented to the microscope, and then surfaced. Surfacing is done with progressively finer abrasives, typically from 120 grit through 400 and often to 600 or beyond, or with a razor blade or sledge microtome for very fine work, until individual cells are resolved. Chalk rubbed into the pores of oak or a smear of white powder can make ring boundaries leap out. Skipping or rushing this stage is the commonest cause of misidentified rings, because a false ring that is invisible on a rough surface is usually obvious on a polished one.

Measurement is then performed on a sliding stage, historically a Velmex or Henson micrometre bench reading to 0.01 or 0.001 millimetres, or increasingly from high-resolution scanned images processed in software such as CDendro, CooRecorder or WinDENDRO. Each ring's total width is recorded, and for climate work earlywood and latewood widths may be recorded separately, or the sample scanned by X-ray densitometry to obtain maximum latewood density, which correlates far more strongly with summer temperature than width does.

The raw widths cannot be used directly for comparison because of the age trend. A young tree adds each year's wood to a small circumference, so a constant volume of new wood produces a wide ring; as the trunk thickens, the same volume spreads over a larger circumference and the ring narrows. Plotted against age, ring width therefore falls in a characteristic negative exponential curve regardless of climate. Standardisation, or detrending, removes this by fitting a curve to each series and dividing each measured width by the value the curve predicts for that year, producing a dimensionless index that averages one and can be compared between trees of different ages. Fitted curves range from a simple negative exponential or straight line, which is conservative and preserves long timescales, to cubic smoothing splines, which remove more but also strip out genuine low-frequency climate variation.

That trade-off has a name: the segment length curse, articulated by Ed Cook and colleagues in 1995. A detrending method cannot reliably recover climate variations longer than roughly the length of the individual samples used, so a chronology built from two-hundred-year segments cannot resolve a millennial trend, however many segments it contains. Techniques such as regional curve standardisation, which fits one average age-trend curve to all samples rather than one curve per sample, were devised to escape this, at the cost of requiring a large and evenly age-distributed sample. Awareness of this limitation is essential to reading any long temperature reconstruction critically.

sections.heading: Which Trees Work, and What Goes Wrong Inside the Wood
sections.body:
Not every tree can be dated, and knowing which cannot is as important as knowing which can. The requirement is a clear annual boundary, and that in turn requires a strongly seasonal climate. In the humid tropics, where growth is continuous or governed by irregular dry spells, many species produce no distinguishable annual rings at all, and tropical dendrochronology is a specialist and comparatively young field relying on the minority of species, such as teak and certain Cedrela, that do respond to a marked dry season. Conversely the technique is at its most powerful in semi-arid and cold-marginal environments where a single limiting factor dominates.

Among usable species, the reliable workhorses are the conifers, especially Pinus, Picea, Larix, Abies, Pseudotsuga and Juniperus, and among broadleaves the ring-porous genera Quercus, Fraxinus, Ulmus and Castanea. Oak is the single most important archaeological species in Europe because it was the preferred structural timber for a millennium and because its rings are unambiguous. Diffuse-porous woods such as beech, birch, poplar, willow, lime and most fruit woods are difficult and frequently undateable, which is why a report may state that a timber could not be dated for reasons of species rather than preservation.

Within a usable sample, four anomalies cause most trouble. A missing or absent ring occurs when growth in a catastrophic year is so slight that no cells are produced at the sampled height, or the ring wedges out and is present on one side of the trunk and not the other; the sequence then appears one year too short and every ring inward is misdated by one year unless crossdating catches it. A false or double ring, sometimes called an intra-annual density fluctuation, forms when a mid-season drought causes a band of thick-walled cells followed by a resumption of growth, mimicking a boundary; the sequence then appears one year too long. Frost rings, bands of collapsed and distorted cells, mark a hard freeze during the growing season and are useful markers in their own right, notably in bristlecone pines. Reaction wood, called compression wood in conifers and tension wood in broadleaves, forms where a tree leans or bears asymmetric load and produces grossly distorted, eccentric rings that must be avoided.

Two further hazards are ecological rather than anatomical. Complacent series from unstressed sites carry too little signal to date. And disturbance events, the death of a neighbouring tree releasing a suppressed sapling into decades of rapid growth, or a defoliating insect outbreak suppressing it, can overwhelm the climate signal for long stretches, which is why several trees from several parts of a stand are always sampled. Wood that has been worked also loses information: a squared beam has had its outer rings cut away, and a radially split board may carry only a narrow wedge of the original sequence, so the archaeologically most informative timbers are often the roughest and least finished ones.

sections.heading: The Long Chronologies
sections.body:
A handful of extraordinary chronologies anchor the discipline, and their construction represents decades of accumulated fieldwork. The Great Basin bristlecone pine, Pinus longaeva, growing on dolomite ridges between about 2,800 and 3,500 metres in eastern California, Nevada and Utah, is the foundation of the American record. Edmund Schulman established in the 1950s that these trees, gnarled and largely dead on the outside, routinely exceed four thousand years of age, and the individual named Methuselah in the White Mountains was dated to a germination around 2833 BC. Prometheus, a bristlecone felled in 1964 in Nevada in circumstances still debated, had at least 4,862 rings. Because dead bristlecone wood erodes rather than rots in that cold arid air, remnant wood lying on the surface extends the chronology to roughly 9,000 years, and in combination with other material the White Mountain sequence exceeds ten millennia.

In Europe the equivalent achievement rests on oak. The German sequence, assembled principally by Bernd Becker at Hohenheim from subfossil oaks buried in the gravels of the Main, Rhine, Danube and their tributaries, together with archaeological and building timbers, now extends past 12,000 years before the present when joined to a preceding pine chronology, and it forms the backbone of the radiocarbon calibration curve for the Holocene. The Irish oak chronology built at Belfast from bog oaks and archaeological material reaches back beyond 5200 BC and, being geographically independent, provides a crucial cross-check.

Other regions contribute distinctive material. New Zealand kauri, Agathis australis, preserved in swamps for tens of thousands of years, provides floating chronologies deep into the last glacial period and has been decisive in measuring radiocarbon behaviour beyond the range of continuous records. Siberian larch chronologies from the Yamal Peninsula and the Taimyr provide millennium-scale Arctic temperature records. Fitzroya cupressoides in Chile and Patagonia yields trees over 3,600 years old. The Aegean Dendrochronology Project at Cornell, begun by Peter Kuniholm in 1973, has assembled long sequences from Anatolian and Aegean timbers that date Bronze and Iron Age monuments, including the tumulus at Gordion associated with the Phrygian king Midas.

These chronologies are not merely records of length. Because they are continuous and exactly dated, they constitute a calendar against which any other annually resolved archive, ice cores, varved lake sediments, corals, historical documents, can be tested and aligned, and disagreements between them become scientific findings rather than nuisances. The realignment of Greenland ice-core layer counts against tree-ring-dated volcanic markers, which shifted parts of the ice chronology by several years and reconciled the dating of the great sixth-century and thirteenth-century eruptions, is a good example of the tree-ring record acting as the arbiter.

Building any of these sequences is generational work. Bernd Becker's Hohenheim laboratory processed tens of thousands of subfossil oak trunks recovered by gravel extraction over some thirty years, and the Belfast chronology represents comparable labour on Irish bog oaks. This is why chronology coverage is so uneven across the world: it reflects where sustained institutional effort has been applied at least as much as where suitable trees grow.

sections.heading: Dendroarchaeology: Dating Buildings, Ships and Objects
sections.body:
The application of tree-ring dating to human artefacts is called dendroarchaeology, and its characteristic product is a felling date, the year, and often the season, in which the tree that supplied a timber was cut down. Because timber for construction was in most pre-modern societies used green, within months or at most a few years of felling rather than seasoned for decades, the felling date usually approximates the construction date closely, and this assumption, tested repeatedly against documentary evidence, generally holds to within a year or two for vernacular buildings.

The reach is remarkable. Thousands of medieval roofs, church spires, barns, bridges, town houses and castle floors across Europe now carry precise construction dates, often overturning stylistic attributions by a century. The Neolithic lake-dwelling settlements around the Alpine lakes of Switzerland, southern Germany and eastern France have been dated timber by timber to individual construction and repair years in the fourth and third millennia BC, producing settlement histories of a resolution unmatched anywhere else in European prehistory. Shipwrecks are dated and, more usefully, provenanced, so that the Mary Rose, the Bremen cog, medieval Baltic wrecks and Viking-age vessels can be tied to specific building traditions and forests.

Two specialist applications deserve mention. Panel paintings, particularly Netherlandish and German works of the fifteenth to seventeenth centuries painted on Baltic oak boards, are dated by measuring the rings visible on the edge of the panel. Since the panel was normally trimmed to remove sapwood, the analyst obtains a date for the last surviving heartwood ring and must add an estimated sapwood allowance plus a seasoning allowance to reach an earliest plausible painting date, which is why such results are stated as an earliest possible date rather than a date of execution. The technique has authenticated and, more dramatically, refuted attributions where a panel proved to come from a tree felled after the supposed artist's death. Musical instruments, above all violins of the Cremonese school, are dated by the spruce of the belly, and the practice has become a routine part of the authentication of high-value instruments.

The archaeological value goes beyond dating single objects. Because felling dates cluster, they reveal building booms and their absence, and hence periods of prosperity, crisis, epidemic or warfare. A sharp collapse in construction dates across a region for a generation is a social signal, and such patterns have been used to trace the demographic impact of the fourteenth-century plague and of the crises of the seventeenth century.

The technique also disciplines architectural history. Before dendrochronology, buildings were dated by the style of their mouldings, joints and carpentry, a method that assumed stylistic features spread and persisted in predictable ways. Tree-ring dates have repeatedly shown that assumption to be wrong in detail: conservative rural carpentry can lag urban fashion by a century, and supposedly diagnostic joint types turn out to span far longer periods than the typologies allowed. The result has been a wholesale rewriting of regional building chronologies, and a general lesson that stylistic seriation is a weaker instrument than it appeared.

sections.heading: Provenancing Timber and Reconstructing Trade
sections.body:
A less obvious but historically potent use of tree rings is determining not when a timber grew but where. The same regional coherence of growth patterns that makes crossdating possible also means that a timber matches best against the chronology of the area it came from, and progressively less well as distance and climatic difference increase. By testing an unknown sample against a network of well-replicated regional chronologies and comparing the resulting statistics, an analyst can often identify the source region to within a few hundred kilometres, and sometimes far more tightly.

The classic case is Baltic oak. From roughly the thirteenth to the seventeenth century, enormous quantities of straight, slow-grown, knot-free oak boards were shipped from the hinterlands of the Vistula, Niemen and Daugava, through Danzig, Königsberg and Riga, to the Netherlands, England and beyond, for use as panel boards, ship planking and fine joinery. Dendroprovenancing identifies this wood unambiguously because its growth pattern differs from western European oak, and it has allowed historians to map the volume and timing of that trade independently of documentary records, to show when supply was interrupted by war, and to date the shift to alternative sources when the Baltic trade declined.

The method has resolved other questions. Timbers in Icelandic and Greenlandic Norse buildings have been sourced to Norway and, in some analyses, to North America, bearing on the extent of Norse westward contact. The construction timbers of colonial buildings in the Americas have been matched to European sources, evidencing the shipping of framing lumber as ballast and cargo. Individual medieval English roofs have been shown to combine local oak with imported boards, revealing procurement strategies invisible in any surviving account.

Provenancing has real limits and they are frequently understated. It is fundamentally a comparison against whatever reference chronologies happen to exist, so a region with no chronology cannot be identified and its timber may be misassigned to the nearest region that does have one. Human selection also biases the record, because the timber that reached distant markets was chosen for quality and may not represent the average growth of its forest. And a strong statistical match to a distant chronology can arise where two regions share a climate regime rather than a location. Careful practitioners therefore treat a provenance attribution as a probabilistic statement supported by the pattern of matches across a whole network, and increasingly combine it with independent evidence from stable isotopes of oxygen and strontium in the same wood.

A related and growing application is the reconstruction of forest history from the timber itself. The average ring width, the number of rings per unit of radius and the size of the parent trees can be read off a building's beams to describe the woodland that supplied it: closely ringed, slow-grown, very large oaks imply mature high forest, whereas fast-grown, wide-ringed timber of small diameter implies managed coppice-with-standards or hedgerow trees. Tracking these characteristics across centuries of dated buildings produces a record of deforestation, replanting and changing woodland management that no written source provides.

sections.heading: Dendroclimatology and the Reconstruction of Past Climate
sections.body:
Because a ring width or density in a climate-limited tree is a measurable response to the weather of a specific year, a network of such trees constitutes an instrument that recorded climate before instruments existed. Dendroclimatology exploits this by calibrating tree-ring indices against the overlapping instrumental record, typically the period since about 1880, deriving a statistical transfer function, and applying it to the pre-instrumental rings to reconstruct temperature, precipitation, drought index or streamflow year by year.

The procedure is disciplined by verification. The instrumental period is split, the transfer function is derived on one half and tested on the other, and skill is quantified by statistics such as the reduction of error and the coefficient of efficiency, which must exceed zero for the reconstruction to beat a simple climatological mean. Reconstructions are quoted with confidence intervals that widen backwards as sample depth falls.

The results have reshaped several fields. In the American Southwest, drought reconstructions extending over two thousand years placed the medieval megadroughts, notably the sustained dry period of the late thirteenth century, in a context that showed twentieth-century droughts to be comparatively mild, with direct implications for the settlement history of the Ancestral Puebloan world and for modern water allocation on the Colorado River, whose 1922 Compact was negotiated using an unusually wet twenty-year instrumental period. Northern hemisphere temperature reconstructions from high-latitude and high-altitude trees, combined with other proxies, produced the widely discussed reconstructions of the 1990s and 2000s. Tree rings also date volcanic eruptions with annual precision through frost rings and abrupt cold years, tying the 536 and 540 events, the 1257 Samalas eruption and the 1815 Tambora eruption to their climatic consequences.

The field's difficulties are real and openly debated. The divergence problem, first described in the 1990s, is the observation that at some high-latitude northern sites the growth response of trees to temperature weakened after about 1960, so that rings underpredict the measured warming; proposed explanations include drought stress, changing snow cover, reduced solar radiation and methodological artefacts, and no consensus has been reached. The segment length curse constrains how much genuine long-term variability any width-based reconstruction can retain. And a reconstruction is only as good as the assumption that the calibrated relationship is stable through time, which is precisely the assumption divergence calls into question. These are genuine, unresolved limitations that a careful reader should hold alongside the method's very real annual precision.

A further caution concerns selection. If chronologies are deliberately built from the most climate-sensitive sites, and if series are screened for correlation with the instrumental record before being included, the resulting network is not a random sample of trees and the apparent strength of the climate signal is inflated. Statisticians have pressed this point hard, and the responses, using unscreened networks, reporting results with and without screening, and preferring density or isotope measurements that respond more directly to temperature, are now standard good practice rather than optional refinements.

sections.heading: Radiocarbon Calibration and the Miyake Events
sections.body:
Dendrochronology and radiocarbon dating are not competitors but partners, and the relationship is asymmetric: radiocarbon depends on tree rings for its accuracy in a way that is not reciprocated. Radiocarbon dating measures the residual carbon-14 in a sample and converts it to an age using a known decay half-life. The conversion assumes a constant atmospheric carbon-14 concentration, and that assumption is false. Production varies with solar activity and the strength of the Earth's magnetic field, and the reservoir is redistributed by ocean circulation, so radiocarbon years and calendar years drift apart, by more than 800 years at points in the early Holocene.

The correction is empirical. Take a tree ring of exactly known calendar year, measure its radiocarbon content, and you have one point on a calibration curve. Do this for thousands of rings across the whole length of the absolutely dated oak and pine chronologies and you have the curve itself, published as successive international consensus versions: IntCal98, IntCal04, IntCal09, IntCal13, IntCal20, with a southern hemisphere counterpart SHCal and a marine curve. IntCal20 rests on tree rings for the last roughly 13,900 years and on other archives, corals, speleothems, foraminifera and macrofossils in varved sediments, beyond that to 55,000 years.

Tree rings also enable wiggle-matching, which sharpens dates on floating sequences dramatically. If a floating chronology has, say, 200 internally dated rings, one can date a series of individual rings at known relative spacings by radiocarbon and slide the resulting pattern of measurements along the calibration curve until the wiggles line up. Because the shape of the curve is distinctive, the fit is far more constraining than any single measurement, often yielding an absolute placement to within one or two decades. This is how many Bronze Age Aegean and Egyptian floating sequences have been anchored.

The most striking recent development is the discovery of Miyake events, named for the Japanese physicist Fusa Miyake, who reported in 2012 a sharp spike in carbon-14 in Japanese cedar rings for the year AD 774 to 775, followed by another for 993 to 994, with further events identified around 660 BC, 5259 BC and 7176 BC. These spikes, attributed to extreme solar particle events, appear worldwide in the same single year, and they act as absolute time markers of extraordinary power: a floating chronology containing a Miyake spike can be anchored to the exact calendar year with no ambiguity at all. The technique has already been used to date Viking settlement timbers at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland to AD 1021, giving a precise year for the earliest known European presence in the Americas, since the wood retained the 993 spike and the felling surface lay exactly twenty-eight rings beyond it.

For a working archaeologist the practical implication is that the two methods should be planned together rather than chosen between. Radiocarbon can be applied to almost any organic material and needs no reference chronology, so it works where dendrochronology cannot; dendrochronology gives an exact year where it works at all. Sampling for both, and reserving material for future wiggle-matching, repeatedly turns an undateable assemblage into a dated one.

sections.heading: The Wider Family: Fire, Landslides, Insects and Rivers
sections.body:
Once the principle of exact annual dating is established, it can be applied to any process that leaves a mark in wood, and a family of subdisciplines has grown up around the idea. Dendropyrochronology, fire history, exploits the fact that a surface fire that fails to kill a tree kills a patch of cambium, and the tree then grows a curled lobe of wood over the wound, producing a fire scar. Because the scar is embedded between two datable rings, and because its position within the ring, in earlywood or latewood, indicates the season, a cross-section from a fire-scarred pine records the exact year and season of every fire it survived. Networks of such trees reconstruct the pre-suppression fire regime of whole landscapes, showing for example that many western North American pine forests burned at intervals of five to twenty-five years before the twentieth century, and this evidence has directly reshaped forest management policy toward reintroducing fire.

Dendrogeomorphology dates landscape processes. A tree partly buried by a debris flow, tilted by a landslide or a creeping slope, scarred by a rockfall or a passing glacier, or with roots exposed by gully erosion, records the event in its wood: burial produces abrupt growth suppression and often adventitious roots, tilting produces eccentric rings and reaction wood beginning in a specific year, impact produces a scar. Mapping such responses across a slope dates individual landslide, avalanche, debris-flow and flood events over centuries, which is decisive for hazard assessment in mountain regions where written records are short. Tree rings likewise date past floods through scars, sediment inclusions and anatomical anomalies in riparian trees.

Dendroentomology reconstructs insect outbreaks. Defoliating insects such as the spruce budworm and the larch budmoth suppress growth for a run of consecutive years in a pattern distinguishable from drought because it affects the host species and not non-host species growing alongside. The larch budmoth record in the European Alps, extending back over a millennium, showed a remarkably regular eight to ten year cycle that appears to have broken down in recent decades, an observation of ecological significance.

Further branches include dendrochemistry, which reads pollution and volcanic fallout histories from elemental concentrations in dated rings, though element mobility across ring boundaries makes this contentious; dendrohydrology, reconstructing river flow; and stable-isotope dendroclimatology, in which the oxygen, carbon and hydrogen isotope ratios of dated cellulose record humidity and source-water composition independently of ring width, and which is increasingly used where widths are complacent.

What unites all of these is the same underlying move: the ring is an annually resolved, permanently archived, spatially fixed record of the tree's circumstances, and almost anything that affected the tree left a trace in it. The constraint is always interpretive rather than chronological. Establishing that a tree was suppressed in a given decade is straightforward; establishing why, when drought, defoliation, shading by a neighbour and root damage can all produce a similar suppression, requires independent evidence, ideally from non-host species growing on the same site.

sections.heading: Limits, Errors and What to Do When Dating Fails
sections.body:
The most consequential uncertainty in dendroarchaeology is not the ring date but what the ring date means. If a timber retains bark, the answer is unambiguous: the outermost ring is the felling year, and its completeness gives the season. If the sapwood is present but incomplete, an estimated allowance for the missing sapwood rings must be added, and these allowances are statistical, derived from measured sapwood counts in trees from that region and species. For English and Welsh oak, a commonly used range is 15 to 40 sapwood rings, with 95 percent confidence; for Irish oak, roughly 26 to 42; for Baltic oak, estimates near 9 to 36 are typical. The published date then reads as a range, and quoting the central value as if it were the felling year is a misreading that has repeatedly propagated through secondary literature.

Where all sapwood has been removed in conversion, only a terminus post quem is possible: the structure cannot be earlier than the last heartwood ring plus a minimum sapwood allowance, but it could be very much later. Timber reuse compounds this. Medieval and later builders routinely salvaged sound timber, and a fifteenth-century roof may contain thirteenth-century beams, betrayed by redundant mortices, empty peg holes and joints that fit nothing. A date on a reused timber dates the tree, not the building, and identifying reuse is a structural and archaeological judgement, not a laboratory one.

Several other failure modes recur. A sample with fewer than about fifty rings will often fail to date at all, because a short pattern is not statistically unique. A complacent series from an unstressed site will fail for lack of signal. A diffuse-porous species may be unreadable. A timber from a region with no reference chronology may date against nothing, however good the sample. And a timber whose growth was dominated by local disturbance rather than regional climate may cross-match poorly even when everything else is right.

When dating fails, the productive responses are to take more samples, since a structure with ten timbers may yield a date from one; to build a site chronology by crossdating the undated timbers against each other, producing a floating sequence that can be anchored later or by radiocarbon wiggle-matching; to test against additional regional chronologies including those for adjacent countries; and, increasingly, to search the sample for a Miyake spike if it is long enough to span one. What should never happen is the acceptance of a marginal statistical match because it suits the expected archaeology, and a reader encountering a reported date should always ask how many samples supported it, what the statistics were, whether sapwood survived, and against which chronology the match was made.

guides.title: Potassium-Argon and Argon-Argon Dating
guides.summary: How the decay of potassium-40 to argon-40 is used to date volcanic rocks, from the physics of the clock and the age equations through laboratory practice, step-heating spectra and single-crystal dating, to the landmark human-origins results it produced and the ways it fails.

sections.heading: Why This Method Underpins Human Prehistory
sections.body:
Before the late 1950s, the deep chronology of human origins was largely guesswork. Louis and Mary Leakey had spent decades excavating Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, and when Mary Leakey found the robust hominin skull catalogued OH 5 in July 1959, the prevailing estimate for the age of the deposits was a few hundred thousand years, extrapolated from sediment thicknesses and faunal comparisons. In 1961 Jack Evernden and Garniss Curtis of the University of California applied a newly developed technique to volcanic ash layers immediately beneath the find and returned an age near 1.75 million years. The result roughly tripled the accepted antiquity of toolmaking hominins overnight and was met with substantial disbelief. It has stood ever since.

That technique was potassium-argon dating, and its later refinement, argon-argon dating, remains the backbone of chronology for the Pliocene and Pleistocene record of human evolution. The reason is a fortunate geological accident. The East African Rift, where much of the early hominin fossil record is preserved, is volcanically active, so the lake and river sediments that entombed those fossils are interleaved with ash falls and lava flows. Each of those volcanic layers carries a clock that started when it erupted. A fossil found between two dated tuffs is bracketed by them, which is how nearly every important early hominin specimen is placed in time.

The method's reach is remarkable. It has dated a lava flow erupted three thousand years ago and meteorites that formed 4.5 billion years ago, spanning six orders of magnitude in time with the same physics. It independently confirmed the age of the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79 to within a century, using only the argon in crystals from the pumice, a test of the technique against known history that few dating methods can attempt. It fixed the Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary, the extinction of the non-avian dinosaurs, at 66.043 million years with an uncertainty of about 43,000 years.

For archaeology specifically, the important boundary is that potassium-argon dating cannot date artefacts or bones. It dates the crystallisation and cooling of volcanic minerals. Its contribution is always indirect: it establishes when the rock enclosing or overlying the archaeology formed, and the archaeological inference depends on the stratigraphic argument connecting the two. That dependence is not a weakness so much as a discipline, and most of the celebrated disputes in the field, including the long argument over the KBS Tuff at Lake Turkana, turned on stratigraphy and sample selection rather than on the physics. The same limitation shapes where the method can contribute at all. In regions without recent volcanism, such as most of western Europe or southern Africa, there are no datable ash layers, and Palaeolithic chronology there has had to be built instead from uranium-series, luminescence, electron spin resonance and palaeomagnetic evidence, which is one reason the African rift record is so much more finely resolved than records of comparable age elsewhere.

sections.heading: Radioactive Decay: The Clock Underneath
sections.body:
Every radiometric dating method rests on one empirical fact: the probability that a given unstable atomic nucleus decays in the next second is a constant, independent of temperature, pressure, chemical state, magnetic field, or how long the nucleus has already existed. Radioactive decay is a quantum tunnelling or weak interaction process occurring inside a nucleus shielded by its own electron cloud, and the energies involved, typically hundreds of thousands to millions of electronvolts, dwarf the few electronvolts available from any chemical or geological process. This constancy has been tested to high precision over a century and across extremes from liquid helium temperatures to the interiors of stars, with only tiny exceptions in a handful of electron-capture nuclides where extreme ionisation strips the electrons the process requires.

From that constant probability the mathematics follows immediately. If each nucleus has probability lambda of decaying per unit time, then in a population of N nuclei the number decaying per unit time is lambda times N.
