Solving that differential equation gives the exponential decay law: the number remaining after time t equals the original number times e raised to the power of minus lambda t. The constant lambda is called the decay constant, and it is more often quoted through the half-life, the time for half the population to decay, which equals the natural logarithm of 2 divided by lambda, approximately 0.693 over lambda.

Dating requires the complementary quantity: not what is left, but what has accumulated. The number of daughter atoms produced equals the original number of parent atoms minus those remaining, which rearranges to give the general dating equation in which time equals one over lambda times the natural logarithm of one plus the ratio of daughter to parent. This is the equation behind every parent-daughter dating method. Note what it requires: you must be able to measure both the surviving parent and the accumulated daughter in the same sample, you must know lambda, you must know how much daughter was present at the start, and the sample must have neither gained nor lost either element since the clock started.

The choice of which decay to use is governed by the half-life relative to the timescale of interest. A half-life much shorter than the age leaves too little parent to measure; radiocarbon, with a half-life of 5,700 years, is exhausted beyond about 50,000 years. A half-life much longer than the age produces too little daughter to detect. The useful range of a system runs roughly from a hundredth of a half-life to several half-lives, which is why an isotope with a half-life near 1.25 billion years turns out to be so well suited to the entire span of geological and human evolutionary time.

sections.heading: Potassium-40: A Uniquely Convenient Isotope
sections.body:
Potassium is the seventh most abundant element in the Earth's crust, making up about 2.1 per cent by mass, and it is a major constituent of some of the commonest rock-forming minerals: feldspars, micas, and clays. That abundance is the first reason the method works so widely. Almost every igneous rock contains a potassium-bearing mineral somewhere.

Natural potassium consists of three isotopes in essentially fixed proportion everywhere on Earth: potassium-39 at 93.2581 per cent, potassium-41 at 6.7302 per cent, and potassium-40 at just 0.0117 per cent, roughly one atom in 8,500. Only potassium-40 is radioactive. Its scarcity is not a problem because modern mass spectrometry can count extremely small numbers of atoms, and its constant relative abundance means the amount of potassium-40 can be inferred from a measurement of total potassium without measuring the rare isotope directly.

Potassium-40 has an unusual property that is central to the method: it decays two ways at once, a phenomenon called branched decay. About 89.5 per cent of decays are beta-minus emissions producing calcium-40, and about 10.5 per cent are electron captures, in which the nucleus absorbs an inner-shell electron, producing argon-40. Expressed as decay constants under the conventional values agreed by Steiger and Jager in 1977, the total decay constant is 5.543 by ten to the minus ten per year, of which the branch to argon is 0.581 by ten to the minus ten per year. The corresponding half-life is 1.248 billion years, meaning that of all the potassium-40 present when the Earth formed, roughly one atom in nine survives.

The calcium branch is far more productive but useless for dating most rocks, because calcium-40 is already the overwhelmingly dominant natural isotope of an abundant element, so the radiogenic addition is undetectable against the background. The argon branch is the opposite. Argon is a noble gas: chemically inert, forming no compounds, fitting into no crystal lattice site by bonding. When a mineral crystallises from molten rock, the argon dissolved in the melt escapes rather than being incorporated, so the mineral starts with essentially none. Every argon-40 atom subsequently found trapped in the crystal was manufactured there by potassium decay. That combination, an abundant parent element and a daughter that the mineral rejects at formation but then cannot lose, is what makes the system so powerful. Incidentally, this same decay explains a curiosity of the air itself: argon makes up 0.934 per cent of the atmosphere, and over 99.6 per cent of it is argon-40 outgassed from the Earth's interior over 4.5 billion years, a fact that also creates the method's most persistent contamination problem. On a planet with almost no primordial argon-36 left in its atmosphere, essentially every argon atom you breathe was manufactured by the same decay the method measures, and any of it that leaks into a vacuum line or clings to a mineral surface is indistinguishable from the argon the sample made itself except by its isotopic composition.

sections.heading: The Age Equation and a Worked Example
sections.body:
Because potassium-40 decays two ways but only one branch produces argon, the standard dating equation must carry a correction. The parent decays away at the total rate, but argon accumulates only at the electron-capture rate, so the observed argon must be scaled up by the ratio of total to argon-producing decay constants to recover the total number of parent atoms that have decayed. The potassium-argon age equation is therefore written as: age equals one over lambda, multiplied by the natural logarithm of one plus lambda over lambda-e times the ratio of radiogenic argon-40 to potassium-40 present. Here lambda is the total decay constant, 5.543 by ten to the minus ten per year, and lambda-e is the electron capture branch, 0.581 by ten to the minus ten per year, giving a branching correction factor of about 9.54.

A worked example makes this concrete. Suppose a laboratory analyses a sanidine feldspar separated from a volcanic ash and reports that the mineral contains 8.00 per cent potassium by mass and 1.20 by ten to the minus ten moles of radiogenic argon-40 per gram. First convert potassium to potassium-40. Eight per cent potassium is 0.0800 grams per gram, which at an atomic mass of 39.1 is 2.046 by ten to the minus three moles of potassium per gram. Multiplying by the isotopic abundance of 0.0117 per cent gives 2.394 by ten to the minus seven moles of potassium-40 per gram.

Now form the ratio of radiogenic argon-40 to potassium-40: 1.20 by ten to the minus ten divided by 2.394 by ten to the minus seven equals 5.013 by ten to the minus four. Multiply by the branching factor 9.54 to get 4.782 by ten to the minus three. Add one and take the natural logarithm, which for so small a number is very nearly the number itself, giving 4.771 by ten to the minus three. Divide by the total decay constant: 4.771 by ten to the minus three divided by 5.543 by ten to the minus ten equals 8.61 by ten to the sixth years. The ash erupted about 8.6 million years ago.

Two features of this arithmetic are worth noticing. Because the logarithm of a small number is approximately the number itself, the age is very nearly linear in the argon-to-potassium ratio for anything younger than about a hundred million years, so a one per cent error in the argon measurement translates to a one per cent error in age. And the calculation depends on measuring two different elements by two entirely different analytical techniques, on two different splits of the sample, with all the risks of inhomogeneity that implies. Removing that particular weakness was the motivation for the argon-argon variant that superseded it.

sections.heading: The Assumptions, Stated Plainly
sections.body:
Every date produced by this method is conditional on a short list of assumptions. Understanding them is not pedantry; nearly every wrong date in the literature is a case of one of them failing, and a competent analyst spends most of their effort testing them rather than making the measurement.

The first is that the mineral contained no argon-40 when it formed. This is the zero-daughter assumption, and it is usually excellent for minerals crystallising from a degassing magma near the surface, because argon is insoluble in silicate melts at low pressure and escapes. It fails systematically in specific circumstances: lavas erupted under deep water, where hydrostatic pressure prevents degassing, minerals that trapped tiny melt or fluid inclusions, and rocks crystallised at depth in argon-rich environments. Argon present at the start is called excess argon and always makes a sample look too old.

The second is that the system has been closed since it formed: no potassium and no argon added or lost. Potassium is mobile in water, so weathering and hydrothermal alteration can remove it, which makes a sample look older, or introduce it, which makes it look younger. Argon is worse, because as a gas that fits nowhere in the lattice it diffuses out whenever the mineral is heated. Every mineral has a closure temperature, the temperature below which argon diffusion becomes negligible on geological timescales, and it varies considerably: roughly 150 to 350 degrees Celsius for potassium feldspar, near 300 for biotite, 350 to 425 for muscovite, and 480 to 550 for hornblende. A date is therefore strictly a cooling age, the moment the mineral passed below its closure temperature, which for a surface volcanic ash is effectively the eruption but for a deep-seated intrusion may be millions of years after crystallisation.

The third is that the potassium isotopic composition is the same everywhere and has not changed, which is very well established, and that the decay constants are accurately known, which is a live issue discussed wherever high precision matters.

The fourth is that any argon that is not radiogenic is atmospheric in composition, so it can be corrected for. This is the workhorse assumption of the whole method. Atmospheric argon has a fixed isotopic ratio of argon-40 to argon-36, long taken as 295.5 following Alfred Nier's 1950 measurement and revised to 298.56 by Lee and colleagues in 2006. Since argon-36 is not produced by any relevant decay, measuring it tells you how much atmospheric argon is present, and multiplying by that ratio tells you how much of the argon-40 to discount. The correction is essential because atmospheric argon adsorbs onto every surface and pervades every vacuum line, and for young samples it can dominate the signal.

sections.heading: What Can Actually Be Dated
sections.body:
The method requires a material that contains potassium, retains argon, formed at a single identifiable moment, and has not been reheated or altered since. In practice that means volcanic and some intrusive minerals, and the choice among them matters enormously for the reliability of the result.

Sanidine, the high-temperature potassium feldspar found in rapidly cooled silicic volcanic ash, is the premier material and the reason so many tephra layers in the East African Rift are precisely dated. It carries 8 to 12 per cent potassium, holds argon extremely well, contains very little calcium and chlorine to complicate the corrections, and forms clean crystals large enough to date individually. Anorthoclase and high-potassium plagioclase are useful where sanidine is absent. Biotite and muscovite are widely available and high in potassium but are prone to alteration to chlorite and to argon loss, and micas suffer particular problems under the neutron irradiation used in the argon-argon variant. Hornblende has a high closure temperature and is excellent for dating slowly cooled rocks but is low in potassium and high in calcium, which increases interference corrections. Leucite and nepheline serve in silica-poor volcanic rocks.

Whole-rock analysis of fine-grained basalt is used where no datable phenocryst exists, which is common for lava flows. It is inherently riskier because a whole rock is a mixture of phases with different retention properties, some of them glassy and prone to both alteration and argon loss. Volcanic glass itself is generally unreliable beyond a few hundred thousand years because it hydrates and devitrifies. Authigenic glauconite formed in marine sediments can be dated but frequently gives ages that are too young because of argon loss.

The practical age range is wide. At the young end, the limit is set by how little radiogenic argon there is to measure against the atmospheric background. Conventional potassium-argon dating struggles below about 100,000 years, though the unspiked Cassignol-Gillot technique has pushed it to a few thousand years on high-potassium lavas. Argon-argon on single sanidine crystals routinely dates material tens of thousands of years old, and the celebrated demonstration on Vesuvius reached AD 79. At the old end there is no upper limit of consequence; meteorites and lunar samples of 4.5 billion years are dated routinely, and the constraint becomes finding a sample that has escaped later heating for that long.

What cannot be dated is equally important: sedimentary rocks in general, since their grains inherit ages from wherever they eroded from, and anything organic, ceramic, or lithic. A stone tool cannot be dated by this method. Its age comes from the volcanic layers around it. The same applies to bone, shell, charcoal, sediment and pottery, none of which contain a mineral that both holds potassium and started life free of argon. The practical skill in applying the technique to an archaeological problem therefore lies in recognising which beds in a section are primary volcanic deposits and which merely look like them.

sections.heading: Collecting a Sample That Can Be Dated
sections.body:
A great many dates fail in the field rather than the laboratory. The commonest causes are collecting altered material, collecting a bed whose stratigraphic relationship to the archaeology is ambiguous, and collecting too little. A useful discipline is to assume the date will eventually be disputed and to gather the evidence that will settle the dispute at the same time as the rock.

Freshness is the first criterion. Reject anything weathered, stained, veined, or crumbly; break through to material that rings under the hammer and shows unclouded crystals. Reject rock cut by later veins or sitting within a metre of a fault. Second, prefer a primary airfall ash, which settled directly from an eruption cloud and represents a single instant, over a reworked ash redeposited by water, which mixes crystals of different ages and is the single most common source of spuriously old results. Primary ashes are typically well sorted, laterally continuous over long distances, have a sharp base, and lack the cross-bedding and rounded grains of a water-laid deposit. Third, collect generously: one to two kilograms of tuff yields ample crystals, whereas a fist-sized piece may not. Finally, collect more than one bed where the section allows it. A pair of dated ashes above and below the horizon of interest brackets it, and two dates that are stratigraphically consistent are worth far more than one date standing alone, because consistency is itself evidence that neither sample has been disturbed.
ingredients: A geological hammer and a set of cold chisels for breaking into unweathered rock; a rock saw or core drill where a specific oriented block is required. Available from any geological supplier.
Heavy cloth or thick polythene sample bags, one to two kilograms capacity, plus permanent marker and waterproof labels written in duplicate, one inside the bag and one outside.
A field notebook and a measured stratigraphic log of the section, recording bed thicknesses, contacts and the exact position of the sampled horizon relative to any archaeological find.
A GPS receiver or a surveyed grid position, and a photographic record of the section with a clearly visible scale bar and the sample point marked.
A hand lens of at least ten times magnification for checking crystal freshness and identifying sanidine, biotite or hornblende phenocrysts in the field.
Dilute hydrochloric acid in a dropper bottle for testing whether carbonate cement is present, which signals secondary alteration.
A compass-clinometer for recording bedding attitude, since a tilted or slumped bed may not be in its original stratigraphic order.
A trowel and brush for cleaning back the exposure by at least twenty to thirty centimetres before sampling, so that the material collected has not been exposed to weathering at the surface.

Nitrile gloves and clean tools, since sweat, tobacco ash and dust from a previously sampled bed are all credible sources of cross-contamination when the target mineral will later be picked grain by grain.

sections.heading: From Rock to Age: The Laboratory Sequence
sections.body: The laboratory route from a bag of tuff to a number with an uncertainty is long, and the greater part of the effort goes into separating a pure, unaltered mineral rather than into the measurement itself. In conventional potassium-argon work the sample must be split, with potassium measured by flame photometry, atomic absorption or inductively coupled plasma spectrometry on one portion and argon measured by mass spectrometry on another. The argon measurement uses isotope dilution: a precisely known quantity of artificial argon-38, an isotope essentially absent from nature, is mixed with the sample gas so that the measured isotope ratios can be converted into an absolute number of atoms. The whole sequence typically takes weeks, and in the argon-argon variant a reactor irradiation adds one to several months.
steps: Dry the sample thoroughly and examine it in thin section or under a binocular microscope before committing to it, to confirm that the target mineral is present, fresh and abundant enough to be worth the several weeks of processing that follow.
Crush the rock in stages, using a jaw crusher then a disc mill, and sieve to a size fraction that liberates individual crystals without shattering them, commonly 250 to 500 micrometres for sanidine.

Wash away the fine dust, then treat briefly with dilute hydrofluoric or nitric acid to strip adhering glass and alteration rinds from the crystal surfaces. This step is short and closely watched, since prolonged acid attack leaches potassium.

Separate the target mineral by density using heavy liquids such as lithium metatungstate, and by magnetic susceptibility using a Frantz isodynamic separator, which cleanly divides feldspar from biotite, hornblende and iron oxides.

Hand-pick the final concentrate under a binocular microscope, rejecting every grain that shows cloudiness, inclusions, adhering groundmass or a different colour. This tedious step does more for accuracy than any instrumental refinement.

For argon-argon work, weigh the picked grains into aluminium or copper foil packets, stack them in a quartz vial interleaved with packets of a flux monitor standard of known age, and send the assembly for neutron irradiation in a research reactor.

After irradiation, wait several weeks for short-lived activity to decay, particularly argon-37 produced from calcium, which has a half-life of 35 days and must be corrected for by decay back to the irradiation date.

Load the sample into an ultra-high-vacuum extraction line and bake the line to remove adsorbed atmospheric argon. Release the gas by resistance furnace or by focused infrared or ultraviolet laser, then clean it over getters that absorb every reactive gas and leave only the noble gases.

Admit the purified argon to a noble gas mass spectrometer and measure the five isotopes at masses 36 through 40, then correct for system blank, mass discrimination, atmospheric argon via argon-36, and interfering neutron reactions on calcium, chlorine and potassium before computing the age.

sections.heading: The Argon-Argon Revolution
sections.body:
The conventional method has a structural weakness that no amount of careful work removes: potassium and argon are measured on different aliquots by different techniques. If the sample is not perfectly homogeneous, the two measurements do not refer to the same material, and the resulting age is meaningless in a way that leaves no trace in the data. It also destroys the sample in a single fusion, so there is no way to test whether the argon came out uniformly or whether part of it had leaked away long ago.

The solution, developed by Craig Merrihue and Grenville Turner and published in 1966, is elegant. Irradiate the sample with fast neutrons in a nuclear reactor. Among the reactions that occur, one converts potassium-39, the dominant and stable isotope, into argon-39 by knocking out a proton. Argon-39 is radioactive with a half-life of 269 years, which is long enough to be treated as stable during an analysis lasting hours and short enough that none exists naturally. The quantity of argon-39 produced is proportional to the amount of potassium-39 present, and therefore proportional to potassium-40, since their ratio is fixed. The parent has, in effect, been converted into a proxy made of the same element as the daughter.

The consequences are large. Both quantities are now measured simultaneously, on the same atoms, in the same mass spectrometer, in a single gas analysis. Sample inhomogeneity ceases to matter. Sample size falls dramatically, from grams to a single crystal weighing under a milligram, because only one measurement must reach precision rather than two. And because the argon can be released in stages rather than all at once, the sample can be interrogated rather than simply consumed.

The price is that the neutron flux inside a reactor is not uniform and cannot be calculated reliably, so the conversion efficiency must be calibrated empirically. This is done by irradiating packets of a standard mineral of independently known age alongside the unknowns, interleaved through the stack so the flux gradient can be interpolated. The calibration is expressed as the J parameter, defined so that J equals the exponential of the total decay constant times the standard's age, minus one, all divided by the measured ratio of radiogenic argon-40 to argon-39 in that standard. The age of any unknown irradiated in the same package is then simply one over lambda times the natural logarithm of one plus J times its own measured argon-40 to argon-39 ratio. Every argon-argon age is therefore a relative measurement, tied to the assumed age of a standard, which is why the values assigned to those standards have been argued over for decades. Irradiation also creates argon isotopes from calcium and chlorine, so a full analysis measures all five argon masses and applies correction factors determined by irradiating pure calcium and potassium salts alongside the samples.

sections.heading: Step Heating and Reading an Age Spectrum
sections.body:
The single most valuable capability the argon-argon method gained is incremental heating. Instead of fusing the sample in one go, the analyst heats it in a controlled series of steps, perhaps ten to thirty of them, from a few hundred degrees Celsius up to fusion, measuring the argon released at each. Because argon-39 sits where potassium sat, and argon-40 sits where radiogenic argon accumulated, every step yields its own apparent age from that fraction of the crystal. Plotting apparent age against the cumulative percentage of argon-39 released produces an age spectrum, and the shape of that spectrum is diagnostic.

An undisturbed sample gives a flat spectrum: every step yields the same age within uncertainty, because argon is distributed exactly as potassium is and nothing has been lost or gained. A sample that suffered partial argon loss during a later reheating gives a spectrum that rises from the low-temperature steps toward a plateau, because argon escaped preferentially from the outer parts of grains and from the least retentive sites, which are also the sites that degas first in the laboratory. The low-temperature steps therefore record a mixture and give ages that are too young, while the high-temperature steps approach the true formation age. A sample containing excess argon typically shows the opposite: anomalously old ages in the first steps, sometimes with a characteristic saddle shape that dips to a minimum in the middle, in which case the true age is no older than the saddle minimum.

A plateau is defined by convention rather than by physics, and the usual criteria require at least three contiguous steps whose ages agree within analytical uncertainty at the two-sigma level, together comprising at least 50 per cent of the total argon-39 released, with an acceptable statistical scatter as judged by the mean square of weighted deviates. When those conditions are met, the weighted mean of the plateau steps is quoted as the age. When they are not, the honest report is that the sample gave no plateau, and any single number extracted from it should be treated as a maximum or minimum rather than a date.

This diagnostic power is what raised the technique from a measurement to an argument. A conventional potassium-argon analysis returns one number and no way of knowing whether it means anything. An argon-argon spectrum returns a shape that reveals whether the assumptions held, and in the failure cases it often reveals what went wrong and roughly when. A staircase spectrum on a hornblende from a metamorphic terrain, for instance, can be modelled to recover both the original formation age and the timing and intensity of a later thermal overprint, which turned the method into the foundation of thermochronology, the study of how rocks cool and are exhumed.

sections.heading: Isochrons and the Trapped Argon Component
sections.body:
The correction for non-radiogenic argon assumes that whatever argon was present at the start had the isotopic composition of modern air. That assumption is testable, and the test is the isochron, a technique borrowed from rubidium-strontium dating and adapted to argon.

The logic is that any measured argon-40 is the sum of two components: a trapped component of unknown but constant isotopic composition, and a radiogenic component proportional to potassium. If several steps or several grains from one sample contain different proportions of trapped and radiogenic argon, then plotting the ratio of argon-40 to argon-36 against the ratio of argon-39 to argon-36 should produce a straight line. The intercept of that line on the vertical axis gives the isotopic composition of the trapped component directly, without assuming it, and the slope gives the radiogenic argon-40 to argon-39 ratio and hence the age. In practice analysts more often use the inverse isochron, plotting argon-36 over argon-40 against argon-39 over argon-40, because the errors behave better and a mixing line becomes a simple straight line between two endpoints.

What makes this powerful is that it converts an assumption into a measurement. If the intercept comes out at an argon-40 to argon-36 ratio of about 298, matching air, the standard correction was justified and the isochron age should agree with the plateau age. If the intercept comes out substantially higher, the sample contained excess argon that was not atmospheric, the conventional correction under-subtracted, and the plateau age is too old while the isochron age may still be correct. Intercepts of several thousand have been measured in minerals from deep intrusions and submarine basalts.

The technique has limits worth stating. It requires genuine spread in the data; if all the steps or grains have nearly the same proportion of trapped argon, the points cluster and the fitted line is poorly constrained, producing an age with an enormous uncertainty that can be mistaken for a real result. It assumes the trapped component was uniform across the sample, which fails if two distinct excess argon reservoirs are present. And a straight line on an isochron plot can also be produced by mixing two populations of different ages, in which case the slope is a meaningless average, so a good isochron is necessary but not sufficient evidence. The strongest practice is to require agreement between a well-defined plateau and an isochron whose intercept is indistinguishable from air, and to treat disagreement between them as a signal to investigate rather than a choice of which number to publish. Where a sample is young or low in potassium, so that atmospheric argon dominates the measured gas, the isochron becomes not merely a check but the only defensible way to extract an age at all, because a small error in the assumed trapped composition would otherwise swamp the tiny radiogenic signal.

sections.heading: Single-Crystal Laser Fusion and the KBS Tuff
sections.body:
Because argon-argon needs only one measurement on one gas sample, the amount of material required fell far enough that a single crystal weighing a fraction of a milligram became analysable. Focusing an infrared or ultraviolet laser onto one grain in a sample chamber fuses it in seconds and releases its argon, so tens of crystals from one ash can be dated individually in a day. The consequence for archaeology was decisive, because it turned a bulk average into a population that can be examined for structure.

The reason that matters is contamination. A volcanic ash falling on a landscape picks up older crystals: xenocrysts torn from the volcano's conduit walls, wind-blown grains from earlier eruptions, and detrital feldspar reworked from older sediment when the ash is redeposited by water. In a bulk analysis of thousands of grains, a small proportion of much older contaminants raises the average age with no visible warning. In single-crystal analysis, they appear as a separate cluster of old ages while the true eruption population forms a tight group at the young end, and the contaminants can simply be excluded on statistical grounds.

The classic demonstration is the KBS Tuff of the Koobi Fora Formation east of Lake Turkana in Kenya, and the episode is worth knowing because it shows the method correcting itself in public. In 1970 Frank Fitch and Jack Miller reported an age of 2.61 million years for the tuff, which mattered enormously because the celebrated cranium KNM-ER 1470, later assigned to Homo rudolfensis, came from just above it. That age implied a large brained hominin considerably older than anything comparable elsewhere, and it conflicted with the faunal evidence, particularly pig lineages, which suggested something closer to 1.8 million years. A protracted and sometimes acrimonious dispute ran through the 1970s. It was settled in the early 1980s when work by Ian McDougall and others, culminating in single-crystal analyses, showed that the older results came from samples contaminated with detrital feldspars reworked into the ash. The accepted age is now 1.87 to 1.88 million years, consistent with the fauna.

The same capability produced the most striking accuracy test the method has undergone. In 1997 Paul Renne and colleagues dated sanidine crystals from the pumice of the AD 79 eruption of Vesuvius, obtaining an age of 1,925 years before 1996 with an uncertainty of 94 years, which is AD 72 plus or minus 94, and which brackets the historically documented date. Dating an event less than two thousand years old with a clock whose half-life exceeds a billion years is a severe test of every correction in the chain, and it passed. The measurement worked only because Vesuvian pumice contains sanidine with roughly 10 per cent potassium and because the crystals were large, fresh and free of excess argon; a low-potassium basalt of the same age would have been hopeless.

sections.heading: Standards, Decay Constants, and the Accuracy Debate
sections.body:
There is an important distinction between precision, meaning how reproducible a measurement is, and accuracy, meaning how close it is to the truth. Modern argon-argon laboratories routinely achieve internal precision better than 0.2 per cent. Accuracy has lagged behind, and the reason is that every argon-argon age depends on two externally supplied numbers that are themselves imperfectly known: the assumed age of the flux monitor standard, and the decay constants of potassium-40.

The most widely used standard is sanidine from the Fish Canyon Tuff of Colorado, a huge Oligocene ignimbrite that provides essentially unlimited homogeneous material. The age assigned to it has moved repeatedly. Values near 27.8 million years were used in the 1980s. Paul Renne and colleagues recommended 28.02 million years in 1998, and that value underpins a large body of published work. In 2008 Klaudia Kuiper and colleagues published 28.201 million years, derived by tying argon-argon analyses of ash layers in Mediterranean marine sediments to the astronomical timescale, which is calibrated by orbitally driven cycles in the sediments themselves and is independent of any radioactive decay constant. In 2010 and 2011 Renne and colleagues published an optimisation that simultaneously fitted the standard's age and the decay constants against independent constraints, arriving at 28.294 million years.

The spread between those recommendations is roughly one per cent, which sounds trivial and is not. One per cent of 66 million years is 660,000 years, which is the difference between an asteroid impact preceding a mass extinction and following it. The recalibration is precisely why the Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary shifted from a long-quoted 65.5 million years to 66.043 million years. It is also why comparing a date published in 1995 with one published in 2020 without checking which standard age each used is a genuine error, and why careful modern papers report the monitor, its assumed age, and the decay constants alongside the result so that later readers can recalculate.

The underlying difficulty with the decay constants is that potassium-40's branching makes them hard to measure directly. Counting experiments must detect the electron capture branch, whose signature is a low-energy X-ray and gamma emission, against a background dominated by the ten times more frequent beta branch, and different counting experiments have disagreed by more than their stated uncertainties. The conventional values fixed by Steiger and Jager in 1977 were adopted for consistency rather than because they were the best measurement, and the systematic uncertainty on the total decay constant is around one per cent. This is the ultimate floor on argon-argon accuracy in absolute terms, though not on the precision of comparing one argon-argon age with another measured against the same standard, which is why the method remains superb for ordering events even where the absolute scale is debatable.

sections.heading: Landmark Results in Human Origins
sections.body:
The chronology of human evolution is, to an unusual degree, a list of argon dates. A brief tour shows both what the method delivers and how it is used stratigraphically.

At Olduvai Gorge, the 1961 and 1965 work of Evernden and Curtis on Bed I established an age near 1.75 to 1.85 million years for the levels containing Oldowan tools and Paranthropus boisei, transforming the perceived timescale of the Palaeolithic. At Laetoli in northern Tanzania, the trail of hominin footprints discovered in 1976 and 1978 lies within the Footprint Tuff, an ash from the nearby Sadiman volcano dated to about 3.66 million years, which is what allows those tracks to be attributed to Australopithecus afarensis and treated as direct evidence of bipedal gait at that date. In the Hadar Formation of Ethiopia, the skeleton AL 288-1, known as Lucy, is bracketed by dated tuffs to about 3.2 million years.

In the Turkana Basin, the dense sequence of dated tuffs, including the KBS and Okote Tuffs, has produced one of the finest chronological frameworks anywhere, permitting the appearance of Homo erectus, of the Acheulean industry, and of the associated fauna to be sequenced at a resolution of tens of thousands of years. At Omo Kibish, argon-argon dating of the tuffs bracketing the Homo sapiens fossils gave an age of 195,000 years with an uncertainty of 5,000, published by Ian McDougall, Francis Brown and John Fleagle in 2005, making them for many years the oldest known anatomically modern humans; a 2022 study by Celine Vidal and colleagues re-dated the overlying Shala volcanic ash and pushed the minimum age to about 233,000 years, an instructive case of the same technique revising its own result by improving the correlation of an ash layer rather than by improving the measurement.

Beyond hominin fossils, argon dating provides the tie points that connect regional archaeological sequences. The Toba supereruption in Sumatra, dated by argon-argon to about 73,900 years with an uncertainty near 320 years, deposited an ash sheet detectable across South Asia and in Indian Ocean cores, giving an instantaneous marker horizon against which the timing of modern human dispersal, and the vigorously debated question of whether the eruption caused a population bottleneck, can be tested. Tephrochronology of this kind, in which a chemically fingerprinted ash dated in one place is recognised in another, extends the reach of a single argon date across continents. The pattern running through all of these cases is worth drawing out. In none of them was the fossil or the artefact dated. In every one, an eruption was dated and the archaeology was placed relative to it by stratigraphy, so the precision quoted for the ash is an upper bound on the confidence that can be attached to the human event, never a substitute for the excavation record that links the two.

sections.heading: Failure Modes and How They Are Recognised
sections.body:
Knowing how a method fails is more useful than knowing how it succeeds, because in practice most of the work consists of detecting failures. There are five recurring ones and each has a diagnostic signature.

Excess argon is argon-40 present at the start, whether inherited from an argon-rich fluid, trapped in melt inclusions, or retained because the magma degassed poorly under pressure. It always makes a sample look older, sometimes by a great deal: young submarine basalts have returned apparent ages of hundreds of thousands of years when they erupted within living memory. Its signatures are anomalously old low-temperature steps, a saddle-shaped age spectrum, and an isochron intercept significantly above the atmospheric argon-40 to argon-36 ratio of about 298.

Argon loss is the mirror image and the commonest problem in old or altered samples. Reheating, deep burial, hydrothermal circulation, or slow diffusion at ambient temperature over very long periods all let argon escape, and every atom lost makes the sample look younger. The signature is a spectrum that climbs from young ages in the early steps toward an older plateau, since the least retentive sites both leaked first in nature and degas first in the laboratory.

Inherited crystals, whether xenocrysts from the volcano's plumbing or detrital grains reworked into the deposit, produce ages that are too old. They are essentially undetectable in bulk analysis and obvious in single-crystal work, where they appear as a scattered old tail beyond a tight young population. This was the root of the KBS Tuff dispute.

Recoil is specific to the argon-argon technique. When a potassium-39 nucleus captures a neutron and ejects a proton, the resulting argon-39 atom recoils about 0.08 micrometres. In a coarse crystal that is irrelevant, but in fine-grained material such as clay, groundmass, or thin mica flakes, a significant fraction of the newly created argon-39 is ejected out of the grain entirely, artificially raising the argon-40 to argon-39 ratio and producing an age that is too old, or redistributed between phases producing a disturbed spectrum. This is why very fine-grained samples are avoided or analysed only in vacuum-encapsulated form.

Alteration is the fifth. Weathering, clay formation and sericitisation of feldspar move potassium and open the argon system, and because the two effects act in different directions the resulting age can be wrong either way. It is the one failure mode most reliably prevented in the field, by rejecting anything that is not visibly fresh, and it is why hand-picking under a microscope remains worth the hours it costs. Two of these five push ages older and two push them younger, which is a useful thing to hold in mind: when a suite of dates from one bed scatters in one direction only, the scatter is diagnostic rather than random, and the extreme value on the contaminated side should be treated as a bound rather than averaged in.

sections.heading: Limits, Cross-Checks, and What to Do When Dates Disagree
sections.body:
Two limits bound the method from outside and cannot be argued away. The first is that it dates rocks, never artefacts. A date is attached to archaeology only through a stratigraphic argument, and that argument is usually the weakest link. Ash layers can be reworked and redeposited long after they fell. Objects can be intruded downward by burrowing animals, by pits, or by trampling. A tuff sampled at one end of a site may be the same bed as one at the other end, or may not. When a date and a stratigraphic expectation conflict, the stratigraphy is the more likely culprit, and the correct response is to re-examine the section rather than the spectrometer.

The second is that the absolute scale is tied to a standard and to decay constants known to about one per cent, so ages measured against different standards are not directly comparable at high precision without recalculation. Anyone comparing dates from different decades should check the calibration each used.

The strongest defence is independent cross-checking, and the Quaternary is unusually well served. Radiocarbon covers the last 50,000 years and overlaps argon-argon at the young end, where both have been applied to the same eruptions with good agreement. Uranium-series dating of speleothems and corals covers roughly the last 600,000 years. Uranium-lead dating of zircon, whose decay constants are known an order of magnitude better than potassium's, can be applied to the same ash beds and has been the principal external check on the argon calibration; the two systems now agree to within a few tenths of a per cent where both work well. Magnetostratigraphy provides a coarse but completely independent framework, since the sequence of geomagnetic reversals is fixed and any argon date must place a sample in the correct polarity chron. Fission track, luminescence, electron spin resonance and tephra geochemistry all add further constraints.

When results disagree, a disciplined sequence helps. Check first whether the dates were calculated against the same standard and decay constants, since about one per cent of apparent disagreement is often bookkeeping. Look at the spectra rather than the summary numbers, and ask whether each has a genuine plateau meeting the conventional criteria. Check whether the isochron intercepts sit at the atmospheric ratio. Ask whether the material was single crystals or bulk, since bulk analyses of tuff are vulnerable to inheritance. Then return to the field relationships and confirm that the sampled bed is what it was assumed to be. In the great majority of historical disputes, including the KBS Tuff, the resolution came from better sample selection and better stratigraphy rather than from better physics, and the sensible expectation is that the next one will too.

guides.title: Thermoluminescence and Optically Stimulated Luminescence Dating
guides.summary: How luminescence dating works: the trapped-charge physics inside quartz and feldspar grains, how a buried sample accumulates radiation dose, and how archaeologists convert that dose into an age for fired pottery, burnt flint and buried sediment, together with the field, laboratory and statistical practice and the ways the method fails.

sections.heading: What Luminescence Dating Measures
sections.body:
Luminescence dating answers a question that radiocarbon cannot: how long ago was this mineral grain last exposed to strong heat or daylight. It does not date the formation of the rock, and it does not date any organic material. It dates an event, and the event is a resetting, either a fire hot enough to empty the mineral's memory or a period of sunlight long enough to do the same. That makes it uniquely suited to the two most common archaeological materials that radiocarbon cannot touch: fired ceramics and stone, and the sediment that buries everything else.

The underlying idea is simple enough to state in a sentence. Certain common minerals, above all quartz and the feldspars, act as natural radiation dosimeters. Buried in the ground, they are continuously bombarded by weak ionising radiation from the decay of uranium, thorium and potassium in the surrounding sediment, plus a small contribution from cosmic rays. That radiation knocks electrons loose inside the crystal, and a fraction of those electrons become stuck in structural defects in the lattice, where they accumulate steadily for as long as the grain remains buried and dark. Heat the grain, or shine light on it, and the trapped electrons are released, recombine, and the crystal emits a faint flash of light. The brightness of that flash is proportional to how much radiation the grain has absorbed since it was last emptied. Measure the flash, calibrate it against known laboratory doses, work out how fast the surroundings deliver radiation, and divide.

The practical significance for archaeology is considerable. Radiocarbon requires organic carbon and runs out of usable signal at roughly 50,000 years. Luminescence needs no organic material at all, and quartz optically stimulated luminescence routinely reaches 100,000 to 150,000 years, with feldspar techniques extending toward half a million years and beyond in favourable conditions. It is the primary method behind current understanding of when modern humans left Africa, when Australia was first occupied, and how the great loess sequences of China and central Europe accumulated. Thermoluminescence on burnt flint has provided most of the chronology for the Middle Palaeolithic of the Levant, a period that sits awkwardly beyond comfortable radiocarbon range.

A further advantage is that the material dated is frequently the material of archaeological interest itself. A radiocarbon date on charcoal from a hearth dates the death of the tree, which may predate the fire by centuries, and dates the charcoal rather than the pot beside it. A thermoluminescence date on the pot dates the firing of the pot. This directness removes an entire category of interpretive argument about association.

The cost of this reach is that luminescence ages carry larger uncertainties than radiocarbon, typically five to ten per cent of the age even when everything goes well, and that the method makes assumptions about the past which cannot always be verified. Understanding the technique properly means understanding those assumptions, because when a luminescence age is wrong it is almost always one of them that has failed rather than the physics.

sections.heading: The Physics of Trapped Charge
sections.body:
A perfect crystal would be useless for dating. What makes quartz and feldspar work is that real crystals are flawed: they contain missing atoms, substituted impurity atoms and dislocations, and each of these distorts the local electric field. In the language of solid-state physics, a pure insulating crystal has a valence band full of electrons, a conduction band that is empty, and a forbidden energy gap between them, about 9 electronvolts wide in quartz. Defects create localised energy levels inside that forbidden gap, and these levels are the traps that make the whole method possible.

When ionising radiation passes through the crystal, it deposits energy and ejects electrons from the valence band into the conduction band, leaving positively charged vacancies called holes behind. Most of these electrons and holes recombine almost immediately and the energy is lost as heat. A minority, however, wander until they fall into a defect level and become stuck. An electron sitting in a trap 1.6 electronvolts below the conduction band cannot escape by ordinary thermal jostling at ambient temperature, because the average thermal energy available at 15 degrees Celsius is about 0.025 electronvolts. Escape requires an improbable statistical fluctuation, and the mean waiting time for that fluctuation, calculated from the Arrhenius relation, can be hundreds of thousands or millions of years. That is the crystal's memory.

Trap depth therefore determines usable lifetime, and different traps are useful for different purposes. Shallow traps, such as the one responsible for the 110 degree Celsius thermoluminescence peak in quartz, empty within hours at room temperature and are useless for dating, though they are extremely useful in the laboratory as a monitor of how the crystal's sensitivity is changing during measurement. The traps used for dating are deeper, corresponding to the 325 degree Celsius region of the quartz glow curve, with calculated lifetimes at 20 degrees Celsius running into tens or hundreds of millions of years, comfortably longer than any age being measured.

Emptying a trap requires supplying the escape energy from outside, and there are exactly two practical ways. Heating the crystal supplies it thermally, and this is thermoluminescence. Shining light of the right wavelength supplies it as a photon, and this is optically stimulated luminescence. In either case the freed electron migrates through the conduction band until it encounters a hole trapped at a different kind of defect, called a recombination centre or luminescence centre. If that centre is radiative, recombination releases the surplus energy as a photon of visible or ultraviolet light. That photon, one of many millions, is what the instrument counts. The intensity of the emitted light is thus a proxy for the number of electrons that were in the traps, which is a proxy for absorbed radiation dose, which is a proxy for burial time.

sections.heading: The Natural Radiation Environment
sections.body:
The clock runs on radioactivity, and understanding where that radioactivity comes from is half of the method. Four sources matter, and they contribute in strikingly different proportions and over strikingly different distances.

The decay chain of uranium-238, with its 4.47 billion year half-life, and the shorter chain from uranium-235, together with the thorium-232 chain at 14 billion years, supply alpha, beta and gamma radiation as they cascade through dozens of intermediate daughters toward stable lead. Potassium-40, which makes up about 0.0117 per cent of all natural potassium and has a half-life of 1.25 billion years, supplies beta particles and a 1.46 megaelectronvolt gamma ray. Rubidium-87 contributes a small beta component, usually a per cent or two of the total. Finally, cosmic rays, principally high-energy muons produced when primary cosmic radiation strikes the upper atmosphere, penetrate the ground and add roughly 0.15 to 0.30 grays per thousand years at the surface, falling off with burial depth and with a dependence on latitude, altitude and the geometry of the overlying ground.

The three types of radiation have radically different ranges in sediment, and this geometry drives almost every decision in sample preparation. An alpha particle travels only about 20 to 30 micrometres in quartz, so it irradiates just the outer rind of a sand grain and does not reach the interior at all. Alphas are also inefficient at producing luminescence relative to the energy they deposit, typically only a tenth to a quarter as effective as beta or gamma, an inefficiency quantified by a parameter called the alpha efficiency or a-value. Beta particles travel roughly 2 to 3 millimetres, meaning a sand grain is fully penetrated but that beta dose comes only from sediment within a few grain diameters. Gamma rays travel about 30 centimetres, so the gamma dose is an average over a sphere of that radius surrounding the sample.

This immediately explains two standard laboratory strategies. In the coarse-grain method, sand-sized quartz grains are etched with concentrated hydrofluoric acid to dissolve away the outer 10 to 20 micrometres, physically removing the alpha-irradiated rind so that the alpha contribution can be ignored entirely. In the fine-grain method, silt-sized particles of 4 to 11 micrometres are used, which are small enough that alpha, beta and gamma all penetrate fully, so all three must be measured and the alpha efficiency determined experimentally.

The 30 centimetre gamma sphere carries a warning that field archaeologists frequently underestimate. If a sample sits within 30 centimetres of a boundary between sediments of different radioactivity, or near a stone wall, a hearth or a void, the gamma contribution is not what a bulk sediment analysis will suggest, and the resulting age can be wrong by a substantial margin.

sections.heading: The Age Equation
sections.body:
The whole of luminescence dating reduces to one deceptively simple expression: age equals equivalent dose divided by dose rate. Everything difficult in the technique lies in measuring those two quantities honestly.

The equivalent dose, universally written as De and pronounced dee-ee, is the amount of laboratory radiation required to induce the same luminescence signal as the sample acquired naturally during burial. It is not measured directly; it is inferred by comparison. You measure the natural signal, then irradiate the same material with known laboratory doses, measure the resulting signals, fit a curve, and read off where the natural signal falls on that curve. The unit is the gray, abbreviated Gy, defined as one joule of absorbed energy per kilogram of material. Typical archaeological equivalent doses run from a fraction of a gray for very recent material to a few hundred grays near the upper limit of the method.

The dose rate, written as a dot over the D or simply as dose rate, is how many grays the sample absorbs per unit time in its burial environment, conventionally quoted in grays per thousand years. Typical values in ordinary sediments fall between 1 and 5 grays per thousand years, with potassium-rich sediments at the higher end and clean quartz sands at the lower. It is calculated from the measured concentrations of uranium, thorium and potassium, converted to dose using standard conversion factors, adjusted for grain size attenuation, adjusted for water content, and added to the cosmic contribution.

A worked example makes the arithmetic concrete. Suppose a sample of quartz from a sand dune yields an equivalent dose of 48.5 grays. Analysis of the surrounding sediment gives 2.1 parts per million uranium, 8.4 parts per million thorium and 1.2 per cent potassium, which after conversion, grain-size attenuation and a water content correction gives a sediment dose rate of 1.72 grays per thousand years, to which a cosmic contribution of 0.18 is added, totalling 1.90. The age is then 48.5 divided by 1.90, which is 25.5 thousand years. Propagating the uncertainties in both terms, typically five to eight per cent, gives an age of roughly 25,500 plus or minus 1,700 years.

The equation also explains why the method's upper limit is not a fixed number of years. Traps are finite, so as dose accumulates the growth curve flattens toward saturation, at which point a small error in signal implies a huge error in dose. Since age is dose divided by dose rate, a sample in a high dose rate saturates sooner in calendar terms. The same mineral may date to 150,000 years in a clean quartz sand and only 40,000 in a potassium-rich silt.

Two features of this arithmetic deserve emphasis. First, the age is a ratio, so a systematic error in either term propagates directly and proportionally into the age. Second, the dose rate is assumed constant over the entire burial period, which is a genuine assumption about the past rather than a measurement, and one that fails if water content changed, if sediment was removed from above, or if uranium migrated in or out of the deposit.

sections.heading: Thermoluminescence: Reading the Glow Curve
sections.body:
Thermoluminescence is the older of the two techniques and remains the method of choice for anything that was heated in antiquity. The measurement itself is straightforward in concept. A small quantity of prepared mineral, typically a few milligrams spread on a stainless steel or aluminium disc, is placed in a light-tight chamber, flushed with nitrogen to suppress spurious signals from surface oxidation, and heated at a controlled rate, conventionally 5 degrees Celsius per second, from room temperature to about 450 or 500 degrees Celsius. A photomultiplier tube counts the photons emitted at each moment. The resulting plot of light intensity against temperature is the glow curve, and it is the primary datum of the technique.

The glow curve is not a single hump. It is a superposition of peaks, each corresponding to a population of traps of a particular depth. Shallow traps empty at low temperature and produce peaks early in the heating ramp; deep traps require more thermal energy and produce peaks later. In quartz the peak near 110 degrees Celsius comes from a very shallow trap that empties within hours at room temperature, so it contains no burial information at all, but because it responds linearly to dose it is invaluable as a monitor of the crystal's changing sensitivity. The peaks in the 325 to 375 degree region come from traps deep enough to be stable over geological time, and it is these that carry the age information. Practitioners test stability by a plateau test: they calculate an apparent equivalent dose at each temperature across the glow curve, and a genuine, thermally stable signal produces a flat plateau of constant dose across a range of typically 300 to 400 degrees. A rising or falling curve with no plateau indicates that the signal is contaminated by unstable traps or by non-radiation-induced light.

Thermoluminescence has one decisive limitation and one decisive advantage. The limitation is that heating destroys the signal, so each aliquot can be measured only once in its natural state, which historically forced the use of multiple-aliquot protocols in which dozens of separate subsamples receive different laboratory doses and the results are combined statistically. This assumes every aliquot behaves identically, which is only approximately true. The advantage is that heat empties traps far more completely than light does. A pot fired at 600 degrees or a flint dropped into a hearth is unambiguously and totally reset, which removes the single largest source of error affecting sediment dating. For fired materials, thermoluminescence remains a robust, well-understood and widely trusted technique, and it is the standard method for authenticating ceramics of disputed origin. In that commercial application a few tens of milligrams drilled from an inconspicuous part of the object are enough to distinguish an antiquity fired two thousand years ago from a modern reproduction fired last decade, since the difference in accumulated dose is enormous and no forger can easily fake it. The one countermeasure, deliberately irradiating a modern fake to raise its apparent dose, leaves detectable signatures in the shape of the glow curve.

sections.heading: Optically Stimulated Luminescence: Light as the Trigger
sections.body:
In 1985 David Huntley, Dorothy Godfrey-Smith and Michael Thewalt published a short paper demonstrating that shining green light on quartz released trapped charge and produced a measurable luminescence signal. That observation transformed archaeological dating, because it meant the clock could be read using the same agent that had reset it in nature: daylight. If sunlight empties the traps that light empties in the laboratory, then any grain that saw daylight before burial has a properly zeroed clock, and ordinary wind-blown or water-laid sediment becomes datable material. Suddenly it was possible to date not just the pot but the layer the pot was lying in, and not just occupied sites but dunes, river terraces, loess, colluvium and cave sediments.

The measurement differs from thermoluminescence in the stimulus, not the principle. The sample is held at a modest constant temperature, usually 125 degrees Celsius to keep the shallow 110 degree trap empty and prevent it from interfering, and illuminated with light of a chosen wavelength. Modern instruments use arrays of blue light-emitting diodes at about 470 nanometres for quartz, and infrared diodes at about 870 nanometres for feldspar. The emitted luminescence is detected at a shorter wavelength than the stimulation so that scattered stimulating light can be filtered out; for quartz, detection is in the ultraviolet near 340 to 380 nanometres through a filter such as Hoya U-340. The signal appears as a decay curve: bright at the instant illumination starts, falling rapidly as traps empty, typically dropping to a few per cent of its initial intensity within one or two seconds.

That decay curve is itself a composite. Quartz optically stimulated luminescence contains a fast component, a medium component and several slow components, each corresponding to a different trap emptied at a different rate. Only the fast component is reliably and rapidly bleached by sunlight, so practitioners deliberately use only the first fraction of a second of signal, subtracting a background taken from the tail of the curve, in order to isolate it. Getting this integration right matters: including slower components imports charge that daylight may not have removed and biases the age upward.

The practical gains over thermoluminescence are large. Optical stimulation empties only the light-sensitive traps and leaves the rest of the crystal intact, so the same aliquot can be measured repeatedly. That single fact enabled single-aliquot protocols, in which one subsample is measured, dosed, measured again and so on, allowing every grain population to serve as its own calibration and removing the assumption that separate aliquots behave alike. It also made the measurement far quicker, since a modern automated reader can carry a carousel of forty-eight discs through a full irradiation and measurement sequence unattended overnight, where the older multiple-aliquot thermoluminescence approach consumed both more material and more of the analyst's time for a less well constrained result.

sections.heading: Quartz and Feldspar: The Two Workhorse Minerals
sections.body:
Almost all luminescence dating is done on one of two mineral groups, and the choice between them is a genuine trade-off rather than a matter of preference.

Quartz is the first choice wherever it is available and behaves well. It is chemically inert, abundant in most sediments, easy to purify, and its optically stimulated luminescence signal bleaches extremely fast in sunlight, with the fast component reduced to under one per cent of its initial value in a few seconds to a minute of direct daylight. Most importantly, quartz shows negligible anomalous fading, meaning its trapped charge is stable in practice as well as in theory. The drawbacks are that quartz saturates relatively early, with the characteristic dose constant of the saturating exponential typically around 50 to 100 grays, which sets a practical dating ceiling near twice that at roughly 150 to 200 grays and therefore ages usually not exceeding 100,000 to 150,000 years. Quartz brightness also varies enormously with geological provenance: quartz from young volcanic terrains is often so dim as to be unusable, a recognised problem in parts of the Mediterranean, Iceland and the tropics.

The feldspars, principally potassium feldspar, are the alternative. They are typically ten to a hundred times brighter than quartz, which makes single-grain measurement far easier, and they saturate at much higher doses, offering the prospect of ages reaching several hundred thousand years. They also contain potassium-40 internally, contributing an internal dose rate of roughly 0.5 to 1 gray per thousand years that is independent of the surrounding sediment and therefore stable. Feldspar is stimulated by infrared light, giving the technique its name of infrared stimulated luminescence, and infrared stimulation conveniently does not excite quartz at all, so a mixed sample can be interrogated selectively.

Feldspar's fatal flaw, discovered by Ann Wintle in 1973, is anomalous fading: the signal decays with time even though the traps ought to be thermally stable for millions of years. The mechanism is quantum-mechanical tunnelling, in which an electron escapes its trap not by acquiring enough energy to climb out but by passing directly through the barrier to a nearby recombination centre. Because tunnelling probability depends on distance rather than temperature, no amount of trap-depth calculation predicts it. Untreated, fading causes age underestimates of 20 to 50 per cent, and it is the reason feldspar was largely abandoned for two decades. It is now managed, and the modern solutions have restored feldspar to central importance, particularly for the older end of the archaeological record where quartz has saturated and can say nothing at all. A common and prudent modern practice is to measure both minerals from the same sample and compare. Where quartz and feldspar ages agree within uncertainty, confidence is high, because two systems with quite different weaknesses have converged. Where they disagree, the direction of the disagreement is itself diagnostic and usually points to fading, incomplete bleaching or an error in the dose rate.

sections.heading: Zeroing: What Event Is Actually Being Dated
sections.body:
Every luminescence age is an age since the last resetting event, and identifying that event correctly is an archaeological judgement rather than a physical measurement. The instrument cannot tell you what emptied the traps; it can only tell you how much dose has accumulated since.

Heating is the cleaner resetting mechanism. Trapped charge is fully released by holding a sample above roughly 400 to 500 degrees Celsius for a few minutes, and even brief exposure to typical fire temperatures achieves substantial emptying. A pot fired in a kiln at 700 to 900 degrees is completely zeroed, and its luminescence age is the age of firing, which is usually close to the age of manufacture and use. A flint tool that fell into a hearth, or was deliberately heat-treated to improve its knapping quality, is likewise zeroed, and its age is the age of that heating event. Burnt stones from hearths, fired daub from burnt structures, and slag from metalworking are all datable on the same principle. The interpretive question is whether the heating event relates to the archaeological event of interest, and a flint heated by a later, unrelated fire will honestly report the later date.

Sunlight is the messier mechanism, and this is where most luminescence controversies originate. Daylight bleaching is rapid but not instantaneous, and it is wavelength dependent, working fastest in the blue and ultraviolet. A quartz grain lying on an open dune surface at midday is reduced to a negligible residual within seconds to minutes and is confidently zeroed. A grain carried in turbid water a metre below the surface may receive a heavily attenuated, red-shifted light dose for only a brief transport episode and may retain a substantial residual signal from its previous burial. A grain plucked from bedrock by a glacier and deposited beneath the ice may never have seen daylight at all.

This produces a systematic distinction between depositional settings that any user of luminescence dates should hold firmly in mind. Aeolian sediments, meaning wind-blown dune sand and loess, are the ideal case and are usually well bleached. Beach and shallow marine sands are generally good. Fluvial, alluvial, colluvial and especially glacial and debris-flow sediments are variably and often incompletely bleached, and in these settings a naive average of grain doses will overestimate the age, sometimes by a factor of several. Cave and rock-shelter sediments occupy an awkward middle ground: some arrived by wind, some by water, some fell from the roof, and some were carried in on feet, so a single sample can contain grains with entirely different bleaching histories. Post-depositional mixing compounds this. Burrowing animals, tree throw, frost heave, trampling and human digging all move grains vertically through a profile, so a securely stratified layer may contain a minority of much younger grains introduced from above or older grains dragged up from below. Recognising and quantifying this mixing, rather than assuming it away, is one of the principal reasons the field moved toward measuring individual grains rather than averaging thousands of them together.

sections.heading: Collecting a Sample in the Field
sections.body:
Field sampling is where luminescence dating is most often ruined, and the failures are unrecoverable: a sample exposed to daylight for thirty seconds has had part of its age erased and no laboratory can restore it. The governing rule is that the mineral must travel from undisturbed sediment to a light-tight container without ever seeing daylight.

Equally important, and more often neglected, is that a luminescence sample is really two samples. The first is the material whose signal will be measured. The second is the surrounding sediment whose radioactivity determines the dose rate, and this must represent a sphere of about 30 centimetres radius around the sampled point because that is the range of gamma radiation. Collecting a beautiful light-tight tube and then forgetting the dose-rate material renders the whole exercise worthless.

Sample position should be chosen for sedimentological clarity rather than convenience. Avoid the top and bottom 30 centimetres of any bed, avoid the vicinity of large stones, roots, burrows and voids, and avoid boundaries between sediments of visibly different character. Record the depth below the modern surface accurately, since the cosmic dose rate depends on it, and note any evidence that a substantial thickness of overburden has been removed since deposition.
ingredients: Opaque steel or thick-walled plastic tubes, roughly 4 to 5 centimetres in diameter and 20 to 30 centimetres long, with caps and lightproof tape
A mallet and a wooden block to drive tubes without deforming them, plus a trowel and a sharp knife for cleaning the section face
Strong opaque bags for bulk dose-rate sediment, at least 500 grams per sample, sealed immediately to preserve field moisture
A portable gamma spectrometer with a probe for in-situ gamma dose measurement, where available, which is far superior to laboratory analysis of bulk sediment for heterogeneous deposits
A tape measure for burial depth, a compass and a notebook, and for night or shelter work a torch fitted with a deep red filter
steps: Clean back the exposed section by at least 20 to 30 centimetres to reach sediment that has never been light-exposed, and identify a homogeneous target bed.
Hammer the opaque tube horizontally into the cleaned face until it is full, keeping it perpendicular to the section so the sediment column stays intact.
Extract the tube, immediately cap both ends, and pack the interior with tissue or foam so grains cannot shuffle and abrade during transport.
Seal both caps with opaque tape and label the exterior with site, context, depth and orientation. Never open the tube outside a darkroom.
Collect at least 500 grams of bulk sediment from within 30 centimetres of the tube position for dose-rate analysis, and seal it at once so field water content is preserved.
If a portable gamma spectrometer is available, insert the probe into the hole left by the tube and record an in-situ measurement for several minutes.
Record burial depth, overburden density, present water table, and any evidence of erosion, disturbance, burrowing or nearby stonework that could distort the gamma field.

sections.heading: Laboratory Preparation of the Mineral
sections.body:
Everything from this point happens under subdued red or amber light, in a laboratory darkroom, because the wavelengths that reset the sample are exactly those in ordinary illumination. Red light at wavelengths above about 600 nanometres carries too little energy per photon to empty the relevant traps at any appreciable rate, so it is safe for the hours of handling required.

The first step is to discard the ends. The outer few centimetres at each end of a sampling tube may have been light-exposed during collection, so these are removed and set aside, sometimes retained for water content and dose-rate measurement. Only the protected core is used for luminescence.

Chemical treatment then strips away everything that is not the target mineral. Dilute hydrochloric acid, typically 10 per cent, dissolves carbonates. Hydrogen peroxide at 10 to 30 per cent oxidises organic matter. The sample is then wet-sieved to isolate a narrow grain size range, most commonly 90 to 250 micrometres for the coarse-grain approach, because a narrow range keeps the beta dose attenuation correction well defined.

Separating quartz from feldspar is the critical step, since even a few per cent of feldspar contamination in a quartz aliquot will contribute a fading signal and bias the age. Density separation using heavy liquids such as sodium polytungstate exploits the density gap: feldspars float at densities below about 2.58 grams per cubic centimetre, quartz sinks below 2.62, and heavy minerals such as zircon sink further still. The quartz fraction is then etched in concentrated hydrofluoric acid, conventionally 40 per cent for 40 to 60 minutes, which dissolves any remaining feldspar preferentially and simultaneously removes the outer 10 to 20 micrometres of each quartz grain, the rind that received the alpha dose. A rinse in hydrochloric acid removes precipitated fluorides, and a final sieve removes grains that etching has reduced below the target size.

Hydrofluoric acid deserves particular caution. It penetrates skin without immediate pain, and the fluoride ion binds calcium in blood and tissue, producing deep burns and potentially fatal hypocalcaemia from exposures that look trivial. It is handled only in a fume hood, in full protective equipment, with calcium gluconate gel immediately available.

For fine-grain work the route differs: the 4 to 11 micrometre fraction is separated by settling in a column according to Stokes' law, and no hydrofluoric etching is performed because the grains are small enough that removing a rind would remove the grain. Fine-grain aliquots are polymineral, containing quartz and feldspar together, so the alpha contribution must be measured and an alpha efficiency determined.

Finally the purified mineral is mounted, either as a monolayer on a disc using silicone oil, or dropped into small holes in a single-grain disc, and is ready for measurement.

sections.heading: Measuring the Equivalent Dose: the SAR Protocol
sections.body:
The single-aliquot regenerative-dose protocol, published by Andrew Murray and Ann Wintle in 2000 and universally abbreviated SAR, is the procedure that made optically stimulated luminescence a routine and reliable technique. It solves a problem that had frustrated the field for years: quartz changes its sensitivity, meaning the light emitted per unit of absorbed dose, during the very measurements used to determine dose. Heating and measuring alter the crystal, so a growth curve built from successive measurements on one aliquot is measuring a moving target.

The solution is elegant. After every measurement, whether of the natural signal or of a laboratory regenerated signal, the aliquot receives a small fixed test dose and that response is measured too. Sensitivity change affects the main signal and the test-dose response in the same proportion, so dividing one by the other cancels the drift. The quantity used to build the growth curve is the ratio, not the raw signal.

Three built-in quality checks make the protocol self-diagnosing, and results failing them are rejected rather than explained away. The recycling ratio repeats one regenerative dose at the end of the sequence; if the sensitivity correction is working, the repeat should reproduce the original within about 10 per cent. The recuperation test measures the response to a zero dose, which should be negligible, conventionally under 5 per cent of the natural signal; a large value indicates charge transferring from other traps. The infrared depletion ratio applies infrared stimulation, which excites feldspar but not quartz, before a blue stimulation; a significant drop reveals feldspar contamination.
steps: Preheat the aliquot, typically 10 seconds somewhere between 160 and 300 degrees Celsius, to empty shallow unstable traps that laboratory irradiation has filled but which would have decayed away during burial.
Stimulate with blue light at 125 degrees Celsius and record the natural luminescence decay curve; integrate the first fraction of a second and subtract a background from the tail.
Give a fixed test dose, apply a lower cut-heat, stimulate again, and record the test-dose response that will normalise this measurement.
Irradiate with a known regenerative dose chosen to bracket the expected equivalent dose, then repeat the preheat, stimulation and test-dose sequence exactly as before.
Repeat with four or five regenerative doses spanning zero to roughly twice the expected equivalent dose, so the growth curve is well constrained on both sides of the natural point.
Include a zero-dose cycle to test recuperation, a repeat of the first regenerative dose to test the recycling ratio, and an infrared-stimulated cycle to test for feldspar.
Plot corrected signal against dose, fit a saturating exponential, and interpolate the corrected natural signal onto that curve to read the equivalent dose.
Validate the whole procedure with a dose recovery test: bleach fresh aliquots, give a known laboratory dose, and confirm the protocol returns it within about 10 per cent.

sections.heading: Determining the Dose Rate
sections.body:
Half of every luminescence age comes from the dose rate, and it is the half more often responsible for systematic error, partly because it is less glamorous and partly because it requires assumptions about the past that cannot be tested directly.

The measurement begins with elemental concentrations. Several techniques are used and each has characteristic strengths. High-resolution gamma spectrometry on a dried, sealed, homogenised bulk sample measures individual radionuclides in the decay chains, which uniquely allows detection of disequilibrium. Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry gives precise total uranium, thorium and potassium but says nothing about chain equilibrium. Thick-source alpha counting and beta counting measure the radiation directly rather than the parent elements. Portable gamma spectrometry in the field measures the actual gamma field the sample experienced, which is the most reliable approach in heterogeneous sediments.

Concentrations are converted to dose rates using published conversion factors, refined several times over the decades, which state how many grays per thousand years result from a given concentration. Roughly, one part per million of uranium in secular equilibrium delivers about 0.11 grays per thousand years of beta and gamma dose combined; one per cent potassium delivers about 0.95.
