These are then adjusted for grain size, because a coarse grain absorbs only part of the beta dose delivered to the surrounding matrix, with the correction depending on grain diameter and reaching 10 to 20 per cent for sand-sized quartz.

Water content is the largest and most troublesome correction. Water absorbs radiation more efficiently per unit mass than mineral matter, so pore water attenuates the dose reaching the grains; as a rule of thumb, each one per cent of water by dry weight reduces the beta dose rate by about 1.25 per cent and the gamma by about 1.14. The correction itself is simple; the difficulty is that the required value is the average water content over the entire burial period, which nobody observed. Analysts measure present field moisture, calculate saturation, consider the palaeoenvironment, and adopt a value with a generous uncertainty, often 5 plus or minus 2 per cent for a dry site. A 5 per cent error in assumed water content translates to roughly 5 per cent in the age.

The cosmic contribution is calculated from burial depth, overburden density, geomagnetic latitude and altitude using the standard formulation of Prescott and Hutton published in 1994, giving about 0.15 to 0.30 grays per thousand years near the surface and falling steeply with depth.

The last check is radioactive equilibrium. The uranium decay chains contain radon-222, a gas, and radium and uranium isotopes of differing solubility, so groundwater can leach or deposit chain members and break the assumption that all daughters decay at the parent's rate. Disequilibrium is common in carbonate-rich and waterlogged settings and is detectable only by high-resolution gamma spectrometry.

sections.heading: Single Grains and the Statistics of Scatter
sections.body:
A conventional aliquot holds hundreds or thousands of grains, and its measured signal is their sum. If every grain shared the same history that would be an efficient way to average out noise. If they do not, averaging conceals precisely the information that matters. Recognition of this drove the development of single-grain dating, in which individual grains are dropped into a disc drilled with a hundred small holes and each is stimulated separately by a finely focused green laser at 532 nanometres.

The results were sobering and illuminating. Even in a well-behaved, well-bleached dune sand, individual grain doses scatter considerably. A large fraction of grains, often 90 to 95 per cent in quartz, emit too little light to measure at all, so the aggregate signal of a conventional aliquot is dominated by a handful of unusually bright grains whose behaviour may not represent the population. Where scatter exceeds what counting statistics and instrument reproducibility can explain, the excess is quantified as overdispersion, expressed as a percentage. Well-bleached, unmixed samples typically show 10 to 20 per cent overdispersion; values of 40, 60 or 100 per cent signal incomplete bleaching, post-depositional mixing, or a heterogeneous gamma field.

Interpreting a scattered distribution requires an explicit statistical model, and choosing one is an interpretive act that should be argued rather than assumed. The Central Age Model of Rex Galbraith and colleagues, published in 1999, returns a weighted mean dose with overdispersion as a fitted parameter, and is appropriate when scatter is symmetrical and the sample is believed well bleached. The Minimum Age Model fits a truncated distribution and returns the dose of the youngest well-defined component, which is the correct choice for a partially bleached fluvial or glacial sample where only the best-bleached grains record the true burial event. The Finite Mixture Model resolves a distribution into several discrete components and suits mixed deposits where two populations of different age have been physically combined.

Distributions are conventionally displayed on a radial plot, a device also due to Galbraith, which shows each grain's dose against its own precision, so that imprecise grains do not visually dominate. Grains consistent with a single dose fall within a band of two standard errors, and a genuine second population appears as a separate ray.

The honest caution is that the choice of model can change an age by tens of per cent, and it is made by the analyst on sedimentological grounds. This is why the Jinmium rock shelter in northern Australia was reported in 1996 as 116,000 years old on conventional multi-grain measurements and revised to around 10,000 years in 1998 when single-grain work showed the older signal came from a minority of unbleached grains weathered out of the shelter's own sandstone walls.

sections.heading: What Can Be Dated, and Over What Range
sections.body:
Anything containing quartz or feldspar that was strongly heated or thoroughly sunlit at a definable moment is a candidate. In practice the material falls into a few well-established classes.

Fired ceramics were the original application and remain the most secure. A potsherd contains abundant quartz and feldspar inclusions, was fired well above the resetting temperature, and yields an age of firing. Precision is typically 5 to 10 per cent, so a genuinely Roman pot might date to 1,850 plus or minus 130 years. This is coarse beside a good radiocarbon determination but is often the only direct date available, and it is the routine method for detecting forged antiquities.

Burnt lithics, above all burnt flint, carry the chronology of the Middle Palaeolithic. Flint contains fine-grained quartz, and a piece that entered a hearth is completely zeroed. The technique underpins the dating of the Levantine Mousterian and of key hominin sites, and it produced the 2017 result placing the Jebel Irhoud hominins in Morocco at about 315,000 years ago, the earliest widely accepted Homo sapiens fossils, an age reached by thermoluminescence on burnt flints because no other method could reach it.

Sediment is the largest modern application by volume. Wind-blown loess and dune sand give the most reliable results, and long loess sequences in China and central Europe have been dated in detail across hundreds of thousands of years. Cave and rock-shelter fills, alluvial terraces, colluvium, tsunami and storm deposits, palaeo-earthquake fault scarps and archaeological occupation surfaces have all been dated, with reliability declining as bleaching becomes less certain.

Burnt structural material extends the list further: fired daub, hearth stones, kiln linings, vitrified fort walls, mortar containing quartz sand, and metallurgical slag. Unburnt building stone can be dated indirectly, because sunlight bleaches a depth-dependent profile a few millimetres into rock, so the moment a block was laid face-down into a wall is recorded in that profile.

There are genuine exclusions. Bone, shell, wood, charcoal and metal contain no suitable mineral and cannot be dated by luminescence at all. Sediments that never saw daylight, such as material deposited directly beneath a glacier, have no resetting event and will report some earlier episode entirely.

The usable range runs from a few decades to several hundred thousand years, but the ends deserve honest statement. At the young end the limit is set by whether the accumulated dose is measurable above zero; in a typical 3 grays per thousand years environment a fifty-year-old deposit carries 0.15 grays, which is measurable in bright quartz but demands careful handling of residuals. Modern analogue studies confirm that recently deposited dune sand returns ages consistent with zero, which is the essential validation. At the old end, quartz saturates at roughly 150 to 200 grays, giving a ceiling commonly between 60,000 and 150,000 years depending on dose rate. Feldspar post-infrared protocols reach 300,000 to 500,000 years, and specialised signals such as thermally transferred optically stimulated luminescence and violet stimulated luminescence have been pushed toward a million years, though with correspondingly larger uncertainties.

sections.heading: How Luminescence Ages Go Wrong
sections.body:
Incomplete bleaching is the commonest cause of an age that is too old. If grains retained a residual signal at deposition, the measured dose includes inherited charge. The effect can be trivial in a dune and severe in a glacial outwash, where residuals equivalent to thousands of years are documented. The diagnostic signs are high overdispersion, a positively skewed dose distribution, and disagreement between quartz and feldspar in a specific direction, since feldspar bleaches more slowly than quartz and so retains more residual. The remedies are single-grain measurement with a minimum age model, and choosing sample locations in sedimentary facies most likely to have been sunlit.

Anomalous fading is the commonest cause of an age that is too young, and it affects feldspar rather than quartz. It is quantified by a fading rate called the g-value, the percentage of signal lost per decade of time on a logarithmic scale, typically 3 to 8 per cent per decade for potassium feldspar. Two responses exist. The correction approach, formalised by Huntley and Lamothe in 2001, measures the g-value and mathematically restores the lost signal, but it is only valid in the linear part of the growth curve and grows unreliable for older samples. The better approach is to use a signal that does not fade appreciably. Post-infrared infrared stimulated luminescence protocols, developed after 2008, first stimulate at a low temperature to deplete the unstable, fading-prone population, then measure at a higher temperature such as 225 or 290 degrees Celsius, isolating a much more stable signal. These protocols carry a larger unbleachable residual, so they trade one problem for a smaller one.

Saturation produces ages that are simply meaningless rather than merely wrong. As the growth curve flattens, a small uncertainty in signal maps onto an enormous uncertainty in dose. The convention is to regard doses above about twice the curve's characteristic dose constant as unreliable and to report them as minimum ages rather than ages.

Dose rate errors are quieter and therefore more dangerous. Wrongly assumed water content, undetected disequilibrium, an unrepresentative bulk sample near a boundary, or unrecognised erosion of overburden changing the cosmic contribution all shift the age smoothly with no diagnostic signature in the luminescence data.

Laboratory failures include feldspar contamination in a quartz aliquot, an unsuitable preheat temperature causing thermal transfer of charge into the measured traps, and quartz that is too dim to measure reliably.

The defence against all of these is convergent evidence. A luminescence age that agrees with radiocarbon, with stratigraphic ordering, with a tephra layer or with an independent method is far stronger than any single determination, and a laboratory that reports its quality-check statistics honestly is telling you how much to trust it.

sections.heading: Origins, Landmark Results and Current Directions
sections.body:
The physics was recognised long before the application. Robert Boyle described a diamond glowing when warmed in 1663. The suggestion that thermoluminescence could date fired material came in 1953 from Farrington Daniels and colleagues at Wisconsin, who saw that ancient pottery ought to have accumulated a measurable signal. Practical archaeological dating was built through the 1960s and 1970s, above all at the Oxford Research Laboratory for Archaeology under Martin Aitken, whose textbooks defined the field and whose laboratory established both the physics and the authentication work that funded much of it.

The transformation came in 1985, when Huntley, Godfrey-Smith and Thewalt showed in a brief Nature paper that green light released trapped charge from quartz, opening sediment to dating. Infrared stimulation of feldspar followed from Hütt and colleagues in 1988. The final enabling step was Murray and Wintle's single-aliquot regenerative-dose protocol in 2000, which made results reproducible between laboratories and turned a specialist art into a standard service.

The landmark applications show what the method uniquely provides. The peopling of Australia rests almost entirely on luminescence, because the arrival lies at or beyond radiocarbon's limit; excavations at Madjedbebe in Arnhem Land, published in 2017, used single-grain optically stimulated luminescence to place occupation at about 65,000 years ago, a result that remains debated on questions of grain mixing rather than of physics. Thermoluminescence on burnt flint provided the Jebel Irhoud age of roughly 315,000 years for early Homo sapiens in Morocco. The Jinmium episode of 1996 to 1998, in which a claimed 116,000 year age collapsed to about 10,000 under single-grain scrutiny, is the field's most instructive cautionary tale and drove the general adoption of single-grain methods.

Current work runs in several directions. Inter-laboratory comparison exercises, in which the same sealed material is circulated among many laboratories, have repeatedly shown that equivalent doses agree well between competent groups while dose rates and therefore final ages scatter more, which has focused attention on water content assumptions and dose rate conversion. Portable and field-deployable readers allow rapid screening of a section before committing to full analysis. Rock surface dating exploits the fact that light penetrates a few millimetres into rock and bleaches a depth profile, allowing the burial of a boulder or the construction of a wall to be dated from the shape of that profile. Luminescence thermochronometry uses the temperature sensitivity of shallow traps to reconstruct rock cooling histories over the past few hundred thousand years. Work continues on extending the datable range through more stable signals and on understanding the physics of fading well enough to correct it from first principles.

The realistic assessment is that luminescence is now a mature, well-validated technique with honestly quantified uncertainties, indispensable wherever radiocarbon cannot reach, and most trustworthy when its practitioners report their quality checks, state their statistical model, and say plainly what event they believe they have dated.

guides.safetyNote: Luminescence sample preparation uses concentrated hydrofluoric acid, which is exceptionally dangerous. It penetrates skin with little or no immediate pain, and the fluoride ion binds calcium in blood and tissue, so a burn covering only a few per cent of the body can cause fatal hypocalcaemia hours after an exposure that seemed trivial. It must be used only in a fume hood, in full protective equipment, by trained personnel, with calcium gluconate gel immediately to hand and a plan for emergency medical care. Radioactive sources used for laboratory irradiation are sealed and licensed, and must never be handled outside the regulatory framework governing them.

guides.title: Relative Dating Methods in Archaeology
guides.summary: How archaeologists put the past in order without knowing calendar dates: stratigraphy and the Harris matrix, association, typology, seriation, cross-dating, chemical tests on bone, and environmental frameworks, together with the pitfalls that mislead them and how relative sequences anchor to absolute time.

sections.heading: Ordering Time Without a Calendar: What Relative Dating Is
sections.body: Relative dating is the family of methods that tell you the order of things in the past, which is older and which is younger, without telling you how old anything actually is in years. It answers the question of sequence rather than the question of age. This may sound like a poor substitute for a calendar, but for most of archaeology's history it was the only tool available, and it remains the discipline's backbone today, because almost everything an excavation reveals is understood first through its position in a sequence and only later, if ever, pinned to a numerical date. The distinction matters conceptually. Absolute dating methods, such as radiocarbon, tree-ring dating, and the potassium-argon technique, produce a number with an error range: this hearth was burning around 3,300 years ago, give or take a few decades. Relative methods instead produce statements of order: this hearth is later than the wall it overlies and earlier than the pit cut through it; this style of pot precedes that one; this grave belongs to the middle phase of the cemetery. Chains of such statements, built link by link, allowed nineteenth-century scholars to construct the entire outline of human prehistory, the Stone, Bronze, and Iron Ages, generations before any laboratory could measure a date. When absolute methods finally arrived in the mid-twentieth century, they did not replace relative dating; they calibrated it, hanging numerical pegs on a framework that stratigraphy and artifact study had already erected. The logical foundations of relative dating are few and robust. The first is superposition: in any undisturbed pile of deposits, whatever is underneath was put there before whatever is on top. The second is association: things found sealed together in the same undisturbed deposit entered the ground at the same time, so dating one dates the others. The third is typological change: the things people make change over time, in style, material, and technique, and once the direction of change is established, objects can be arranged along it. Everything else, seriation curves, cross-dating between regions, chemical comparisons of buried bone, pollen zonation, is machinery built on those three foundations. It is worth being honest about what the machinery can and cannot bear. Relative sequences are local by nature; a sequence of layers is true for one trench, and extending it across a site, a region, or a continent requires argument, not assumption. Order is also not tempo: two adjacent layers may be separated by an afternoon or by five centuries, and nothing in superposition alone says which. And every relative method rests on the assumption that the ground has not been secretly rearranged, an assumption that burrowing animals, tree roots, later diggers, and collapsing structures conspire against. Archaeologists therefore treat relative dating not as a single measurement but as a web of mutually checking observations, and the strength of the web, rather than any single strand, is what carries the weight of the past.

sections.heading: Foundations Borrowed from Geology: Steno, Smith, and Deep Time
sections.body: Archaeology did not invent its dating logic; it inherited it from geology, and the inheritance is worth tracing because the principles arrive with their original justifications attached. The founding statement is usually credited to Nicolas Steno, a Danish anatomist working in Florence, who in 1669 articulated the law of superposition: strata are deposited in sequence, with the lowest laid down first, because each layer needs something already solid beneath it to settle on. Steno added two companions that archaeologists still use daily. The principle of original horizontality holds that sediments settle in roughly level sheets, so strongly tilted or folded layers must have been disturbed after deposition. The principle of lateral continuity holds that a layer originally extended until it thinned out or met a barrier, so matching layers on either side of a later cut, a river gorge or a Victorian cellar alike, were once continuous. A century and a half later the English surveyor William Smith, digging canals through the 1790s and 1800s, noticed that each rock stratum carried its own characteristic fossils and that the same fossil assemblage always appeared in the same order wherever he traveled. His principle of faunal succession let him correlate strata across all of England and publish, in 1815, the first geological map of an entire country. Substitute potsherds for fossils and Smith's method is precisely how archaeologists correlate the phases of distant settlements: distinctive artifact types succeed one another in a consistent order, so an assemblage identifies its place in the sequence wherever it turns up. The third geological gift was time itself. James Hutton in 1788 and Charles Lyell in the 1830s argued that the earth's features result from ordinary processes, deposition, erosion, uplift, running at ordinary rates over immense spans, a doctrine called uniformitarianism, summarized as the present being the key to the past. This mattered enormously for human history, because the biblical chronology then dominant allowed only about six thousand years for everything. When stone tools were found sealed in ancient river gravels alongside the bones of extinct elephants and rhinoceros, at Hoxne by John Frere in 1797, and decisively in the Somme gravels studied by Boucher de Perthes in the 1840s, the geological reading of those gravels forced the conclusion, publicly accepted by leading British scientists in 1859, that humanity was vastly older than written records. That single relative-dating argument, tools beneath undisturbed ancient deposits, created prehistory as a subject. The transfer of geological logic into excavation practice was gradual and initially crude; nineteenth-century diggers often shoveled through sites in arbitrary spits, recording depth alone. It matured through figures such as General Pitt-Rivers, who from 1880 recorded finds by layer with obsessive precision on his Cranborne Chase estates, and Mortimer Wheeler, whose grid-and-baulk excavations in the 1920s to 1940s kept standing sections of every trench so the stratification could be read, drawn, and argued from. By then archaeology possessed geology's rules and had begun adding refinements of its own, because human sites break ground in ways rivers never do.

sections.heading: How Archaeological Layers Form: Deposits, Surfaces, and Site Formation
sections.body: To read a sequence of layers you must first understand how layers come to exist, a subject archaeologists call site formation processes. An archaeological site is an accumulation of events, each of which either adds material, removes it, or rearranges it. Natural additions include windblown sand and dust, waterlaid silts, slopewash creeping downhill, volcanic ash, and the slow rain of decaying vegetation; in temperate climates these processes alone can bury an abandoned floor under several centimetres per century, though rates vary enormously with setting. Human additions are usually faster and lumpier: floors are laid and re-laid, walls of mud brick or turf melt back into thick loam when abandoned, hearths build up lenses of ash and charcoal, middens grow from daily rubbish, and whole platforms of imported soil are dumped to level ground for building. In long-occupied towns of the Middle East these processes stacked settlement on settlement until the accumulated mound, called a tell, stood tens of metres above the plain; the great tells of Mesopotamia and the Levant are effectively layer cakes of successive villages and cities spanning thousands of years. Removal is just as important and easier to overlook. People dig pits for storage, rubbish, burials, and foundations; they rob out old walls for reusable stone; they terrace hillsides and scrape yards clean. Erosion planes off exposed surfaces. Every removal event creates what analysts call an interface, a surface that is not a deposit but the record of something taken away, and interfaces carry chronological information exactly as deposits do: the moment of a pit's digging is an event in the sequence just as real as the moment of its filling. Rearrangement, finally, is the saboteur. Earthworms, studied for exactly this effect by Charles Darwin in his last book in 1881, continually pass soil through their bodies and can sink small objects many centimetres below the surface they were dropped on while sorting a stone-free worm-worked layer above; moles, rabbits, rodents, and root systems churn material between layers; frost heave lifts stones; ploughing homogenizes the top twenty to thirty centimetres of any cultivated site into a single mixed horizon. Later humans are the most energetic rearrangers of all, digging their features down into older deposits so that ancient objects end up in young fills. The practical consequence of all this is that a layer is not a slice of time but a body of material with a history: a formation event, a source for its contents, and a career of disturbance afterwards. The excavator's questions are correspondingly specific. What put this deposit here, and over how long, an afternoon's dump or a century of floor sweepings? Where did its contents come from, freshly discarded or scooped up with older soil? And has anything moved since? Only after those questions are answered does the layer's position in the pile translate into a statement about time, which is why modern excavation records soil texture, colour, inclusions, and boundaries with such apparent fussiness: those details are the evidence from which formation, and therefore meaning, is inferred.

sections.heading: Reading the Section: Stratigraphy in Excavation Practice
sections.body: Excavation destroys its own evidence as it proceeds, so stratigraphic reading is organized around capturing relationships before they vanish. The classic instrument is the section: a deliberately preserved vertical face of soil, kept straight and clean, in which the stack of deposits can be seen edge-on like the layers in a cut cake. Where the sequence is deep and well differentiated, a single drawn and photographed section can summarize centuries: a buried topsoil at the base, a rammed-chalk floor above it, a lens of charcoal and burnt daub from a fire, a thick dump of levelling rubble, a mortar spread from later construction, and the dark loam of abandonment sealing everything. Reading such a face rests on a small toolkit of observations. Layers are distinguished by colour, texture, compaction, and inclusions, differences often subtle enough that excavators clean the face with a trowel and view it in low-angle light, or spray it lightly with water, to make boundaries legible. The nature of each boundary matters as much as the layers it separates: a gradual mottled transition suggests slow accumulation or biological mixing, while a knife-sharp line suggests a deliberately laid surface or an episode of trampling or erosion, and a boundary that truncates the layers beneath it, cutting across their edges, is the signature of removal, an interface where something, a pit, a terrace, an erosion event, took material away. Tip-lines, the sloping streaks visible inside a dumped fill, even record the direction from which a pit or ditch was backfilled. From these observations the excavator applies superposition, but with archaeological caution, because human sites violate the geological ideal constantly. Deposits banked against a standing wall can be later than deposits on the wall's other side at the same height; a collapsed roof can deposit older material on top of younger; and the contents of a layer, the sherds and coins inside it, date the layer's material, not necessarily its deposition, since old rubbish is endlessly recycled in soil. The rule that survives all this is that physical relationships, which deposit overlies which, which cut truncates which, are the facts, and depth below the modern surface is nearly meaningless by itself, a lesson learned painfully from early excavations recorded in arbitrary spits. Field practice has accordingly split into two traditions. Section-led excavation, associated with Mortimer Wheeler and refined by Kathleen Kenyon at Jericho in the 1950s, digs in a grid of squares separated by standing baulks whose faces preserve continuous sections. Open-area excavation, which became standard for complex urban and rural sites from the 1960s onward, removes deposits one at a time across a wide area in the reverse of the order they accumulated, recording each in plan; it sacrifices the permanent standing section but follows each layer's true extent and reveals features, post holes, hearths, foundation trenches, that narrow trenches dismember. Most modern projects blend the two, and both feed the same product: a record of every deposit and interface, each given a unique context number, with its physical relationships to its neighbours explicitly noted, which is the raw material of sequence-building.

sections.heading: The Harris Matrix: Turning Layers into a Sequence
sections.body: A drawn section shows the sequence along one vertical slice, but a real site is three-dimensional, and by the 1970s large urban excavations in cities like Winchester and London were producing thousands of deposits whose relationships no single drawing could hold. The solution was devised in 1973 by Edward Harris, working on the Winchester material, and is now used worldwide under the name of the Harris matrix. Its insight is that for dating purposes only three relationships between any two recorded contexts matter: one is earlier than the other, established when one physically overlies, fills, or is cut into the other; the two are equivalent, being severed parts of what was originally a single deposit; or they have no direct physical relationship at all. Every other nuance of shape and composition, however important for interpretation, is irrelevant to sequence. Harris's second insight was that a context's essential stratigraphic position is fully captured by its immediate neighbours only: the things directly above it and directly below it. Relationships with remoter contexts follow logically and need not be recorded. This reduction lets the whole site be drawn as a single diagram, the matrix, in which each context is a numbered box, boxes are connected by lines running downward from later to earlier, and equivalent contexts are joined side by side. Reading upward from the bottom traces the site's growth; any two boxes connected by a downward path are in fixed chronological order, while boxes on parallel branches, say the fills of two separate pits that never touch, are of unknowable relative age on stratigraphic evidence alone, and the diagram honestly displays that ignorance as the absence of a connecting path. Building the matrix is a discipline as much as a drawing. Each context sheet records the numbers of every context above and below; the matrix is assembled from those assertions, and contradictions, a claimed loop in which A is above B, B above C, and C above A, are logically impossible and flag a recording error to be resolved while the evidence may still be checkable. Once the full diagram exists, the analyst simplifies it into phases: groups of contexts, such as all the construction deposits of one building, that belong to a single episode of activity, producing a site history of manageable chunks, construction, occupation, destruction, abandonment, rebuilding, each phase bracketed by the phases before and after. The matrix also disciplines the use of finds. Artifacts date deposits, not the reverse, only through argued association, and when a datable object is assigned to a context, the matrix instantly propagates the consequences: everything below that context must be earlier than or contemporary with the object's deposition, everything above later. A single well-stratified coin can thereby constrain hundreds of contexts at once. The method's limits are the limits of stratification itself: it records order, never duration or gaps, and it is only as good as the excavator's identification of contexts and interfaces in the ground. But as a bookkeeping instrument for sequence it has no rival, and it made the relative chronology of even the most tangled urban sites tractable.

sections.heading: Cuts, Fills, and Features: Dating Events That Remove Evidence
sections.body: Much of what people do to the ground subtracts rather than adds, and handling subtraction correctly is where archaeological stratigraphy most clearly parts company with geology. Consider the simplest case, a rubbish pit. Its history contains at least three distinct events. First the pit was dug: an act that created no deposit at all, only a cut, the interface where the digger's spade truncated whatever layers already existed. Then the pit was filled, perhaps in one dump, perhaps in many episodes distinguishable as separate fills with their own tip-lines and lenses. Finally later deposits sealed the filled pit over. The chronological grammar of this little story repays careful statement. The cut is later than every layer it truncates, since you cannot dig through what is not yet there. The fills are later than the cut, and each fill is later than the fill beneath it. The sealing layer is later than the uppermost fill. Crucially, the cut and its fills can be separated by any amount of time: a defensive ditch dug in one century may silt up over the next three, so treating a ditch and its contents as one dated event is a standard beginner's error. Equally crucially, the objects inside a fill date the filling at best, never the digging, and even the filling only loosely, because fill dirt is usually scraped up from the surroundings and arrives pre-loaded with older artifacts. The habit of recording cuts as first-class entities, with their own context numbers, entered standard practice with the single-context recording systems of the 1970s, and it transformed the dating of exactly the features that matter most on many sites: graves, whose cut marks the burial event while the objects in the backfill may be centuries older; post holes, where the pit dug for the post, the packing around it, and the void or rot-fill left when the post decayed are three separately datable elements; wells, quarries, cellars, and foundation trenches. Foundation trenches deserve special note because they date buildings. A wall footing is normally set in a trench dug from some contemporary ground surface, and identifying the level from which that trench was cut establishes which surfaces the builders stood on, and therefore which occupation deposits precede the building; artifacts sealed in the construction trench's backfill give the wall a maximum age. Robber trenches, dug long after abandonment to steal the stone out of buried walls, replay the same logic in reverse and are a common trap, since a robbed wall survives only as a stone-flecked trench whose fill is far younger than the building it outlines. The general principle underlying all these cases is that events, not objects, are what a site chronology is made of, and many of the most important events, digging, demolition, robbing, erosion, leveling, are represented in the ground purely by interfaces. A sequence built only from deposits, ignoring the surfaces between them, systematically misses the destructive half of human behaviour and will misdate the constructive half in consequence.

sections.heading: Association and Assemblage: Dating by the Company Things Keep
sections.body: Objects rarely carry their age on their face; they borrow dates from their companions. The principle of association states that items found together in a genuinely sealed, undisturbed deposit entered the ground at the same time, so establishing the date of one establishes the date of deposition for all. A grave is the exemplary case: the skeleton, the brooch at the shoulder, the pot at the feet, and the beads at the neck were placed in the earth in a single event, so a coin among them whose minting date is known from written records anchors the whole group, and by extension gives at least one fixed point for every other grave containing brooches or pots of the same types. Association is thus the bridge over which dates travel from historically documented objects, coins, inscriptions, datable imports, into the mute mass of everyday material. The strength of the bridge depends entirely on the integrity of the sealing, and archaeologists grade their trust accordingly. A closed find, a hoard buried in a single pot, an intact tomb, a room buried by volcanic ash, carries the highest confidence. An ordinary occupation layer is weaker, since it may have accumulated over decades and suffered mixing. A ploughed field surface is weakest of all, an open find in which association means little more than shared geography. Two systematic complications must be reasoned through even in good deposits. The first is time-lag: objects have use-lives, and what is buried together was discarded together, not made together. A coin circulates for decades before it is lost; an heirloom sword may be a century old at burial; fine pottery is curated longer than cooking ware. Association therefore dates deposition, and the manufacture dates of the objects inside scatter backward from that moment by their varying use-lives. The second is residuality, the presence of much older material accidentally incorporated when soil was moved, which is discussed in its own right as a pitfall but enters here as the reason a deposit is dated by its latest reliable object, never its average. From association grows the working concept of the assemblage: the total set of artifact types that occur together repeatedly across many contexts and sites. When the same combination, say a particular pot form, a brooch style, and a glass bead type, recurs in grave after grave and layer after layer, it defines a chronological horizon, a slice of time during which that combination was in circulation. Assemblages, not single objects, are what regional chronologies are really made of, precisely because they average out the quirks of individual use-lives. The nineteenth-century organization of European prehistory was built this way: Christian Jürgensen Thomsen, arranging the Danish national collection from 1816 and publishing in 1836, sorted closed finds by their material associations to demonstrate that stone tools, bronze, and iron represented three successive ages rather than a jumble, and his student Jens Worsaae then verified the order stratigraphically in Danish bogs and burial mounds. That three-age system, an achievement of pure associational reasoning, remains the top-level framework of Old World prehistory.

sections.heading: Terminus Post Quem and Terminus Ante Quem
sections.body: Two Latin phrases carry most of the logical weight when relative sequences meet datable objects, and using them precisely is what separates rigorous dating arguments from wishful ones. A terminus post quem, abbreviated TPQ and meaning the limit after which, is the earliest possible date for a deposit, fixed by the youngest datable thing inside it. A layer containing a coin struck in AD 337 was deposited in or after 337; it cannot be older than its own contents. It can, however, be arbitrarily younger, because the coin may have circulated for sixty years before it was dropped, or been dug up and redeposited centuries later. A TPQ is therefore a one-way gate: it forbids earlier dates and says nothing against later ones, and the deposit's true date tends to sit somewhat after the TPQ by an amount that depends on the object's typical use-life, a residue of uncertainty that no logic can squeeze out. The complementary limit, the terminus ante quem or TAQ, the limit before which, is rarer and more precious: a date by which the deposit must already have existed. TAQs come from overlying events whose dates are known. Everything beneath the ash that buried Pompeii on the eruption date of Vesuvius in AD 79 was in place by that day; everything cut by a wall whose construction is documented to a given year is older than that year; everything sealed under a dated mosaic floor precedes the floor. Between a TPQ from below-or-within and a TAQ from above, a deposit is bracketed, and where written history is rich, as in Roman or medieval towns, the brackets can close to within decades. Several disciplined habits follow from the logic. The latest object rules: a fill with two hundred first-century sherds and one thirteenth-century sherd has a thirteenth-century TPQ, however inconvenient, unless the intruder can be shown to be genuinely intrusive, delivered later by a root hole or burrow, which is an argument about site formation that must be made, not assumed. Coins are the classic TPQ instruments because minting dates are precise, but they must be identified and their circulation spans considered; a worn coin testifies to a long gap between minting and loss. Manufactured goods with documented production ranges, clay tobacco pipes with makers' marks, dated bottle glass, printed ceramics with registry marks, serve the same role on post-medieval sites, and on prehistoric sites the function is taken over by types whose currency is fixed by cross-reference elsewhere. The propagation of termini through a stratigraphic sequence is where the Harris matrix earns its keep: a TPQ in one context flows downward as a TAQ for nothing, but upward it constrains every later context, since whatever overlies a post-337 deposit is itself post-337; conversely a securely dated horizon high in the sequence hands a TAQ to everything beneath it. Whole site chronologies are assembled by shuttling these limits up and down the matrix until every phase is squeezed between the tightest available pair, and the honest residue, phases bracketed only loosely, is reported as such rather than split by guesswork.

sections.heading: Typology: The Logic of Ordering Things by Form
sections.body: Artifacts change through time the way everything made by cultural beings changes: gradually, directionally over stretches, and with enough consistency that form can serve as a clock. Typology is the method that exploits this, classifying objects into types by shared attributes of shape, material, decoration, and technique, and then arranging the types into a developmental order. The method was systematized in late nineteenth-century Scandinavia, above all by Oscar Montelius, who between the 1870s and his classic 1903 statement of method divided the Scandinavian Bronze Age into six sequential periods using thousands of closed finds. His procedure remains the template. First, classify: reduce the continuous variety of, say, bronze axes to a manageable set of types defined by explicit attributes, flat axes, flanged axes, palstaves, socketed axes. Second, hypothesize a developmental order using internal evidence, and here Montelius leaned on the observation that artifacts carry vestigial features, elements that were functional in an ancestral form and survive as decoration in descendants, the way early socketed axes retain cast imitations of the flanges and stop-ridges that earlier forms needed structurally, or the way chariot-shaped razors keep a loop where a working handle once was. The direction of change runs from functional to skeuomorphic, a term for an ornamental vestige of a once-practical feature. Third, and decisively, test the hypothesized order against closed finds: if axes of type B repeatedly occur in hoards and graves with objects that stratigraphy or other associations show to be intermediate in date, while type A consistently keeps earlier company and type C later, the seriated order is confirmed; a single secure closed find combining supposedly distant types forces revision. Typology is thus not an aesthetic intuition but a hypothesis-testing loop between form and association. Its power in practice is enormous because certain artifact classes evolve quickly and are ubiquitous. Pottery is the workhorse: fabric, rim form, base form, surface treatment, and decoration all drift measurably within generations, and sherds are nearly indestructible and discarded in quantity, so a trained ceramicist can assign a handful of sherds to a phase of a regional sequence on inspection. Metalwork, brooches above all, evolves even faster in some periods; coins are typology perfected by the state, with dated issues; stone tools change more slowly but carry the deep Palaeolithic sequence, from Oldowan choppers through Acheulean handaxes to prepared-core and blade technologies, that organizes the first three million years of the human record. The method's assumptions must be kept in view, because each is violated somewhere. Change is not always gradual: styles can be revived deliberately, and archaism misleads. It is not always directional in the same sense everywhere: a type invented in one region arrives late in another, so typological phases are local until proven otherwise. Function complicates form: a plain cooking pot may stay unchanged for centuries beside rapidly evolving fine ware, so different classes tick at different rates. And typology dates manufacture traditions, not the day an individual object was buried. Handled with those cautions, and always anchored back to stratigraphy and association, typology remains the most widely applied relative dating instrument in existence.

sections.heading: Seriation: Petrie's Sequence Dating and Frequency Curves
sections.body: Seriation is typology made quantitative: instead of ordering individual types, it orders whole collections, graves, pits, site phases, by the mix of types they contain, on the principle that assemblages closest in composition are closest in time. Its founding achievement is one of the intellectual landmarks of archaeology. In 1899 the Egyptologist Flinders Petrie faced roughly nine hundred predynastic graves from cemeteries at Diospolis Parva in Upper Egypt, each containing pottery but nothing historically datable, since the graves predated Egyptian writing. Petrie recorded the pottery types present in each grave on a slip of card and physically rearranged the slips until types showed coherent runs: each pottery type concentrated in a continuous block of graves, appearing, flourishing, and disappearing without gaps. The ordering that best satisfied all types simultaneously he took as the cemeteries' chronological sequence, and he divided it into fifty numbered sequence dates, S.D. 30 through 80. He fixed the direction of time using typological drift, notably the degeneration of functional wavy ledge handles on jars into mere painted squiggles, and the scheme, refined, still underpins predynastic Egyptian chronology, its sequence dates later shown by radiocarbon to span roughly the millennium before 3000 BC. What Petrie had invented, contextual seriation based on presence or absence, was generalized in the twentieth century into frequency seriation, which uses proportions rather than mere presence. The empirical regularity behind it is the battleship curve: plot a type's share of an assemblage against time and the shape is a slow rise from rarity, a broad peak of popularity, and a slow decline to extinction. Given assemblages of unknown order, one seeks the arrangement in which every type's frequency bars form such a single-peaked curve. American archaeologists, above all James Ford working on Mississippi Valley ceramics in the 1930s to 1950s, made this the standard tool for ordering surface collections from hundreds of sites, and a famous 1966 study by James Deetz and Edwin Dethlefsen verified the whole logic against colonial New England gravestones, whose carved dates let the death's-head, cherub, and urn-and-willow motifs be watched succeeding one another in exactly the predicted battleship curves, at slightly different times in different towns. That last observation names the method's chief caution: seriation orders assemblages along a gradient of similarity, and time is only one possible gradient. Geographic distance, social class, and site function can also structure similarity, a rural parish lagging urban fashion, a poor cemetery lacking rich types, so a seriation must be checked against independent evidence, stratigraphy above all, before its axis is read as time, and even then its direction, which end is early, must be supplied from outside. Assemblages must also be comparable in kind and drawn from one cultural tradition, and each should represent a short interval, since long-accumulating deposits smear the curves. Within those constraints seriation is uniquely powerful where stratification is absent, ordering shallow sites, ploughed scatters, and cemeteries that superposition can never touch, and its modern descendants use correspondence analysis and related multivariate statistics to extract the same orderings algorithmically, with the archaeologist still responsible for proving the axis means time.

sections.heading: Cross-Dating: Linking Sequences Across Regions
sections.body: Every stratigraphic column and every seriation is an island of local order, and cross-dating is the method of building bridges between islands, transferring chronological position, and ultimately calendar dates, from regions that have them to regions that do not. The mechanism is the traded object. When an artifact manufactured in one cultural sphere turns up stratified in another, it links the two sequences at that point: the deposit containing the import cannot be earlier than the import's manufacture, and if the import's date is known historically, the whole local phase around it inherits an anchor. Before radiocarbon, this was the only way prehistoric Europe could be dated in years at all, and the anchor of anchors was Egypt, whose king lists, regnal years, and occasional astronomically fixable records provide a written chronology reaching back to about 3000 BC. Dates flowed outward along trade routes in both directions of inference. Egyptian and Egyptianizing objects, scarabs, faience, inscribed stone, found in Aegean contexts dated Minoan Crete and Mycenaean Greece: Arthur Evans framed the Minoan sequence at Knossos this way in the early 1900s. Aegean products found elsewhere then carried the dates onward, Mycenaean pottery in its recognizable phases turning up from Sicily to the Levant, and metal types and faience beads relayed the framework, with diminishing precision, into temperate Europe. The logic has well-understood failure modes that any user must weigh. Transport takes time and objects have use-lives, so an import is always somewhat older than its foreign findspot, occasionally much older: Egyptian antiques circulated for centuries, and a scarab may be an heirloom or even an ancient forgery, so single links are weak and cross-dating lives on repeated, consistent associations in both directions. Identification must be secure, since local imitations of prestigious imports are common and date differently. And the method inherits every error in the anchor chronology: the long-running argument between high and low chronologies for the Bronze Age eastern Mediterranean, turning partly on the dating of the Thera volcanic eruption, shows how a shift of decades at the anchor propagates everywhere downstream. A related instrument is the horizon: a distinctive style or artifact that spread very widely in a short time, so its appearance marks approximately the same moment across its whole range. Historic examples make the idea concrete, such as the near-instant spread of particular Roman terra sigillata forms across the empire, datable within decades by kiln records and dated sites; prehistoric examples include widespread bell beaker pottery in third-millennium Europe or Chavín art styles in the Andes. Horizons let regional sequences be aligned wholesale rather than link by link, at the cost of assuming rapid spread, which must itself be demonstrated. When radiocarbon arrived it did not retire cross-dating but audited it, largely vindicating the Egyptian-anchored web in the east while famously breaking some of its longer extrapolations, as when calibrated dates showed megalithic monuments in Atlantic Europe to be older than the eastern Mediterranean models they had been assumed to copy, a correction Colin Renfrew publicized in the 1970s as the collapse of the diffusionist short chronology.

sections.heading: Chemical Relative Dating of Bone: Fluorine, Uranium, and Nitrogen
sections.body: Buried bone is chemically restless, and its slow exchanges with the surrounding soil can be read as a relative clock for materials from the very same deposit. Three elements carry the signal, remembered as the FUN methods. Fluorine diffuses from groundwater into bone's mineral framework, hydroxyapatite, converting it gradually to the more stable fluorapatite; the longer a bone lies in fluorine-bearing ground, the more fluorine it accumulates, and the process effectively never reverses. Uranium, similarly dissolved in trace amounts in groundwater, is likewise progressively absorbed by buried bone and can be measured nondestructively by counting its radioactivity. Nitrogen runs the opposite way: fresh bone contains about four to five percent nitrogen in its protein, collagen, which decays after burial at a rate governed by temperature, moisture, and microbes, so nitrogen content falls with time in the ground. None of these processes runs at a universal rate; fluorine uptake in one gravel bed proceeds utterly differently from uptake in a chalk downland, so the measurements can never yield an age in years. What they can do, powerfully, is answer one precise question: have these bones, found in the same deposit, actually been buried for the same length of time? Contemporaneous bones from one deposit share a groundwater history and should show similar fluorine, uranium, and nitrogen values; an intrusive or planted bone betrays itself by mismatched chemistry. The method's celebrity case is the destruction of the Piltdown fraud. From 1912 gravel diggings at Piltdown in Sussex had yielded fragments of a thick human braincase together with an apelike jaw, celebrated by some as the missing link and increasingly anomalous as genuine human fossils accumulated elsewhere. In 1949 Kenneth Oakley applied a fluorine test: the Piltdown bones held far less fluorine than the genuinely ancient animal fossils from the same gravels, showing they were not ancient members of that deposit. The full reanalysis published with Joseph Weiner and Wilfrid Le Gros Clark in 1953 added the nitrogen evidence, the jaw retaining nearly fresh-bone protein levels, and closer inspection revealed artificial staining and filed-down teeth: the find was a modern orangutan jaw planted beside a medieval-to-recent human skull. A forty-year-old phantom that had distorted accounts of human evolution was deleted by a relative dating test costing a few milligrams of bone. The same trio settled a genuine question at Swanscombe in Kent, where fluorine analysis confirmed that a human skull's fragments belonged with the interglacial fauna of their gravel terrace, and it has been used repeatedly to sort mixed cave assemblages, where bones of many ages tumble together, into burial cohorts before expensive absolute methods are applied. The methods' limits are inherent in their chemistry: they compare only materials from effectively identical burial environments, ideally the same layer of the same site; they are qualitative or at best semi-quantitative; and modern absolute techniques have taken over most of their former ambitions. But as a cheap internal consistency check on associations involving bone, and as the instrument that killed archaeology's most damaging forgery, they remain the textbook demonstration that relative dating includes the laboratory as well as the trench.

sections.heading: Environmental Frameworks: Pollen Zones, Varves, and Volcanic Ash
sections.body: Nature writes its own stratified records, and archaeology dates itself relatively by tying cultural material into them. The most widely used is the pollen record. Pollen grains have walls of sporopollenin, among the most decay-resistant organic substances known, and in waterlogged, acidic settings, peat bogs and lake beds, they accumulate in sequence and preserve for tens of thousands of years, each grain identifiable to plant genus or sometimes species under a microscope. Counting the proportions of pollen types through a vertical core yields a vegetation history: in northwest Europe, the retreat of the last glaciation is followed by successive dominance of birch, then pine, then hazel and mixed oak forest, then the elm decline around 5,000 years ago, a sharp drop in elm pollen coinciding with the arrival of farming, then increasing grasses, cereals, and weeds of cultivation as clearance spread. Early twentieth-century workers, building on the Blytt-Sernander division of postglacial climate into named periods such as Boreal, Atlantic, and Sub-Boreal, formalized these changes into numbered pollen zones, and an archaeological find from a bog or lake edge could be dated by which zone's pollen surrounded it: an axe haft from the hazel-dominated zone is older than one from above the elm decline. Within a single bog such placements are secure superposition; between regions they inherit the caution that vegetation change was not simultaneous everywhere. Annually layered sediments provide a second natural framework. Proglacial lakes deposit varves, paired coarse-summer and fine-winter laminae, one couplet per year; the Swedish geologist Gerard De Geer, counting and matching varve sequences from lake to lake from the 1880s onward, built a year-by-year chronology of the Scandinavian deglaciation thousands of years long, the direct methodological ancestor of tree-ring dating. Archaeological material associated with a counted varve sequence, or with shorelines graded to it, borrows its place in that ladder. The third great framework is volcanic. A large eruption spreads a layer of ash, tephra, across huge regions in days; each eruption's glass shards carry a distinctive geochemical fingerprint identifiable even in microscopic, invisible concentrations, called cryptotephra, in peat and lake cores far from the volcano. A recognized tephra is therefore an isochron, a surface of identical age wherever it occurs: everything beneath it everywhere is older than the eruption, everything above younger, and once the eruption itself is dated by any means, every sequence containing the layer inherits the date instantly. Iceland's historically recorded eruptions knit together the chronologies of North Atlantic settlement sites; the Vesuvius ash of AD 79 seals Pompeii and Herculaneum to a single day; the massive Thera eruption ties Aegean Bronze Age deposits together even while its own absolute date remains argued over; and ash from the Toba supereruption about 74,000 years ago serves as a marker horizon across South Asia. Ice cores add a final ledger, their annual layers recording volcanic acid spikes and other events that increasingly cross-tie all these archives. For the archaeologist the common logic is the same: these natural sequences are stratigraphy with wider reach, and every secure tie into them converts local site order into regional, sometimes hemispheric, relative chronology.

sections.heading: Surface Chemistry Clocks: Obsidian Hydration, Patina, and Weathering
sections.body: Between strict relative methods and true absolute dating lies a family of techniques based on the slow, cumulative alteration of exposed surfaces, useful chiefly for ordering material and only cautiously for estimating age. The best developed is obsidian hydration. Obsidian, volcanic glass prized everywhere it occurs for its razor edges, absorbs atmospheric and soil moisture into any freshly fractured surface; the water diffuses inward, creating a hydrated rim that thickens with time and shows under high magnification as a distinct band on a polished thin section, typically a few micrometres wide, with a measurable optical boundary. Every flake struck in toolmaking starts a new rim at thickness zero, so the rim on an artifact's worked surface records time since manufacture. Introduced by the geologists Irving Friedman and Robert Smith in 1960, the method is genuinely quantitative in its measurement but only conditionally so in its interpretation, because the rim grows at a rate that depends strongly on temperature, roughly doubling with modest warming, on the glass's chemical composition, which varies by volcanic source, and on humidity. Within a single site, where artifacts share one burial climate and often one obsidian source, rim thicknesses provide an excellent relative ordering, cheap enough to run on hundreds of pieces, and calibrated against radiocarbon-dated contexts they can be converted to approximate years; transported across climates or sources without recalibration they mislead badly. Related logic applies to other materials, always more loosely. Flint and chert develop patina, a white or glossy surface alteration, and deeply patinated pieces in a mixed surface scatter are, other things equal, older than fresh ones, though soil chemistry so dominates the rate that the comparison is only safe within one field. Exposed rock surfaces accumulate rock varnish, a dark manganese-iron film, relevant to dating petroglyphs pecked through it, and weathering rinds thicken on boulders in datable glacial deposits; lichen colonies on stone grow at measurable rates, exploited as lichenometry to order features like moraines and stone monuments over the last few centuries. All these surface clocks share a common set of hazards that must be checked case by case. The clock resets on damage: a retouched or re-flaked obsidian tool carries rims of two ages, which is itself useful for detecting reuse but ruins naive dating. The environment controls the rate, so comparisons are valid only within uniform conditions. And several of the phenomena, patination especially, can stall or even reverse. Used within those limits, surface methods fill a real niche: they order the enormous quantities of undatable lithic material that dominate surface archaeology in obsidian-rich regions like Mesoamerica, the North American Great Basin, and Anatolia, they flag mixed collections by revealing bimodal rim distributions, and they extend rough chronology to landscapes where nothing organic survives for radiocarbon. They also teach the general lesson of this whole class of evidence: a physical process only becomes a clock when its rate is known or held constant, and the archaeologist's first duty with any such method is to ask what, besides time, drives the measurement.

sections.heading: Pitfalls: Disturbance, Residuality, and Intrusion
sections.body: Every relative dating argument assumes the ground has kept its order, and the commonest serious errors in archaeology come from cases where it has not. The failure modes deserve to be known individually, because each has its own signature and its own remedy. Residuality is the presence of material older than the deposit containing it, and it is not an anomaly but the normal condition of settlement soil: every time earth is dug, moved, or re-deposited, it carries its old artifacts along, so a medieval pit fill in a Roman town routinely contains far more Roman sherds than medieval ones. The deposit's date is set by its latest reliable material, but residuality does its damage subtly, by sheer weight of numbers tempting the excavator to date a context by its majority content, and by starving late phases of distinctive finds so they masquerade as earlier. The diagnostic clues are abrasion and size, since much-recycled sherds are small and edge-worn, and the remedy is discipline about the latest-object rule combined with awareness of how much earlier activity there was on the spot to be recycled. Intrusion is the mirror image: material younger than its deposit, delivered downward. The carriers are specific and worth listing. Deep-burrowing animals move objects both ways; worms sink small finds below surfaces they were dropped on; roots open channels down which small objects and even seeds travel; desiccation cracks in clay soils swallow surface material a metre deep; and later features whose edges went unrecognized in excavation, a pit cut invisible against a similar fill, quietly donate their young contents to an old layer. Small, dense items, seeds, beads, coins, teeth, are the most mobile, which is why a single anomalous find should provoke a site-formation argument rather than an instant re-dating. Wholesale disturbance has grander agents. Ploughing amalgamates the upper strata of most lowland sites into one mixed horizon, erasing all vertical order while roughly preserving horizontal patterning, which is why ploughzone archaeology leans on seriation and spatial statistics instead of stratigraphy. Erosion and redeposition can move entire coherent-looking soil bodies downslope, artifacts included, so a terrace or valley fill may be a secondary context whose contents share transport, not contemporaneity; rolled, abraded artifacts and sorted sediments are the tell-tale. Frost churning in periglacial climates, gravity slumping into old features as their fills compact, and the collapse of buildings, which lays roof material over floor material in reverse order of construction, all invert or scramble local sequences in ways an alert excavator can recognize and model. Reoccupation and curation confuse in a different register: people reuse old monuments, rebury heirlooms, and dig up and redeposit their own ancestors, so genuinely associated groups can contain objects centuries apart in manufacture. None of these hazards is fatal; all are manageable by the same three habits. Record formation evidence, boundaries, sorting, abrasion, articulation, as carefully as the finds. Prefer arguments resting on many contexts to those resting on one. And treat every date-bearing object as a witness whose testimony must be cross-examined for how it got where it was found, not merely read off.

sections.heading: From Relative to Absolute: How the Two Kinds of Dating Work Together
sections.body: Radiocarbon dating, announced by Willard Libby in 1949, and the family of physical methods that followed did not make relative dating obsolete; they made it more valuable, because numbers and order constrain each other, and modern chronology is built from their combination. The relationship runs in both directions. Absolute methods calibrate relative frameworks: a handful of radiocarbon dates through a pollen core turns its zones into a dated environmental history; dates on key graves turn a seriated cemetery sequence into a timeline; and the tree-ring record, itself relative matching of ring-width patterns until anchored on living trees, now supplies the calibration curve that converts radiocarbon measurements into calendar years. In return, relative evidence disciplines the numbers. Every laboratory date carries statistical uncertainty, typically decades for radiocarbon, and some carry undetected errors from contamination or from dating the wrong event, old wood from a long-lived timber giving the tree's growth date rather than the building's construction. Stratigraphy exposes such misfits mercilessly: if a sample from a lower layer yields a younger date than a sample sealed above it, at least one measurement or one association is wrong, and the matrix says exactly which relationships are at stake. Since the late 1990s this mutual constraint has been formalized in Bayesian chronological modelling, implemented in widely used programs such as OxCal. The stratigraphic order of samples is entered as prior information, mathematical statements that context 12 is earlier than context 8, and the radiocarbon likelihoods are then combined with those priors to produce posterior date ranges for every event, ranges routinely two to three times narrower than the raw dates alone. The approach re-dated Stonehenge's construction phases, resolved the internal sequence of Neolithic long barrows to within lifetimes in the work of Alasdair Whittle and Alex Bayliss, and has become standard wherever sequences are deep and samples plentiful. The practical division of labour on a modern excavation follows from all this. Relative methods remain the primary structure: single-context recording and the Harris matrix organize the site into a sequence and phases; typology and seriation date the mass of finds against regional frameworks and sort what is worth absolute dating; association and the termini rules decide which samples genuinely date which events. Absolute dates are then spent strategically, on short-lived, single-event materials, a cereal grain, an articulated bone, from contexts whose stratigraphic position will let each result constrain many others through the model. Where absolute methods cannot reach, and the gaps are real, iron and stone without organic association, arid surface scatters, periods where the calibration curve flattens into plateaus such as much of the Iron Age around 800 to 400 BC, relative methods still carry the chronology alone. The deepest lesson of the partnership is conceptual. Archaeology's subject is not points in time but order, duration, and succession, which built what, what replaced what, how fast things changed, and those are relational questions. Absolute dating supplies the scale; relative dating supplies the structure; and a site report that muddles either is wrong in ways the other will eventually reveal.

guides.title: Seriation and Typology
guides.summary: How archaeologists put the undated past in order: the logic of artifact classification, the history and mechanics of typological and seriational dating from Thomsen and Petrie to computational methods, worked examples, and the assumptions and failure modes of the whole apparatus.

sections.heading: Ordering the Past Without Calendars
sections.body: Archaeology's founding problem is time. Objects come out of the ground mute: a potsherd, a bronze pin, a stone blade carries no date stamp, and for most of the discipline's history there was no laboratory technique that could supply one. Radiocarbon dating did not exist until 1949, and even today it cannot date a coin, costs money, requires organic material, and delivers ranges rather than points. Yet archaeologists routinely arrange thousands of graves, village sites, and artifact styles into sequences spanning centuries, often correctly to within a generation. The intellectual machinery that makes this possible rests on two linked ideas: typology, the disciplined classification of artifacts into types based on their observable attributes, and seriation, the arrangement of those types or the assemblages containing them into a serial order that reflects the passage of time. Together they constitute relative dating, which answers the question of what came before what without necessarily saying when, as opposed to absolute dating, which attaches numbers to years. The core insight is deceptively simple: things made by people change through time in patterned, directional ways. Automobile tailfins, telephone handsets, typefaces, and trouser cuts all rise in popularity, peak, and fade, and anyone shown photographs of unfamiliar cars can arrange them roughly by decade using nothing but stylistic drift. Seriation formalizes that everyday intuition into a method with explicit assumptions, reproducible procedures, and known failure modes. Its importance is hard to overstate. Before the radiometric revolution, virtually the entire chronological skeleton of world prehistory, the ordering of Egyptian predynastic cultures, the phases of the European Bronze Age, the ceramic sequences of the American Southwest and Southeast, the periodization of Greek vase painting, was built by typological and seriational reasoning, and when radiocarbon arrived it largely confirmed the orderings while correcting the absolute spans attached to them. The methods remain indispensable now, because most archaeological material still cannot be directly dated: surface surveys recover millions of sherds from plowed fields with no stratigraphy at all, cemetery excavations yield grave groups whose bones may be poorly preserved, and museum collections hold artifacts excavated a century ago with minimal records. Seriation also does something absolute dating cannot: it measures the tempo of change itself, revealing whether styles turned over quickly or slowly, spread from a center or arose everywhere at once. The chapters of the story ahead run from the Danish museum cupboards where the three-age system was born, through Flinders Petrie sorting nine hundred Egyptian graves with slips of cardboard in 1899, to the mid-century American debates about whether types are discovered or invented, to matrix algebra and correspondence analysis on modern computers, and finally to a cemetery study of New England gravestones that tested the whole apparatus against dated stones and watched it work. Throughout, the same discipline applies: every ordering is a hypothesis, every type is a tool, and the method's power comes precisely from knowing the assumptions well enough to notice when they break.

sections.heading: What a Type Is: The Logic of Archaeological Classification
sections.body: Classification precedes chronology, because you cannot count what you have not defined. An archaeological type is a class of artifacts defined by a recurring combination of attributes, where an attribute is any observable characteristic: the material, the shape of a rim, the angle of a shoulder, the temper mixed into clay, a painted motif, a technique of flaking. A single pot has hundreds of describable attributes; a type is a deliberate selection among them, a claim that this particular bundle of features co-occurs often enough, and varies meaningfully enough, to be worth naming. Archaeologists distinguish several kinds of types by purpose. Morphological or descriptive types simply summarize form for cataloging. Functional types group objects by inferred use, scrapers, hoes, cooking jars, and tend to be poor time markers because basic tasks persist for millennia. Historical or temporal types, the workhorses of seriation, are defined precisely because their attribute bundles proved to change through time; the American archaeologist Alexander Krieger argued in an influential 1944 paper that the test of a valid type is exactly this demonstrable historical significance, its consistency in time and space. Stylistic attributes, decorative choices with many functionally equivalent alternatives, make the best temporal markers precisely because nothing but fashion constrains them: a cord-marked surface works no better or worse than a plain one, so the choice between them tracks social convention, and convention drifts. Below the type sits the mode, a term the Yale archaeologist Irving Rouse promoted for a single recurrent attribute state, such as a specific rim form or paint color, that can be tracked independently; above it sit wares and traditions that bundle types into larger historical units. The type-variety system, developed in the late 1950s for the ceramics of the American Southwest and the Maya lowlands, formalized a hierarchy in which a type is subdivided into varieties reflecting finer variation in time, space, or workshop. Good typological practice follows rules that sound pedestrian and matter enormously. Definitions must be explicit enough that two independent workers sort the same collection the same way; boundary cases must be handled by stated criteria rather than intuition; the classification must be exhaustive and its classes mutually exclusive for the material at hand; and lumping versus splitting is a decision about analytic purpose, not a fact about the world. A chronology built on types that only their author can recognize is not reproducible science. It is equally important to understand what a type is not. A type is not necessarily a category the makers themselves recognized; the mental templates of ancient potters, what archaeologists call emic categories, may or may not align with the etic classes an analyst constructs, and the method does not require that they align. Nor is a type a claim that every member is identical; it is a region in a continuous space of variation, drawn where the density of specimens clusters. Treating types as convenient, explicit, revisable instruments rather than metaphysical discoveries keeps the machinery honest, and disputes over precisely this point produced one of American archaeology's most instructive controversies.

sections.heading: The Three-Age System and the First Ordered Past
sections.body: The first successful large-scale ordering of prehistory came out of a museum storeroom in Copenhagen. In 1816 the Danish crown appointed Christian Jürgensen Thomsen, a merchant's son with no university training, to organize the Royal Commission's growing collection of national antiquities. Faced with cabinets of uncatalogued axes, urns, swords, and ornaments, Thomsen did something quietly radical: instead of arranging objects by beauty or material value, he arranged them by the hypothesis that Denmark's past fell into three successive technological ages, an age of stone, an age of bronze, and an age of iron. The scheme itself had classical ancestors, Lucretius had speculated along the same lines, but Thomsen turned speculation into method through what he called closed finds: groups of objects demonstrably deposited together at one moment, above all grave groups and hoards. If a particular style of pot repeatedly occurs in graves with bronze weapons and never with iron ones, the pot belongs to the bronze age; if a brooch type occurs with early iron swords, it belongs to early iron. By chaining thousands of such associations, Thomsen could assign even isolated objects to their age by their stylistic company, and when the museum opened to the public in 1819 its rooms embodied the sequence. He published the system in 1836 in a guidebook, the Ledetraad til Nordisk Oldkyndighed, and it spread across Europe within a generation. What Thomsen had discovered, without the vocabulary, was the associational logic on which all later seriation rests: contemporaneity is inferred from co-occurrence, and time from patterned changes in what co-occurs. His successor Jens Jacob Worsaae supplied the stratigraphic proof. Excavating in Danish burial mounds and peat bogs in the 1840s, Worsaae showed that where deposits were layered, stone-age material genuinely lay beneath bronze, and bronze beneath iron, converting a museum arrangement into a tested chronological claim. This mattered enormously, because it demonstrated that human time, like geological time, was deep, structured, and recoverable from the ground, decades before Darwin made deep human time a biological necessity. The three-age system also established the template that later workers refined: divide time into periods defined by material culture, subdivide as evidence accumulates, and let associations police the boundaries. Its limits were real and instructive. The ages are stages of technology, not fixed dates, and they begin and end at different times in different places; iron reached Scandinavia two thousand years after it reached Anatolia, and some regions, like Australia, never had a bronze age at all, so exporting the labels uncritically produced confusion that took a century to clean up. The system also says nothing about tempo within an age, and its coarse tripartite rhythm concealed enormous variation. But as a proof of concept it was decisive: material culture, properly classified and associated, contains its own history. Every subsequent development, Montelius's fine-grained periods, Petrie's sequence dates, Ford's frequency curves, is an elaboration of the Copenhagen insight with sharper tools and smaller time slices.

sections.heading: Pitt-Rivers, Montelius, and the Typological Method
