Magnetometry also assigns no dates and no depths beyond rough modeling. It answers one question superbly, where is something, and disciplined projects treat its beautiful plots as maps of hypotheses, not of proven archaeology.

sections.heading: Geophysics on the Ground II: Radar, Resistance, and Induction
sections.body:
Ground-penetrating radar, GPR, is the geophysical method that adds the dimension magnetometry lacks: depth. An antenna dragged across the surface emits electromagnetic pulses, typically between 100 and 1000 megahertz, and records echoes returned wherever the ground's electrical properties change, at a buried wall top, a floor, a grave cut, a pipe, the water table. Travel time converts to depth once the local wave velocity is known, usually 0.06 to 0.15 meters per nanosecond, calibrated against a target of known depth. Frequency sets the trade-off: a 500 megahertz antenna resolves features of a few centimeters but sees perhaps a meter or two down; a 200 megahertz antenna reaches several meters at coarser resolution. Single lines produce radargrams, vertical slices through the ground, but archaeology's standard product is the time slice: a dense grid of lines processed into plan-view maps of reflectivity at successive depths, so an interpreter can page downward through a site, watching a Roman building's walls appear at 40 centimeters and its earlier predecessor emerge at 90. GPR's triumphs include mapping unmarked graves, cathedral and abbey interiors through floors, and, in the Stonehenge landscape's motorized surveys, hundreds of hectares imaged in three dimensions. Its master variable is soil: dry sand, gravel, chalk, and masonry are transparent; wet, saline, or heavy clay soils absorb the pulse and can reduce penetration to almost nothing, an honest and sometimes decisive limitation.

Earth resistance survey, the oldest technique in the kit, injects a small current between electrodes and measures the soil's resistance, which is governed almost entirely by moisture held in pore spaces. Stone walls and compacted surfaces hold little water and read high; moisture-retaining ditch and pit fills read low. The classic twin-probe frame, two mobile electrodes on a hand-carried beam paired with remote fixed probes, samples on a half-meter grid at walking pace, and produces plots in which masonry buildings appear with photographic clarity, which made resistance the traditional tool for villas, abbeys, and formal gardens. It is slower than magnetometry, works poorly in drought or waterlogged extremes when contrasts vanish, and its depth of investigation is set by probe spacing. Its deeper cousin, electrical resistivity tomography (ERT), plants lines of dozens of electrodes and inverts thousands of four-electrode measurements into true cross-sections meters deep, the tool of choice for ramparts, mounds, buried valleys, and harbor sediments.

Electromagnetic induction (EMI) instruments measure conductivity, resistance's inverse, and magnetic susceptibility simultaneously, without ground contact, from a sensor slung above the surface; they map large areas fast, follow moisture and soil variation well, and serve as reconnaissance where probes are impractical, though their resolution of small features is coarser. Around these core methods cluster specialized ones: seismic refraction for deep sediments, microgravity for voids and crypts, and magnetic susceptibility sampling for activity areas. Method choice is a matter of physics against target: burnt and cut features favor magnetometry, masonry favors resistance and GPR, depth questions favor GPR and ERT, and integrated surveys deploying several sensors over the same grid, then interpreting the overlaid results, are the professional standard precisely because each instrument's blindness is another's specialty.

sections.heading: From Anomaly to Archaeology: Interpretation, GIS, and Ground-Truthing
sections.body:
Every technique in this guide terminates in the same object: an anomaly, a pattern in an image or a plot that differs from its background. The intellectual discipline of remote-sensing archaeology is the chain of inference that turns anomalies into claims about the past, and the chain has definite links. The first is georeferencing: every image, model, and survey grid must be fixed in a common coordinate system, because interpretation is fundamentally the act of overlaying evidence, the 1946 vertical photograph on the LiDAR local relief model on the magnetometer plot on the nineteenth-century estate map, and seeing whether independent measurements agree. A geographic information system is the workbench for this, and national inventories, historic environment records, sites-and-monuments databases, are its institutional memory: a newly noticed cropmark is checked first against what is already recorded within and around it.

The second link is morphology and context. Interpreters classify anomalies by shape, size, orientation, and association: a subcircular ditched enclosure of 30 meters with a single east-facing causeway sits in a known later-prehistoric repertoire; a strict rectangle with rounded corners and internal range suggests Roman military engineering; a narrow rectilinear grid ignoring the terrain is more likely a Victorian drainage scheme than an ancient field system. Association carries weight, a ring ditch amid a barrow cemetery is probably a plowed barrow; the same ring beside a wartime airfield may be a gun emplacement, and so does the landscape's known geomorphology, since periglacial ice-wedge polygons, palaeochannels, and solution hollows are the classic natural mimics of archaeology. Honest interpretation records confidence explicitly and preserves alternatives rather than forcing every mark into a site.

The third link is ground-truthing, and it is not optional. Fieldwalking collects surface artifacts whose dates and densities test whether an anomaly coincides with occupation debris. Coring and augering establish whether a magnetic ditch anomaly really contains a cut and fill, and how deep. Small, targeted excavation remains the ultimate arbiter, converting geophysical geometry into stratigraphy, dating evidence, and environmental samples; a trench across one ditch terminal can date an entire cropmark complex that no sensor could place in time. The professional literature is candid that remote sensing without ground observation systematically over- and under-counts: some brilliant anomalies dissolve into geology, and excavation regularly finds features, postholes, graves, shallow floors, that every instrument missed.

The final link is publication and archive. Because marks are ephemeral and instruments improve, the primary data, flight photographs, point clouds, raw grids, are deposited so future workers can reprocess them; national mapping programs transcribe interpreted features into layered inventories with source citations for every line. The mature deliverable of remote-sensing archaeology is therefore not a picture of a site but an auditable, cumulative map of evidence, in which any user can trace a plotted ditch back to the July 1976 oblique or the 2019 gradiometer grid on which it rests, and judge the inference for themselves.

sections.heading: Planning a Drone Survey of a Suspected Site
sections.body:
Remote sensing rewards preparation over improvisation, and a small drone photogrammetry survey is the version of the craft most readers could actually execute, so it serves as the worked example. The intellectual step comes first: define what question the survey answers. Detecting subtle earthworks argues for a low-sun flight or drone LiDAR; catching crop stress argues for midday flatness, a multispectral camera, and the right week of the growing season; recording a standing ruin argues for oblique orbits and elevation facades. The physical parameters follow from the question through one number, ground sampling distance, which falls as the aircraft flies lower, and one constraint, overlap, which SfM processing needs at roughly 75 to 80 percent forward and 65 to 70 percent side. Legal parameters bracket everything: most jurisdictions require registration and a competency certificate, cap altitude near 120 meters, demand visual line of sight, and prohibit flight over uninvolved people and near aerodromes, and landowner permission is required, as is checking whether the site itself is legally protected, since even non-contact survey of scheduled monuments can require consent.

Accuracy planning is what separates a measurement from a picture. Ground control points, high-contrast targets laid across the site and surveyed with centimeter-grade GNSS, or an RTK-equipped drone, tie the model to real coordinates; without them a model can float meters from truth and stretch subtly across its length. Weather is an instrument setting: a uniformly overcast, low-wind day gives even lighting for mapping, while a clear morning within two hours of sunrise gives the raking light that makes earthworks legible, two different surveys, often worth flying both.
ingredients: Small quadcopter with a mechanical-shutter mapping camera, ideally RTK-capable, plus spare batteries
Flight-planning app that flies autonomous lawnmower grids with set altitude and overlap
8 to 12 ground control targets and a survey-grade GNSS receiver, or RTK for the drone
Pilot registration and certificate as required locally, airspace check, insurance, and written landowner permission
Field notes: site sketch, wind and light log, and a checklist of flight parameters
Processing software (structure-from-motion) and a computer with a capable graphics card
steps: State the survey question, choose the product it needs (orthophoto, elevation model, or both), and pick season and time of day to match.
Complete the legal work: airspace and site-protection checks, permissions, and a safe takeoff area.

Plan the grid: altitude for the target ground sampling distance (about 90 to 110 meters for 2 to 3 centimeters per pixel), 75 to 80 percent forward and 65 percent side overlap, camera straight down, plus one oblique cross-grid for stronger geometry.
Lay out and survey ground control targets around the perimeter and center, logging each.
Fly the mission in steady conditions, watching battery margins and keeping visual contact; re-fly any strip with dropped frames.
Process in SfM software: align photos, mark control points, build the dense cloud, then export the orthophoto and digital surface model.
Interpret with multiple visualizations (hillshades from several azimuths, slope, local relief), map candidate features in a GIS with confidence levels, and archive raw data and reports.
Ground-truth the best anomalies by walkover and, where justified and permitted, geophysics before drawing conclusions.

sections.heading: Ethics, Looting, and the Politics of Seeing
sections.body:
The power to find sites from a desk raises questions the discipline's founders never faced, and modern practice treats them as core method rather than afterthought. The sharpest is disclosure. Precise coordinates of an unprotected site, published in a paper, a database, or an enthusiast forum, are equally legible to looters, and the same commercial imagery archaeologists use to find sites has been used to strip them; metal-detecting raids and organized digging have followed publicity often enough that many national inventories now fuzz coordinates for sensitive sites, and projects weigh, case by case, what resolution of location any output should carry. The mirror application is surveillance of destruction: time-sliced satellite imagery lets researchers count looting pits and quantify damage at scale, as Sarah Parcak's team did across Egypt after 2011 and as multiple monitoring programs did during the Syrian and Iraqi conflicts, producing evidence used by heritage agencies, courts, and the antiquities trade's regulators. Remote sensing is thus simultaneously the looter's reconnaissance and the strongest instrument ever built for catching looting in the act; which effect dominates depends on governance, and practitioners are participants in that governance whether they choose to be or not.

A second cluster of issues concerns consent and ownership of the seen landscape. Aerial and satellite instruments do not stop at property lines or reservation boundaries, and communities have their own interests in what is revealed: burial grounds and sacred places may be exactly the features descendants do not want mapped, published, or visited. Indigenous data-sovereignty frameworks, and plain courtesy, imply consulting affected communities before survey where feasible and before publication always, sharing data back, and accepting that some knowledge may be held rather than broadcast. Drones add a domestic version: they photograph homes, workers, and livestock incidentally, and flying them lawfully and considerately, announced, permitted, away from people, is part of professional competence. Colonial patterns shadow the field's history, foreign projects extracting imagery and publishing abroad, and the practical correctives are unglamorous: local partnership, capacity building, depositing archives in the host country, and publishing in accessible venues.

Third is the honesty of claims. Remote sensing is spectacle-friendly, lost cities announced from LiDAR make headlines, and the gap between anomaly and demonstrated archaeology invites inflation. Responsible practice states what was measured, what was inferred, and what remains untested; resists the passive-voice miracle in which an algorithm discovers anything; and credits the ground: the 60,000 Maya structures were counted by human interpreters and verified by field crews walking transects. Data ethics extends to preservation itself: point clouds and imagery of monuments since damaged, Palmyra, Bamiyan-adjacent sites, Ukrainian churches, have become the only surviving record, which argues for open, redundant archiving, while the disclosure dilemma argues for controlled access; mature repositories resolve the tension with tiered permissions rather than a single policy. The discipline's ethical center of gravity is easily stated: seeing is an intervention, and the standards that govern excavation, permission, stewardship, publication, accountability, govern the view from above no less.

sections.heading: Limits, Pitfalls, and What to Do When the Ground Disagrees
sections.body:
Every mature user of archaeological remote sensing carries a private museum of failures, and the field's honest literature dwells on them, because the failure modes are systematic and learnable. The first family is geological and agricultural mimicry. Periglacial ice-wedge polygons produce crisp networks of cropmark lines that have been mapped as field systems; solution hollows in chalk mimic pits; palaeochannels curve convincingly like ditches; and modern land use contributes pipe trenches, removed hedgerows, drainage schemes, vehicle headlands, and the circular scars of center-pivot irrigation and fairy-ring fungi. The defenses are comparative: check the geomorphology mapping, ask whether the pattern respects or ignores topography as archaeology would, seek independent confirmation from a second technique, and treat perfect regularity with suspicion, since nature is irregular and so, differently, is antiquity.

The second family is absence misread. No instrument detects everything: pasture hides cropmarks, clay hides GPR targets, leveled sites hide from LiDAR, non-magnetic features hide from magnetometers. A blank survey is therefore weak evidence of emptiness, and development decisions premised on negative geophysics have been embarrassed by excavation often enough that professional guidance insists blank results be reported with explicit statements of what the method could not have seen under the conditions flown or walked. The inverse error, over-interpretation, is fed by pareidolia and enthusiasm; the internet era supplies steady examples, from Google Earth patterns announced as Atlantis, which proved to be sonar survey track lines, to seasonal mowing marks celebrated as henges. The corrective habits are procedural: multiple independent data sets before claims, explicit confidence grading, peer review by interpreters who did not make the discovery, and the standing rule that extraordinary announcements await ground-truthing.

The third family is technical. Misgeoreferencing silently shifts an entire interpretation off its true position; SfM models without control points bow and stretch; LiDAR ground-classification erases subtle banks or manufactures terraces from dense brush; radiometric drift in thermal sensors paints gradients that look like buried roads; interpolation artifacts in coarsely gridded geophysics create linear ghosts aligned with the survey grid. Each has a known remedy, control points, raw-data inspection, calibration passes, azimuth-varied visualization, and the general remedy is preserving primary data so that processing can be audited and redone.

When the ground disagrees with the imagery, the ground wins, but the disagreement itself is information. A trench that finds a natural channel where the plot promised a ditch calibrates every similar anomaly on the plot; a magnetometer blank over an excavated building teaches what that soil cannot show; a cropmark that never returns in twenty years of flying still exists in the archive, dated and located, awaiting a drier summer or a better sensor. The discipline advances exactly this way, by iterating between the view from above and the truth from below, and its accumulated archives, photographs from 1906, film from orbit in 1965, point clouds from last year, constitute one of archaeology's few genuinely renewable resources: evidence that improves not by re-excavating the past but by re-asking it questions.

guides.title: LiDAR in Archaeology
guides.summary: How laser scanning from aircraft, drones and tripods reveals ancient landscapes hidden under forest and vegetation — the physics, the survey and processing workflow, the visualisation methods, the landmark discoveries, and the limits and ethics of the technique.

sections.heading: Seeing Through the Canopy: Why LiDAR Changed Archaeology
sections.body:
For most of the discipline's history, finding archaeological sites in forest meant walking through it. A survey
team cut transects with machetes, recorded what it stumbled across, and extrapolated. In tropical rainforest a
good field season might cover a few square kilometres, and the resulting maps recorded the monumental core of a
site — the pyramids and plazas somebody could see — while the ordinary houses, terraces, field walls, causeways
and reservoirs surrounding them stayed invisible under vegetation. Whole categories of evidence about how many
people lived somewhere, how they fed themselves and how their settlements were organised were therefore missing,
not because archaeologists were uninterested but because they were unreachable.

Airborne laser scanning changed that arithmetic in a single decade. In April 2009, a survey aircraft operated by
the United States National Center for Airborne Laser Mapping flew roughly 200 square kilometres of dense forest
around the Maya city of Caracol in Belize over four and a half days. Arlen and Diane Chase had spent
twenty-five years mapping that city on foot and had recorded about 23 square kilometres of settlement. The laser
data, processed into a bare-earth terrain model, revealed the whole urban landscape at once: thousands of
structures, agricultural terraces covering hillsides, causeways linking outlying plaza groups to the centre. A
generation of fieldwork was matched in days, and then vastly exceeded.

What followed was not merely faster mapping but a shift in the questions the discipline could ask. When the
PACUNAM LiDAR Initiative published its survey of 2,144 square kilometres of northern Guatemala in the journal
Science in 2018, it reported some 61,000 structures, extensive defensive works, and causeways and wetland field
systems implying agricultural intensification on a scale earlier population estimates had not accommodated.
Estimates of Classic Maya lowland population were revised sharply upward. In Cambodia, surveys of Angkor in 2012
and 2015 covering nearly 2,300 square kilometres exposed a gridded urban landscape, water-management features and
previously unknown cities on the Phnom Kulen plateau. In the Bolivian Amazon in 2022, laser data revealed
monumental Casarabe settlements with platform mounds, causeways and canals in a region long characterised as
incapable of supporting complex society. In 2024, similar work in the Upano Valley of Ecuador described urban
landscapes with thousands of platforms and road networks dating back more than two millennia.

The technique's power comes from an almost unreasonable physical fact: a forest canopy, however dense it looks
from above, is full of small gaps. A laser system firing hundreds of thousands of pulses per second will send a
fraction of them — sometimes only 1 or 2 per cent in the worst rainforest, often 20 to 40 per cent in temperate
woodland — all the way to the ground and back. Collect enough pulses and those few ground returns are sufficient
to reconstruct the surface beneath the trees at a resolution of a metre or better, and human earthworks measured
in tens of centimetres of relief become visible across whole landscapes.

sections.heading: The Physics: Measuring Distance With Light
sections.body:
LiDAR — Light Detection and Ranging — is conceptually a tape measure made of light. The instrument emits a very
short pulse of laser light, waits for the reflection, and measures the elapsed time. Because light travels at
299,792,458 metres per second in vacuum and very close to that in air, the range is simply half the round-trip
time multiplied by that speed. The halving matters: light must travel out and back, so one nanosecond of
round-trip time corresponds to about 15 centimetres of distance. Achieving the few-centimetre ranging precision
that archaeology needs therefore requires timing electronics resolving well under a nanosecond, which is routine
in modern instruments.

The pulses themselves are extremely short and quite energetic. A typical topographic system emits pulses lasting
around 3 to 10 nanoseconds — a pulse only a metre or two long in space — at a wavelength of 1,064 nanometres in
the near infrared, generated by a neodymium-doped yttrium aluminium garnet laser. Near-infrared is chosen because
vegetation reflects it strongly, atmospheric absorption is low, and eye-safety limits are more permissive than at
visible wavelengths. Bathymetric systems designed to penetrate water instead use 532-nanometre green light,
produced by frequency-doubling the same laser, because water absorbs infrared within centimetres but transmits
green; such systems can reach roughly one to one and a half times the Secchi depth, meaning perhaps 10 to 20
metres in clear water and only 2 to 3 metres in turbid estuaries.

Two properties of the emitted beam govern what the data can resolve. Beam divergence, typically 0.25 to 0.5
milliradians, sets how the spot grows with distance: at 1,000 metres above ground, a 0.3-milliradian beam
illuminates a footprint about 30 centimetres across. Anything smaller than that footprint is averaged into a
single measurement, so footprint size is a hard floor on spatial detail. Pulse repetition frequency sets how many
measurements per second are possible; modern systems run from about 100 kilohertz to well over a megahertz, and
many use multiple-pulses-in-air techniques, firing the next pulse before the previous return arrives and
disentangling them by timing logic, to sustain high rates from high altitudes.

Crucially, the returning signal is not a single clean echo. A pulse that clips a branch, passes through a gap,
grazes understorey and finally strikes soil produces a series of reflections spread over tens of nanoseconds.
Discrete-return systems detect peaks in that train and record up to four or five distinct returns per pulse, each
with its own range and intensity. Full-waveform systems instead digitise the entire returning signal, typically
sampling at 1 gigahertz — one sample every 15 centimetres of range — and store the profile for later analysis.
That ability to record several surfaces along one line of sight is precisely what allows the technique to
separate canopy from ground.

sections.heading: Anatomy of an Airborne Laser Scanning System
sections.body:
An airborne laser scanner measures range along a line of sight, but a range alone is useless: to turn it into a
coordinate on the Earth, the instrument must know exactly where the aircraft was and exactly which way the beam
was pointing at the microsecond the pulse left. An operational system is therefore four instruments working
together, and understanding the division of labour explains most of what can go wrong.

The laser rangefinder provides the distance. A scanning mechanism sweeps the beam across the flight path so that
a single aircraft pass covers a swath rather than a line. Several scanner geometries are in use and each leaves a
recognisable pattern on the ground. An oscillating mirror sweeps back and forth, producing a zigzag or sinusoidal
track with points bunched at the swath edges where the mirror slows and reverses. A rotating polygon mirror
produces a series of straight parallel lines all scanned in the same direction, giving more even coverage. A
Palmer or nutating scanner traces overlapping ellipses, which has the useful property of viewing each ground
point from two different directions and so seeing into gaps and vertical faces that a single-look geometry would
miss. Fibre-optic scanners produce parallel lines with very stable geometry.

Position comes from a Global Navigation Satellite System receiver, logging at 1 to 2 hertz. Alone that is far too
coarse and too imprecise, so it is combined with an inertial measurement unit — a package of accelerometers and
gyroscopes sampling at 200 to 500 hertz — which tracks the aircraft's roll, pitch and heading continuously and
fills in position between satellite fixes. The two are fused in a Kalman filter, the satellite data anchoring the
inertial system's inevitable drift and the inertial system supplying the high-rate attitude the satellites
cannot. Positioning is normally processed differentially against a ground reference station within a few tens of
kilometres, or against a network correction service, after the flight rather than in real time.

The accuracy budget is dominated by attitude, not by ranging. The laser measures distance to a few centimetres,
but an angular error of 0.005 degrees in the measured aircraft attitude translates to about 9 centimetres of
horizontal error at 1,000 metres of range, and the error grows with altitude and with distance from the swath
centre. Typical delivered accuracies for archaeological survey are 5 to 15 centimetres vertically and 15 to 40
centimetres horizontally, with vertical performing better because the geometry is more favourable and because
vertical errors can be checked and corrected against flat, hard surfaces.

The system must also be calibrated for boresight — the small, fixed angular misalignments between the laser
scanner's axes and the inertial unit's axes. These are solved for by flying calibration patterns over a site with
sloped roofs or similar features and adjusting until overlapping swaths agree. Uncorrected boresight error is the
classic cause of data in which adjacent flight lines are visibly offset from one another.

sections.heading: Planning a Survey: Density, Altitude, Season and Cost
sections.body:
The single most consequential decision in an archaeological laser survey is made before the aircraft takes off,
and it is the choice of point density. Density is quoted in pulses or points per square metre and determines
everything downstream, because in forested terrain only a fraction of emitted pulses reach the ground. In open
farmland almost every pulse returns from the surface, so 4 points per square metre yields 4 ground points per
square metre. Under closed temperate woodland perhaps 20 to 40 per cent penetrate. Under multi-storey tropical
rainforest the figure can fall to 1 to 5 per cent. A survey specified at 15 pulses per square metre over
rainforest may therefore deliver only 0.3 ground points per square metre — one point every 1.8 metres — which is
just enough to build a 1-metre terrain model but not enough to resolve a low house platform confidently. This is
why tropical projects commonly specify 15 to 40 pulses per square metre while a survey of ploughed English
downland may be adequate at 4 to 8.

Density is bought with flying time, and flying time with money. Lower altitude concentrates the same pulse rate
into a narrower swath, raising density but requiring more flight lines. Slower ground speed does the same.
Overlapping adjacent swaths by 20 to 50 per cent both doubles density in the overlap and provides the redundancy
needed to detect and correct flight-line misalignment. Typical archaeological survey altitudes run 600 to 1,200
metres above ground for fixed-wing aircraft, with scan angles deliberately restricted to plus or minus 15 to 20
degrees from vertical rather than the 30 degrees or more used for general topographic mapping, because a
near-vertical look has a far better chance of finding a gap straight down through canopy.

Timing matters enormously in temperate and deciduous regions. Flying under leaf-off conditions, in late autumn
through early spring, can raise ground-return density by a factor of two to five compared with the same site in
summer. In evergreen and tropical forest that lever does not exist, which is one reason tropical work demands
higher specified densities. Ground conditions matter too: dry, low, senescent understorey is far more permeable
than a flush of new growth, and standing water absorbs infrared entirely, leaving voids over flooded ground that
are easily mistaken for real depressions.

Costs have fallen sharply but remain substantial. Airborne survey is commonly priced per square kilometre with a
large fixed mobilisation charge, so small projects pay a heavy premium and large blocks are far more efficient
per unit area. This economic structure has encouraged consortium projects and, equally important, the reuse of
data flown by others. Enormous quantities of national laser coverage exist for flood modelling, forestry and
mapping — the Environment Agency's open release of English data at 1-metre and finer resolution, the Netherlands'
AHN programme, and comparable national datasets in Denmark, Finland, Slovenia, Poland and elsewhere. Much
significant archaeology has been found by reprocessing such data at no acquisition cost at all, and checking what
already exists should always precede commissioning a flight.

sections.heading: From Pulses to a Point Cloud
sections.body:
The immediate product of a survey is not a map but a point cloud: a very large, unstructured list of
three-dimensional coordinates, each with attributes. A moderate archaeological block of 100 square kilometres at
20 points per square metre contains two billion points, so the practicalities of storage and handling are not a
trivial afterthought.

Each recorded point carries more than position. Intensity records the strength of the returned signal, a rough
proxy for surface reflectance at 1,064 nanometres, useful for distinguishing bare soil from vegetation or wet
from dry ground, though it is affected by range, incidence angle and scan geometry and needs normalisation before
it can be compared across a survey. Return number and total returns record where in the echo train the point sat
— a point that is the fourth of four returns from a pulse is very likely to be ground, while a sole return in
forest is likely to be canopy top. GPS time stamps each point, permitting reconstruction of which flight line
and which moment it came from. Scan angle records how far off nadir the beam was pointing, which matters because
edge-of-swath points are both less accurate and less likely to have reached the ground.

The standard interchange format is LAS, defined by the American Society for Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing,
a binary format with a fixed header and per-point records. Its compressed variant LAZ, developed by Martin
Isenburg, typically achieves five- to tenfold compression losslessly and has become the practical default for
distribution. Both carry an ASPRS classification code per point, and the codes worth knowing are 1 for
unclassified, 2 for ground, 3, 4 and 5 for low, medium and high vegetation, 6 for building, 7 for noise and 9 for
water. Newer point-cloud formats such as COPC and Entwine allow cloud-hosted data to be streamed and queried by
region without downloading whole tiles, which matters when national datasets run to trillions of points.

Before classification, the cloud needs cleaning. Gross outliers — points hundreds of metres above the terrain
from birds, cloud, aerosol or from spurious multiple-pulse resolution, and points far below it from multipath
reflections off water or wet roads — must be removed, usually by a statistical filter that rejects points whose
elevation lies many standard deviations from their local neighbourhood. Flight lines must then be checked against
one another in the overlap zones; a systematic vertical offset between adjacent strips, or a tilt across the
swath, indicates a boresight or trajectory problem and is corrected by a strip adjustment that solves for small
rotations and translations per line. Skipping this step produces terrain models with faint linear ridges running
along flight-line boundaries, and those artefacts have on more than one occasion been briefly mistaken for
ancient field boundaries or trackways.

sections.heading: Ground Classification: The Step That Makes Archaeology Possible
sections.body:
Everything archaeological in an airborne dataset depends on one processing step: separating the points that
struck the ground from the points that struck vegetation, buildings and everything else. The output, a bare-earth
digital terrain model, is what reveals earthworks; the alternative, a digital surface model including the canopy,
shows only trees. Ground classification is an algorithmic problem with no perfect solution, and its settings are
the single largest source of variation between two analysts working from identical raw data.

Several families of algorithm are in general use. Morphological filters slide a structuring element of increasing
size over the cloud and progressively remove points that rise too sharply above their surroundings, on the logic
that vegetation is locally high and terrain is not. Progressive TIN densification, introduced by Peter Axelsson
in 2000 and implemented in the widely used TerraScan software, begins by selecting the lowest point in each cell
of a coarse grid, builds a triangulated surface from those seed points, and then iteratively adds any point lying
within a specified distance and angle of the existing triangles, growing the surface upward into the true terrain
without climbing into vegetation. Multiscale curvature classification, published by Jeffrey Evans and Andrew
Hudak in 2007, works by repeatedly fitting smooth surfaces at several scales and rejecting points above a
curvature-dependent threshold. The cloth simulation filter of Wuming Zhang and colleagues in 2016 inverts the
point cloud and drapes a simulated fabric of specified rigidity over it from below, taking the points the cloth
settles on as ground; it is intuitive to tune and performs well on gentle terrain. Open implementations exist in
LAStools, PDAL, WhiteboxTools, CloudCompare and GRASS GIS.

The parameters that matter most are the assumed maximum terrain slope, the cell size of the initial seed grid,
and the tolerance for adding points. Their interaction produces two opposite and equally destructive failures.
Set too aggressively, the filter strips genuine archaeological relief: a house platform, a burial mound or a
rampart is a locally raised feature, and a filter that removes locally raised things will happily shave it away.
Set too conservatively, low vegetation, brash, fallen timber and shrubs are retained as ground, producing a noisy,
hummocky surface in which real features are indistinguishable from bushes.

The practical response is to treat classification as an interpretive act rather than a black box. Run more than
one algorithm or more than one parameter set over the same block and compare the resulting terrain models; a
feature present in all of them is far more trustworthy than one that appears in a single aggressive run. Where a
site is important, manually reclassify a sample area by eye, using cross-sectional profiles through the cloud to
see directly what the algorithm decided, and use that as a check on the automated result. Above all, record the
software, version and parameters used, because a terrain model without that provenance cannot be properly
interpreted by anyone else.

sections.heading: Visualisation: Making Faint Relief Visible
sections.body:
A bare-earth terrain model is a grid of elevation values, and elevation values are not directly interpretable by
eye. The archaeological features of interest are often only 10 to 50 centimetres high sitting on terrain that
varies by tens or hundreds of metres, so a straightforward greyscale elevation image shows the hill and hides the
earthwork entirely. Visualisation — the family of techniques for rendering the model so that small local relief
becomes visible — is therefore not cosmetic but analytical, and different methods reveal genuinely different
features.

Analytical hillshading is the traditional starting point. It simulates illumination from a notional sun at a
chosen azimuth and elevation, typically 315 degrees and 45 degrees, and shades each cell according to the angle
between its surface normal and the light. It produces an immediately legible, three-dimensional-looking image, but
it has a serious and often overlooked defect: features running parallel to the illumination direction cast no
shadow and effectively disappear. A linear bank aligned with the light is invisible, which has led to real
features being missed for years in published imagery. The remedy is to generate several hillshades from different
azimuths and combine them. Multi-directional hillshading blends the results, and the approach of David Devereux
and colleagues in 2008 runs a principal component analysis over sixteen hillshades and displays the leading
components, producing an illumination-independent image.

Sky-view factor, developed by Klemen Zakšek, Krištof Oštir and Žiga Kokalj in 2011, measures for each cell the
proportion of the hemisphere of sky visible from it, sampling a set of directions out to a chosen radius. Points
inside a ditch see less sky and render dark; points on a bank see more and render bright. Because the result
depends on local geometry rather than on a light source, no orientation is favoured, and the technique is
outstanding for ditches, hollow ways, quarry pits and terracing. Positive and negative openness, from Ryuzo
Yokoyama's 2002 work, are closely related measures using maximum zenith and nadir angles along sampled azimuths.

Local relief modelling, described by Ralf Hesse in 2010, takes a different approach: it removes the large-scale
landform by smoothing the terrain and subtracting the smoothed version from the original, leaving only deviations
at scales smaller than the smoothing radius. Choosing a radius of, say, 15 metres isolates features of roughly
that size and smaller and renders them against a flat background, which is extremely effective for low, broad
features such as ploughed-out barrows or field lynchets. Slope maps, simply the gradient magnitude, are useful for
sharp-edged features such as revetments and terrace risers.

No single method dominates. Best practice is to produce a suite — multi-directional hillshade, sky-view factor,
openness, local relief model, slope — and examine them together, often blended as coloured layers over one
another. The free Relief Visualization Toolbox from the Slovenian research group behind sky-view factor packages
most of these, and comparable tools exist in QGIS, SAGA, GRASS and WhiteboxTools.

sections.heading: What Archaeological Features Actually Look Like
sections.body:
Learning to read a terrain model is a visual skill acquired by looking at many examples, but the underlying logic
is consistent: laser scanning detects shape, so it finds anything that still has topographic expression, and it
finds nothing that does not. Reading the imagery is a matter of recognising the geometry that human activity
produces and of distinguishing it from the geometry that geology, water, trees and modern machinery produce.

Settlement features usually appear as clusters of low, flat-topped rectangular or oval platforms, often only 20
to 60 centimetres high, arranged around open spaces. In Maya contexts these platforms occur in groups of three to
five around a shared patio, and once the eye learns that pattern it becomes visible across whole landscapes.
Larger structures — pyramids, temple platforms, palace compounds — are unmistakable, but the interpretive value
usually lies in the humble platforms, because it is those that support population estimates. Enclosures and
fortifications appear as continuous banks with an accompanying ditch, and the relationship between the two is
diagnostic: a ditch outside the bank generally suggests defence, a ditch inside may suggest a boundary or a
ritual enclosure, as in British henge monuments.

Agricultural features are among the technique's greatest successes because they cover enormous areas and are
almost impossible to map on foot. Terraces appear as sets of roughly parallel contour-following risers stepping
down a slope. Ridge and furrow, the corrugated signature of medieval European open-field ploughing, appears as
regular parallel undulations with a wavelength of 5 to 10 metres, often with a distinctive reversed-S curve
produced by turning an ox team. Lynchets — soil banks accumulated at the downslope edge of long-ploughed fields —
appear as contour-parallel steps. Raised fields, drainage canals and causeways in wetland contexts appear as
regular geometric grids.

Communication and water features show as linear anomalies. Roads and causeways appear as raised straight or gently
curving embankments, sometimes with flanking quarry ditches; hollow ways, worn down by centuries of traffic,
appear as linear depressions, often braided where users skirted a muddy stretch. Reservoirs and tanks appear as
rectangular depressions with retaining banks.

Industrial and extractive traces are abundant and easily overlooked. Charcoal-burning platforms appear as small
level circles 8 to 15 metres across cut into slopes, sometimes in their thousands. Mining appears as lines of
shallow bell-pits, as opencast scars, as leats and as spoil heaps. Ridge-and-hollow patterns from quarrying,
peat cutting and clay extraction are pervasive in European woodland.

The essential discipline is that morphology alone does not date anything, and that many natural forms mimic
cultural ones. Frost polygons, solifluction lobes, tree-throw hollows, landslip scars, natural levees and modern
forestry drainage all generate regular geometry.

sections.heading: Beyond the Aircraft: Drone, Terrestrial and Bathymetric Scanning
sections.body:
Airborne survey dominates landscape archaeology, but three other laser platforms serve different scales and are
now routine parts of the toolkit.

Uncrewed aerial vehicles carrying compact laser scanners occupy the middle ground between aircraft and tripod.
Because a drone flies at 40 to 120 metres rather than 1,000, the same pulse rate concentrates into a far smaller
area, and densities of several hundred to over a thousand points per square metre are achievable. Small, light
sensors have made this practical. The trade-off is coverage: a battery-limited drone might survey 0.2 to 1 square
kilometre per flight day depending on regulations and terrain, against hundreds of square kilometres for an
aircraft. Drone laser scanning is therefore the right tool for a single site or a small block requiring very fine
resolution — a hillfort's rampart sequence, a deserted village, the microtopography of a barrow cemetery — and
the wrong tool for regional survey. It is also the only practical way to obtain repeat surveys cheaply, which
makes it valuable for monitoring erosion, looting damage or slope movement at threatened sites.

Terrestrial laser scanning uses a tripod-mounted instrument that sweeps a full or partial sphere from a fixed
station, recording millions of points at millimetre to few-millimetre precision within ranges of a few metres to
several hundred. It is the standard method for recording standing buildings, rock-cut monuments, quarry faces,
cave interiors, rock art panels and open excavation surfaces. Because a single station sees only what is in
direct line of sight, complete coverage requires many stations registered together, either by surveyed targets or
by cloud-to-cloud alignment algorithms. Handheld and backpack scanners using simultaneous localisation and mapping
techniques trade precision — typically a few centimetres — for enormous speed, and can record a complex
underground site by walking through it, which has transformed the documentation of caves and mines.

Bathymetric laser scanning uses green 532-nanometre light to penetrate water and map submerged topography. Its
depth performance is governed by water clarity rather than by instrument power, reaching roughly one to one and a
half Secchi depths, so it excels in clear coastal shallows, lakes and springs and fails in turbid rivers and
estuaries. Where it works it maps submerged prehistoric landscapes, harbours, fish traps, causeways and shipwreck
mounds continuously across the land–water boundary, a zone traditionally split awkwardly between terrestrial and
marine survey methods.

These platforms are complementary rather than competing, and a mature project often uses all of them: airborne
data to find and contextualise, drone data to resolve a chosen site, and terrestrial scanning to record specific
structures at recording-grade precision. Because all produce point clouds in the same coordinate framework, they
merge readily into a single multi-scale model.

sections.heading: Landmark Projects and What They Overturned
sections.body:
A handful of surveys carry most of the discipline's evidence about what the technique can do, and each corrected
a specific long-held assumption.

Caracol, Belize, flown in 2009 and published by Arlen Chase, Diane Chase and colleagues in 2011, was the
proof-of-concept for tropical forest. It demonstrated that the ancient Maya landscape was not a scatter of ceremonial
centres in wilderness but a continuously modified terrain of terraces, causeways and residential groups, and that
the sustaining area of a city was far larger and more intensively farmed than survey-based reconstructions
suggested.

The PACUNAM LiDAR Initiative in Guatemala, whose first results appeared in Science in 2018 under the lead
authorship of Marcello Canuto and Francisco Estrada-Belli, scaled that finding to 2,144 square kilometres of the
Petén, documenting some 61,000 structures, 106 kilometres of causeway, extensive wetland field systems and
unexpectedly elaborate defensive works including ditches, ramparts and fortified strongholds. The defensive
evidence in particular revised views on the scale and organisation of Classic Maya warfare, and the agricultural
evidence supported population estimates several times higher than earlier consensus.

Angkor, Cambodia, surveyed by Damian Evans and the Khmer Archaeology LiDAR Consortium in 2012 and again in 2015,
covered nearly 2,300 square kilometres and revealed the formally planned urban grid within the temple enclosures
themselves, dense occupation across areas thought empty, and an entire previously unmapped urban complex on the
Phnom Kulen plateau. It also mapped the water-management network in enough detail to inform debate about whether
hydraulic failure contributed to the settlement's decline.

Angamuco in Michoacán, Mexico, surveyed by Christopher Fisher and colleagues, mapped a Purépecha urban landscape
built on a lava flow with a structure count in the tens of thousands, illustrating that the technique works
equally well on rugged volcanic terrain that defeats conventional survey.

In Amazonia, the assumption that pre-Columbian societies there were small and mobile has been comprehensively
dismantled. Heiko Prümers and colleagues reported in Nature in 2022 on Casarabe-culture sites in the Llanos de
Mojos of Bolivia, including the centres of Cotoca and Landívar, with stepped platforms, conical pyramids over 20
metres tall, and radiating causeways and canals extending for kilometres. In 2024, work led by Stéphen Rostain in
the Upano Valley of Ecuador described thousands of earthen platforms and a network of wide, straight roads dating
from roughly 2,500 years ago.

In Europe, the impact has been less dramatic but arguably broader, because national datasets flown for other
purposes cover entire countries. Reprocessing of such data has mapped Roman roads and camps, medieval field
systems, hillforts, charcoal-burning platforms and mining landscapes in numbers that would have been unimaginable
by conventional means, and has done so at essentially zero acquisition cost. The lesson repeated in every one of
these cases is the same: the visible monuments were never the whole of the record, and the missing part was
usually the part that mattered for understanding how people actually lived.

sections.heading: Ground-Truthing: Turning Anomalies Into Archaeology
sections.body:
A terrain model produces candidate features, not archaeological sites. An anomaly is a shape; converting it into
an interpretation with a date, a function and a cultural attribution requires fieldwork, and projects that skip
this step routinely publish counts that later prove substantially wrong. Reported false-positive rates from purely
desk-based identification vary widely with terrain and feature type, but figures of 10 to 40 per cent are common
and can be far higher in geologically complex or heavily forested ground. The verification workflow below is the
standard sequence.
steps: Build a mapped inventory first. Digitise every candidate as a point or polygon in a geographic information system with a consistent attribute scheme recording morphology, dimensions, confidence on a simple three- or five-point scale, and which visualisation it was seen in.

Have a second analyst independently map a sample block without seeing the first result, then compare. The disagreement rate between two competent analysts is the honest measure of how reliable the whole inventory is, and it is usually larger than expected.

Cross-check against every existing record before going to the field: historic maps, aerial photographs, geological mapping, soil survey, forestry and drainage records, mining plans and the regional heritage database. A great many anomalies resolve immediately into documented quarries, wartime installations, forestry ditches or field boundaries shown on a nineteenth-century map.

Stratify a field sample rather than visiting the most exciting candidates. Select across confidence classes, feature types, land covers and terrain settings, including a deliberate sample of areas where nothing was mapped, so that both false positives and false negatives can be estimated.

Navigate to each selected anomaly with a survey-grade or at least sub-metre positioning device, since typical handheld accuracy under canopy is poor enough to leave you standing beside the wrong bump.

Record what is physically present: dimensions measured with tape and level, a described profile, surface material, vegetation, disturbance, and photographs from fixed bearings. Note explicitly when nothing is there.

Apply minimally invasive testing where permitted and appropriate — auger transects, small test pits, geophysical survey with magnetometry or ground-penetrating radar, or examination of exposures in tree-throws, animal burrows and eroding edges.

Obtain dating evidence where the question requires it, from diagnostic artefacts, from radiocarbon on charcoal or organic material in secure contexts, or from optically stimulated luminescence on buried surfaces beneath banks and mounds.

Feed the results back into the desk assessment. Recompute the accuracy of each confidence class, revise the identification criteria, and rescan the imagery with the corrected eye, since the feedback loop typically finds features missed on the first pass.
Publish the verification rates alongside the counts. An inventory quoted without a measured error rate cannot be used quantitatively by anyone else.

sections.heading: Tools, Data Sources and a Practical Working Setup
sections.body:
A great deal of serious archaeological laser analysis is done on ordinary hardware with free software, using data
somebody else paid to collect. The barrier to entry is now low enough that the main constraint is knowledge
rather than budget, and assembling a working setup is a matter of a few well-chosen components.

Hardware requirements are driven by point-cloud handling rather than by raster analysis. Memory is the binding
constraint: 32 gigabytes is comfortable for tile-by-tile work and 16 is workable if tiles are kept small, while
raster visualisation of an already-generated terrain model runs happily on far less. Fast local storage matters
more than processor speed for most operations, since these workflows are dominated by reading and writing very
large files. Working in tiles of 500 metres or 1 kilometre square with a generous buffer overlap avoids most
memory problems and avoids edge artefacts in neighbourhood operations such as sky-view factor.

The commonest practical mistake is to accept a supplied terrain model without question. Data delivered for flood
modelling or forestry has been ground-classified with parameters chosen for those purposes, frequently smoothing
away exactly the low relief archaeology depends on. Wherever the raw or minimally processed point cloud is
available, reclassify it, and compare the result against the supplied product before drawing conclusions.

A sensible order of work is to acquire the point cloud, remove gross outliers, check flight-line agreement,
classify ground, interpolate a terrain grid at a resolution matched to actual ground-point density — typically
0.5 to 1 metre, and never finer than the data genuinely supports, since an over-fine grid manufactures very
convincing noise — then generate a suite of visualisations, and only afterwards begin interpreting. Scripting
that pipeline so it can be rerun with altered parameters repays the initial effort many times over, because the
parameters will certainly change.
ingredients: Open national laser datasets: England's Environment Agency coverage, the Netherlands' AHN programme, Denmark's national model, Finland's and Slovenia's open data, and the United States Geological Survey's 3DEP holdings distributed through OpenTopography. Check licence terms, which are usually permissive but vary.
OpenTopography, a free portal serving both raw point clouds and derived products worldwide, including many research-project datasets released after publication.
LAStools for fast point-cloud filtering, tiling, ground classification and terrain-model generation; several core tools are free, others licensed.
PDAL, the open Point Data Abstraction Library, for scriptable and reproducible processing pipelines defined in plain text.
CloudCompare, free and open, for interactive inspection, cross-sections, manual reclassification and cloud-to-cloud comparison.

The Relief Visualization Toolbox from the Slovenian research group that developed sky-view factor, which produces hillshade, multi-directional hillshade, sky-view factor, openness and local relief models from a terrain grid.
QGIS with GRASS and SAGA providers, or WhiteboxTools, for raster analysis, digitising and map production at no cost.
A geographic information system project template with a consistent anomaly-recording schema, so that inventories from different analysts and projects remain comparable.
Sub-metre or survey-grade satellite positioning for fieldwork, since consumer accuracy under tree canopy is often 5 to 15 metres.

sections.heading: How It Compares With Other Remote Sensing
sections.body:
Laser scanning is one instrument among several, and choosing between them depends entirely on what physical
property distinguishes the target from its surroundings. Understanding the complementarity prevents both wasted
money and false expectations.

Photogrammetry — reconstructing three-dimensional shape from overlapping photographs using structure-from-motion
software — produces superficially similar point clouds at a fraction of the cost, and for bare or lightly
vegetated ground it is often the better choice, delivering colour with the geometry. Its fundamental limitation is
that it can only reconstruct surfaces the camera can see. Under a closed canopy it reconstructs the canopy. There
is no photogrammetric equivalent of a pulse slipping through a gap and returning from the forest floor, which is
precisely the capability that makes laser scanning transformative in woodland.

Conventional aerial photography remains extremely powerful for levelled sites, because it detects cropmarks and
soilmarks rather than relief. A ditch ploughed flat two thousand years ago has no topography for a laser to find,
but its deeper, damper fill still makes cereal grow taller and stay green longer in drought, producing a mark
visible from the air. Laser scanning and aerial photography therefore find largely different populations of
sites, and a landscape assessed by only one of them is systematically biased.

Satellite imagery contributes multispectral and very-high-resolution optical data over vast areas at low cost,
and has been used effectively for desert and steppe archaeology and for monitoring looting and conflict damage.
Declassified Cold War imagery, notably the CORONA series flown between 1960 and 1972, is uniquely valuable because
it records landscapes before the agricultural intensification and urban expansion of the later twentieth century
destroyed them.

Synthetic aperture radar penetrates cloud and, at longer wavelengths, dry sand to depths of a metre or two, which
has revealed buried palaeochannels in the Sahara. It does not usefully penetrate vegetation for archaeological
purposes in the way laser does, and its resolution and interpretive complexity limit routine use.

Ground-based geophysics operates at an entirely different scale and answers a different question. Magnetometry
detects magnetic contrasts from burning, ditch fills and iron; earth resistance detects moisture contrasts;
ground-penetrating radar images buried structures in three dimensions to depths of a few metres. These methods see
below the surface, which laser scanning categorically cannot. The natural workflow is hierarchical: laser survey
to map the landscape and identify targets, aerial photography to catch what has been levelled, then geophysics on
selected areas to characterise what lies beneath, then excavation to date and interpret. Each stage narrows the
area and increases the cost per hectare by roughly an order of magnitude, which is exactly why the cheap
wide-area stage is worth doing first and doing well.

sections.heading: Automated Detection and the Problem of Scale
sections.body:
The technique has created a problem of its own success. A national dataset contains more candidate features than
any team can examine by eye. Manual inspection of high-quality visualisations runs at perhaps 1 to 10 square
kilometres per analyst-hour depending on terrain complexity and feature density, so a single country's coverage
represents decades of specialist attention. Two responses have developed: automate the looking, or distribute it.

Automated detection began with template matching and morphological rules — searching for circular raised features
of a given diameter range, for instance — and such approaches work respectably for geometrically stereotyped
targets such as burial mounds, charcoal-burning platforms and mining pits. They fail on anything variable in
shape. Since the mid-2010s the field has shifted to convolutional neural networks trained on annotated examples,
following the general trajectory of computer vision. Published applications include detection of grave mounds and
charcoal kilns in Scandinavian forest, mining pits in central Europe, and Maya structures in Mesoamerican
datasets. Reported performance is often good on the region a model was trained in and degrades sharply when the
same model is applied elsewhere, because terrain, vegetation, data density and processing all differ. Transfer
between datasets remains the central unsolved difficulty.

Two structural problems limit how far automation can go. The first is class imbalance: archaeological features
occupy a minuscule fraction of any landscape, so a detector with an apparently excellent false-positive rate per
unit area still generates an unusable flood of candidates when run over thousands of square kilometres. A
detector producing one false positive per square kilometre yields a hundred thousand of them across a
medium-sized country. The second is training data: supervised learning requires large, consistently annotated
examples, and archaeological inventories are notoriously incomplete, inconsistently defined and biased toward
where people have already looked, so a model trained on them learns those biases too.

Crowdsourcing has proved a genuinely effective complement. Projects inviting volunteers to inspect terrain
visualisations online — the Dutch Heritage Quest initiative among the most successful — have mapped very large
numbers of features, with multiple independent inspections of each tile providing a built-in consistency measure
that a single expert working alone cannot supply. The practical consensus emerging is a hybrid: automated
detection to prioritise where humans should look, human interpretation to decide what things are, and field
verification to establish what is actually there. Fully automated inventories are not, at present, trustworthy
enough to publish unchecked, and papers claiming otherwise should be read with attention to whether the reported
accuracy was measured on a held-out region or merely on a held-out portion of the same block. Two figures should
always be reported together: recall, the proportion of real features found, and precision, the proportion of
detections that are real. A method can be tuned to excel at either one alone, and quoting only the flattering
number is the commonest way such results mislead.

sections.heading: Ethics, Access and Who the Data Belongs To
sections.body:
Producing a precise map of every undocumented archaeological site across a region creates obligations, and the
discipline has had to work these out quickly because the technology arrived faster than the norms.

The most immediate concern is looting. A published high-resolution terrain model with coordinates is an
efficient targeting tool for anyone wishing to dig illegally, and this is not hypothetical: illicit excavation is
a major and continuing destroyer of archaeological evidence worldwide, and metal-detecting damage to newly
mapped sites has followed data releases in several countries. Practice has converged on a graduated response
rather than blanket secrecy. Aggregated or generalised locations are published; precise coordinates for
vulnerable classes of site are held in restricted heritage databases available to researchers and land managers;
full-resolution data may be embargoed or released at reduced resolution. There is genuine, unresolved tension
here, because openness improves science, allows reanalysis and lets landowners and planners avoid destroying
sites unknowingly, while restriction protects. Reasonable practitioners disagree, and the right balance is
usually assessed site class by site class rather than as a single policy.

The second concern is the relationship with descendant and Indigenous communities. Laser surveys are frequently
flown over lands that are ancestral, currently occupied, or subject to unresolved title claims, and the resulting
data may bear directly on those claims — sometimes supporting them, by documenting long and dense occupation, and
sometimes exposing sacred places their custodians would prefer not to be mapped or publicised. Consultation
before flying, agreement about who holds and controls the resulting data, and community authority over what is
published are increasingly treated as prerequisites rather than courtesies. The CARE Principles for Indigenous
Data Governance — collective benefit, authority to control, responsibility and ethics — are the most commonly
cited framework, and they sit deliberately alongside rather than inside the open-data FAIR principles, because
open by default and community-controlled are not automatically compatible.

A third concern is more mundane but affects the record permanently: archiving. A processed terrain model is an
interpretation, dependent on classification software, version and parameters. If only the derived raster is
archived, later researchers cannot reprocess with better algorithms, and much of the data's long-term value is
lost. Good practice archives the raw or minimally processed point cloud, the full trajectory and calibration
metadata, and a written processing history, in a repository committed to long-term preservation. Several early
archaeological surveys are already effectively irreproducible because only images were kept.

Finally, there is credit and capacity. Much survey over the global South has been commissioned and analysed by
institutions elsewhere. Equitable practice means local co-authorship, training, and data held in and accessible
from the country of origin rather than solely in a foreign repository.

sections.heading: Limits, Failure Modes and Misinterpretation
sections.body:
The most important limitation is categorical rather than technical: airborne laser scanning measures the shape of
the ground surface and nothing else. It does not see beneath the surface. A site levelled by ploughing, buried by
alluvium, sealed under a modern town or built of materials that have decayed without leaving relief is invisible
to it, no matter how dense the survey. In intensively cultivated lowlands, where a large proportion of the
archaeological record has been flattened, the technique may return almost nothing while aerial photography and
geophysics return a great deal. Any statement that a survey found no archaeology in an area must be read as
finding no surviving topographic expression of archaeology.

Vegetation sets the practical limit on data quality. Dense bamboo, spiny understorey, rhododendron thickets and
young conifer plantations can reduce ground returns to near zero, leaving voids in the terrain model that are
often not obvious in a rendered image because interpolation fills them smoothly. Producing and inspecting a map
of ground-point density alongside the terrain model is essential, and any feature — or any apparent absence of
features — in a low-density area should be treated as unproven. Standing water and saturated ground absorb
infrared and generate the same problem.

Processing artefacts mimic archaeology convincingly. Flight-line boundaries can produce faint linear ridges or
tonal bands that look like trackways or field boundaries. Interpolation across data gaps generates smooth
lens-shaped rises. Tiling can produce edge effects that appear as regular rectilinear patterning across a
landscape, which is particularly seductive because rectilinearity reads as cultural. Aggressive ground filtering
truncates the tops of mounds and platforms, subtly changing their apparent morphology; conservative filtering
leaves bushes that look like small cairns. Any feature that aligns suspiciously well with a tile edge, a flight
line or a data boundary deserves scepticism before excitement.

Natural landforms are the largest source of genuine misinterpretation. Tree-throw mounds and their paired
hollows, periglacial patterned ground, solifluction lobes, sinkholes, natural levees, landslip terraces, drumlins
and beach ridges all produce regular, sometimes strikingly geometric relief. So do modern features: forestry
drainage grids, plough headlands, silage clamps, wartime training earthworks, pipeline scars and unmapped
twentieth-century quarrying. Consulting geological mapping and recent aerial photography before interpreting is
not optional.

When results look wrong, the diagnostic sequence is consistent. Check ground-point density first, since most
puzzling absences are data problems. Reprocess with different classification parameters and see whether the
feature survives. Examine raw cross-sectional profiles through the point cloud rather than the rendered image,
because a profile shows directly what the algorithm decided. Compare against a second visualisation method, since
artefacts are frequently method-specific while real relief is not. Check the feature against historic mapping.
Then, and only then, go and look at it on the ground — which remains, after every technological advance, the only
way to know what is actually there.

guides.title: Ground-Penetrating Radar and Geophysical Survey
guides.summary: How archaeologists see beneath the ground without digging: ground-penetrating radar, magnetometry, earth resistance and electromagnetic survey, how each method works, when it fails, how surveys are laid out and processed, and famous discoveries made this way.

sections.heading: Seeing Beneath the Soil: What Geophysical Survey Does for Archaeology
sections.body:
Archaeology's central dilemma is that excavation, its most powerful tool, destroys what it studies. A trench can be dug only once; whatever relationships between soil layers, walls and objects existed at that spot are converted into records and finds, and the site itself is gone. Geophysical survey offers a way around the dilemma: physical instruments passed over the surface measure properties of the ground beneath, magnetism, electrical resistance, radar reflectivity, conductivity, and from the patterns in those measurements archaeologists infer what lies buried, all without turning a single spade of earth.

The logic rests on contrast. Human activity changes soil physically. A ditch dug in the Iron Age and long since filled in holds looser, more humic, often more magnetic soil than the subsoil around it. A buried stone wall is more electrically resistant than the damp earth beside it and reflects radar energy where soil does not. A hearth or pottery kiln, fired a thousand years ago, carries a permanent magnetic signature. None of these targets is visible from the surface, but each disturbs some measurable field, and an instrument sensitive to that field, moved systematically across a site, maps the disturbance. The archaeologist's skill lies in choosing the right instrument for the expected targets and soils, and in reading the resulting maps critically.

The payoff operates at two scales. At the scale of a single site, survey guides excavation: instead of gridding a field with exploratory trenches and hoping, a team can place one precise trench across an anomaly to date and characterize it, saving seasons of labor and sparing the rest of the site. At the scale of whole landscapes, survey does what excavation never could. Motorized arrays towing banks of sensors now cover tens of hectares a day, and projects around monuments such as Stonehenge have mapped thousands of buried features, pits, enclosures, trackways, across kilometers of ground that will never be dug at all, changing interpretations of entire regions.

The field has its own history of quiet ingenuity. The first deliberate archaeological resistance survey was carried out by Richard Atkinson at Dorchester-on-Thames in England in 1946, adapting a technique from geology. Magnetometry entered archaeology in 1958, when Martin Aitken and Edward Hall of the Oxford Research Laboratory for Archaeology used an early proton magnetometer to locate Roman pottery kilns near Water Newton, the Roman town of Durobrivae, proving that fired clay could be found from the surface. Ground-penetrating radar, developed for glaciology, engineering and the military, spread into archaeology through the 1980s and 1990s as computing made its torrents of data manageable. Today the standard toolkit, radar, magnetometer, resistance meter and electromagnetic induction, is deployed from garden plots to entire buried Roman towns.

It is worth saying at the outset what survey is not. It does not find gold, it does not identify objects, and it does not date anything. It finds contrasts, ambiguous, patterned contrasts, and everything after that is interpretation, which is why the best surveys end not with a pretty map but with a targeted excavation that tests what the map seems to say.

sections.heading: How Ground-Penetrating Radar Works: Pulses, Echoes and Travel Time
sections.body:
Ground-penetrating radar works on the same principle as a ship's echo sounder, but with radio waves instead of sound and soil instead of water. A transmitting antenna held against the ground fires an extremely short pulse of electromagnetic energy, lasting around a nanosecond, downward into the earth. The pulse travels through the soil until it meets a boundary where the electrical properties of the material change, the top of a buried wall, the edge of a filled pit, a stone, a pipe, the water table. At each such boundary part of the energy reflects back toward the surface, where a receiving antenna records it. The instrument measures one thing with great precision: the two-way travel time, in nanoseconds, between transmission and each returning echo.

Time becomes depth through velocity. Radar waves move through air at the speed of light, thirty centimeters per nanosecond, but ground slows them dramatically: typical dry sand passes the wave at twelve to fifteen centimeters per nanosecond, ordinary loams around ten, and wet clay-rich soils at six or less. If the velocity of the local soil is known, each echo's travel time converts directly to the depth of the reflector that produced it. Velocity can be estimated from the shape of reflections, measured by surveying over a target of known depth, or looked up from soil type, and getting it right is what turns a radar record from a picture into a measurement.

A single spot measurement, one pulse and its echoes, is called a trace. The instrument does not take one; it takes hundreds per second while the operator drags or pushes the antenna along the ground, and stacks the traces side by side into a profile called a radargram, a vertical slice through the ground along the line walked, with distance across the page and travel time, effectively depth, down it. Modern systems trigger from an odometer wheel so traces are spaced evenly, commonly every two to five centimeters, regardless of walking speed. Survey a whole grid of closely spaced parallel lines and the profiles can be assembled by software into a three-dimensional block of reflectivity, which is where radar's most famous archaeological images come from.

What makes a boundary reflective is the contrast in a property called the relative dielectric permittivity, which describes how a material stores electrical energy in the radar wave's oscillating field, and which in soils is governed overwhelmingly by water content. Air has a permittivity of 1, dry sand around 3 to 5, most damp soils somewhere between 8 and 25, and fresh water about 80. The bigger the mismatch across a boundary, the stronger the echo: an air-filled void under a stone slab is a spectacular reflector, a damp wall foundation in damp soil a subtle one. Reflection strength also carries a polarity, and a wave passing into a slower material flips differently than one passing into a faster material, a detail experienced interpreters use to tell, for instance, a void from a solid.

The elegance of the method is that it is entirely non-invasive, rapid, and sensitive to exactly the kinds of compact, hard, dry features, walls, floors, tombs, road surfaces, that other techniques often miss. Its price is paid in physics, in the trade-offs of frequency and the tyranny of soil conditions, which the next sections take in turn.

sections.heading: Antenna Frequency: The Trade-Off Between Depth and Detail
sections.body:
Every ground-penetrating radar survey begins with one decision that constrains everything after it: the antenna's center frequency. Radar antennas are built around a characteristic frequency, common archaeological choices being 200, 250, 400 or 500 megahertz, with 100 megahertz and below for deep work and 900 megahertz to 2.6 gigahertz for very shallow, fine-grained targets such as voids in concrete. The choice is a bargain between seeing deep and seeing detail, and no antenna gives both.

The physics is straightforward. Lower-frequency waves are longer, and long waves suffer less attenuation, the progressive absorption and scattering of energy by the ground, so they penetrate farther before the echoes fade below the noise. But resolution, the ability to distinguish two nearby reflectors or to detect a small one at all, scales with wavelength too, and as a working rule a reflector needs to be on the order of a quarter wavelength thick to produce a clear, separate echo. A 100 megahertz wave in typical soil is roughly a meter long, so it resolves features at the scale of a quarter meter and coarser: fine for a buried ditch or a tomb chamber, hopeless for a mosaic floor's bedding layers. A 900 megahertz wave, around eleven centimeters in the same soil, sees those thin layers beautifully, but may be exhausted within the first meter of ground.

In practical archaeological terms, the middle band earns its popularity. A 400 or 500 megahertz antenna in reasonably cooperative soil resolves features of ten centimeters or so and reaches two to three meters deep, which covers most burials, foundations, floors and pits on most sites. A 200 or 270 megahertz antenna trades detail for reach, useful over deeply stratified urban sites, tells, or where targets may lie four or five meters down. Deep alluvial landscapes and geological questions call for 100 megahertz or lower, with antennas so large they are towed rather than carried. Some modern systems duck the choice by carrying two frequencies at once, or by using arrays of many antennas that record dense swaths in a single pass.

Frequency also interacts with the ground itself, because attenuation is not fixed: conductive soils devour high frequencies preferentially. The same 400 megahertz antenna that profiles three meters of dry sand may see forty centimeters into wet clay. Experienced surveyors therefore think in terms of a budget, the total signal loss the survey can tolerate, spent jointly by frequency, soil and target depth, and they test on site: a few trial lines with different antennas over a known or suspected feature reveal within minutes what the ground will permit that day.

One more variable rides along with frequency: the footprint.
