A radar antenna does not illuminate a pencil-thin line but a cone widening with depth, broader for lower frequencies, so a deep survey senses a larger, blurrier patch of ground at the target depth than the neat profile suggests. This is why line spacing in serious mapping surveys is tied to frequency and target size, quarter-meter spacing or finer for high-resolution work, and why the most detailed published surveys, such as the mapping of complete Roman towns, collected lines as close as twelve and a half centimeters apart. Detail is bought line by line, and the frequency decision sets the price.

sections.heading: Reading a Radargram: Hyperbolas, Layers and False Echoes
sections.body:
A raw radargram looks nothing like a buried site. It is a curtain of wiggles and gray bands, and learning to read it means learning a small vocabulary of characteristic shapes and an equally important vocabulary of illusions. The single most diagnostic shape is the hyperbola, an inverted U. A compact object, a boulder, a pipe, a skull-sized void, a tomb corner, reflects energy not only when the antenna is directly above it but also from several meters before and after, because the radar cone is wide; the echo's travel time is shortest at closest approach and longer on either side, so the object draws itself as an arc peaking over its true position. Far from being a nuisance, hyperbolas are gifts: their width encodes the wave velocity of the soil, and fitting a model curve to a clean hyperbola is the standard way to calibrate depth for the whole survey.

Extended flat reflectors write different signatures. A buried surface, a floor, a road, a paving of stone, a compacted courtyard, appears as a continuous horizontal or gently undulating band. A wall crossed at right angles appears as a short, strong, often hyperbola-capped segment repeating at the same position on adjacent profiles, and its alignment only becomes obvious when many profiles are viewed together in plan. Strata such as flood silts or windblown sand draw long parallel bands; a pit or ditch cut through them interrupts the bands and often shows as a sag or a bowl of reflections where the layered fill dips. The water table, where soil saturates, can print a strong continuous reflector that has nothing to do with archaeology, and bedrock does the same.

Then come the illusions. Because the antenna cone also spreads sideways and upward, radargrams record things that are not below the antenna at all. A stone wall standing beside the survey line, a metal fence, a parked car, even the surveyor's own body can reflect energy that arrives late and masquerades as a deep feature; these air-wave reflections betray themselves by their velocity, drawing hyperbolas with the wide, shallow shape of travel at the speed of light. Multiples are echoes that bounce twice, ground to surface to ground again, printing a ghost of a strong reflector at exactly double its travel time. Ringing, a ladder of closely spaced repeating bands, appears when the antenna couples badly with the ground or passes over metal, and can wallpaper over everything beneath it. Dry stone walls at the surface, rebar in concrete, and buried corrugated iron each produce recognizable, and recognizably misleading, textures.

Interpretation therefore leans on redundancy and context. A real buried feature should appear consistently on neighboring lines, at consistent depth, forming a coherent shape in plan; an artifact of the method usually will not. Depths should be sanity-checked against anything known, a visible section, a service record, a previous excavation. And the interpreter should always know what was on the surface, which is why good field practice logs every fence, path, drain cover and tree along each line. The radargram never lies about travel times; it simply answers a stranger question than the one asked, and reading it well means constantly re-translating between echo space and the buried world.

sections.heading: Soils and Site Conditions: When Radar Works and When It Fails
sections.body:
The most important fact about ground-penetrating radar is that the ground gets a vote. No instrument setting can rescue a survey in soil that absorbs the signal, and no method is more site-dependent, which is why an honest radar practitioner talks about soils before targets. The governing property is electrical conductivity: soils that conduct electricity well convert the radar wave's energy into tiny currents and heat, attenuating it within decimeters. The two great conductors in soils are clay and salt.

Clay minerals carry surface electrical charges and hold water films, making clay-rich ground both conductive and lossy. Wet, heavy clay is the radar surveyor's despair; penetration can collapse to a few tens of centimeters even at low frequency, and what returns is often smeared and ringing. Salts dissolved in soil water do the same damage: coastal flats washed by seawater, arid soils crusted with evaporite salts, ground salted by de-icing along roads, and some heavily fertilized fields all drink the signal. In such conditions radar is simply the wrong tool, and magnetometry or resistance survey should carry the project instead.

At the other pole, radar's paradise: dry sand, gravel, chalk, volcanic ash, and massive dry masonry all pass the signal generously. Deserts have produced radar profiles tens of meters deep; clean quartz sand can carry a 200 megahertz pulse ten meters or more. Ice and snow are so transparent that radar's first great successes were glaciological, and the same transparency once famously deceived: aircraft lost under Greenland's ice were found by radar hundreds of feet down. Between the extremes lie the loams and silts where most archaeology happens, workable but variable, with penetration of one to four meters that shifts with the weather.

Moisture cuts both ways and changes by the day. Water raises a soil's dielectric permittivity steeply, so moisture contrasts create the very reflections radar sees; a bone-dry, homogeneous sand can be almost featureless precisely because nothing contrasts. Light rain a few days before survey can improve results by re-establishing contrast between, say, a damp ditch fill and a drier gravel. Saturation, on the other hand, raises conductivity and drowns the record. Frozen ground is often excellent, since ice is resistive; the spring thaw is often terrible. Repeating a survey in a different season is a legitimate, and sometimes transformative, strategy.

Surfaces and clutter set further conditions. Radar needs good contact, so ploughed clods, dense scrub, rubble and standing crops degrade data, while mown grass, bare earth, pavement and building floors are ideal; radar is, notably, the one major method that works indoors and through concrete, which makes it the tool of choice inside standing churches, mosques and historic buildings where graves and crypts are sought beneath floors. Metal is opaque: reinforced slabs, buried sheet iron and dense service runs shadow everything below them. Overhead, mobile phones and radio masts rarely trouble modern systems, but buried live cables announce themselves and confuse records. The disciplined habit is a walkover before the first line: note slopes, wet patches, services, surface metal, and vegetation, and write down a prediction of what the ground will allow. Comparing that prediction with the first trial profiles is the fastest education the site can offer.

sections.heading: From Radargram to Map: Processing and Time Slices
sections.body:
Raw radar data are a stack of noisy vertical slices; the images that make headlines, ghostly plans of villas and ships, are the product of a processing chain, and understanding that chain is part of reading the results honestly. Processing does not add information; it rearranges, filters and re-scales what was recorded so that human eyes can find the patterns, and each step has assumptions that can mislead if applied thoughtlessly.

The standard sequence begins with housekeeping. Time-zero correction aligns every trace so that the moment the pulse enters the ground sits at the top of the record, since electronics drift and the true surface otherwise wobbles. Dewow, a low-cut filter, removes a slow bulge that transmitters superimpose on every trace. Because echoes weaken exponentially with depth, gain functions amplify later arrivals so deep reflections become visible alongside shallow ones; gain is cosmetic but indispensable, and over-gained sections manufacture apparent features from noise. Background removal subtracts the average trace from every trace, erasing the horizontal banding that plagues radargrams and revealing dipping and localized reflections, at the cost of also erasing genuinely flat archaeology such as floors if applied too aggressively. Band-pass filtering cuts frequencies outside the antenna's useful range, and migration, the most elegant step, uses the measured wave velocity to collapse each hyperbola back to the point that generated it, turning arcs into compact objects and restoring the true geometry of dipping surfaces.

Then comes the step that changed archaeological radar from a profiling tool into a mapping tool: the time slice. With a grid of closely spaced parallel profiles in the computer, software resamples the data into a three-dimensional volume and cuts it horizontally, extracting the reflection amplitude everywhere within a chosen travel-time window, say between twenty and twenty-four nanoseconds, and painting it in plan. The result is a map of reflectivity at an approximately constant depth, and a sequence of slices descends through the site like the pages of a flip-book: topsoil clutter in the first slices, then wall lines snapping into rectilinear clarity, then floors and streets, then natural. Features that are invisible as isolated wiggles on single profiles become unmistakable when their alignment across dozens of profiles is seen from above; it was time-slice mapping at tight line spacing that let teams publish the complete street plan of the buried Roman town of Falerii Novi, temple, bath block, market and a monumental arcade among them, without excavation.

Honesty in presentation is the final processing step. A slice's nominal depth depends on the velocity model, so captions should give travel time as well as estimated depth, with uncertainty. The processing sequence should be reported, because a skeptical reader needs to know whether that faint rectangle survived background removal or was created by it. Amplitude color scales can be chosen to flatter; grayscale with stated clipping is the sober default. And interpretation drawings, the neat inked plans of walls and pits derived from slices, must be published alongside, never instead of, the data images. The professional bodies of archaeological geophysics publish guidance to exactly this effect, and the discipline's credibility rests on the distinction between what the ground returned and what the interpreter believes it means.

sections.heading: Magnetometry: Mapping Ditches, Hearths and Kilns by Their Magnetic Ghosts
sections.body:
If radar is archaeology's scalpel, magnetometry is its scythe: the fastest of the major methods, mowing whole landscapes into maps, and the first choice for prospecting unknown ground in most of temperate Europe. A magnetometer measures the strength of the Earth's magnetic field, about 48,000 nanotesla in northern Europe, with a sensitivity of a tenth of a nanotesla or better, and archaeological features betray themselves as local distortions of a few nanotesla, parts per ten thousand of the ambient field, superimposed on it.

Two physical effects write those distortions. The first is thermoremanent magnetization: iron oxide minerals in clay, when heated past about 580 degrees Celsius, the Curie point of magnetite, lose their magnetic memory, and as they cool they re-magnetize aligned with the Earth's field of that moment, permanently. Every kiln, hearth, furnace, burnt house and dump of fired brick is therefore a little fossil magnet, and fired features produce the strongest, crispest anomalies in the repertoire, which is why magnetometry's first archaeological triumph, in 1958, was finding Roman pottery kilns. The second effect is subtler and vastly more widespread: magnetic susceptibility enhancement. Topsoil, enriched by burning, decay and soil bacteria, contains more fine-grained magnetic minerals than the subsoil beneath it. Any hole dug in antiquity and refilled, ditch, pit, grave, posthole, ends up packed with enhanced topsoil-derived fill, and reads as a faint positive anomaly against the quieter subsoil. Whole settlement plans, enclosure ditches, roundhouse rings, storage pit clusters, roads flanked by ditches, emerge from exactly this contrast.

The workhorse instrument is the fluxgate gradiometer, a pair of directional sensors mounted vertically half a meter to a meter apart. Subtracting the two readings cancels the Earth's field and its diurnal wanderings, along with distant interference, leaving only sharp local gradients, precisely the signature of near-surface archaeology. Carried on a light frame at a steady walk, sampling several times per meter along lines a meter apart or towed as multi-sensor arrays behind a vehicle, gradiometers routinely cover one to several hectares a day, and motorized cesium and fluxgate arrays with satellite positioning have surveyed thousands of hectares in single projects. Depth reach is modest, most sensitivity lies in the top meter or so, and an anomaly's breadth roughly signals its source's depth.

Reading a magnetic map has its own conventions. Data are usually displayed in grayscale at a tight range, commonly a few nanotesla either side of zero, so faint ditches show; ferrous rubbish, horseshoes, wire, ploughshares, saturates as paired black-white dipoles that experienced eyes discount automatically. Igneous geology can shout over archaeology, fired features can be confused with lightning strikes, and modern services, fences and vehicles lay stripes of interference, which is why surveyors dress metal-free, no steel toecaps, zips or phones near the sensors, and keep grids away from parked cars.

Magnetometry's blind spots complete the picture: it barely sees stone, since most building stone is magnetically quiet, so a masonry villa may appear only as the ditches and pits around it. On the sites where radar excels, dry masonry under floors, magnetometry is weakest, and the reverse holds equally, which is why the two methods are so often flown in tandem over the same grid.

sections.heading: Earth Resistance Survey: Finding Walls and Ditches with Electrical Current
sections.body:
Earth resistance survey is the oldest of archaeology's geophysical methods and still one of the most trusted, precisely because its physics is domestic: damp soil conducts electricity, dry stone does not. Pass a small current through the ground between electrodes and measure the voltage; the ratio gives resistance, and resistance maps moisture. A buried stone wall holds less water than the soil around it and reads high. A silted ditch, humic and moisture-retentive, reads low. The method sees, in effect, a moisture shadow of the archaeology, and on the right site it draws building plans with a clarity magnetometry cannot match.

The standard field instrument is a frame carrying two probes half a meter apart, the twin-probe array, connected by cable to a distant pair of fixed remote probes that complete the circuit and calibrate away the wider ground. The operator walks the grid, pressing the frame's probes into the turf at each sample station, typically every meter, or every half meter for building detail, taking the logged reading, and stepping on; an experienced pair covers a fraction of a hectare to perhaps half a hectare in a day, an order of magnitude slower than magnetometry, which is why resistance is usually a second-stage tool, deployed over targets rather than landscapes. Wheeled multi-probe carts and towed square arrays speed the work where ground allows, and the same physics scaled up becomes electrical resistivity tomography, lines of dozens of electrodes that image vertical slices meters deep, invaluable over deep features such as ramparts, mottes and buried valleys.

Probe geometry sets depth. The rule of thumb for the twin-probe array is that sensitivity reaches roughly as deep as the mobile probe separation, so the standard half-meter frame senses approximately the top half to three-quarters of a meter, where wall footings and floors live. Widening the separation deepens the view at the cost of resolution, and repeat surveys at two separations can crudely separate shallow from deep anomalies.

Everything about the method is seasonal. Resistance depends on soil moisture contrast, and contrast comes and goes with the weather: after weeks of drought the whole site may read uniformly high, after saturating winter rain uniformly low, and in both states the archaeology fades. The classic best conditions are a drying spell after a damp period, when soils drain differentially, walls drying first, ditch fills last. Old hands schedule resistance survey for late spring and early summer in Britain for exactly this reason, and the same physics explains cropmarks and parchmarks, the drought-summer phenomenon in which buried walls print themselves as yellowed stripes in grass, effectively a resistance survey performed by the sky.

Interpretation carries fewer traps than radar or magnetometry but is not trap-free. Tree roots dry the soil and mimic high-resistance features; paths and compacted ground read high; buried pipe trenches, backfilled loosely, read low and ruler-straight. Geology intrudes where gravels and clays interfinger. The compensations are ample: resistance is indifferent to ferrous litter and urban magnetic noise, works close to fences and buildings where magnetometers are blinded, needs no exotic electronics, and its maps, walls white, ditches dark, are the most intuitively legible products in archaeological geophysics. On a masonry site with cooperative moisture, a resistance plot can look startlingly like an excavation plan, achieved for the price of a few days' walking.

sections.heading: Electromagnetic Induction, Susceptibility and Metal Detection
sections.body:
Between radar and the galvanic methods sits a family of instruments that measure the ground by induction, without touching it. An electromagnetic induction meter, EMI in the trade, carries a transmitter coil driving an alternating magnetic field into the soil; that field induces faint eddy currents in conductive ground, and those currents broadcast a secondary field that a receiver coil detects. From the returned signal the instrument derives two properties at once: the soil's electrical conductivity, the inverse of the resistance that probe arrays measure, and its magnetic susceptibility, the same property that underwrites magnetometry. One pass, two maps, no ground contact.

That combination makes EMI the utility player of archaeological prospection. Because nothing needs to be pushed into the ground, the meters stride over baked earth, frozen turf, gravel and stubble that stop resistance frames cold, and they thrive exactly where radar drowns: conductive, clayey and salt-affected soils return strong induction signals, so EMI is the default method on alluvial plains, estuarine silts and the heavy soils of, for instance, large parts of the Low Countries, where multi-coil instruments towed behind small vehicles have mapped buried medieval landscapes, paleochannels and World War One trench systems alike. Coil spacing sets depth: small hand-held meters integrate the top meter or so, while larger multi-coil sleds read several depth ranges simultaneously and allow crude layered modeling. The conductivity channel excels at moisture-holding features, ditches, channels, clay floors, while the in-phase susceptibility channel flags burning, occupation soils and brick.

Magnetic susceptibility deserves its own line in the toolkit even without full survey. Because human occupation enhances topsoil susceptibility, measuring it, with a field loop pressed to the ground or on soil samples in the laboratory, offers a cheap wide-mesh prospecting technique: sample a plough field on a twenty-meter grid, contour the values, and occupation areas emerge as susceptibility highs worth surveying properly. The same measurements help interpret magnetometer data, since they reveal whether the local soils can generate strong anomalies at all.

The humble metal detector is an induction instrument too, a transmitter-receiver coil pair tuned to the strong secondary fields of discrete metal objects in the top decimeters. Within archaeology it has two honorable roles: systematically gridded detecting of ploughsoil, logging every find to coordinates, recovers the artifact scatter that plowing has already lifted from stratigraphy, and on excavations detectors check spoil heaps and pre-scan surfaces for the small coins and fittings trowels miss. Around them sits a larger, contested world: hobby detecting recovers vast numbers of objects, some reported through schemes such as England's Portable Antiquities Scheme, which has logged well over a million finds, and some looted from protected sites. The instrument is neutral; the difference is recording, permission and law, which vary sharply by country.

Two further siblings complete the family. Frequency-domain and time-domain metal detectors scale up into deep industrial locators used for pipes, cables, drums and unexploded ordnance, and archaeology borrows them for exactly those targets when clearing ground. And low-frequency EMI merges, at the far end, into the induction tools of utility mapping, a reminder that most anomalies under a modern field are recent: knowing what a water main, a land drain and a field boundary look like in every instrument's data is as much a part of the archaeological skill set as recognizing a Roman ditch.

sections.heading: Planning and Walking a Survey Grid
sections.body:
Every method in this guide produces its map by the same discipline: measurements taken at known positions, dense enough to resolve the targets, over a grid tied to the real world. The glamour is in the instruments, but the quality of a survey is decided by tapes, pegs and patience, and the classic field routine is worth learning in its standard form even in the satellite-positioning era, because it is what makes datasets comparable, repeatable and publishable.

Planning starts with a question, not a machine. What features are plausible here, at what size and depth, in what soils? A Roman masonry villa in free-draining loam argues for resistance and radar; an Iron Age ditched enclosure on magnetically quiet subsoil argues for magnetometry; deep alluvium argues for EMI and low-frequency radar. From the expected target size follows the sampling interval, the rule being that a feature must be crossed by at least two, preferably several, readings or lines: a two-meter ditch permits one-meter traverses, a half-meter wall demands half- or quarter-meter density. From site area and the chosen density follows the time budget, and from the time budget, often, a two-stage design: fast magnetometry everywhere, then slow, dense methods over the anomalies that matter.

The field grid is traditionally laid as squares of twenty or thirty meters, set out with tapes and optical squares or, now, with survey-grade satellite receivers, and marked with pegs, plastic, bamboo or wood, never steel where a magnetometer will pass. The grid must be tied to permanent mapping, national grid coordinates or well-described local monuments, so that an anomaly found this year can be relocated, and excavated, years later to centimeter accuracy. Within each square the instrument is walked in parallel traverses, either all in one direction, slower but cleaner, or zigzag, faster but prone to small positional shear between alternate lines that processing must correct. Consistent walking pace, consistent instrument height and orientation, and honest logging of every square's conditions, weather, ground state, obstacles, interference sources, are the unglamorous core of data quality.

Modern practice increasingly replaces the string grid with continuous positioning: instruments log against real-time-kinematic satellite fixes or robotic total stations, motorized arrays sweep open fields, and the operator's job shifts toward keeping swaths overlapping and sensors healthy. The principles do not change, sampling density, positional integrity, metadata, and hand layout remains essential in woodland, inside buildings and on small urban sites where satellites fail.
steps: Define the archaeological question, the expected feature types, sizes and depths, and choose methods and sampling intervals that can actually resolve them in the local soils.
Walk the site first: map slopes, wet ground, services, fences, surface metal and vegetation, and record everything that could produce false anomalies.
Establish a baseline along one site edge with tapes or satellite positioning, and set out grid squares, commonly twenty by twenty meters, marking corners with non-magnetic pegs.
Tie at least three grid points to permanent real-world coordinates so the survey can be georeferenced and any anomaly relocated later for excavation.
Configure and test the instrument over known quiet ground each morning, checking drift, sensor balance and, for radar, the time-zero and a velocity estimate from a test hyperbola.
Survey each square in parallel traverses at the planned line and sample spacing, keeping pace and sensor height constant, and re-walk any line the logger flags as faulty.
Record metadata for every square as it is finished, direction walked, conditions, anomalies noticed, interference encountered, before moving the tapes.
Back up raw data on site at least daily, then process conservatively, keeping the unprocessed files untouched so every image can be regenerated and audited.
Interpret anomalies against the surface observations and historic maps, grade each one by confidence, and propose ground-truthing before any claim is made public.

sections.heading: Famous Discoveries: Falerii Novi, the Gjellestad Ship and Stonehenge's Hidden Landscape
sections.body:
The clearest way to grasp what these methods can do is through the surveys that changed expectations, and three from the last two decades stand for the whole discipline. Each answered a question excavation could not have touched at the same scale, and each was published with its data, which is why they bear retelling.

Falerii Novi, fifty kilometers north of Rome, was a walled Roman town of about thirty hectares, founded in 241 BC and slowly abandoned in the early medieval period; its circuit walls still stand in open farmland, with the town itself entirely buried and unexcavated. It had already been magnetometer-mapped in the 1990s, itself a landmark, when a British-Belgian team returned with a towed ground-penetrating radar array, collecting profiles at 12.5 centimeter spacing across the whole town, and published the results in 2020. The time slices resolved the town in astonishing depth and detail: a temple, a market building, a grand bath complex, a public monument of a type unparalleled, a great colonnaded enclosure near the south gate, and, running beneath the streets, the aqueduct network, visible as it looped the town rather than merely feeding it. Beyond the buildings, the survey demonstrated something methodological: that a complete Roman town could be studied as urban fabric, room by room and phase by phase in places, without a trench, and that the sheer data volume, tens of millions of traces, was now the discipline's central challenge.

Gjellestad, in Ostfold, southeastern Norway, showed the opposite scale: a single target of national importance. In 2018, archaeologists from the Norwegian Institute for Cultural Heritage Research, asked to assess a field beside the great Jell Mound before agricultural drainage works, drove a motorized radar array over it and found, among the traces of a vanished cemetery and settlement halls, an unmistakable ship: a twenty-meter keel-shaped anomaly lying in a ploughed-flat burial mound half a meter beneath the topsoil. Trial trenching confirmed a Viking-age ship burial with the keel surviving, and in 2020 and 2021 it was fully excavated, Norway's first Viking ship excavation in about a century, driven by the discovery that fungal decay was destroying the remaining timber. The sequence, radar find, targeted confirmation, rescue excavation, is the textbook relationship between survey and digging.

Around Stonehenge, survey rewrote a landscape. The Stonehenge Hidden Landscapes Project, led by the University of Birmingham with the Ludwig Boltzmann Institute for Archaeological Prospection, towed motorized magnetometer and radar arrays across roughly ten square kilometers between 2010 and 2014, mapping hundreds of buried features: new henges, barrows, pit alignments and the huge Durrington Walls enclosure's hidden details. Building on that coverage, a consortium announced in 2020 a ring of massive pits, each on the order of ten meters across and five deep, arcing more than a kilometer from Durrington Walls, a monument scale nobody had imagined the Neolithic landscape contained. Whatever each pit proves to be, the point stands: only landscape-scale geophysics could even pose the question.

Three different scales, town, grave, landscape, one lesson. The methods do not replace excavation; at Gjellestad they triggered it, at Falerii they will guide whichever trenches are ever cut, and around Stonehenge they generated a decade of targeted digging. Survey finds and frames; the spade still decides.

sections.heading: Beyond Archaeology: Graves, Utilities, Voids and Forensics
sections.body:
The same physics that finds a Roman wall finds a water main, a mine shaft or a clandestine grave, and archaeological geophysicists share their instruments with a wide world of applied survey. Knowing those neighboring trades matters even for the purely archaeological reader, partly because their targets litter every site, and partly because their standards and cautions are instructive.

Utility location is the largest of these trades. Before roads are cut or foundations dug, surveyors sweep the ground with electromagnetic pipe-and-cable locators, which induce or trace signals along conductive services, and with ground-penetrating radar, which also catches the non-conductive ones, plastic gas pipes, clay drains, fiber ducts. Radar sees a pipe crossed at right angles as a crisp hyperbola, and an experienced operator can distinguish a metal main from a plastic one by polarity and ringing. The trade's hard-won rule is codified in standards such as the United Kingdom's PAS 128, which grades every detected utility by how it was found and how confident its position is: a lesson archaeology has absorbed into its own guidance, that an anomaly's confidence must travel with it. The other rule is blunter: no survey is exhaustive, which is why legal digging still requires the utility-marking call and careful hand excavation near indications.

Forensic search applies archaeology's toolkit to recent tragedy. Ground-penetrating radar is the standard instrument for suspected clandestine graves, because a burial disturbs soil layering and often leaves a subtle void or slump, and it can search floors, patios and cellars non-destructively; it was famously used in the 1994 investigation at 25 Cromwell Street in Gloucester, England, and more recently in the search, begun in earnest in 2020, for unmarked mass graves from the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre in Oaklawn Cemetery, where radar anomalies guided excavations that found coffined burials. Cadaver dogs, soil probes and careful stratigraphic excavation complete the forensic sequence, and practitioners emphasize the same discipline as archaeology: radar indicates, it never identifies, and a grave-shaped anomaly may be a root hollow, so conclusions wait for the ground truth. The same is true, poignantly, of searches at former residential school sites in Canada from 2021 onward, where radar results have been reported precisely and properly as probable graves pending confirmation.

Engineering and hazard survey rounds out the family. Radar maps voids under roads and runways, sinkholes in karst, abandoned mine workings, and the deteriorating rebar inside bridge decks; resistivity tomography images dam cores and landslide slip surfaces; magnetometry sweeps former battlefields and ranges for unexploded ordnance, a serious concern on twentieth-century European sites, where archaeological magnetometer maps are routinely screened for bomb-sized dipoles before any machine cuts a trench. Marine cousins, sidescan sonar, sub-bottom profilers and towed magnetometers, do the same work underwater, finding wrecks from the Mary Rose era to lost aircraft.

For the archaeologist, the practical takeaways are three. First, every modern site is layered with the signatures of these other trades' targets, services, drains, made ground, and learning their look in each instrument prevents embarrassing interpretations. Second, their safety rules apply on archaeological ground too: utilities and ordnance do not care why you are digging. And third, their professionalized reporting, confidence grading, method statements, auditable data, is the standard archaeological survey should meet, and increasingly does.

sections.heading: Ground-Truthing: Tying Anomalies to the Real Ground
sections.body:
A geophysical map is a hypothesis, and the discipline's integrity lives in how hypotheses are tested. Ground-truthing, checking anomalies against the actual soil, is not an optional epilogue; it is the step that converts patterns into knowledge, calibrates every future survey on similar ground, and catches the interpretive failures that every method commits. The forms it takes run from a hand auger to a full excavation, and choosing among them is itself a design decision.

The lightest tools touch the ground barely more than the survey did. A soil auger or gouge core, hand-driven at the center of an anomaly and at a control point beside it, recovers a column that can confirm a humic ditch fill, a rubble spread, burnt material or undisturbed natural in minutes, at the cost of a few centimeters' hole; on many projects a morning of augering sorts a map's anomalies into archaeological, geological and modern with striking efficiency. Test pits, meter squares dug by hand, go further, exposing enough of a feature to photograph, draw and date from finds. The strongest test is a targeted trench cut perpendicular across an anomaly, wide enough to read the feature in section: its shape, fills, finds and relationships, which is what finally names a radar reflector as a wall footing of a particular period rather than a band of bedrock.

The scientific yield flows in both directions. Excavation dates and characterizes what the instruments saw; just as importantly, it teaches what the instruments were actually responding to. Measuring the excavated feature, its depth, width, fill properties, ideally with laboratory magnetic susceptibility and moisture measurements of its soils, turns one trench into a calibration for the whole landscape: now the survey team knows what a two-meter ditch in this subsoil looks like at this sample density, and every similar anomaly on the map inherits that confidence. Well-run projects loop the process, survey, trench, re-interpret the survey, and sometimes re-survey with another method over the freshly understood ground.

Failure cases are part of the record, and publishing them is a professional obligation the field has learned to honor. Anomalies dissolve on excavation into tree throws, animal burrows, ice-age frost cracks, geological pipes in chalk, or twentieth-century rubbish; conversely, trenches reveal archaeology the survey never registered, shallow graves in dry sand, stone walls in magnetometer data, features below radar's local penetration. Recorded honestly, both kinds of miss refine expectations; suppressed, they corrupt the literature into overconfidence. Guidance from bodies such as Historic England and the professional archaeological institutes therefore asks that reports state methods, instrument settings, sampling densities, processing steps and confidence for each interpretation, exactly so that later workers can judge what an absence of anomalies does and does not mean.

There is also a conservation logic to ground-truthing sparingly. On protected sites, the whole point of survey is to spare the archive in the ground, so the test excavation is kept minimal, placed where it answers the most questions per square meter, and sometimes replaced entirely by archival calibration, comparing the survey with old excavation records or standing remains. The mature relationship is symbiotic: geophysics makes excavation surgical, excavation makes geophysics meaningful, and neither alone deserves the confidence the pair have earned together.

sections.heading: Limits, Ethics and Good Practice in Survey Work
sections.body:
Every instrument in this guide measures a physical property, not the past, and the final skill of the discipline is knowing, and saying, what the measurements cannot support. The limits fall into three families: physical, interpretive and ethical, and each has practical consequences for how surveys should be commissioned, conducted and reported.

The physical limits are absolute. No method sees everything: magnetometry misses stone, resistance fades when moisture contrast fails, radar drowns in conductive clay, and everything blurs with depth. Small features escape coarse sampling by simply falling between lines, so a blank map at one-meter traverse spacing says nothing about graves half a meter wide. Deep features escape every shallow-sensing method; urban stratigraphy meters thick, or features under alluvium, may be beyond any surface instrument. The honest formula, drilled into every practitioner, is that absence of evidence in a survey is not evidence of absence in the ground, and a survey report that cannot bring itself to say so plainly should be distrusted. The corollary is that negative results still have value when their limits are quantified: a magnetometer survey that would certainly have detected a ditched enclosure, and found none, genuinely constrains what a field can contain.

The interpretive limits are subtler because they are human. Anomaly maps invite pattern-hunting, and the eye completes rectangles that the data only gesture toward; the professional defenses are independent interpretation by more than one worker, publication of data images alongside interpretations, confidence grading of every claimed feature, and the discipline of proposing a testable identification rather than an evocative one. Sensational claims from unverified survey data, lost cities, hidden chambers, have repeatedly embarrassed the field when trenches or further work deflated them; the corrective is not silence but sequence: survey, then test, then announce. Guidance documents from national heritage agencies and the professional geophysics organizations codify this, along with archiving standards so that raw data outlive the interpreter and can be reprocessed as methods improve.

The ethical limits bind hardest. In most countries, geophysical survey on protected monuments requires consent even though it is non-invasive, partly to control the follow-on temptation to dig, and metal detecting on protected sites is criminal in many jurisdictions; permission of the landowner is everywhere the minimum. Survey data are also power: a published map of a rich, shallow cemetery is a looter's shopping list, so responsible projects consider what to release at what precision, sometimes generalizing locations in public outputs while archiving the detail with the heritage authority. Where surveys concern graves, and above all recent or contested graves, communities and descendants come first: the searches at former residential schools in Canada and at Tulsa have modeled a practice in which affected communities commission, control and interpret the work, and where the language of results, probable, consistent with, pending confirmation, is chosen with care because the stakes are human, not academic.

Good practice, condensed: ask a clear question; choose methods that can answer it in the local ground; sample densely enough to resolve the targets; record conditions and settings; process transparently and archive raw data; grade confidence; test before claiming; publish misses as well as hits; respect law, landowners and descendants. An instrument does none of this by itself. The method's real sensor, as the discipline likes to say, walks behind the machine.

guides.safetyNote: Geophysical survey itself is low-risk, but acting on its results is not. Never dig based on a survey image alone: radar and other instruments routinely miss buried electricity cables, gas lines and other utilities, and striking one can be fatal. Before any excavation, use the official utility-marking service for your country, in the United States call 811 several days ahead, and treat every unexpected pipe, cable or drum as live and hazardous until proven otherwise. Fieldwork also means traffic, uneven ground, weather and, on some sites, unexploded ordnance or contaminated soil; follow the site owner's rules and local law, since surveying and digging on protected archaeological sites without a permit is illegal in most countries.

guides.title: Underwater and Maritime Archaeology
guides.summary: How archaeologists find, excavate, record and conserve shipwrecks, sunken cities and drowned landscapes, from side-scan sonar and diver excavation to raising the Mary Rose and the Vasa, plus the law that separates science from treasure hunting.

sections.heading: What Underwater and Maritime Archaeology Actually Study
sections.body:
Underwater archaeology is ordinary archaeology carried out where water covers the evidence; maritime archaeology is the study of how humans have lived with the sea, whatever the site's current state. The two overlap heavily but are not the same. A shipwreck lying in 40 meters of water is both; a Roman harbor now silted into dry farmland is maritime but not underwater; a prehistoric village drowned by a rising lake is underwater but not maritime. Together they cover ships and boats, cargoes, harbors, anchorages, fish traps, bridges, crannogs, wells, ritual deposits in bogs and springs, submerged prehistoric land surfaces, aircraft lost at sea and even entire drowned towns. The discipline's founding insight, argued forcefully by the American pioneer George Bass, is that none of this requires a new kind of science, only ordinary archaeological method executed under difficult conditions: the same careful excavation, recording and publication expected on land, with the diving as a means rather than the point.

Why go to the trouble? Because water preserves what land destroys, and because ships are uniquely informative objects. A wreck is often a closed find, a single moment sealed in one event: everything aboard was in use together on the day of loss, unlike a land site where centuries of occupation mix. Archaeologists call this the time capsule quality, and it makes wrecks priceless for dating and for reconstructing trade. A single cargo can rewrite economic history; the Uluburun ship, sunk off Turkey around 1320 BCE, carried ten tons of Cypriot copper, a ton of tin, Baltic amber, African ebony and ivory, Canaanite jars and Mycenaean pottery, a physical cross-section of Late Bronze Age exchange no text records.

The field is young. Helmet divers salvaged artifacts in the nineteenth century, and sponge divers found the Antikythera wreck in 1900, but recovery without recording is salvage, not archaeology. The turning point came with the aqualung, developed by Jacques Cousteau and Emile Gagnan in 1943, which freed divers from hoses and made precise seabed work possible. In 1960 George Bass, then a graduate student, directed the excavation of a Bronze Age wreck at Cape Gelidonya, Turkey, applying full land-standard method underwater for the first time, mapping every object before lifting it. Britain followed with the Mary Rose project, Sweden with Vasa, and by the 1970s universities were training specialists. Today the discipline spans warm-water classical wrecks, cold-water medieval ships, submerged Stone Age forests and robotic surveys in kilometers of water.

It is worth naming what maritime archaeology is not. It is not treasure hunting, which sells the evidence; it is not souvenir collecting; and it is not only about ships. Some of its most important recent work concerns landscapes: reconstructing Doggerland, the drowned plain beneath the North Sea where Mesolithic people hunted, or mapping the submerged shorelines that early humans followed out of Africa. The sea floor holds the largest unread archive of human history, and this field is the discipline of reading it without destroying it.

sections.heading: How Shipwreck Sites Form and Change Over Time
sections.body:
A wreck on the seabed is not a ship, and treating it like one leads to bad interpretation. Between the sailing vessel and the site the archaeologist maps lies a chain of transformations that the discipline calls site formation processes, a framework given its classic statement for wrecks by the British archaeologist Keith Muckelroy in his 1978 book Maritime Archaeology. Muckelroy described the wrecking event as a series of filters and scrambling devices: each stage removes some material, moves some, and rearranges the rest, and the analyst's job is to run the film backward.

Consider the sequence. A ship strikes rock or founders in a storm. Some cargo and gear may be jettisoned before loss; people escape with valuables; rigging and boats float away. As the hull sinks it may break, scattering material along a debris trail that can run for hundreds of meters and, for deep losses, spread as items of different weight sink at different speeds. On the bottom, salvage often begins within days; historical divers with bells and grapples stripped guns and cargo from accessible wrecks for centuries, and a site may show the neat absence of everything a contemporary salvor valued. Then the sea gets to work. Storm waves and currents roll and winnow light material; wooden structure above the seabed is colonized and eaten; iron concretes; sand ripples bury and re-expose the remains in cycles. Within a few decades most wrecks in shallow water collapse into a low mound, stabilizing when everything perishable above the sediment line is gone and what remains is buried or too heavy to move.

The crucial mercy in this destruction is burial. Whatever sinks into soft sediment, or is buried by the collapsing hull and ballast above it, leaves the oxygenated zone where biology operates and enters a slow, dark, stable world. This is why wrecks so often survive as a lens-shaped slice of the lower hull, the turn of the bilge, packed with cargo, while the upper works are simply gone, and why the first question at any new site is not what is visible but what the sediment might hold. It is also why environment predicts preservation better than age: the Baltic Sea, cold, brackish and hostile to the wood-boring shipworm, keeps seventeenth-century ships standing upright with masts, while a tropical reef reduces a hull to ballast stones and cannon in a generation.

Understanding formation processes has practical consequences. Excavators distinguish primary deposits, material lying where the wrecking placed it, from material reworked by storms or salvage, and they read scattered sites as physics problems: a trail of progressively heavier objects points along the ship's dying course. Site managers use the same science in reverse, reburying exposed timbers under sandbags or sediment because exposure is the enemy, and monitoring scour around wrecks that act as reefs and dig their own graves. And every field report now records not only what was found but the processes evidently at work, because a site is not a snapshot of a ship; it is the current frame of a process still running.

sections.heading: Why Water Preserves and Destroys: Anoxia, Shipworm and Corrosion
sections.body:
The underwater environment runs two opposite regimes at once, and every wreck is a map of which regime governed which part. Above the seabed, in oxygenated water, destruction is fast and biological. The most notorious agent is the shipworm, Teredo navalis, not a worm but a bivalve mollusk with a vestigial shell it uses as a drill; its larvae settle on wood and tunnel through it, riddling a hull plank in months and consuming exposed wooden structure in warm seas within years. Gribble crustaceans chew surfaces, fungi and bacteria finish the job, and storms and abrasion do the mechanical work. This is why warm, salty, shallow sites keep almost no wood: the classical Mediterranean wreck typically survives as a cargo mound of amphoras over the few timbers the cargo's weight pressed into the sediment.

Below the sediment line, or in naturally hostile water, the rules invert. Buried in fine mud, wood lies in an anoxic world where the borers and most microbes cannot live, and organic materials survive on timescales land archaeology can only envy: rope, leather shoes, wooden bowls, textile fragments, seeds, insect remains, even ships' biscuit have come intact from wrecks centuries or millennia old. Two famous environments extend this mercy to whole ships. The Baltic is too brackish for Teredo, which needs fuller salinity, so hulls there stand for centuries; the Black Sea below about 150 meters is permanently anoxic, and robotic surveys since 2015 have imaged more than sixty ships on its floor, including a Greek trading vessel from around 400 BCE lying essentially complete, mast still stepped, after twenty-four centuries. Cold, low light and stable chemistry are the librarians of the deep.

Metals follow their own electrochemical logic. Iron in seawater corrodes actively, but a curious protective process intervenes: corrosion products, sand and marine growth cement into a hard crust called concretion around the object. Inside a concretion, the original iron may persist, or may dissolve entirely, leaving a perfect hollow mold of itself; excavators routinely x-ray concretions and cast their cavities with epoxy to recover the shape of a vanished tool. Cast iron cannon survive centuries; thin wrought iron may be a ghost. Copper and its alloys corrode slowly and poison marine growth around them, which is why bronze statues and fittings emerge recognizable after two thousand years; the Antikythera mechanism's bronze gears survived where iron would not have. Gold is untouched by seawater, silver converts to sulfides but survives, and lead endures almost indefinitely. Where different metals touch, galvanic couples accelerate the loss of the less noble partner, a detail that lets corrosion scientists like those who studied the Titanic predict a wreck's remaining lifespan.

The practical laws follow directly. Digging deeper into the anaerobic zone yields disproportionately more organic material. Everything stable underwater is stable only there: lift waterlogged wood into air and it begins to collapse within hours as water leaves cell walls that water was holding up, and freshly raised iron begins weeping acid as trapped chlorides react. Recovery without conservation is destruction on a delay, which is why the conservation laboratory, described later, is not an afterthought but half the discipline.

sections.heading: Finding Sites: Side-Scan Sonar, Magnetometers and Sub-Bottom Profilers
sections.body:
Most wrecks are found before anyone gets wet. The modern survey suite is a boat towing or carrying three complementary instruments, each answering a different question, plus positioning good enough to come back to the same square meter, which differential satellite navigation now provides almost for free.

Side-scan sonar answers the question: what is lying on the seabed? A torpedo-shaped towfish streams sound in wide fans to either side and builds an acoustic photograph of the bottom from the pattern of echoes and shadows, imaging swaths hundreds of meters wide at resolutions that, on modern high-frequency systems, can show individual timbers and the debris trail of a scattered wreck. Its images read like raking light on a field: objects standing proud cast long acoustic shadows, and an experienced interpreter can tell a rock outcrop from a boiler from a hull at a glance. Multibeam echosounders, mounted on the hull, complement side-scan by measuring exact depths across a swath, producing three-dimensional terrain models in which a wreck appears as a measurable mound; the standing Baltic ships have been mapped this way in near-photographic relief.

The magnetometer answers a different question: is there iron here? Towed well behind the boat to escape its magnetic noise, it measures tiny distortions in the Earth's magnetic field caused by ferrous masses, cannon, anchors, fastenings, engines, even the fired clay of a cargo of bricks, whether exposed or buried. Sensitivity is startling: a single cannon can be detected tens of meters away, and a systematic survey run in tight parallel lanes, mowing the lawn in surveyors' slang, produces a contour map of magnetic anomalies to be dived or probed one by one. Magnetometry found many of the most famous colonial-era wrecks, and it remains the only practical way to detect a wooden ship whose visible remains are entirely buried, betrayed by its iron skeleton.

The sub-bottom profiler answers the third question: what is under the seabed? Firing low-frequency pulses that penetrate sediment and return from buried layers and objects, it draws vertical acoustic cross-sections in which a buried hull appears as a hyperbolic reflector interrupting the neat strata. It is the instrument of drowned landscapes as much as wrecks, tracing buried river channels, peat beds and old land surfaces beneath the mud, which is how the contours of Doggerland under the North Sea have been mapped using, in part, seismic data donated by the oil industry.

Survey design matters as much as hardware. Researchers begin in archives, with charts, wreck registers, insurance records and newspaper accounts narrowing the search box; they then lay out systematic lanes with overlap, because a hole in coverage is exactly where the target will be. Aerial and satellite methods add a shallow-water layer: harbor moles, fish traps and roads show through clear water in aerial photography, and airborne lidar bathymetry maps coastal seabeds from aircraft. Increasingly, autonomous underwater vehicles run the lanes by themselves, and machine-learning classifiers pre-sort thousands of sonar contacts. But every anomaly list ends the same way it did in 1960: someone goes down to look.

sections.heading: Excavating Underwater: Airlifts, Dredges, Grids and Trowels
sections.body:
Underwater excavation is land excavation translated into a medium that steals time, warmth and visibility, and the translation is remarkably faithful. The governing rule is identical: excavation destroys the site as it proceeds, so nothing is moved until its position and relationships are recorded. What changes is the toolkit and the clock.

The clock rules everything. Air supply and decompression limits fix how long divers can work; at 30 meters a diver on air has perhaps twenty productive minutes before decompression obligations mount, and the Uluburun excavation at 44 to 61 meters ran on paired dives of about twenty minutes, twice a day, for eleven seasons, totaling more than 22,000 dives. Deeper or longer work brings mixed gases, staged decompression, or saturation systems; cold brings drysuits and shortened attention; and every project budget is largely a translation of bottom time into money. Modern projects increasingly put closed-circuit rebreathers on archaeologists, quadrupling useful time at depth, or move the archaeologist into a one-atmosphere observation role while a remotely operated vehicle handles the deepest tasks.

Sediment is moved with water and air rather than shovels. The airlift, introduced to archaeology in the earliest Mediterranean excavations, is a rigid pipe rising toward the surface into which compressed air is injected at the bottom; the rising bubbles create suction at the mouth, and the excavator feeds sediment into it much as one would use a vacuum cleaner, with the spoil discharged down-current or onto a screening barge where every basketful is sieved for small finds. In shallower water the induction or water dredge, driven by a pump jetting water through a venturi, does the same job. In skilled hands these are precision instruments held near, never against, the deposit, while the actual digging is done with the same trowels, brushes and fingers used on land; fragile surfaces are cleaned by gently fanning a hand to waft silt into the suction. The constant enemy is the silt-out: one careless fin stroke can drop visibility to zero for an hour, so excavators work with exaggerated stillness, trim their buoyancy finely and plan tasks down-current.

Order is kept exactly as on land. Sites are divided by datum points and, where useful, physical grids of scaffold pipe or plastic leveled over the wreck; excavation proceeds in layers within defined units, every find receives a number, a spot elevation and coordinates before lifting, and finds are raised in labeled trays and lifting bags rather than pockets. Timbers are tagged individually, often with numbered plastic labels nailed on, because a disassembled hull of a thousand pieces must be reassemblable on paper. Probes and test trenches establish how deep and how far the deposit runs before commitment, since opening more of a site than a team can conserve is the cardinal management sin; many projects deliberately excavate half a wreck and rebury the rest for a better-equipped future.

The end state of a modern excavation is frequently not a cleared site but a stabilized one: exposed structure recorded and then reburied under sediment and sandbags, the archive of drawings, photographs and samples standing in for the wood left safely in the dark.

sections.heading: Recording and Mapping: From Tape Measures to Photogrammetry
sections.body:
Recording is the conscience of excavation, and underwater it has undergone the discipline's biggest revolution in a generation. The classical toolkit was direct measurement: baselines of tape stretched between datums, offsets measured from them, and above all trilateration, fixing each point by distance from three or more known points, since compass bearings and right angles are treacherous to a floating observer. The Mary Rose and other great excavations were mapped with the Direct Survey Method, in which hundreds of tape distances from fixed datums to labeled points were fed to software that adjusted them into a best-fit three-dimensional model, with residuals flagging bad measurements. Alongside the tapes went drawing: planning frames, gridded squares laid over the seabed, guided divers drawing plans on matte plastic film with pencil, the one writing technology indifferent to immersion. It worked, at the price of enormous bottom time; a single complex square could consume a day of diving.

Photography always promised more speed, and stereo-photographic mapping was tried as early as the 1960s, but water fought back with light absorption, color loss and the impossibility of getting far enough from a large site to see it whole. Mosaics of overlapping photographs were laboriously assembled by hand for decades. The transformation came in the 2010s from an unexpected direction: structure-from-motion photogrammetry, software that takes hundreds or thousands of overlapping ordinary photographs, finds matching features among them, solves for the camera positions and builds a dense, measurable, photo-textured three-dimensional model. A diver or robot now swims a systematic pattern over a wreck with a camera, an hour of imagery replaces a season of tape work, and the output is a millimeter-to-centimeter accurate model in which any distance can be measured later, any plan or section extracted, and successive years compared to detect change. Scaled by ranging poles or coded targets fixed to the site, checked against a handful of direct measurements, photogrammetry has become the default site plan almost overnight, and it works from the shallowest harbor to the deepest robotic survey; the Titanic was captured whole in 2022 as a model built from over 700,000 images.

The recording system extends beyond geometry. Every context, layer, timber and find carries structured records: context sheets adapted from land archaeology, timber sheets noting species, tool marks, fastenings and joints, photographs with scales and labels, sample logs for dendrochronology and residues. Position on the planet comes from satellite positioning of surface buoys or vessels transferred acoustically to the seabed; ultra-short baseline acoustic systems track divers and robots in real time against the ship's position. Video, once a luxury, is now continuous, and dive logs tie every image to person, time and task.

Two principles govern all of it. First, record as if the site will be destroyed tomorrow, because parts of it will be, by the excavation itself if nothing else. Second, the archive outranks the objects: a wreck fully recorded and left in place has told most of its story, while a hold full of artifacts without positions is cargo again, not evidence. The tape measure taught the discipline that ethic; the camera has simply made it affordable.

sections.heading: Conserving Waterlogged Finds: PEG, Freeze-Drying and Electrolysis
sections.body:
Everything raised from the sea is a rescue case, and conservation is where wrecks are won or lost. The core problem with organic materials is that water is holding them up. In waterlogged wood the cellulose that gave cell walls their strength has hydrolyzed away over centuries, leaving a fragile lignin sponge whose cells are full of water; the object looks sound on the seabed, but dry it in air and capillary forces collapse the weakened cells, shrinking and cracking the wood by as much as half its volume within days. The conservator's task is to replace the water with something that will stay.

The standard answer is polyethylene glycol, PEG, a waxy water-soluble polymer. The object is immersed in a PEG solution that starts dilute and is gradually strengthened over months or years, so the polymer diffuses into the cell structure and replaces the water; low molecular weight grades penetrate deeply to bulk degraded cell walls, heavier grades consolidate surfaces. Small objects then go to a vacuum freeze-drier, where remaining water sublimates away as vapor without ever exerting capillary pull, and the result is a stable, handleable object that keeps its excavated shape. This PEG and freeze-dry pipeline is now routine for everything from combs to logboats. Whole ships get the heroic version: the Vasa was sprayed with PEG for seventeen years, from 1962 to 1979, and the Mary Rose for nineteen, from 1994 to 2013, followed by years of controlled air drying, and both projects continue to manage their giant patients today, tuning humidity to a few percent and monitoring chemistry deep in the timbers. Sulfur compounds absorbed from anoxic harbor mud, oxidizing to sulfuric acid inside PEG-treated wood, emerged in the 2000s as the Vasa's chronic disease, and treating and monitoring such acid is now a research field of its own.

Metals fight a different battle. Iron soaked in seawater is loaded with chloride ions, and in air these drive runaway corrosion; untreated cast iron guns split themselves apart within years, weeping orange and shedding scale. The remedy is to pull the chlorides out. Objects are kept wet from the moment of lifting, mechanically cleaned of concretion, then washed for months in alkaline baths, or, for robust items like cannon and anchors, treated by electrolytic reduction: the object is made the cathode in a tank of electrolyte, a low current drives chloride out toward anodes, and corrosion products are partially reduced. Treatments for a large gun run months to years, after which the metal is rinsed, dried and sealed with wax coatings. Silver and copper alloys receive gentler versions; gold needs nothing but cleaning. Ceramics and glass must be slowly desalinated in changes of fresh water, or soluble salts left inside will crystallize in dry air and spall the surfaces off a jar that survived two millennia of seabed.

Two rules from this laboratory world reach back and govern the whole discipline. First, never lift what you cannot conserve; a project's excavation permit is, morally and often legally, a promise of decades of tank space, chemistry and curation. Second, keep everything wet until the conservator says otherwise; a find drying in a boat's bilge on the ride home can lose more information in an afternoon than the sea took in a thousand years.

sections.heading: Raising Whole Ships: The Mary Rose and the Vasa
sections.body:
Two projects define the heroic end of the discipline, and between them they taught the world most of what it knows about lifting and keeping a whole wooden ship. The first, chronologically, is the Vasa. This 64-gun Swedish warship, built at enormous expense for King Gustavus Adolphus, sailed on her maiden voyage from Stockholm on 10 August 1628, heeled in a light gust before a crowd of thousands, flooded through her open lower gunports and sank within about 1,300 meters of her berth, killing around thirty people; the inquest, unable to blame the king's own approved dimensions, punished no one. She settled upright in about 32 meters of cold, brackish harbor water where shipworm cannot live, and there she stood for three centuries. The amateur researcher Anders Franzen, reasoning precisely from that absence of shipworm, hunted her systematically through the 1950s with a home-made coring sampler, striking black oak in 1956. Navy divers then tunneled six passages beneath the hull with water jets, threaded steel cables through, and in a two-stage operation lifted her between pontoons, first walking her underwater into shallower berths in 1959, then breaking the surface on 24 April 1961, watched live on television. She came up astonishingly whole, some 95 percent original, complete with hundreds of carved sculptures, and after seventeen years of PEG spraying and decades of climate management she stands in her own museum in Stockholm, which now receives on the order of a million and a half visitors a year and doubles as a permanent laboratory for waterlogged wood chemistry.

The Mary Rose is the English mirror image. A carrack of Henry VIII's navy, rebuilt to carry heavy guns, she capsized in the Solent on 19 July 1545 while maneuvering against a French invasion fleet, in full view of the king ashore; of a crew of about 500, hardly three dozen survived. She lay heeled into soft sediment, which entombed her starboard half in anaerobic mud while tide and biology erased the exposed port side, a textbook demonstration of formation processes. Rediscovered in 1971 after a sonar-guided search inspired by the historian and diver Alexander McKee, she became the largest underwater excavation ever mounted: between 1979 and 1982 more than 500 volunteer divers under archaeologist Margaret Rule logged over 22,000 dives, emptying and recording the hull's contents, some 19,000 artifacts that amount to a sealed cross-section of Tudor shipboard life, longbows by the score, surgeons instruments, musical instruments, the skeletons of the crew and of the ship's dog. On 11 October 1982, cradled in a purpose-built steel frame after the hull had been drilled and bolted to a lifting frame, the surviving half-ship was raised on live television watched by tens of millions, surviving one heart-stopping slip of the crane rig. Nineteen years of PEG spraying and controlled drying followed, and she is displayed in Portsmouth today facing a gallery of her own contents.

The paired lessons: preservation environment is destiny; patient survey finds what legend cannot; and the lift is the easy part, a single day standing between decades of excavation before and decades of conservation after. Every subsequent proposal to raise a hull is measured against these two, and most, on that measure, wisely choose to record and rebury instead.

sections.heading: Ancient Wrecks of the Mediterranean: Uluburun, Antikythera and Kyrenia
sections.body:
The Mediterranean is the discipline's classical heartland, and three wrecks there mark the span from the Bronze Age to the threshold of Rome, each transformative in its own way. The oldest is Uluburun, found in 1982 by a Turkish sponge diver off a cape near Kas who described metal biscuits with ears, instantly recognizable to archaeologists as oxhide-shaped copper ingots. The wreck lay brutally deep for divers, 44 to 61 meters, and its excavation by George Bass and Cemal Pulak of the Institute of Nautical Archaeology, over eleven seasons from 1984 to 1994 and more than 22,000 dives, remains a benchmark of method at the edge of air-diving limits. The cargo, dated around 1320 BCE, reads like a royal manifest of the Late Bronze Age world: ten tons of Cypriot copper in 354 oxhide ingots, a ton of tin, about 175 glass ingots in cobalt blue and turquoise, Canaanite jars of terebinth resin, ebony logs from Egypt, hippopotamus and elephant ivory, ostrich eggshells, Baltic amber, a gold scarab naming Nefertiti, weapons and seals from half a dozen cultures, and the oldest known wooden writing tablet, its wax pages lost. No text describes such a voyage; the ship itself is the document, physical proof of palace-scale exchange linking Egypt, the Levant, Cyprus, Mycenaean Greece and beyond.

At the other end of antiquity lies the Antikythera wreck, a large Roman-period ship lost around 70 to 60 BCE off a small island between Crete and the Peloponnese, found by Symi sponge divers in 1900. Its salvage in 1900 and 1901, by helmet divers working at desperate depths around 45 to 60 meters, one killed and two paralyzed, was the first great underwater recovery: bronze and marble statues including the Antikythera Youth, luxury glass, jewelry, and an unregarded lump of corroded bronze that split open in the museum to reveal gear wheels. That object, the Antikythera mechanism, studied across a century and finally read by x-ray computed tomography in the 2000s, is a geared astronomical computer of at least thirty bronze gearwheels that modeled the cycles of sun and moon, predicted eclipses by the Saros cycle and tracked the four-year round of Greek games, a machine whose sophistication would not be matched in the surviving record for well over a millennium. Cousteau worked the site in 1976, and renewed excavation since 2014, using closed-circuit rebreathers and even a pressurized exosuit, continues to recover statuary and, in 2016, human remains.

Between the two in scale but foundational for ship construction is the Kyrenia ship, a small Greek merchantman of the late fourth century BCE found off northern Cyprus in 1965 and excavated by Michael Katzev from 1968 to 1969. About 14 meters long, she carried some 400 wine amphoras, mainly Rhodian, almonds by the thousand, and 29 millstones as saleable ballast, the working inventory of a coasting trader; four sets of eating utensils suggest her crew. More than half her pine hull survived, revealing shell-first construction, planks edge-joined by thousands of mortise-and-tenon joints before frames were inserted, the signature technique of ancient Mediterranean shipwrights. Conserved in PEG and displayed in Kyrenia castle, she became the first ancient ship rebuilt in replica for sea trials; the sailing replica Kyrenia II, launched in 1985, showed such hulls could make brisk passages and handle heavy weather, turning naval archaeology into experimental science.

sections.heading: Deep-Water Archaeology: ROVs, AUVs and Wrecks Beyond Diving
sections.body:
Ordinary scientific diving effectively ends around 50 to 60 meters, and technical diving stretches only a little further at great cost in time and risk. The average depth of the ocean is about 3,700 meters. Nearly the whole seafloor, and every ship ever lost over deep water, therefore lies beyond human presence, and its archaeology belongs to machines. The enabling instruments are the remotely operated vehicle, an unoccupied robot flown from a surface ship through a power-and-data tether, seeing through cameras and sonar and working through hydraulic manipulators, and the autonomous underwater vehicle, a free-swimming torpedo-shaped robot that runs pre-programmed survey lanes with sonar and cameras and needs no cable. Between them, with ship-based multibeam sonar and acoustic positioning, they extend survey, photography, photogrammetry and even delicate recovery to any depth; work-class ROVs operate routinely at 3,000 to 6,000 meters.

The demonstration case was the Titanic, found on 1 September 1985 at about 3,800 meters by a joint French-American expedition under Jean-Louis Michel and Robert Ballard, first by towed camera sled and the sonar of the French vessel, then explored in 1986 by the submersible Alvin and the small camera robot Jason Junior. Ballard, a Navy-funded oceanographer, went on to find the Bismarck at about 4,700 meters in 1989 and, with others, to argue that the deep sea is history's greatest museum. The record depth for a surveyed wreck now stands with the American destroyer USS Johnston, sunk in 1944 and surveyed by crewed submersible at about 6,460 meters in the Philippine Trench in 2021, and the USS Samuel B. Roberts nearby at about 6,900 meters in 2022.

Deep water changes the science as well as the access. Below the reach of storm waves, sunlight and, in special basins, oxygen itself, preservation can be extraordinary: the Black Sea surveys led by expeditions including Ballard's from 1999 and the Black Sea Maritime Archaeology Project from 2015 to 2017 mapped more than sixty ships between the medieval period and classical antiquity, among them the complete Greek trader from about 400 BCE noted earlier, imaged by ROV photogrammetry with rudder and mast in place. Deep sites also skip most human interference; they are time capsules unopened even by salvors. Against this stand new threats that arrived with the technology: deep trawling plows wreck sites invisibly, and commercial salvage companies operate the same ROVs archaeologists do. The legal fight over the SS Central America gold, recovered from about 2,200 meters in the late 1980s, and the dispute over the Spanish frigate Nuestra Senora de las Mercedes, whose 500,000 coins a court ordered returned to Spain in 2012, made deep water the front line of the treasure question.

Methodologically, robots have quietly imposed the discipline's own best standards. An ROV cannot pocket a souvenir; everything it does is logged, positioned and recorded on video by default, and survey-first, minimal-recovery projects are the norm because lifting anything from 4,000 meters is expensive. The emerging model, pioneered on projects like the Mardi Gras wreck in the Gulf of Mexico at 1,200 meters, treats the deep site as a laboratory to be documented exhaustively and sampled sparingly, with the archive, not the artifact hoard, as the product. The machines, built to serve oil fields and navies, have ended up enforcing archaeology's conscience at depths its founders never expected to reach.

sections.heading: Sunken Cities and Drowned Landscapes: Port Royal, Thonis-Heracleion and Doggerland
sections.body:
Ships are only half the underwater archive; the other half is land that stopped being land. Settlements go under by three main routes, each leaving a different kind of site: sudden catastrophe, slow subsidence and the long rise of the sea since the last Ice Age.

Catastrophe made the most famous example. Port Royal, Jamaica, was the boomtown of the seventeenth-century Caribbean, a harbor city of privateers and merchants with a reputation as the wickedest city on Earth. At 11:43 on the morning of 7 June 1692, recorded by a pocket watch later recovered from the seabed, an earthquake liquefied the sand spit beneath it, and roughly two thirds of the town slid into the harbor within minutes, killing perhaps 2,000 people at once and as many again in the aftermath. The submerged streets, excavated notably by Texas A&M University teams in the 1980s and 1990s, preserve buildings with fallen walls, hearths, and household goods lying where the quake dropped them, a Pompeii in ten meters of water, and one of the very few archaeological sites anywhere datable to the minute.

Subsidence and shifting deltas claimed the Egyptian port of Thonis-Heracleion, which stood at the Canopic mouth of the Nile and handled the Greek trade of late pharaonic Egypt. Built on compressible delta clays, undermined by earthquakes and floods, it sank piecemeal into Aboukir Bay early in the first millennium CE and vanished so completely that scholars debated whether Thonis and Heracleion were two cities; the underwater surveys of Franck Goddio's team, which relocated the city in 2000 about 6.5 kilometers offshore under some ten meters of water and sediment, proved they were one. The finds are staggering in scale: colossal five-meter statues of a pharaoh, a queen and the god Hapy, the intact naos of the temple of Amun-Gereb, gold coins and ritual barques, and more than seventy ancient ships lying in the buried harbor basins, one of the largest ancient fleets known. Alexandria's own royal quarter, including districts associated with Cleopatra's palace, lies similarly drowned a few meters down in the neighboring harbor.

The grandest submergence needed no earthquake at all. At the Last Glacial Maximum, about 20,000 years ago, sea level stood roughly 120 meters lower than today, and the continental shelves were inhabited plains. The North Sea's southern basin was Doggerland, a country of rivers, marshes and hills where Mesolithic Europeans hunted and fished until the rising sea, and possibly a tsunami generated by the Storegga submarine landslide around 6200 BCE, finished its drowning. It is archaeology's invisible homeland: trawlers have dredged up its harpoons, worked bone and mammoth remains for over a century, and since the 2000s projects led from Bradford and elsewhere have mapped its buried river valleys across thousands of square kilometers using donated oil-industry seismic data, sampling its sediments for DNA and pollen. Every continent has an equivalent, from the drowned shorelines that early people followed out of Africa and along the Pacific rim of the Americas to submerged Aboriginal sites recently confirmed off northwestern Australia. Rising seas took the first chapters of the human story; this branch of the field is learning to read them through the water.

sections.heading: Law, Ethics and Treasure Hunting: Who Owns a Wreck?
sections.body:
Nothing shapes underwater archaeology's daily reality more than law, because the sea is crowded with competing claims and full of things that look like money.
