The traditional legal instruments were the marine salvage law of the admiralty courts, built to reward rescuing property in peril, and the law of finds for abandoned property, both catastrophically ill-suited to heritage: they reward speed and recovery, exactly the behaviors that destroy archaeological context. Under their logic, commercial companies through the late twentieth century mined historic wrecks as private assets, and the sale of the cargo was the point of the enterprise.

The counter-principles crystallized slowly. Sovereign immunity gives warships and other state vessels continuing protection: a sunken warship remains the property of its flag state regardless of age or location, which is why Spain won the Mercedes case in United States courts in 2012, forcing the return of some 500,000 silver and gold coins lifted by the salvage firm Odyssey Marine from the frigate blown up by the Royal Navy in 1804, and why war graves such as the Arizona at Pearl Harbor are protected outright. National heritage statutes claim and regulate wrecks in territorial waters, as Britain's Protection of Wrecks Act 1973 does for designated sites, and the United States Abandoned Shipwreck Act of 1987 transferred most historic wrecks in state waters to state ownership, pulling them out of the salvage courts.

The global standard is the UNESCO Convention on the Protection of the Underwater Cultural Heritage, adopted in 2001 and in force since 2009, now ratified by more than seventy states. Its rules distill the discipline's ethics into law: underwater cultural heritage means all traces of human existence underwater for over one hundred years; preservation in situ is the first option to be considered; commercial exploitation for trade or speculation is fundamentally incompatible with protection, so recovered heritage may not be sold; and an annex of thirty-six rules sets professional standards for any intervention, from project design and funding through conservation and publication. States parties agree to close their ports and markets to illicitly recovered material. Major maritime powers including the United States and Britain have not ratified, citing concerns over sovereign immunity and jurisdiction, but both broadly follow the annex rules in practice, and the convention has become the reference point even where it does not formally bind.

The ethical argument beneath the law is worth stating plainly, because the treasure-hunting question never dies. A cargo dispersed at auction is data destroyed: provenience, association and the unglamorous ninety-five percent of finds that carry the history are sacrificed to market the shiny five percent. Companies promising archaeology plus profit have repeatedly delivered neither, and the economics are stark; salvage ventures have far more often consumed investors' money than returned it, while the knowledge cost is total and permanent. Museums and journals now generally refuse commercially recovered material, which removes its scientific value from the market side too. Meanwhile looting persists at every scale, from souvenir-stripping by sport divers, which emptied many accessible wrecks of their portable fittings within a generation of scuba's arrival, to industrial illegal salvage of Second World War naval graves in Southeast Asia for their low-background steel and brass. The working rules for any individual are simple: look, photograph, enjoy, report, and leave the site as found; the law increasingly says the same thing ethics always did.

sections.heading: Maritime Archaeology on the Shore: Harbors, Fish Traps, Logboats and Landing Places
sections.body:
Some of maritime archaeology's richest evidence never requires a dive tank, because coastlines are archives in their own right. The sea's edge has always been the busiest zone of maritime life, and everything built there, harbors, slipways, boatyards, fish traps, lighthouses, salt works, wrecks driven ashore, gets preserved in mud, sand and marsh or exposed twice daily between tides.

Harbors are the monumental end of the record. Ancient engineers built on a scale that still surprises: at Caesarea Maritima in modern Israel, King Herod's builders around 22 to 15 BCE sank timber forms filled with hydraulic concrete, made with volcanic pozzolana shipped from the Bay of Naples, to create two vast artificial breakwaters enclosing a harbor where no natural shelter existed, a project studied jointly by divers and land excavators since the 1970s. Roman Portus, the imperial port of Rome, survives as silted basins two kilometers inland, its hexagonal inner harbor now a lake in farmland, excavated with geophysics and trenches like any land site. The lesson generalizes: coastlines move, and yesterday's waterfront may today be under a meadow or under ten meters of water, so harbor studies stitch together cores, seismic profiles, standing ruins and archival charts to reconstruct where the water actually was in any century. Buried ships turn up in these sediments constantly, from the thirty-plus Roman vessels found in the silted harbor at Pisa from 1998 onward to medieval hulls under Oslo and Bergen and the dozens of ships, including the seventeenth-century Vasa-era warships, revealed by construction digs in Stockholm.

The intertidal zone preserves humbler and often older structures. Wooden fish traps, fences of stakes and wattle funneling fish into baskets on the falling tide, survive by the hundred around the coasts of Ireland, Britain and France, some radiocarbon dated to the Mesolithic and many to the early medieval centuries; stone tidal weirs ring coasts from Brittany to the Pacific. In the Severn estuary, prehistoric footprints of adults, children and animals are preserved in laminated muds beside trackways and hunting camps. Logboats, the simplest and longest-lived watercraft, dugout hulls hollowed from single trunks, surface regularly from riverbeds, lake muds and reclaimed land across the world; the Pesse canoe from the Netherlands, about 3 meters of hollowed Scots pine dated to roughly 8000 BCE, is the oldest known boat of any kind, and Danish, Irish and African finds carry the type through every later millennium. Ship burials extend the maritime record inland: at Sutton Hoo in England the ship itself had rotted to a ghost, every plank gone, but its exact form survived as stains and rows of iron rivets in the sand, excavated in 1939 with brushes rather than regulators.

Methodologically this shoreline work blends every field skill archaeology has: walkover survey timed to extreme low tides, drone photogrammetry racing the flood, dendrochronology on waterlogged stakes, sediment coring for past sea levels, and oral history from fishing communities who often know exactly where the old weirs and wrecks lie. It is also the most accessible face of the discipline, where trained volunteers monitor eroding sites through programs like England's CITiZAN and Scotland's SCHARP, photographing and measuring what each winter's storms expose and destroy. The rising sea that first drowned these coasts is now eroding them faster than professionals alone can record, which makes the beach, not the deep, the discipline's most urgent frontier.

sections.heading: Getting Involved: Training, Careers and Avocational Archaeology
sections.body:
Underwater archaeology looks like a closed guild from outside, but it is one of the few sciences where trained volunteers still make first-rank contributions, and there are well-marked doors in. The professional route runs through a university degree in archaeology or anthropology followed by a specialized graduate program; the recognized centers include the Nautical Archaeology Program at Texas A&M University, founded around George Bass's Institute of Nautical Archaeology, the maritime archaeology programs at the University of Southampton and Flinders University in Australia, and counterparts in Denmark, the Netherlands and elsewhere. Alongside the degree, a professional needs scientific diver certification, in North America usually under American Academy of Underwater Sciences standards and in Britain the Health and Safety Executive scuba qualification, plus the unglamorous employable skills the job actually runs on: survey and photogrammetry processing, geographic information systems, conservation basics, small-boat handling and report writing. Employment splits among universities and museums, government heritage agencies that manage wreck registers and permits, navies and, increasingly, the commercial sector, where offshore wind farms, pipelines and dredging projects are legally required to assess and avoid heritage, making development-led marine archaeology the field's biggest employer in several countries.

For everyone else, the avocational path is real and respected. Britain's Nautical Archaeology Society runs an internationally taught training scheme, from one-day introductions through recorder and surveyor grades, and its graduates have discovered, surveyed and monitored protected wrecks for decades; licensed volunteer teams look after many of Britain's designated sites. In the United States, state programs such as Florida's underwater archaeology preserves, Maryland's and the Great Lakes marine sanctuaries train sport divers to document rather than strip wrecks, and avocational groups work alongside professionals on surveys. Sport divers with no formal role at all still matter enormously as the discipline's eyes: a large share of known wrecks were first reported by recreational divers and fishermen, and the etiquette is simple and binding, look and photograph freely, move and take nothing, and report finds to the responsible agency, in Britain the Receiver of Wreck, elsewhere the state or national heritage office. A single uncontexted souvenir subtracts more knowledge than most divers imagine, and in many jurisdictions it is also a crime.

Nor does participation require diving at all. Shore-based programs monitoring the intertidal zone, like England's CITiZAN, welcome anyone who can walk a beach with a phone camera; archives hold undigested wreck records, charts and insurance registers that reward patient landlubbers; museums need volunteers in conservation labs and finds rooms; and photogrammetry processing, sonar interpretation and database work are done at desks. Crowdsourced transcription of ships logs has even turned historic weather observations into climate data, a reminder that maritime records serve many sciences.

For a reader who wants to go deeper into the literature, the classic starting points are Keith Muckelroy's Maritime Archaeology from 1978 for theory, George Bass's books for the great excavations, and the published reports of the Mary Rose and Vasa projects for what total commitment looks like. The sea keeps most of history's unread pages, museums display the recovered ones, and between them there is room for almost any set of hands. The only real entry requirement is the discipline's founding promise: record first, respect the context, and leave the past legible for the next reader.

guides.safetyNote: Underwater archaeology is diving first and archaeology second, and diving carries real risks. Never dive without recognized training and certification, never dive alone, and follow depth and no-decompression limits exactly; decompression sickness, nitrogen narcosis and running out of gas are life-threatening. Wreck sites add their own hazards, including entanglement in nets and lines, sharp corroded metal, unstable structures that can collapse, silt-outs that erase visibility in seconds, and, on some wrecks, live munitions or leaking fuel, so never penetrate a wreck interior without specific overhead-environment training. Cold water, currents and boat traffic kill unprepared divers every year. If you find what you think is a wreck or artifact, do not lift it; note the position and report it to the responsible heritage agency, both because untrained recovery destroys evidence and because in most countries removing material from wreck sites without a permit is illegal.

guides.title: Experimental Archaeology
guides.summary: How archaeologists test ideas about the past by rebuilding and using ancient technology: stone tools, fire making, houses, farming, pottery kilns, metal smelting, ships, and megalith moving, plus how such experiments are designed and what they can and cannot prove.
guides.safetyNote: Replicating old technology involves genuinely dangerous work. Flintknapping throws razor-sharp flakes and fine silica dust, so wear eye protection, work outdoors or with ventilation, and keep flakes off the ground where feet and pets go. Fire making, pit firing, and metal smelting involve open flame, temperatures above 1,000 degrees Celsius, and molten metal that spatters violently on contact with moisture; keep water and extinguishing material at hand, wear natural-fiber clothing and proper gloves, and never smelt or cast without an experienced person present. Moving heavy stones and timbers crushes hands and feet, so plan lifts, use sound rope, and keep bystanders clear.

sections.heading: What Experimental Archaeology Is and What It Is Not
sections.body:
Experimental archaeology is the practice of testing ideas about the human past by actually doing the things past people did, under conditions controlled and recorded carefully enough that the results count as evidence. If an archaeologist wants to know how long it takes to fell an oak with a bronze axe, how many people are needed to drag a four-tonne stone, whether grain keeps through winter in a sealed underground pit, or what microscopic polish forms on a flint blade used to harvest wheat, no amount of staring at excavated objects will answer the question. The experiment supplies the missing link between the static archaeological record, the broken and buried things we dig up, and the dynamic living behavior that produced them. Archaeologists borrowing a term from the philosopher of science approach call this middle-range research: building reliable bridges of inference between what we find and what people did.

The discipline has a strict and a loose sense, and confusing them causes most of the arguments about it. In the strict sense, an experiment has a hypothesis, defined variables, controls, measurements, and enough documentation that someone else could repeat it. Firing thirty replica pots in a reconstructed kiln while logging temperatures with thermocouples, then comparing the color and hardness of the results with excavated sherds, is an experiment. In the loose sense, the label gets attached to any hands-on engagement with old technology, from craft demonstrations at museums to festival re-enactments. That work has real value for education and for generating hunches, and skilled craft practice produces knowledge of its own, but a weekend spent dressed as an Iron Age farmer is not a controlled trial, and careful practitioners distinguish experimental archaeology from experiential activities. The field's professional network, EXARC, which links open-air museums and researchers across dozens of countries, spends a good deal of effort keeping that boundary honest.

It is equally important to be clear about what a successful experiment demonstrates. Showing that a balsa raft can drift from Peru to Polynesia proves that such a voyage was possible, not that it happened. Showing that one method raises a Stonehenge-sized lintel proves nothing about which method Neolithic builders used, only that at least one workable method existed within their means. Philosophers call this the problem of equifinality: many different past processes can produce the same material result. Experiments therefore work best in the negative and the comparative. They can kill a hypothesis outright, as when a proposed tool material simply cannot do the claimed job, and they can rank hypotheses by efficiency, labor, and byproducts, whose traces can then be sought in the ground.

Done well, the method delivers something almost no other branch of archaeology can: numbers. Hours of labor per cubic meter of ditch, kilograms of charcoal per kilogram of iron, hectares of grain per family per year, days at sea per crossing. Those numbers turn vague stories about the past into testable models of economies, and they anchor the rest of this guide, which follows the method through its history, its rules, and its most famous applications, from flint and fire to ships and standing stones.

sections.heading: A Short History: From Victorian Curiosity to a Scientific Discipline
sections.body:
People have tested old technology for almost as long as they have collected it. In the nineteenth century, as museums filled with stone tools and bronze weapons whose uses were disputed, a first generation of scholars tried them out. The Danish archaeologist Sven Nilsson experimented with stone tools to infer their functions in the 1830s and 1840s, and in England John Evans, a paper manufacturer and antiquarian, knapped his own flint implements partly to expose the forgeries then flooding the market, since a man who could make a hand axe could recognize a fresh one. Augustus Pitt Rivers, often called the father of scientific excavation, tested replica weapons and recorded how earthworks on his estates weathered. This early work was ingenious but usually informal: one man, one trial, a paragraph in a report.

The twentieth century supplied the spectacles and then the rigor. Thor Heyerdahl's 1947 Kon-Tiki voyage, drifting a balsa raft from Peru into Polynesia in 101 days, put the experimental approach on front pages worldwide, though professionals then and now note that it demonstrated possibility rather than history. The genuinely scientific turn came in the postwar decades. In 1960 British researchers built the experimental earthwork on Overton Down in Wiltshire, a chalk bank and ditch seeded with buried materials, designed from the outset to be sectioned at planned intervals across 128 years, an experiment still running and covered later in this guide. In Denmark, the Historical-Archaeological Research Centre at Lejre opened in 1964, a permanent campus where reconstructed prehistoric houses, fields, and workshops could host long-running trials. Britain followed in 1972 when Peter Reynolds founded Butser Ancient Farm in Hampshire, a working Iron Age farm run for decades as a laboratory, whose results on crop yields, grain storage, and roundhouse design overturned several textbook claims.

The discipline gained its charter in 1973 when the Cambridge archaeologist John Coles published Archaeology by Experiment, followed in 1979 by Experimental Archaeology, books that collected scattered trials into a method with stated rules: use the materials and technology plausibly available to the culture in question, repeat trials, quantify results, and publish failures as well as successes. In the same era, Soviet researcher Sergei Semenov's traceology, the microscopic study of use wear on tools validated by experiment, reached western readers in translation and founded an entire laboratory subfield. François Bordes in France and Don Crabtree in the United States raised flintknapping from a curiosity to a research skill and trained a generation of lithic analysts.

Since the 1980s the field has professionalized and spread. Dedicated journals and the EXARC network link hundreds of open-air museums and university laboratories; degree programs at institutions such as the University of Exeter teach experimental design; and the method has expanded from technology into taphonomy, the study of what happens to bones, seeds, and structures after deposition. The arc of the field's history runs from gentlemen trying out axes, through heroic voyages, to thermocouples, load cells, and statistics, and the best modern work keeps something of all three: curiosity, nerve, and measurement.

sections.heading: Designing an Archaeological Experiment: Variables, Controls, and Authenticity
sections.body:
A good archaeological experiment begins the way any experiment does, with a question sharp enough to be answered. How many person-hours does it take to produce a polished stone axe from raw flint? Does a thatched roundhouse need a smoke hole? At what temperature does this clay fabric turn the color of the excavated sherds? Vague ambitions such as understanding Bronze Age life cannot be tested; the craft of design is mostly the craft of narrowing. From the question follow the variables. The experimenter must decide which factors to hold constant, which to vary deliberately, and which cannot be controlled and must at least be measured and reported, such as weather during an outdoor firing. Replication matters for the same reason it does in any laboratory: a single trial confounds the method being tested with the skill and luck of the person testing it, so serious programs repeat trials across multiple operators and occasions and report ranges, not single numbers.

The issue peculiar to archaeology is authenticity, and it operates on a sliding scale that honest reports state explicitly. At the highest level, everything is period-correct: tools of stone or bronze, materials gathered as past people would have gathered them, techniques within the culture's known repertoire. That level is expensive and sometimes impossible, and it is not always necessary. If the question concerns how a kiln heats, building it with modern shovels changes nothing that matters, though firing it with the wrong fuel would. Experimenters therefore distinguish the variables that bear on the hypothesis, which must be authentic, from the scaffolding, which need not be. Trouble arrives when the distinction is drawn carelessly, as when a stone-moving trial uses modern low-stretch rope at a strength no plant-fiber cordage could match, quietly transforming the result. A related trap is the skill differential: a modern person with two years of flintknapping stands in for an ancient knapper with a lifetime of practice from childhood, so absolute performance numbers are usually minimums, and comparative designs, where the same operators test method A against method B, are more trustworthy than absolute ones.

Measurement and recording turn activity into evidence. Modern programs log time and labor per task, instrument firings and smelts with thermocouples, weigh every input and output, photograph stages, and increasingly video entire processes so that others can audit technique. Crucially, they also collect the byproducts: the flake scatters, ash spreads, slag heaps, and butchery marks the activity generates, because those byproducts are what survives archaeologically, and matching them against excavated patterns is often the entire point. An experiment that produces the right product but the wrong debris has probably found the wrong method.

Finally, good design plans for publication before the first trial, including of failure. A kiln that cracks, a raft that founders in the harbor, a storage pit that rots are all informative results, and a literature that reports only triumphs systematically overstates how easy the past was. The checklist that emerges is short and demanding: a falsifiable question, stated variables, authentic materials where it matters, repeated trials, quantified results, collected byproducts, and a full report either way. Every famous experiment in the sections that follow can be graded against it, and several of the most famous lose marks.

sections.heading: Flintknapping: Replicating Stone Tools and Reading the Debris
sections.body:
Stone tools are the longest-running technology in human history, spanning more than three million years, and for most of the archaeological record they are nearly all that survives. Understanding them experimentally begins with fracture mechanics. Flint, chert, and obsidian break conchoidally, meaning a blow of the right force and angle drives a crack through the stone in a predictable shell-shaped wave, detaching a flake with edges that can be sharper than surgical steel; freshly struck obsidian edges taper to molecular thinness and have occasionally been used in modern surgical trials. Because the fracture is lawful, knapping is learnable and its products are readable. A knapper strikes flakes from a core with a hard hammerstone, switches to a soft hammer of antler or dense wood for thinner, flatter flakes, and may finish an edge by pressure flaking, pushing flakes off with an antler tine. Each technique leaves diagnostic scars, bulbs, and platforms on both flake and core.

The modern research tradition was built largely by two men. François Bordes in France, a superb knapper, replicated the Middle Paleolithic repertoire and used his skill to argue about what Neanderthal tool types meant. Don Crabtree in Idaho, self-taught over decades, worked out the demanding techniques behind spectacular pieces such as fluted Folsom points and published the recipes so others could verify them. Their students established replication as ordinary laboratory practice: a lithic analyst today learns to knap the way a chemist learns glassware. From that practice came systematic experiments. Knappers produced complete reduction sequences, from raw nodule to finished tool, and kept every flake, building reference collections that let excavators read a scatter of debris, the debitage, as a transcript: which techniques were used, at what stage the knapper worked at this spot, whether the products were carried away, even, in famous refitting studies where excavated flakes are glued back into their original nodule, where an individual sat and how they turned the stone.

Experiments also answered performance questions that speculation had argued about for a century. Replicated hand axes butcher animal carcasses effectively, and trials comparing tool forms measure cutting efficiency, edge life, and resharpening costs. Hafting experiments, mounting stone points on spears and darts, then firing them into carcasses or ballistic gel with calibrated force, established how impact fractures on excavated points differ from trampling damage, giving archaeologists a way to tell weapons from knives. Heat-treatment trials confirmed that burying flint under a fire for hours changes its fracture properties, improving knappability, a deliberate technology now documented tens of thousands of years back, with South African evidence for heat-treated silcrete reaching beyond seventy thousand years.

For the reader tempted to try, flintknapping is among the most accessible experimental crafts, and among the most instructive failures. The first lesson every novice learns is respect for the skill embodied in even a crude prehistoric flake; the second is that the ground around a knapper fills with razor-edged debris that remains dangerous indefinitely, which is itself an archaeological insight, since prehistoric camps must have managed the same hazard. Work over a tarp, wear glasses and a leather pad, avoid breathing the dust, which contains fine silica, and keep your reference pile: your own debitage is your first dataset.

sections.heading: Making Fire the Old Way: Friction, Sparks, and Time Trials
sections.body:
Fire is the foundational technology, and how past people made, kept, and used it is a classic experimental question because fire-making kits rarely survive in the ground. Wood rots, and what remains is mostly indirect: hearths, charcoal, heat-altered stone. Experiments fill the gap in two directions, testing which methods work with which materials, and generating the byproducts, char, ash signatures, and wear on stone strikers, that excavators can then recognize.

Friction methods dominate the ethnographic record and the experimental literature. In the hand drill, the simplest kit, a straight stalk is spun between the palms against a softwood hearth board; friction grinds off hot wood dust that collects in a notch until, at roughly the temperature of a scorching oven, it fuses into a glowing coal that can be transferred to tinder and blown to flame. The bow drill adds a cord-wrapped bow and a bearing block, multiplying speed and downward pressure and making fire accessible to people without conditioned palms and in worse weather; experimenters routinely produce a coal in under a minute with a good kit. Trials across wood species produced practical knowledge that matches ethnography: soft, dry, non-resinous woods such as willow, lime, cedar, and mullein stalks make reliable hearths and spindles, while dense or resin-soaked woods glaze and fail. The percussion method strikes sparks not from steel, which belongs to later periods, but from flint struck against iron sulfide minerals, pyrite or marcasite, whose faint sparks will catch on prepared tinder fungus. This is not conjecture: Ötzi, the Copper Age man frozen in the Alps around 3300 BCE, carried true tinder fungus with traces of pyrite, a complete Neolithic fire kit, and Paleolithic pyrite nodules with wear grooves are known from sites in Europe.

Beyond ignition, experiments target fire management, which mattered more daily than fire starting. Reconstructed hearths measure fuel consumption per hour of cooking or warmth; trials with earth ovens, pits of fire-heated stones, quantify how long stones hold cooking heat and how often they crack, producing the fire-cracked rock that litters prehistoric sites; experiments keeping embers alive in banked ashes or carried in fungus and bark containers show that a household could avoid re-ignition for days, which reframes how often the difficult friction methods were actually needed. Archaeologists have also burned down whole reconstructed houses, as at Lejre in Denmark, partly to study how burned buildings collapse and what patterns the fire leaves for excavators to interpret.

As a home experiment, friction fire is achievable, humbling, and safe if treated seriously. Choose dead, dry wood, cut a proper notch over a bark catch-tray, and prepare the tinder bundle before you begin, because a coal dies in an unready nest. Expect failure for hours before the first success; that learning curve is itself data about the value of skill in the past. Keep water at hand, clear the ground for a meter around, and remember that the experiment ends with an actual fire, which must have somewhere safe to live. The experience permanently changes how you read a prehistoric hearth: not as a pile of ash, but as the running heart of a household economy that someone had to feed, bank, and guard every single day.

sections.heading: Rebuilding Houses and Earthworks: Roundhouses, Burned Halls, and Overton Down
sections.body:
Buildings are among the most informative reconstructions because excavation gives so little to work from: postholes, a hearth, perhaps a ring of collapsed daub. Everything above the ground line, walls, roof pitch, smoke management, lifespan, is inference, and experiments test the inferences by building the building and living with the consequences. The most famous program is Butser Ancient Farm in Hampshire, founded by Peter Reynolds in 1972, where large British Iron Age roundhouses have been reconstructed from specific excavated ground plans, including a house based on the Pimperne ring nearly thirteen meters across, with tonnes of thatch on a conical roof. The reconstructions produced immediate, textbook-changing results. Generations of illustrators had drawn roundhouses with smoke holes at the apex; the experimental houses showed that an apex hole turns the roof into a chimney, drawing the hearth fire upward and threatening to ignite the thatch, whereas without a hole the smoke rises, pools harmlessly in the high cone above head height, and seeps out through the thatch, incidentally smoking the roof timbers against insects and preserving stored food hung in the rafters. Absence of evidence for smoke holes turned out to be evidence of good engineering.

Reconstruction also generates lifecycle data that no excavation can. How much timber, hazel rod, straw, and labor does a house consume to build, and then to maintain, year on year? Butser and the Danish center at Lejre, running since 1964, have tracked reconstructed houses through decades of weathering, repair, and eventual decay, and Lejre has deliberately burned reconstructed houses to study how a burning building collapses, what temperatures its daub reaches, and what the resulting deposit looks like in section, giving excavators of genuinely burned prehistoric houses across Europe a comparative key. Maintenance numbers feed directly into economic models: a house that demands a wagonload of thatching straw every few years ties its household to a predictable acreage of cereal cultivation, and the posthole diameters that survive underground can be read against the known loads of the experimental roofs.

The boldest experiment in this family concerns not buildings but the ground itself. In 1960, researchers built an earthwork on Overton Down in Wiltshire, a chalk bank about two meters high beside its quarry ditch, with samples of leather, textiles, wood, bone, and buried pottery sealed inside at known positions, and a second earthwork on sandy heathland at Wareham in 1963 for comparison. The design commits future generations: the banks are sectioned at planned intervals, one, two, four, eight, sixteen, thirty-two years and onward, with the final excavation scheduled 128 years after construction, in 2088. The excavations so far, including the thirty-two-year section in 1992, transformed understanding of site formation. The sharp-edged bank slumped and the ditch half-filled within the first few years and then stabilized, meaning the weathered profile an excavator sees formed almost immediately, not gradually; buried turf lines compressed and migrated; textiles and leather vanished quickly in the alkaline chalk but survived differently in acid sand; and buried pottery moved measurably as the bank settled. Every excavator who reads a ditch section today is, knowingly or not, using Overton Down's calibration, which is exactly what a discipline-scale experiment is for.

sections.heading: Ancient Farming Trials: Crops, Ards, and the Underground Granary
sections.body:
Prehistoric agriculture left seeds, pollen, field boundaries, and tools, but the numbers that make a farming economy intelligible, yields per hectare, labor per season, storage losses, must come from experiment. The longest-running trials are again Butser's. Peter Reynolds grew the actual crop species of the British Iron Age, principally the hulled wheats emmer and spelt along with hulled barley, on plots cultivated with replica tools, and did so year after year for decades so that good and bad seasons both entered the record. The results overturned the prevailing picture of Iron Age farming as bare subsistence. The old cereal varieties, grown in mixtures and on soils worked by ard, returned yields that compared respectably with, and in some years exceeded, medieval figures, implying that Iron Age Britain could generate substantial surpluses, which in turn helps explain the grain-rich hillforts and the export trade Roman authors mention. Trials also quantified the ard itself, the symmetrical scratch-plough of prehistory: unlike the later mouldboard plough it does not turn a furrow, so effective cultivation means cross-ploughing the field in two passes at right angles, a practice that experiments connected directly to the criss-cross ard marks preserved under excavated barrows and blown sand across northern Europe.

The most elegant single experiment concerned storage. British Iron Age sites are riddled with large pits, and for a long time many archaeologists doubted grain could survive months underground in a wet climate. Reynolds cut pits into the chalk, filled them with threshed grain, sealed the mouths airtight with clay, and opened them after winter, repeating the trial across many years and pit shapes. The mechanism proved beautiful: grain at the damp walls germinates, and respiration by grain and microbes consumes the pit's oxygen and replaces it with carbon dioxide, which shuts the whole mass into dormancy. Losses in a well-sealed pit ran to a few percent at the skin of the deposit, and the sprouted skin itself formed part of the seal. A sealed pit is also a hidden and fireproof granary, and the experiments showed seed corn overwintered this way remained viable for spring sowing. Storage, not yield, is the hinge of any grain economy, and a technology this effective, invisible except as an empty hole, rewrote estimates of how much wealth an Iron Age community could bank.

Processing experiments complete the chain from field to meal. Harvesting trials with replica sickles of flint and bronze measured cutting rates and left the diagnostic silica gloss on flint blades that use-wear analysts now read as harvest evidence. Threshing and winnowing trials established the distinctive chaff and weed-seed signatures each processing stage leaves, which archaeobotanists use to identify what activity happened where on a site from charred residues alone. Grinding experiments on saddle querns, the back-and-forth stones of prehistory, and later rotary querns measured flour output per hour and per person, revealing the sheer daily grind, hours of a household's female labor by most ethnographic parallels, hidden inside every loaf, and showed how quern grit enters flour, which is visible as wear on prehistoric teeth. Baking and brewing trials in reconstructed ovens close the loop, turning experimental harvests into food whose residues, burnt crusts, sprouted grain, fermentation vessels, can be matched against finds. The cumulative result is a farming year with numbers attached at every step.

sections.heading: Pottery and Kilns: Clay, Temper, and Reading Fire in a Sherd
sections.body:
Pottery is the archaeologist's favorite material because it is nearly indestructible once fired, endlessly variable, and everywhere. Experimental work asks how sherds acquired the properties we measure in them, hardness, color, porosity, cracking, sooting, and the answers turn every excavated fragment into a record of choices made by a potter and a firing crew. The chain begins with clay preparation. Raw clay shrinks as it dries and steams internally as it fires, so potters knead in temper, sand, crushed shell, crushed old pottery called grog, chopped plant material, or crushed rock, to open the fabric. Experiments systematically varying temper type and quantity, then testing vessels over cooking fires and in thermal-shock cycles, showed that temper choices ethnographers recorded are engineering decisions: shell and grog resist the repeated heating of cooking pots far better than a dense untempered fabric, which explains why cooking wares and fine serving wares from the same site so often differ in fabric. What once read as tribal custom now also reads as materials science.

Forming and firing experiments reconstruct the production sequence. Most prehistoric pottery was built without a wheel, by pinching, coiling, and beating with paddle and anvil, and replication established the diagnostic traces each method leaves, coil fractures, join lines visible in x-ray, paddle facets, so that a sherd can testify to its own manufacture. Firing is where experiment matters most, because temperature and atmosphere are invisible in the finished pot until you know the code. Open firings and pit firings, the universal early methods in which pots and fuel burn together, are fast and fuel-cheap; instrumented replications show them typically peaking between about 600 and 900 degrees Celsius, holding peak heat only minutes, and swinging unpredictably between oxidizing and smoky reducing conditions, which produces the mottled surfaces and dark fire clouds characteristic of much prehistoric ware. Built kilns, which separate fuel chamber from pot chamber, reach 1,000 degrees and beyond, hold heat longer, and give the potter control of atmosphere: air-rich firing burns iron minerals red and orange, while a smothered, smoke-filled finish turns wares grey to black and can deposit the lustrous carbon of burnished blackware. Experimenters have replicated everything from Roman updraft kilns to Greek three-stage iron-reduction glosses, in the Greek case working out the precise oxidation-reduction-reoxidation cycle that makes red-figure vases red and black exactly where the painter intended.

Failure is half the harvest. Replica firings crack pots by steam explosion when drying was rushed, dunt them by cooling too fast, and underfire them to crumbling softness, and each failure mode matches waster sherds found dumped at production sites, letting excavators identify kilns and workshops from the rejects alone. Post-firing experiments carry the story into use: cooking porridges and stews in replica pots builds the soot patterns, carbonized crusts, and absorbed lipid residues that laboratories now extract from ancient sherds, and controlled use of replicas is how residue chemists validated that milk fats, meat fats, and plant waxes can be told apart after millennia. For a careful amateur, a small pit firing of hand-built, well-dried, generously tempered pots is an achievable and deeply instructive experiment, provided it is treated as real fire management on cleared ground with water standing by, and the honest measure of success is not beauty but survival rate, which for first firings is rarely above half.

sections.heading: Recreating Ancient Metallurgy: Copper, Bronze, and the Bloomery
sections.body:
Metal production is the experimental field where replication is least optional, because almost nothing about it can be inferred from the finished object alone. A bronze axe tells you its shape and its alloy, but the furnace, the fuel budget, the failure rate, and the choreography of a pour are gone, surviving only as slag, broken moulds, and burnt clay, and those byproducts only speak once experiments have produced their like under known conditions. Copper comes first historically and experimentally. Smelting trials reduce green copper carbonate ores such as malachite with charcoal in crucibles and small clay furnaces, and they establish the entry price of the Metal Ages: sustained temperatures around 1,100 degrees Celsius and a controlled, air-blown, oxygen-poor environment, achievable with pot bellows or blowpipes but far beyond any cooking fire. The experiments make sense of the archaeology of early smelting sites, where fragments of tuyeres, the clay nozzles that carry blast into the fire, and small slag cakes are often all that remains. Alloying trials adding tin show why bronze conquered: it casts more cleanly at lower temperature and work-hardens to a serviceable edge, and replica bronze tools felling trees and harvesting grain performed far better than pure copper in comparative tests.

Casting experiments reconstruct the foundry. Replicas poured into open stone moulds, two-part clay moulds, and lost-wax investments reproduce the seam lines, casting flaws, and mould debris of excavated material, and they restore respect for the craft: a successful pour requires dry moulds preheated to the right temperature, metal fluid enough to fill a sword's length before freezing, and nerve, since molten bronze meeting a damp mould spits explosively. Trials also measure economics, how many castings a clay mould survives, how much metal is lost per pour, how long a workshop day yields, numbers that turn hoards of scrap and failed castings into legible industrial waste.

Iron required a different revolution, and the bloomery experiments that reconstructed it are among the field's largest sustained programs; hundreds of documented smelts have been run by researchers and dedicated independent smelters across Europe and North America. The key fact is that a bloomery furnace, a clay shaft charged from the top with roasted ore and charcoal and blown through tuyeres, never melts the iron. It reduces ore to a spongy, white-hot mass of metal and trapped slag, the bloom, which must be dragged out and consolidated by repeated hammering and reheating that squeezes the slag out drop by glowing drop. Experiments quantify the appetite of the process: several kilograms of charcoal per kilogram of usable iron, with the charcoal itself representing several times its weight in wood, so a season of iron making consumes a measurable slice of forest, an environmental signature archaeologists can seek in pollen records. Slag from experimental smelts, tapped or furnace-bottom, matches excavated slag closely enough that a field walker can now diagnose a smelting site from a handful of it. Smithing experiments complete the chain, showing how bloom iron is folded and welded into tools, how steel edges are made by controlled carbon uptake, and what distinctive hammerscale, the glittering flakes shed at the anvil, settles into a smithy floor, which is how excavators find the workshop even when the anvil is long gone.

sections.heading: Experimental Voyages: Kon-Tiki, Polynesian Navigation, the Trireme, and the Sea Stallion
sections.body:
Sea trials are the most dramatic branch of experimental archaeology, and the most instructive about the method's limits, because the sea grades harshly and the sample size is usually one. The modern tradition begins with Thor Heyerdahl's Kon-Tiki in 1947: a balsa log raft built with traditional materials, sailed and drifted about 7,000 kilometers from Callao in Peru to the Tuamotu Islands in 101 days, to support his theory that South Americans settled Polynesia. As an experiment it succeeded narrowly and failed broadly, a distinction worth learning. It proved a balsa raft could survive the crossing, a real result that silenced one class of objection; it proved nothing about what actually happened, and the accumulated evidence of linguistics, archaeology, and genetics shows Polynesia was settled from the west by Austronesian voyagers, though genetic studies have since found traces of South American contact within Polynesia. Possibility is not history.

The deeper answer to Heyerdahl was another experiment. In 1976 the Polynesian Voyaging Society built Hokule'a, a performance replica of a double-hulled voyaging canoe, and sailed her from Hawai'i to Tahiti with the Micronesian navigator Mau Piailug directing the crossing by stars, swells, and birds, without instruments. The voyage demonstrated that traditional wayfinding could hold a course across 4,000 kilometers of open ocean and hit a target island group, transforming scholarly opinion about deliberate two-way Polynesian voyaging and, beyond scholarship, helping ignite a cultural revival of voyaging across the Pacific that continues today. Where Kon-Tiki tested a drift, Hokule'a tested a skill, and the skill was the real historical question.

European programs put numbers on ancient naval architecture. The trireme Olympias, a full reconstruction of a classical Athenian warship launched in 1987 and crewed by 170 volunteer rowers, tested the long-disputed three-level oar arrangement: she reached sprint speeds around nine knots, sustained cruising under oar, and executed the tight turns ancient tactics demand, while also revealing the brutal ergonomics of the middle and lower benches, the water budget of a rowing crew in Mediterranean heat, and why fleets beached at night. The Viking Ship Museum at Roskilde in Denmark built the Sea Stallion from Glendalough, a thirty-meter replica of the longship Skuldelev 2, whose excavated timbers had shown it was built of Irish oak around 1042. With a crew of some sixty volunteers she sailed from Roskilde around Scotland to Dublin in 2007 and back in 2008, logging speeds, leeway, sea-keeping, and crew endurance in North Sea conditions, data that no tank test of a hull model could supply, alongside quieter findings about watch systems, wetness, and morale that are themselves history: the ship is a machine whose moving parts are people.

The rules that separate these voyages from stunts are the ordinary rules of the discipline applied at scale: build from excavated evidence rather than imagination, state which materials are compromises, instrument everything, and publish the log honestly, including the towing, the breakages, and the harbor days. Read that way, each successful passage retires a claim of impossibility, and each measured failure, a sprung plank, an unrowable rig, an exhausted crew, quietly redraws the map of what ancient seafaring could and could not have been.

sections.heading: Moving Megaliths: Sledges, Rollers, Walking Statues, and Wet Sand
sections.body:
How did people without wheels, cranes, or draft animals move stones weighing as much as loaded trucks? The question attaches to Stonehenge, whose largest sarsen stones weigh on the order of twenty-five tonnes and whose smaller bluestones, two to four tonnes each, originate in the Preseli hills of Wales some 225 kilometers away; to the moai of Rapa Nui, Easter Island, multi-tonne statues that stand kilometers from the quarry where they were carved; and to megalithic tombs, Egyptian colossi, and standing stones worldwide. Because the movers left no manuals, the field belongs to experiment, and the experiments have converged on a reassuring general answer while staying honestly divided on particulars: human muscle, organized and multiplied by simple mechanics, is entirely sufficient, and the true constraint was social, the ability to feed and coordinate a large willing crew.

The workhorse experiments use sledges. Trials in Britain, Denmark, and Japan, including a well-documented 1990s trial that moved a forty-tonne concrete replica of a Stonehenge sarsen, established practical coefficients: a heavy stone lashed to a stout timber sledge, hauled over greased timber rails or sleepers, moves with roughly one to two pullers per tonne on level ground, while dragging on bare earth can demand several times that, and rollers, the favorite of older illustrations, prove treacherous under real loads, wandering and jamming unless confined in a track. Levering experiments show small crews can inch multi-tonne stones without any hauling at all, walking a block forward on alternating pivots. For raising, trials tipped stones into prepared sockets over a ramp edge and hauled them upright with ropes over timber shear-legs, and lintels have been raised on cribs of stacked timber, layer by layer, a slow, safe method well within Neolithic carpentry. None of this proves which methods Stonehenge's builders chose, but it prices every candidate in person-days, and it makes the monument legible as an organizational feat, plausibly hundreds of people working seasons, rather than a physical mystery.

Two modern experiments changed pictures that had stood for decades. On Rapa Nui, islanders' own tradition says the moai walked, and in 2012 archaeologists Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo tested it: three small teams with ropes rocked a 4.35-tonne standing replica side to side, and its D-shaped base, wider than it is deep with a forward lean carved into the unfinished statues found along roads, converted the rocking into steps. Eighteen people walked the statue a hundred meters in under an hour. The experiment did not merely add a method; it matched the archaeology, explaining why statues abandoned in transport stand upright along the roads and why those roads are flat rather than rutted by sledges, and it removed the need for the timber-hungry log-rolling story often blamed for the island's deforestation. In Egypt, a tomb painting from Deir el-Bersha of around 1900 BCE shows a worker pouring water before a sledge hauling a colossal statue; long dismissed as ritual, the detail was vindicated in 2014 when physicists at Amsterdam measured sand friction and found that properly damp sand roughly halves the pulling force, because water bridges stiffen the grains and stop the sledge ploughing. The lesson generalizes: ancient images and traditions of technique deserve testing before dismissal, because at least twice now the depicted method turned out to be the good engineering.

sections.heading: Use-Wear and Residue Analysis: Experiments Under the Microscope
sections.body:
Not all experimental archaeology moves boulders; much of the field's daily value is generated at a laboratory bench, where experiments answer the most basic excavation question of all: what was this object actually used for? The founding figure is the Soviet researcher Sergei Semenov, whose decades of work, published in Russian in 1957 and reaching the West as Prehistoric Technology in 1964, established traceology. Semenov's insight was disciplined: use leaves mechanical traces, striations, edge rounding, micro-fractures, polishes, and the way to read them is not intuition but experiment, using replica tools on known materials for known durations and cataloguing the resulting wear. His laboratory worked bone, hide, wood, and stone with replicated tools and built the first reference atlas linking wear patterns to tasks.

The method matured through blind testing. In the 1970s Lawrence Keeley developed high-power microwear analysis, reading distinctive micro-polishes formed on flint edges by different contact materials, wood, bone, hide, antler, and the silica-rich gloss of harvested cereals, at magnifications of a few hundred times. Its credibility rests on a famous test: colleagues used replica flint tools on materials Keeley was not told about, and his blind identifications of both the worked material and the used edge were correct in the large majority of cases, a validation exercise that remains a model for how archaeological science should audit itself. Since then, use-wear laboratories worldwide have run thousands of controlled experiments, extending the reference libraries to obsidian, quartz, bone tools, and ground stone, and adding quantitative surface metrology to the analyst's trained eye. Every conclusion of the form these blades were used to scrape hides rests on such an experimental library.

Residue analysis grew alongside wear analysis and depends on experiment just as completely. Replica tools used to process plants pick up starch grains and phytoliths; those used on animals retain blood films, collagen, and fat; adhesives such as birch tar, the tar Neanderthals distilled from bark, survive as hafting traces. Laboratory programs process known materials with replica tools, then bury the tools in different soils for months and years to learn what survives, what migrates, and what modern contamination looks like, without which every exciting residue claim would be unfalsifiable. Parallel experiments validated pottery lipid analysis: cooking known foods in replica pots, then extracting the absorbed fats, showed that ruminant fats, pig fat, dairy fat, and plant oils retain distinguishable chemical signatures for millennia, the foundation on which the prehistory of milk drinking has been rewritten from potsherds.

A related experimental family, taphonomy, studies what happens to things after use. Butchery experiments with stone tools on carcasses established how cut marks differ from carnivore tooth scores and trampling scratches, distinctions on which claims about the earliest meat eating stand or fall. Bones weathered in the open for known years, seeds charred at controlled temperatures, and replica graves monitored through seasons all calibrate the record's distortions. The common thread across this whole bench-scale field is epistemological: archaeology constantly infers invisible past dynamics from visible present statics, and the only way to license those inferences is to run the dynamics under observation, in the present, and watch what statics they leave. That is experimental archaeology at its purest, even when nothing in the room is larger than a microscope slide.

sections.heading: Living History, Open-Air Museums, and the Experiential Borderland
sections.body:
Surrounding the strict experimental core is a broad, lively borderland of reconstruction done primarily for education, heritage, and experience, and the relationship between the two is closer to symbiosis than rivalry. Open-air museums are the shared habitat. Lejre in Denmark, Butser in England, the Archeon in the Netherlands, Guédelon in France, and hundreds of similar sites maintain reconstructed houses, workshops, fields, and animals, staffed by interpreters who plough, spin, smith, and cook before the public. The museums keep alive craft skills that formal archaeology needs but cannot maintain in-house, thatching, coppicing, traditional carpentry, warp-weighted weaving, and their buildings, occupied and repaired for decades, are effectively long-running experiments in structural lifespan whether or not anyone framed a hypothesis at the start. The professional network EXARC, with member organizations in dozens of countries, exists precisely to connect these institutions with university researchers so that the daily practice generates recorded knowledge.

The flagship of the borderland is Guédelon in Burgundy, where since 1997 a crew of masons, carpenters, blacksmiths, tilers, and rope makers has been building a thirteenth-century castle from scratch using only period methods, quarrying stone on site, mixing mortar to medieval recipes, raising walls with human-powered treadwheel cranes. Guédelon calls itself an archaeological experiment in the broad sense, and its harvest is real: masons rediscovered practical geometry and seasonal work rhythms, the site produced answers about mortar curing and scaffolding that consultants on real castle restorations now use, and lime-burning and pigment-making trials there feed conservation science. Yet it also illustrates the boundary: a project whose purpose includes tourism and employment cannot freeze variables or repeat trials, so its knowledge is craft knowledge, invaluable and hypothesis-generating, but not controlled measurement.

Re-enactment and living-history groups form the outer ring. At their best they achieve astonishing material authenticity and embody skills, marching in period equipment, sailing traditional rigs, cooking a whole year's calendar of historical food, that generate what practitioners call experiential knowledge: how heavy the mail shirt really feels by afternoon, how much light a tallow lamp truly gives, how a shield wall actually constrains movement. Academic archaeology has grown steadily more respectful of this knowledge while insisting on the distinction: experience tells you what it is like, experiment tells you what is the case, and converting the first into the second requires the machinery of design, controls, and publication described earlier in this guide. Trouble arises mainly when the conversion is skipped, when a re-enactor's practice is quoted as proof, or when, conversely, academics dismiss embodied expertise that could have saved a flawed experiment.

For a reader who wants in, the borderland is the open door. Open-air museums recruit volunteers and run courses in knapping, smelting, bronze casting, and traditional building; EXARC publishes an accessible journal and lists member sites worldwide; universities increasingly welcome skilled amateurs into formal experiments, because a program that needs sixty rowers or twenty hauliers cannot staff itself. The honest path is to hold both values at once: full enthusiasm for the lived experience, and full discipline about what any given day of it does and does not demonstrate about the past.

sections.heading: Limits, Criticisms, and Good Practice: What an Experiment Can Never Tell You
sections.body:
Experimental archaeology earns its keep, but it carries structural limits that every user of its results should know, because the difference between a strong claim and an overreach usually lies in respecting them. The first and deepest limit is logical. An experiment operates in the present, on present materials, with present people, and however authentic the setup, its conclusion takes the form this works or this fails, never this happened. The problem of equifinality, many possible pasts converging on one material present, cannot be experimented away; it can only be narrowed, by showing that some candidate methods fail outright, that others produce byproducts absent from the record, and that the surviving candidates differ in testable ways. The strongest experimental claims are therefore negative or comparative, and the weakest are triumphant reconstructions announced as revelations of how it was done.

The second limit is the experimenter. Ancient practitioners learned their crafts from childhood inside living traditions; modern replicators are usually adults with years, not lifetimes, of practice, so absolute performance figures, hours to make an axe, days to cross a strait, systematically overstate ancient difficulty. Skill also cuts the other way: a brilliant modern knapper may unconsciously use motor solutions no ancient knapper had, and a modern crew's morale, nutrition, and safety constraints differ from any ancient crew's. Related is the authenticity trap discussed earlier, the quiet substitution of modern rope, steel supports, or weather forecasts at exactly the point where the hypothesis lives. The third limit is statistical. Sea voyages, castle builds, and forty-tonne stone hauls are experiments with a sample size of one, unrepeatable for cost reasons, so their results are demonstrations of existence, not distributions, and should be quoted as such. Publication bias compounds this: failed experiments are less written up, so the literature reads as if the past always worked.

Criticism from within the discipline has sharpened practice into something like a professional code. State the hypothesis and the level of authenticity claimed, variable by variable. Repeat wherever repetition is affordable, and use multiple operators to separate method from skill. Instrument and quantify, because numbers can be audited and adjectives cannot. Collect and publish the byproducts, since debris is what the archaeological record actually keeps. Report failures with the same care as successes. Involve, and credit, the craft experts whose hands carry knowledge the literature lacks. And where experiments touch living cultures, as with Pacific voyaging or Indigenous technologies anywhere, conduct them with rather than merely about the communities whose heritage they reconstruct, a standard the Hokule'a tradition set early and well.

Read with these limits in mind, the field's real achievement comes into focus. Experimental archaeology has not told us what happened; nothing can. It has done something almost as valuable: it has repeatedly replaced impossible, miraculous, or condescending stories about past people with priced, engineered, achievable ones, and it has built the reference libraries, wear atlases, residue signatures, slag types, weathering curves, through which mute objects now testify. Its lasting lesson is a habit of mind as useful outside archaeology as within it: when you catch yourself saying they could never have, or it must have been done this way, stop, and go find out.
